units.t: "Those who manage to follow the plot in cowboy movies can understand politics in the Westfjords. The same laws apply there." Such was the theory of Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson, member of parliament and a Westfjords man to the marrow. "In the Wild West," said Ólafur, "the clashes of the outlaw gangs revolved first and last around the water holes. Out here in the west, it is the freezing plants. It's that simple." I was preparing my candidacy for the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) in the Westfjords constituency for the elections in the summer of 1967. The winter before, Ólafur and I often sat talking as we prepared for the campaign. Few could offer more colorful descriptions of the shades of human life and the political struggles out west than Ólafur. He became completely animated and carried on with his speech.
"Instead of gun barrels being wielded in the battle over the freezing plants, money and political favors are the means that get the job done."

I was headed into the firing line of politics. In the scattered rural districts, politics had almost everywhere been marked by clashes between two main camps for most of the century. On one side, the Independence Party men and the money power in Reykjavík mustered their forces, and on the other, the Progressives fought with the strength of the Federation (Sambandið) and the cooperative societies. The political parties were the backers in this struggle, and the power to ration credit in the banks and public funds was worth its weight in gold. The political battles were fought over that no less than over seats in parliament and in governments. In the Westfjords, politics was known for being hard. Word there had it that votes followed the freezing plants.

Thus the story went that when the ice house at Kaldrananes was near bankruptcy in the winter of 1948, a "Bjarnarfjörður man in a brown coat" came to Reykjavík with the message that if a buyer could be found for the plant, the parliamentary seat for Strandasýsla would be included in the bargain. That was my father's constituency before the electoralthe

change of precedent in 1959. The day before Eggert Kristjánsson announced his candidacy for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in Strandasýsla, he purchased the freezing plant. From a letter my father sent to the people of Strandir, it is clear that he viewed the matter with grave seriousness. He gave his all in the election campaign and won, receiving 504 votes against Eggert's 275. Eggert was bitterly disappointed when the votes had been counted, according to the biography of Ólafur Thors. He had to console himself with owning the freezing plant. This was the exception.

Stories about my father had followed me for as long as I could remember. He became a member of parliament and prime minister when I was six years old. I had grown up at the keyhole of politics in the Prime Minister's Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn) by the Tjörnin pond. It was always far from my mind to make politics my life's work. I studied engineering in the United States and considered that a sure guarantee that I would not go into politics. I doubted whether participation in politics was desirable at all. Perhaps I surprised myself most of all when I entertained the idea of following in my father's footsteps in the Westfjords, when he retired from parliament in 1967, after having sat in the Althing (Alþingi) for 33 years without interruption.

For me, the question of candidacy revolved around whether I intended to take part in politics with body and soul. If I offered myself as a candidate, it would be to gain influence and make my mark. Those Westfjorders who approached me were surely thinking along similar lines. Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson often recounted that many of those who supported my candidacy in the constituency had done so because they believed they saw in me a man of the future who was likely to rise to leadership in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and in government.

This was how the Westfjorders had always thought, and perhaps it is no wonder. Many of the nation's strongest leaders have had roots in the Westfjords. Jón Sigurðsson, the national independence hero of the Icelanders, was from Hrafnseyri by Arnarfjörður and a member of parliament for the people of Ísafjörður. Skúli Thoroddsen, district magistrate and newspaper editor in Ísafjörður, was one of the nation's foremost leaders in the independence struggle, not to mention Hannes Hafstein, who rose to prominence as district magistrate of the Ísafjörður region.

The leading figures of the Progressive Party in the Westfjords had always been at the forefront of national affairs. Tryggvi Þórhallsson was both party chairman and prime minister, and the same was true of my father. Other parties had likewise fielded strong leaders in the west. Ásgeir Ásgeirsson, prime minister and president of Iceland, was a member of parliament for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) in Vestur-Ísafjarðarsýsla. He was in fact originally in the Progressive Party. Hannibal Valdimarsson was a Westfjorder through and through, and Vilmundur Jónsson, director of public health and member of parliament for the Social Democratic Party, was for a long time a physician in Ísafjörður. Many more could be named.

This heritage troubled me less than it might have once the campaign was underway, because my ambition was in harmony with the mindset of the local people. It was probably just as well, though, that I did not know the giant yardsticks by which new men were measured until after I had decided to run. Had I known of them beforehand, it is by no means certain that things would have gone the same way.

One thing I understood quickly: the Westfjorders choose those who hold firmly to their interests in the Althing (Alþingi). In the Westfjords, elections are as much about men as about issues or parties. Ásgeir Ásgeirsson, later president, held his ground even though he left the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and joined the Social Democrats. Hannibal Valdimarsson was elected to parliament despite party-hopping and constantly new names on the candidacies he was involved in. It was therefore essential for me to get to know the voters personally if I intended to run at all.

When it came to it, I was only offered the third seat on the Progressive Party's list of candidates. I was not entirely pleased with that offer. This was less advancement than I had had in mind when I entertained the idea of running. A committee of thirty had chosen Bjarni Guðbjörnsson, bank manager in Ísafjörður, for the first seat and Halldór Kristjánsson from Kirkjuból for the second seat. I came to the conclusion that it would be "absurd" to accept the offer if one looked first and foremost at "my interests and career prospects in this connection." The party's interest, however, was unquestionably that I should take the plunge.

I would have had plenty of tasks to turn to even if politics had been left aside. I worked energetically on building up research affairs as director of the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins), which was both a good position and enjoyable work. In the evenings and on weekends I occupied myself with carpentry and finishing work on the family's new house at Mávanes in Arnarnes. In the summers the family sought the company of my parents at their summer house at Klettur in Borgarfjörður or set off on trips around the country. Edda and I had had our second child in the spring of 1966, a daughter, who was given the name Hlíf. We already had Hermann, who was two years old. Life smiled upon me, whatever all the political bustle might bring.

In the government offices, the Restoration Government (viðreisnarstjórnin) was serving its second term, with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) held firmly in the grip of the Independence Party men. Bjarni Benediktsson had taken over the office of prime minister after Ólafur Thors withdrew due to failing health. As time went on, I hardened in my opposition to the Restoration Government but was at the same time dissatisfied with the Progressive Party's performance in opposition. I found the parliamentary group old-fashioned and sluggish in both defense and attack. Nevertheless, much seemed to me to indicate that the Restoration Government could be toppled in the 1967 elections. I wanted to add my weight to those scales.
The Struggle over the List

I decided to offer myself as a candidate and accept the third seat on the list in late autumn 1966. It was not without difficulty, however, that a final list was put together. The nomination committee's proposal assumed that Sigurvin Einarsson would retire from parliament. He had sat in parliament alongside my father for the constituency for years. Instead of moving him from the second seat to the first, it was proposed that he would not be on the list at all. The majority of the thirty-member committee considered renewal desirable, and Sigurvin received only 13 votes for the first seat at its meeting.

Sigurvin had strong supporters in Barðastrandarsýsla, and they could not bear the thought of his stepping down. They therefore demanded a primary election to change the composition of the list. They wanted Sigurvin in the first seat. They sent their demands to the party leadership in the Westfjords, signed by 300–400 voters. This was a considerable number in a constituency that had about 5,400 on the electoral roll. Fewer than two hundred votes needed to shift between parties for a parliamentary seat to be won or lost.

I was not averse to a primary but wanted the vote to cover all three top seats. It appears in letters that I sent to my supporters around this time that I fully intended to seek a higher place on the list. Various people feared, however, that a primary would leave deep wounds. This dispute lasted four months.

When one month of the year 1967 had passed, a meeting was called in Ísafjörður attended by Eysteinn Jónsson, the party chairman, his executive director, Þráinn Valdimarsson, and influential men from the constituency in addition to the candidates. Guðmundur Einarsson of Brjánslækur led Sigurvin's supporters. He had become very hard of hearing, if not deaf. This turned out to be a long meeting, because all answers had to be written on paper for Guðmundur.

At the beginning of the meeting, Eysteinn stressed that the primary proposal should not be dismissed, since that would look very bad. Others opposed a primary vehemently. I describe what followed in a letter to Brynjólfur Sæmundsson, agricultural advisor in Hólmavík:

First Sigurvin was spoken to, but he and his followers were adamant that it was out of the question for Sigurvin to withdraw. Then that singular event occurred: Halldór Kristjánsson from Kirkjuból showed such great nobility and social maturity that he decided to give up his seat, if that might lead to peace being achieved over the candidacy. Halldór has grown greatly in stature through this.

Sigurvin accepted this at once, and it seemed to various people that he diminished in the same measure as Halldór grew. In his shoes I myself would far rather have wanted to let the voters decide whether I should have a seat on the list, rather than accept such a sacrifice. This nonetheless prevailed, and it was agreed at the meeting to work toward the list being composed as follows:
1. Sigurvin Einarsson 2. Bjarni Guðbjörnsson 3. Steingrímur Hermannsson 4. Halldór Kristjánsson 5. Guðmundur Óskarsson 6. Jónas Jónsson, etc.

This was illustrative of the party loyalty of Halldór of Kirkjuból. It seemed to know no limits. He is a Progressive by conviction, a man of social solidarity raised in the spirit of the youth movement. Time and again he stood for election where he had to content himself with a hopeless seat. Despite his great qualities, intelligence, and good sense, he did not have the popularity to lead the list. He was perhaps too deeply rooted among his fellow countrymen to be at the forefront in the constituency, paradoxical as that sounds. I quickly found on my travels, however, that the list was stronger after the change. Sigurvin was considered to have done well as a member of parliament, and Halldór did not enjoy the same support outside the party as within it. Halldór from Kirkjuból, on the other hand, rose greatly in my esteem.

Sigurvin Einarsson was from Barðastrandarsýsla. I later learned on my travels that his supporters in the rural districts there showed him, for the most part, complete loyalty, even though various people thought he had grown old. Sigurvin was gray-haired and wore black, round spectacles, which gave him a striking appearance. Sigurvin was notably intelligent and radical in his views. He had long been one of the fiercest opponents of the military presence at Keflavík Airport among the members of parliament of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). He was renowned for his kindness to children, being a former primary school teacher. He was less successful, however, in attracting support from young people.
The First Campaign Trips

As soon as I had decided to run, I began preparations for the candidacy, whatever came of the disputes over the list. I wanted to be prepared if a primary election were called. I took unpaid leave from my work at
the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) in order to travel around the constituency and meet voters. In total, I was away from work for three months that winter.

When I began my travels around Strandir late in 1966, I immediately set myself the goal of visiting every farm and as many workplaces as possible in the villages. Probably no one had undertaken this since the Westfjords constituency was created out of five single-member constituencies in 1959. The old constituencies were Strandasýsla, Barðastrandarsýsla, Vestur-Ísafjarðarsýsla, Norður-Ísafjarðarsýsla, and Ísafjörður, which was a separate constituency. There had been considerable rivalry between these areas, and its remnants played a part in making more people willing to settle on an outsider as a candidate. I quickly sensed this rivalry and tried to bridge the gap. I emphasized that I was a representative of all Westfjorders and not just of particular areas.

Because of the great number of people I intended to visit and meet, I took with me a tape recorder that I kept in the car. After each visit, I read information and other things I wanted to remember onto the tape. I usually recorded names, the number of children on the farm in question, the scale of the farming, the residents' main interests, and where I thought the household stood politically. My wife Edda and her sister Inga Lára typed up these records when I returned home. In this way I acquired detailed accounts of all my travels around the Westfjords.

I benefited from these first trips for a long time. The records proved especially useful when I met the people again on later trips, some months or even years later. I would then look them up in the card index to refresh my memory of the household and recall the interests and concerns of the voters. I had no particular precedent for this method, and in fact I am not aware of other politicians having employed the same practice.

Some part of this card index has unfortunately been lost, but most of it I still have. Various stories circulated about this behavior of mine. Some of them were based on misunderstanding. It was claimed, among other things, that I concealed a recording device under my clothes and thus had every word spoken to me on tape. That, of course, was absurd.

I visited Strandir in two rounds. In addition, in late autumn 1966 I went on a kind of exploratory trip. The first person I met was Jónas R. Jónsson at Melar. He was considered left-leaning and was critical of my candidacy. Jónas is still a left-leaning man of social solidarity and cooperation with firm views on national affairs. I often stayed with Jónas and his wife Elín Þórhallsdóttir on my travels around Strandir, and we frequently sat talking late into the evening. In time he became a staunch supporter
of mine and was on our list of candidates in three elections, including in fourth place in 1978.

Jónas at Melar was a hard-hitting candidate and an entertaining man at meetings. On one occasion, after Matthías Bjarnason had become the leading figure of the Independence Party men out west, he was boasting of his part in the construction of the Djúpvegur road. Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson was then in third place and felt compelled to point out the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) role in advancing the matter, since the party had been in government at the time. Matthías could often be prickly at meetings. He snapped at Ólafur that he did not understand why he was butting into this discussion, since he had been crawling around in diapers when the road construction was decided. Jónas at Melar then took the floor and said he could attest that Matthías had been so precocious that he had never come near a chamber pot.
But Matthías was yet another sad example of how often child prodigies come to little when they get out into life. The roof nearly came off the community hall at this retort.

Jónas's neighbor was Vilhelm Steinsson. He was also a staunch Progressive but a man of great temper, and Jónas was always on edge as elections approached and invariably considered his support uncertain. A story was told from my father's time that Vilhelm had thrown rocks after his car when he drove past the farmyard without stopping. "I'll never vote for that devil again," Vilhelm is said to have bellowed, and he repeated this every single day up to the election. When Jónas at Melar spoke with him after the polls had closed, however, he said with a wry grin: "Of course I voted for the bastard."

When I had become a substitute member of parliament, Vilhelm was as cantankerous as ever, and once again Jónas at Melar saw reason to fear for his support. He therefore suggested to me that I send Vilhelm a telegram on his birthday. I followed this advice, and Vilhelm is said to have been most pleased as a result, and not a cross word about me passed his lips after that.

I intended to work my way through the farms from Munaðarnes in the north and southward. When I got north, the ground proved very wet, which made the journey difficult. The going was in fact hard in many places, but I had a good jeep and managed remarkably well to get around, especially after I acquired a large Blazer jeep of the old type. Sometimes, though, I had to take unconventional routes. The moors and ridges were often nearly impassable. On one of my trips I was stuck for four hours in a bog up in the middle of Steingrímsfjarðarheiði. Then I felt what it was to be alone in the car. I probably would have given up quickly if I had not enjoyed this kind of rough going as much as

as I in fact do. I thus managed to reach every farm in Strandasýsla except one, Tindur in Miðdalur in Steingrímsfjörður. The river was in violent flood. That farm was abandoned a few years later. So I never got there.

In Strandir, most people were probably curious to meet Hermann's son, whatever party they belonged to. Everyone knew my father. He had long since become an idol to a great many people of Strandir. The story was told that when my father was prime minister, an unnamed Independence Party man had expressed astonishment that the people of Strandir still believed in Hermann, as seldom as he showed himself up north. One of Pabbi's staunchest supporters, Ragnar Valdimarsson in Hólmavík, is said to have replied that they also believed in God, even though He had never been seen in Strandir.

I felt that people greatly appreciated my coming to every farm regardless of where the household stood politically. Admittedly, support for the Progressive Party was overwhelming in Strandir, but there were Independence Party men here and there. All spoke of my father with respect, however. At first I found the comparison a big pill to swallow. The yardstick applied to me was Hermann Jónasson. It was not easy to measure up to that. Most often, though, this was enjoyable. Some of the old men became quite animated and recounted stories from my father's first election campaign, which was fresh in the memory of many of them. He too had covered a lot of ground on his first campaign trip. He made it, however, on foot and not in a jeep like me.

Devotion to my father still lives on in various old people of Strandir. Sixteen years after his death, I received a short letter from Aðalheiður Þórarinsdóttir from Ós in Strandasýsla, an 87-year-old resident of the Grund nursing home. She was married to Magnús Gunnlaugsson, and Gunnlaugur Sigmundsson, former member of parliament, is the couple's grandchild. Aðalheiður's letter was written in October 1992, a little over a year after I left the office of prime minister for the last time. The memory of my father evidently still occupied this venerable old lady, even though a quarter of a century had passed since he held a seat in the Althing (Alþingi). The letter contained these words, accompanied by a verse:
Thinking of Hermann Jónasson, prime minister, member of parliament for us people of Strandir.
Many famous sons has Iceland had, who have increased its renown and might. Yet our highest hope of help was the superman Hermann Jónasson.
Unavoidable Poison and Exceptional Hospitality

At the start of the trip around Strandir, I set myself the goal of reaching 20 farms a day. I had intended to spend half an hour at each farm. These plans proved unrealistic. My stops frequently became twice as long. I did not bring up politics first, but rather sought news of the people themselves, the farming, and the state of affairs in the area. I asked questions rather than preached. Everywhere I was expected, because news of people's movements traveled fast on the rural party line. Coffee was on the pot everywhere and delicious cakes on the tables.

I had never drunk coffee before. During these weeks I sometimes had to sip 20 cups a day and even more. This was an unavoidable poison, because it would have been rude to decline a sip. The cream cakes that had been brought out or fetched from the freezer lost their appeal as time went on. I missed not getting ordinary food. Everyone wanted to do their best for me, and as was the custom of the land, nothing was considered finer than coffee and cakes. Later on this changed, thankfully. Then I would sit down at the table with the household if I arrived at mealtime and could ask for milk instead of coffee without being considered a weak-stomached milksop and a hopeless candidate.

Guðmundur Valgeirsson was the undisputed leader in his district and wrote a great deal in Tíminn. He lives at Bær in Trékyllisvík. The Valgeir family is very large in Árneshreppur, where many of Guðmundur's brothers still live, all of them staunch Progressives. Their sister, Laufey, was married to Bjarni Jónsson from Asparvík and later of Bjarnarhöfn on Snæfellsnes. There my son Hermann spent five summers in the countryside. Guðmundur is now in his nineties and still the same as ever. He has a sound opinion on every matter and still sends me letters on various subjects. Two years ago I got a line from him in which he warned against the "New Zealand way," an extreme form of free-market liberalism in economic management, which he said was a reckless folly.

Many of my father's long-standing supporters quickly became my best advisors, friends, and backers in Strandir. Ólafur Einarsson at Þórustaðir was one of the chief instigators of my candidacy. Ólafur was the district officer in Bitra and a true chieftain in his district. At Ólafur's home a dram was usually offered before or after the meal, and a toast was then drunk to the future and to the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). He was an exceptional host to visit. My wife Edda came with me to Strandir for the first time in 1968. We ate an excellent dinner at Ólafur's and accepted lodging for the night. When it was time to retire, it turned out that his wife Friðmey Guðmundsdóttir had made up for us the marital bed of her and Ólafur. We tried to protest, but it was to no avail.

Ólafur moved to Reykjavík in his old age, but his heart always remained tied to his home district. He often came north with me on my trips there. "Got to hitch a ride to the countryside," as he put it.

Another older man was Guðmundur Ragnar Guðmundsson at Bær on Selströnd, a great hunter and a good marksman. He welcomed me with open arms from our first acquaintance. In his home and that of his wife Margrét Guðbrandsdóttir, my father's name was held in high esteem. I was received without question as if I were a son, and the best food was set before me. Margrét never called me anything but "dear Steingrímur." It was a pleasure to talk with these people about bygone times, and they had a great many stories to tell.

Many more people of Strandir could be named. From many I received sound advice, lodging, or good support. I was pleased with the reception in Strandir and continued my journey around the Westfjords full of confidence. I felt I was managing to dispel mistrust, and a great awakening took place, not least among the younger men. Among them may be named Brynjólfur Sæmundsson, agricultural adviser, Jón Alfreðsson, now cooperative manager in Hólmavík, Karl Loftsson, now branch manager in Mosfellsbær, Páll Þorgeirsson, and Sigurður Jónsson at Stóra-Fjarðarhorn.

I was greatly taken with the people of Strandir, their industry and diligence. The life there was good, even better than I had imagined. I had, to be sure, become acquainted with fine Icelandic rural life in Skagafjörður in my younger years and learned from my father to appreciate it. Those memories, however, had begun to fade after years spent in the big cities of the United States.

The reception in the rural districts of the Westfjords constituency was in fact good everywhere. The farmers generally held their heads high. They were confident that their work was appreciated and a national necessity. The farmers I visited were free men. Attitudes toward the countryside have changed in the time that has since passed. Thirty years ago, farmers enjoyed general respect in society. Back then, those voices from Reykjavík proclaiming that the nation's farmers are parasites on Icelandic society were unknown.

These critical voices can be traced in some part to dissatisfaction with the agricultural system, overproduction, and subsidies. Overproduction in agriculture was a nearly unknown problem before the days of the Reconstruction Government (viðreisnarstjórnin). In fact, there had been occasional shortages of agricultural products since the end of the war, both domestically and abroad. Partly for this reason, the Reconstruction Government had introduced a system of export subsidies whose main objective was increased production. The export subsidy system was sometimes named after the ministers Ingólfur and Gylfi, and the legislation was called the Ingólfur Laws (Ingólfslög). By 1967 it had already had the consequence that production was at the outermost limits of what the market could bear. As time went on, the Ingólfur Laws led to overproduction, as is well known.

It came to the point that everyone saw the arrangement was deeply flawed, but it nevertheless proved difficult to tamper with the export subsidies. I became well acquainted with that when I became Minister of Agriculture in 1978.
The Red Town

Ísafjörður was the capital of the constituency. I spent a great deal of time there while the campaign lasted. The constituency's main campaign office was also in Ísafjörður. Working there was Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson, mentioned earlier. Among other things, he energetically handled our publishing matters and was editor of the young Progressives' campaign paper. Few had as good an insight into the mindset of the people of the Westfjords as Ólafur. He seemed to know where the great majority of them stood on every issue.

We named our campaign paper "Your Choice – Your Future" (Þitt val – þín framtíð) after the publication we young Progressives in Reykjavík had put out before the 1963 elections. It covered matters as varied as the herring price, transportation by sea and land, promotion of swimming as a sport, improved organization of trade education, one-sided employment, theater, and healthy social life along the coast, in addition to which half a page was devoted to a demand for more accurate weather forecasts! Ólafur was also largely responsible for the fact that many articles were directed at young people, urging them to secure my election.

The young man who occupies the battle seat on the Progressives' list is a source of dread to the opponents in the election campaign here in the west. Young people! Let us pay our share of the funeral costs of the current government. We do that by electing Steingrímur Hermannsson to parliament.

In Ísafjörður we were not a large party. The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) had a large following there, resting on old foundations, which showed itself among other things in the fact that the Social Democrats controlled the cooperative society. They drew much of their support from workers, tradesmen, and fishermen. The Social Democratic Party had long held the reins in the town council of Ísafjörður, which in years past was called "the red town." What hampered the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) most was that organized party work was scant, and poor track had been kept of the support we nonetheless had. That made it all the more necessary, I felt, to set to work briskly. We built the Progressives' association almost from the ground up by merging the existing associations of older and younger men. This brought many excellent men into the work.
Much the same story could in fact be told elsewhere in the Westfjords. Wherever I went, I immediately set about rebuilding the Progressive associations, not least the associations of younger

men. I placed particular emphasis on reaching the younger generation, which I felt had been neglected. Among them there was also a certain mistrust at first, and I was made to feel that it was not enough merely to be the son of Hermann Jónasson. Mistrust of this kind, however, always vanished as soon as we got down to work. There the young party members did their part no less than I. A particular awakening took place in Hólmavík, Suðureyri, and Flateyri, to name a few examples. Countless people could be named from the tough-minded party associations that came into being there.

Before the 1963 elections, my father had gotten me to transport the party's candidates between campaign meetings. The reason was that I owned a first-rate mountain vehicle, a Dodge Weapon, R 3030. It had originally been an ambulance which I had refitted. It was well equipped, with massive tires and a powerful winch. The equipment came in handy, since the going was often difficult on the mountain roads. On that trip I was entirely unaware that I myself would later stand for election in the west. I do not know, though, whether that thought lay behind it in my father's mind. With that trip, one might say, he raised the first cairns on my road to candidacy. On this journey I got to know the party's key men in each place.

Among the first to whom my father introduced me was Jón Jóhannsson, tax director in Ísafjörður, one of the foremost leaders of the Progressives in the Westfjords. He was tall of stature and had a lordly, even magisterial bearing. He had been a police officer before taking up the office of tax director. He was well respected by the people of Ísafjörður. For a great many years Jón published Ísfirðingur, the Progressives' paper in Ísafjörður, without ever accepting a single króna for his trouble. He was so productive at gathering advertisements and so thrifty that after decades of publishing he handed the paper back to the party with a fat balance in a savings account.

Bjarni Guðbjörnsson was our other foremost leader in the town, and he occupied the second seat on our final list in the constituency in 1967, as mentioned earlier. He had completed his lower secondary examination and been a driver for several years. Bjarni later took a teaching qualification and joined the staff of the Fisheries Bank (Útvegsbankinn) that same year. Before long he became branch manager in Ísafjörður and earned the nickname Bjarni in the Bank. He was a warm man, a friend to his friends, and a good fellow. Bjarni was one of those who urged me to stand for election in the Westfjords. When I sought a higher place on the list at the next elections, however, he had second thoughts.

Bjarni had comprehensive knowledge of the employment affairs of the people of Ísafjörður, was conservative in his political views, but a most courteous gentleman. Sparring at meetings was not his strong suit, and the people of the Westfjords therefore perhaps did not see in

him a future leader of the party. Bjarni, on the other hand, was popular in Ísafjörður and drew support from far and wide. His work was naturally colored by the fact that the banking system was interwoven with politics in those years. It was said that Bjarni would read from the annual accounts of the Fisheries Bank (Útvegsbankinn) at campaign meetings. In that way he demonstrated how great and important the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) support for employment affairs in the Westfjords was. This was not considered anything remarkable.

Before one municipal election in Ísafjörður, Kristján Jónsson from Garðsstaðir predicted 400 votes for the Progressive Party. This was considered an incredible figure, since the party's support had usually been around 200 votes. "Eh, yes," said Kristján in his characteristic voice, "that's right, the Progressive Party has only 200 votes, but Bjarni and the bank have the other 200."

Kristján from Garðsstaðir was one of the staunchest Progressives in Ísafjörður, and indeed anywhere you might look. He had become an old man. More amusing stories are probably told about Kristján than about any other Icelander. He was as devoted a supporter of the Federation of Cooperatives (Sambandið) as is humanly possible, peculiar in his manners, and liked to begin sentences with a questioning grunt. He was a favorite of the country's impressionists because of his distinctive voice and verbal tics. One of the most famous stories about Kristján tells of when he arrived at a filling station on his last drops of gasoline. He glanced at the pump and remarked: "Eh, is this Shell? No, then I'd rather drive without gasoline!" Shell was the conservatives' oil company. He could not bring himself to do business with it. And that was that.
"You're nothing but a damned wretch!"

In Ísafjörður, as elsewhere, the Progressives contended with supporters of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in business and fishing operations. Baldur Jónsson was one of the party's pillars in that struggle. He had built up the Ice-House Company of Ísafjörður (Íshúsfélag Ísfirðinga) and then Norðurtanginn with a blend of toughness and diligence. Baldur was a hot-tempered man but tremendously entertaining.

After I had become a substitute member of parliament, Einar Ingvarsson, branch manager of the National Bank (Landsbankinn), was to be transferred south. He and Baldur were great friends. Once when I was driving down Hafnarstræti in Ísafjörður, I saw Baldur waving to me. I stopped the car and he jumped in and said without preamble: "Those devils down south are planning to transfer Einar. That must not happen! You have to prevent it." I permitted myself to point out that I was only a lowly substitute member of parliament and in the opposition besides, so it was unlikely I could have any influence. Baldur reacted furiously and yanked the car door open. I just managed to stop before he leapt out. He stuck his head back in and said: "You're

nothing but a damned wretch," and slammed the door so hard that something was knocked out of place, so that it could not be opened. I had to go to a workshop to have the lock repaired — but the branch manager was transferred south.

Baldur and I nevertheless became good colleagues and friends. Before all was said and done, he himself moved south and was, among other things, chairman of the Progressive Association (Framsóknarfélagið) in Garðabær. I hired him to work in the Ministry of Fisheries during my time as minister in 1980.

When I was on the campaign trip with my father in Ísafjörður in 1963, I was directed to lodge at the home of Jóhann Júlíusson, fishing-vessel operator, and Margrét Leósdóttir, his wife. I stayed there without exception on my visits to Ísafjörður during the twenty years I was engaged in politics there, and indeed longer. And I was always handed the keys to the family car for my use the moment I had landed. The home often saw many guests, and the lady of the house attended to everyone with a special warmth. She was light-hearted and cheerful and delightful in conversation, being highly knowledgeable and talkative. I also remember well Margrét's quality of showing understanding and fairness even when she disagreed with people. That I found worthy of imitation.

The affection this couple showed one another was unique. Never did a harsh word pass between them, and in that household one never needed to ask for help. Margrét faithfully backed her husband in his large fishing operation, and he lent her a hand whenever needed. They took me in at once as if I were their own son.

Much could be said of Jóhann Júlíusson, and many could learn from him. He moved to Ísafjörður at a young age together with his father, Júlíus Geirmundsson from Fljótavík in Hornstrandir, and a great many siblings. Jóhann began working as a taxi driver but soon started a fishing operation with a small boat together with his brother, Þórður. Little by little they expanded the operation. Jóhann and his partners bought their first trawler in the later trawlerization wave in 1972. I remember that once when I stayed with him in those years, he was worried about the debts resting on the ship. He could not bear being in debt. He remarked that perhaps the most sensible thing would be to sell and clear out the debts. Fortunately, he did not do so. I sometimes claim that I talked him out of the sale that evening, but he refuses to admit it.
In the years that followed, the trawler operation went exceedingly well.

Despite tremendous success, he always showed restraint and thrift. When the trawler came to land, Jói Júl, as he is often called, was the first down to the dock, whether by night or by day. Everything the ship needed for its next trip was then ready — cables and fishing gear, provisions, or anything else. The trawler, Júlíus Geirmundsson, was not only one
the greatest fishing vessel of the Westfjords but also always like new, because it was carefully maintained.

After Jóhann withdrew from the fishing operation and his son Kristján largely took over the business, he assisted his wife Margrét in the shoe shop, Leó's Shoe Store (Skóverslun Leós), which Margrét's brothers had long run on the main street in Ísafjörður. This illustrated their relationship well. Margrét was quoted as saying in jest that the old man was of some use. He was, however, made in such a peculiar way that whenever he happened to send customers home with two shoes for the same foot, he was far too inclined to waive the price of the shoes as compensation for their having to come back to the shop to correct the mistake.
The Federation, the Progressives, and Tíminn

I learned right away in the market towns that where the cooperative societies were strong, the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was strong. The cooperative manager in each place was usually the first person I went to see. The position almost without exception carried with it being the party's chief agent and leader. This was especially true where the Federation of Cooperatives (Sambandið) also ran a freezing plant or fish processing. Ever since the days of Jónas from Hrifla, the interests of these communities had been considered so interwoven with the interests of the Federation and the Progressive Party that the representatives of each made little distinction between them. By the time I entered politics, these attitudes had taken deep root. What was good for the cooperative was good for the community and thereby for the party.

No one was in any doubt about this connection, and Tíminn, the organ of the Progressive Party, carried campaign news about it all. Everyone who deposited their goods with the cooperative received Tíminn daily, and the subscription was deducted from their credit. I do not know whether many asked to be excused from the paper, or whether that was even possible. This arrangement, however, remained in place for a long time despite considerable criticism, and when the editorial board of Tíminn was informed that the Federation intended to abolish this compulsory subscription, I was certainly one of those who took that outcome hard.

The cooperative managers were usually my hosts on campaign trips and my chief advisers on the concerns of the voters, just as their predecessors had been a pillar of support for the Progressive Party's candidates through the years. The occasional cooperative manager had been all at once cooperative manager, fish processor, and member of parliament on top of everything else.
Eiríkur Þorsteinsson at Þingeyri was such a man. He had been a member of parliament and held the reins in his home district. Stories circulated about the imperiousness

of him, and things had been turbulent for a while. In the wake of it he received the nickname "blood-axe." The Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) support was for most of that time solid in Þingeyri, and that was surely due not least to Eiríkur's efforts. Another cooperative manager of the old school was Ólafur E. Ólafsson at Króksfjarðarnes. He was called "both emperor and king" in those parts. Ólafur gave me immeasurable help. He naturally knew every single person in "his district." Some thought it worse that he also believed he knew all their needs, wishes, and desires. Once I came to a farm in Reykhólasveit where the housewife complained that Ólafur was altogether too autocratic. For example, he had refused to stock work trousers for women for sale in the cooperative because he believed that womenfolk ought to wear skirts.

Widely around the Westfjords, younger men with progressive attitudes were running the cooperative societies. They proved no less of a great support to me than the old men. In Patreksfjörður, Svavar Jóhannsson was cooperative manager until he took over the local branch of the Cooperative Bank (Samvinnubankinn). His namesake, Svavar Júlíusson, then took over the cooperative. With him and his excellent wife Helga Þórðardóttir I first stayed in 1973 and was their guest regularly for many years afterward. We often sat long into the evening discussing life and existence no less than the affairs and needs of the country.

Another imaginative cooperative manager from the ranks of the younger men was Kári Einarsson, electrical engineer. He took over the cooperative at Bíldudalur from Pétur Þorsteinsson. Kári was married to Sigrún Magnúsdóttir. Sigrún was a skeptic in politics, and we debated a great deal. In the end she agreed to stand for the district council in Bíldudalur and became a tough local-government politician. Sigrún later ran for the Reykjavík city council, where she still holds a seat for the Progressive Party. She is now married to Páll Pétursson, a minister of the Progressive Party. Sigrún sometimes says that I made her a Progressive.

Pétur Þorsteinsson, who had been cooperative manager at Bíldudalur, had taken over the fishing operation at Tálknafjörður. Before long he became all-powerful in the place. Pétur not only supported my candidacy at the outset but also guided me greatly and proved wise in counsel in every respect. When I had spent a few days in Patreksfjörður, Tálknafjörður, and Bíldudalur, I asked Pétur whether it was not obvious that the units in this area needed to be enlarged through consolidation. Given the proximity, the cooperatives, the schools, and all public services could be merged, if the roads were improved. Pétur answered gravely: "It is true that the roads need fixing, but if you intend to spread that propaganda here — that the cooperative should be moved to Patreksfjörður — then you had best withdraw your candidacy at once."

Pétur knew his home folk. The rivalry between communities was as strong as ever. Before all was over, however, all the cooperatives had gone bankrupt and the freezing plants were headed the same way. Most of the villages have fared badly because of quota speculation and the consequences of reduced fishing allowances. Conservatism and the fear of rationalizing surely played their part in the development. Commerce shifted to Ísafjörður following bankruptcies rather than through organized consolidation. As a result, Ísafjörður alone has managed to defend its position. The town has changed less than the smaller places in the Westfjords and has even grown and strengthened. In the villages, however, only roadside kiosks and video rental shops remain.
"It's beautiful here when the fish are biting"

In the election campaign I paid special attention to the fishing villages. There, I reckoned, the swing vote was chiefly to be found. I went to every workplace I could manage and visited a great number of homes. In the villages the atmosphere was different from the countryside. There, life revolved around fish. I liked to talk with people on their home ground whenever possible: in the freezing plants, the baiting sheds, and at other workplaces. When I entered a home, there was no lack of hospitality.

In the fishing communities there were difficulties in those years. The trawler industry had collapsed some time earlier, and fishing was mainly done from boats. Cod fishing had been declining for several years, but the herring had kept the nation afloat. When the herring disappeared, it was therefore hard not only on the herring boats but on the fishing industry and society as a whole. Nevertheless, I found no sign of despair in the people. Everyone was a participant in the working life, and the refrain was often: "It's beautiful here when the fish are biting."

Patreksfjörður was of course an important place on account of its population. I combed the town, so to speak, and wrote detailed notes about everything that met my eyes, the people I met, the matters they cared about, and so on. One of my most reliable allies in Patreksfjörður was Bjarni Hermann Finnbogason. He was chairman of the labor union and our campaign manager. On my first trip he had organized visits to many homes in the town. I was taken aback and asked whether the men of the house would be home in the middle of the day. He said they would not, but their wives would all be home because there was no fish at the freezing plant. It was necessary to meet them no less than their husbands. That day we were guests in 24 homes and accepted coffee in all of them. My stomach was queasy when I lay down to sleep after that coffee-guzzling.
I thank the higher powers that the theory that cream was lethal had not reached the west. I think it was to my stomach's
saved my life that I got cream in my coffee in many places during that election campaign.

Many of the fishing villages in the Westfjords enjoyed a new period of prosperity in the 1970s. Patreksfjörður benefited, like other places in the west, when the left-wing government broke the stagnation in the development of the rural areas and the fishing industry in 1971. There, as in many other places around the country, businesses run by Progressives and Independence Party men competed for room to operate. The Vatneyri brothers led the Independence Party men, while Bogi Þórðarson ran the cooperative movement's freezing plant. Bogi informed me about the politics in Patreksfjörður and where the shoe pinched in fisheries matters. We became good friends as time went on, and I hired him as my assistant when I became Minister of Fisheries in 1980.

In the villages it was the same story everywhere in those years. If a man had grit in him, he rowed out to sea and brought home provisions, so long as he had some sort of small boat at his disposal. There was no quota then. Competition in business also served the communities well as long as there was enough catch to process. The freezing plants competed to attract the boats' catches and good workers.

That picture has changed completely. When the catches contracted at the beginning of the 1980s, it hit these places hard. The build-up turned into its own opposite. Two freezing plants were then competing for raw material that was barely enough for one to scrape by. Political ambition and generous patronage had in many places encouraged such grand ventures. People built big and took loans for a substantial part of the construction. Price indexation, which was introduced throughout the country's entire banking and credit system, meant that it no longer paid to be in debt. Anyone could foresee the outcome.

I well remember what a fine man from Flateyri said to me about the necessity of tying businesses to their home communities. In Flateyri, Einar "the Rich" Sigurðsson ran a trawler operation until one fine day he sailed away and left the place virtually helpless. The operating figures had not shown sufficient profit. With the arrival of the quota system and the free transfer of catch rights, the inhabitants of every other settlement in the Westfjords can tell a similar story. The Westfjords were poorly equipped for the battle over capital and fishing rights that the quota system called for. Many were then forced to merge with others or sell. They remain behind as tenants of other parts of the country.
The Conservative Strongholds
Bolungarvík was a great stronghold of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) under the all-seeing eye of Einar Guðfinnsson, the fishing-vessel operator. About him I say in my notes:

Einar Guðfinnsson is the absolute ruler of Bolungarvík, one might say. All the main businesses are in his hands or his sons', and likewise the largest shop. Einar's sons are fine-looking men, but the old man will nonetheless decide whatever he wants. He is popular in Bolungarvík. People feel he has often lent a helping hand to those in need, and he is credited with the building up of the town. Some, however, find him rather domineering.

I met Einar in his freezing plant and found it instructive to talk with him. I also quickly discovered that Progressives (framsóknarmenn) were hidden here and there in the town. One of our foremost leaders was Guðmundur Magnússon at Hóll. One might also mention Kristján Júlíusson, a teacher, who was usually called Krjúl. That was his byline under articles in Tíminn, where he was a correspondent. He was an exceptionally intelligent and well-made man, but because of a disability he walked with a limp. Kristján spared no effort when it came to the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and me. He regularly picked me up in Ísafjörður and organized meetings and gatherings.

On these trips Kristján had the custom of stopping the car at Ósvör, where Óshlíð lies behind and Bolungarvík comes into view. There he lit his pipe. After I had witnessed this a few times, I asked him what it was about. He said he paused at this spot to let the stowaways out. They would hitch a ride with the car where accidents had happened on the slope. I did not argue with him. He seemed to be serious.

Transportation past Óshlíð was in fact a major political issue. The road there had long been considered dangerous because of avalanches and rockfalls during thaws. When I was the driver on my father's campaign tour in 1963, it was doubtful whether it was passable. I wanted to put it to the test, but Jón Jóhannsson, the tax director, forbade such recklessness. Since we knew that transportation matters were a sensitive subject in the eyes of the people of Bolungarvík, we were, on the other hand, extremely displeased to be the only candidates who did not travel the slope. It ended with Jón reaching an agreement with all the candidates that they would accompany us by boat. The people of Bolungarvík are said not to have found that a very manly expedition.

Súðavík was another "conservative den," as hardline party men put it. At Langeyri I met Björgvin Bjarnason, brother of Matthías the member of parliament, a convinced conservative. Björgvin ran a fish-processing operation but was very eccentric and solitary. His mind was consumed with improvements in fish processing, and among other things he had had a machine built to shell shrimp, of his own invention. We got along well and he showed me this marvel. News of this spread through all the districts, for it was considered a great and unexpected mark of confidence. He showed the machine to only a chosen few.

The only harsh reception I can recall receiving was at Hattardalur. There two fierce dogs attacked me from behind with open jaws when I knocked at the door. It seemed obvious to me that they cared nothing for guests. In a fluster I kicked toward the beast that was more forward, and the clog I was wearing landed under his jawbone. The dog flew into the air and landed howling on his back. With that, the curs crawled away. When the farmer Jón Björnsson came to the door, I told him what had happened and said I hoped the wretched dog had not broken his jaw. He, however, took this lightly and said that in that case the dog would have deserved it.
"Then the Engine Came into the Boat"

My acquaintance with the people of the Westfjords is the equivalent of attending many universities. That is how I have put it ever since my first election campaign in 1967. That acquaintance alone would have been reason enough for me to run for office. There the common people were at work, and nowhere did anyone give in despite hardships in the economy or natural disasters. The story embodied in the people's organizations and ways of working was for me an inexhaustible fund of learning. From conversations with older people one could learn much about a time that had vanished but was preserved in stories and memories.

At Lambavatn on Rauðisandur lived Ólafur Sveinsson, father of Magnús Torfi, who later became a minister for the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna). Ólafur was very old when I ran for office but both talkative and entertaining. He especially welcomed the extension of the fishing limits, which he considered the greatest public benefit of the century. He also wanted to extend them further out. Ólafur told me that he remembered the days when British trawlers dragged their nets so close to shore at Rauðisandur that one could read their names on the ships' sides without binoculars.

Júlíus Kristjánsson at Efri-Tunga in Örlygshöfn was another old man whom it was memorable to get to know. I intended to stop only briefly with him but stayed a long while, for Júlíus had much on his mind. Among other things, he told me

a striking story about the consequences of technological change. In his youth, men went every year to the fishing station in Kollsvík. From there it is a short row to the fishing grounds. He praised the life at the fishing station but also told me of various hardships the station men had to endure. Sometimes a boat would break apart on landing and lives were lost.

The old man remembered above all, though, stories of how merry things were when the girls came to gut the catch. "That's where I met my sweetheart," said this seasoned man, his eyes growing moist. At that very moment she appeared in the doorway with coffee for us. Her name was Dagbjört Torfadóttir, and she was still elegant though she had reached her later years. Júlíus reminded me of the tough characters in the road work at Vatnsskarð when they grumbled about the bulldozer. "Then the engine came into the boat," he said, gazing out the window as if looking back on days gone by. "And then it was all over." Fishing operations largely ceased in Rauðasandshreppur with the arrival of motorboats and moved into Patreksfjörður.

In the outer coves of the Westfjords the same story could be told in many places. Dozens of people had once lived there, and many times that number in the fishing stations during the catch season. In those days men rowed out in open boats and fished as close to shore as possible. After engines came into the boats, it became possible to row farther out to fish. The people moved into the villages and sought the comforts of the towns. The outer coves remained behind, only a shadow of their former selves. Evidence of this could be seen in many places.

Another memorable man was the Reverend Þórarinn Þór at Reykhólar. He too was a resolute supporter of mine and rallied people far and wide. Þórarinn was a reformer in spirit, and one of his chief interests was the matter of primary schools. In my account of a visit to him there is a detailed overview of these issues. The education laws that had been enacted in 1946 had never been enforced in the rural districts of the Westfjords, even though more than 20 years had passed since their adoption. Children began school two years later than in the capital area, at 9 years of age. On top of this, the school term lasted only three months. Rural children thus received only 15 months of schooling, compared with 42 months of compulsory schooling in the towns. The result was that only the occasional teenager completed the national examination (landspróf), which was the prerequisite for further study.
This worried me greatly, and I became interested in reforms. I say in my notes:

This serious situation can be traced to a great many things. Parents are expected to teach their children to read and write before they come to the primary schools. This fails in the vast majority of cases, and it may be said that the children are unable to read or write when they come to school at 9 years old — at least far too many of them. The teaching in the countryside is, moreover, compressed and often aimed solely at the examinations, because there is competition between
teachers over good examination results. Teaching is then often done pell-mell, cramming for what is to be tested next, but such teaching is of little worth.

I was also worried that the teaching was bound to be uneven in quality, since one man taught an entire school everything that was to be learned, from spelling to arithmetic and everything in between. Some of the teachers were in fact outstanding and worked miracles in these scattered settlements. They were not many, however, and their numbers were dwindling.

Shortly before I took up the matter, a proposal had been voted down for a joint school for five districts with a combined population of 500. In that way a large school with specialized teachers was to have been established. This solution was not without its flaws, however. The children would be far from their parents for a large part of the year and would miss out on their loving care, which I considered the most important provision for the journey into life. Nevertheless, I supported these reform proposals of Þórarinn and others who considered education more important than most other things. On the other hand, I had doubts about the farmers' ambitions in school matters and said of them in my notes:

It stands very much in the way of healthy development in school matters that there seems to be very little understanding among farmers of increased education for their children. Many seem most relieved that it is not possible to get children into secondary schools, since these are always full, and people generally do not have enough foresight to reserve a school place for their child one or two years in advance.

This is certainly a harsh judgment, and fortunately not all farmers were guilty of the same fault in these matters. In this respect attitudes have also changed greatly for the better, and the building up of secondary schools in the countryside has met a greatly increased demand for them.
The Chosen Land of the Hermits

My mind was very much occupied with the election campaign, the tightly packed schedule, the next farm and settlement, and the next meeting. Yet I could not avoid being deeply moved by the surroundings that met my eyes on my travels. The nature of the Westfjords and Strandir is powerful, like the people who inhabit these areas. It is, however, somewhat divided into two extremes, like various other things. The Strandir coast stretches northward with expanses of vegetated moorland. From there the people of Strandir draw their broad-mindedness and open spirit. Strandasýsla is one of the most fertile counties in the country. There, soil erosion measures only one percent, and

that does not surprise me. The Westfjords, on the other hand, are adorned with towering mountains and narrow valleys. That is the chosen land of the hermits. On calm summer evenings it is as if every living thing stops breathing in these fjords. And the sea hardly stirs except to recall the perfect mirror image of the mountains, which the surface of the water preserves like a cherished memory. Then there is nowhere lovelier to be.

One of my father's most devoted supporters was named Sigurjón Sigurðsson, a hermit at Grænanes, a little croft between Staðardalur and Selárdalur in Steingrímsfjörður. Visiting him was memorable. He kept all my father's New Year's articles in a neat stack under his bed. From there he pulled them out now and then to read and lift his spirits. Sigurjón owned a Russian jeep that was undrivable because it lacked a tie-rod end. I undertook to procure one and brought it to him on my next trip. Thus the jeep was put back into service. Sigurjón admittedly had no driver's license, but he got his neighbors to drive him into Hólmavík when needed.

Not everyone had the manner of a hermit, even if they lived in remote places. In Selárdalur I visited Hannibal Valdimarsson and spent a pleasant while with him and his wife Sólveig. Hannibal was taciturn about the end of the left-wing government in 1958, but I said I believed that outcome had had bad consequences for the labor movement and its part in national affairs. He said only that it could not have been helped. We walked out beyond the farmhouse to the sheep sheds. On the way we clambered over a fence. Hannibal then remarked that my father would have thought nothing of jumping over it. I therefore had no choice but to jump over the fence on the way back, and it went off without mishap.

I also visited Gísli at Uppsalir on this trip and met him outside. He was not very talkative. I understood hardly a single word of the little he said, but I believed I could make out something like one yes and two noes. Gísli later became famous throughout the country after Ómar Ragnarsson's television program about him.

Memorable men of unusual habits lived no less in the villages than in remote valleys, however. The Reverend Stefán Eggertsson was one of the many fine Progressives at Þingeyri. He concerned himself not only with the heavenward journeys of the departed but also devoted special care to the affairs of the local airfield. He maintained the hangar, painted the gates, and saw to it that everything was kept up as well as could be wished. He had set up an amusing control tower, which was the cabin of an old boat. The same story could be told of the emergency shelter on Hrafnseyrarheiði. He stopped there regularly to make repairs. The Reverend Stefán always kept a long-wave radio switched on in the parsonage in case anyone in distress needed assistance. He cared greatly about

travelers. I made use of this on my journeys, since I had a two-way radio in the car. I often sent word ahead of me through the radio when I was passing by Þingeyri. I stayed with the Reverend Stefán quite often, and talking with him was especially rewarding.
"Very Slippery Is the Path of the Ascetic Life"

Some of the Westfjord people I had come to know in my father's house. After every party congress and central committee meeting of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), my father invited the constituency's delegates home and held a feast for them. At these gatherings I became acquainted with most of the party's leading men long before I ever considered taking part in politics. There I met Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson for the first time. He was then at the Teachers' College. This was in 1966. I asked Ólafur, among other things, how support stood at Suðureyri on Súgandafjörður. "Not well, not well," said Ólafur. "Most people there follow the Social Democrats, if they don't vote for the conservatives." Ólafur added, however, that if I could get Eðvarð, son of Sturla Jónsson the district officer, to work with me, then we would be saved.

I got in touch with Eðvarð, and at some point when I was in Patreksfjörður I got passage on a coast guard vessel to Suðureyri. Eðvarð received me on the breakwater where the ship docked. The handshake was firm, and so the man proved to be. He became one of my best co-workers and allies in the Westfjords. I never stayed anywhere else but with him and his wife Arnbjörg Bjarnadóttir when I came to Suðureyri. About our first meeting I wrote a few years later in Eðvarð's guestbook:
When I took his hand, it seemed clear to me, for the grip was strong and warm, that no one could stand up against us, if we rowed on the same side of the boat.

Eðvarð did not take conventional routes. He took me to every workplace, into every baiting shed, and aboard every boat. Wherever a living soul was to be found. When people looked up from their work, he took me by the shoulder and said: "This man here is Steingrímur Hermannsson. You should vote for him." I found this a strange procedure, but the fact is that the Progressive Party grew from being a small party at Suðureyri into being the largest party in the place. All of it was under Eðvarð's leadership.
The baiting sheds proved in fact to be a kind of parliament of the common people in the Westfjords. In few places were there fiercer debates on national affairs. The baiting menwere

also tough customers in debate, after years of training in their conversations over the bait tubs. There was no shortage of shots fired at me, both hard questions and pithy assertions. On one thing, though, they all seemed able to agree. "The middleman rabble and the office crowd down south" were worthless parasites on "the honest working people out around the country."

Suðureyri was one of the most delightful places I have ever known. I would make a detour to get there for district festivals and Þorri feasts. I traveled from Ísafjörður on skis or by snowmobile if nothing better was available. It was a lively village. The inhabitants numbered between four and five hundred, and everyone was a comrade. The district festivals were held by the Progressive association, but everyone came to them, whatever party they belonged to. Afterwards people went from house to house, and there was great merriment. People competed at tossing off verses, which were recorded in guestbooks, and men tested their strength at arm wrestling (sjómaður) and other trials of strength. The festivities often lasted until near morning. In Eðvarð's guestbook I once left behind this verse:
Very slippery is the path of the ascetic life, and far from my inclination. At Suðureyri I sat over a glass, with song and dance and joy.

This was a very good community life, and a similar story could be told of the other fishing villages in the Westfjords. People worked from dawn to dusk when there was fish to be had. At such times there was not a soul on the streets, and I went to meet the people in the freezing plant. In those days there were no European Union regulations to forbid the teenagers from having their share in the windfall. It seemed to me that these people nonetheless felt happy — and much happier than now. This vitality disappeared with the quota and with the people who followed it to other parts of the country. I cannot escape the thought that priceless cultural treasures were thereby lost, for much vanished with this way of life. The village is now like a faint shadow of what it was in earlier times.
"Will You Bring Us the Electricity?"

From Ísafjörður I visited the farms along the Djúp. I tried to get as far in as was at all possible. I visited Súðavík and the farms all the way to Eyri in Hestfjörður. It was not possible to get any farther then. My last round before campaign meetings took all my time was to the farms around Inn-Djúpið. More of them were inhabited then than now. I came to every single farm except one. Vigur was

left out, unfortunately. A road ran from Ögur and around Skötufjörður. On the eastern side there was a farm, or hovel, called Hjallar. There lived one Steingrímur Pétursson, with his wife Vilborg Ólafsdóttir and several children. They received me extremely warmly. The couple's farm seemed to me one of the most inhospitable I encountered in the Westfjords, and the housing very poor.

It cannot be denied that in the Westfjords there were, here and there, settlements and farms that were poorly built even though it was well into the 1960s. Even in Strandasýsla there were hovels here and there that can hardly be described. They were, however, more common out west in the fjords. There the farming was often not as flourishing and the spirit of cultivation different. No one starved, but some of the dwellings were not fit for human habitation. Cleanliness was in some places in short supply, though in most places water had been piped into the farmhouses. When I came to Garðsstaðir in Ögurvík I knocked on the door but no one answered. I opened the door and was nearly bowled over as a hen came flying out of the house and brushed against my head. On another visit I had to edge along the wall to avoid falling into the cellar.
Several floorboards had broken and a huge hole gaped open. Once I sat down through a worn-out sofa onto the floor — it was both broken and springless. These were exceptions, however.

Modern conveniences, on the other hand, were not to be found everywhere. The most remote farms still lacked telephones, and in some places electricity had not yet been brought in. There the first question was often: "Will you get us the electricity?" I would often swear solemn oaths that it would be done. It was a matter of fairness. Television was also becoming a major point of emphasis. Those who lived in remote places wanted to receive television broadcasts no less than others. Over the following years I spent a great deal of time in parliament working to bring such broadcasts about. By the time I became Minister of Transport just over a decade later, this was mostly complete. I then pushed for the automatic telephone system to reach all Icelanders. An extensive plan was drawn up for that project.
Transport and roads were an eternal concern in the countryside, and no less by the fjords, where one had to cross heaths and ridges to reach the next settlement.

In the Westfjords, electricity, television, and the telephone have long since become a self-evident part of daily life. There are video players in nearly every home and video-rental shops in every village. The roads are admittedly still of varying quality. But a revolution has taken place compared to how things were.

Around Djúp there was unfortunately considerable rivalry between districts and farms. It hindered the prosperity of the settlement there. For example, relations in Nauteyrarhreppur were so poor that people there could not attend the same church. A church was therefore built at Melgraseyri even though there was already another at Nauteyri a short distance away. This endemic rivalry also showed itself in the so-called Westfjords Plan (Vestfjarðaáætlunin). It

went toward the construction of outbuildings. In Djúp the plan fell completely apart because people could not work together. Each and every farmer sent for a work crew from Reykjavík, with the attendant cost.

Things were altogether different in Árneshreppur in Strandir. There Guðmundur Valgeirsson worked to build solidarity among the people. The farmers formed a building crew and got a master builder — a Strandir man who had moved away — to come up from the south. They then went from farm to farm and built for one another, so the cost was far lower than the estimates had projected.

Traveling around Djúp in 1968 I ran into Halldór Þórðarson from Laugaland on the road. There had been sea ice and considerable hardship that year. Halldór was in low spirits, as was to be expected, since the hayfields were damaged. After we had talked for a while, he remarked: "Do you think the damned government will give us a hardship grant?" I said I did not know, but people had to hope. On the same trip my route took me to Árneshreppur. There, everyone who could lift a finger was hauling driftwood up from the shore. I joined the group and was well received. I remember well that old Guðmundur Guðmundsson at Melar said: "Yes, times are hard now, Steingrímur. Now everyone must fend for himself as best he can. We have no time to attend your meeting tonight." This described well the attitudes in Strandir and around Djúp. The meeting was in fact held, and every seat was filled.
Guðmundur at Melar himself sat in the front row.

In the decades that have since passed, the position of the Westfjords has changed completely, and the people of the Westfjords feel they have less influence than before. Many of them have remarked to me that they find the constituency's group of members of parliament rather lacking in vigor. The Westfjords now have no minister or member of parliament in a position of real influence. I have tried to placate these friends of mine by pointing out that Sighvatur Björgvinsson is chairman of his party and a former minister. Not a single Strandir man's brow lifted at those words.
Campaign meetings and flying barbs

In the Westfjords constituency, thirteen joint campaign meetings were held in the run-up to elections — and still are to this day. They are a remnant of the old constituency arrangement, and any proposal to change this system is poorly received. These meetings were instructive for me and proved a good school for political battles later on. The first meetings were held in Árneshreppur in Strandir and at Hólmavík, and the last in Ísafjörður. By the time the round of meetings began at the end of May, I had made all the trips around the constituency that I had intended.
There were two meetings each day, with the exception of the Ísafjörður meeting. All the top candidates went to that one, but for the others we divided into teams. The arrangement

of the meetings was usually the same, with two candidates speaking for each ticket. First came the keynote speeches, which were the longest; a second speaker from each party gave a considerably shorter address, and finally there were closing remarks. It often fell to me to deliver the keynote, except when Sigurvin was along. At the end I generally handled the responses.

Voters attended these meetings in great numbers. Many came in their best clothes and in a festive mood. Meetings were judged by whether they offered some entertainment no less than by what issues were under discussion. There was thus never any lack of flying barbs, personal attacks, or even juvenile pranks. Famous is the story of the clash between Sigurður Bjarnason from Vigur and Hannibal Valdimarsson. Sigurður is said to have poked Hannibal with a pencil while he was at the podium. When Sigurður had repeated the trick several times, Hannibal lost control of himself and slapped Sigurður across the face. The audience stared, thunderstruck, unable to make head or tail of Hannibal's rage. In my own speeches I tried to steer clear of needless quarrels and to emphasize the issues and the future. I soon found, however, that I was expected to answer for myself, and preferably at full volume.
I would then often save that for the closing remarks of the meeting.

The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) was the chief opponent of us Progressives. Sigurður from Vigur led its list. I never got into a bad clash with him. That can probably be traced to my placing primary emphasis on sticking to the issues. I had heard that the meetings were first and foremost a cockfight and that harder-fought battles were hard to find. Nor were nicknames spared. At the first meeting I attended, Halldór from Kirkjuból called Sigurður "the fledgling from Vigur." He reacted angrily and responded by belittling Halldór's manner of dress. He said Halldór belonged in the cowshed. I do not think Sigurður gained anything from that remark. Otherwise, the candidates often became the best of friends. We were not unlike a traveling theater company where the actors are the greatest of pals between performances. On stage, however, we staged spectacular battles every evening.

Halldór at Kirkjuból rose still further in my esteem at these campaign meetings. He was a superb debater and had an exceptional memory. It was incredible to hear him recount what some candidate had said at a campaign meeting four or eight years earlier. No one ever dared to contradict him, for it was invariably quoted correctly.

Halldór was a sincere man of the people but careless about his appearance. There was no denying that some found Halldór old-fashioned and reactionary. Perhaps it played some part that he was a teetotaler of the old school, while among the majority
of the young people, the youth-association spirit had given way to greater liberality in these matters.

Matthías Bjarnason is among the most memorable of my opponents. He was in second place on the Independence Party list in 1967 and had sat one term in parliament. Matthías went at it hard at meetings and could be witty. It sometimes seemed to me that he made do with jeering and cared less about arguments. Matthías's criticism of me was more often than not personal and veiled, rather than a matter of the issues I championed being to his displeasure. He insinuated far and wide that I was an outsider born with a silver spoon in my mouth, far too partial to American attitudes and right-leaning accordingly. In this way he sought to sow distrust of me among the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) supporters. I was therefore glad to have put in many months of work and tireless travel to get to know the voters personally.
That is the only way to prevent such malicious gossip from taking root. Some of it, though, was hard to guard against.

Matthías was tireless in dreaming up stories about his opponents and spreading them wherever he went. Many of them are surely still alive. Once, when a truck driver by the name of Svavar Friðbergsson was doing road work on Botnsheiði above Súgandafjörður, Matthías Bjarnason and Pétur Sigurðsson, members of parliament for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), came by. Matthías knew that Svavar had supported me in the 1967 elections. He took Svavar aside and said: "Things have turned ugly with Steingrímur now. Don't you know he has started carrying on with Beta, the wife of Þorvaldur Garðar." Þorvaldur was one of Matthías's chief rivals for the leadership of the Independence Party men in the west. Svavar said he did not believe it. Matthías then said, as proof, that he had seen me and Beta together at Hótel Borg a few days earlier.
