When I came to Súgandafjörður shortly afterward, Eðvarð Sturluson put the story to me. I was naturally astonished. "Matthías says he saw the two of you together at Hótel Borg," was the refrain. I could not help but laugh. Elísabet, Þorvaldur's wife, and I had served together on the class committee in secondary school. The group had recently met to prepare the class's graduation anniversary. The meeting was at Hótel Borg. Matthías and Pétur sat two tables away from us.
The Restoration Government Holds On

In my campaign speeches I emphasized the future and the changes that were needed in each place. The economic life of the Westfjords seemed to me lacking in variety, as in many respects it still is today. The livelihood of the inhabitants was based on fishing and farming. Businesses and farms were in most places small in scale. I therefore thought it necessary to broaden the foundation of economic life as much as possible by promoting larger and stronger units. When I read these old speeches and my notes from the meetings, I am actually surprised at how full they are of new ideas in economic matters. I spoke in favor of a sawmill in Strandir so that the driftwood could be put to better use. I wanted to buy a shrimp-peeling machine for Hólmavík and set up shrimp-meal processing afterward. I wanted to search for ocean quahog and for markets for shellfish.

At Króksfjarðarnes I spoke in favor of greenhouse cultivation at Reykhólar, and at three meetings I pointed out the conditions and possibilities for fish farming and fish cultivation, which I believed had a very great future. Already in this first election campaign of mine I got into a clash with Matthías Bjarnason over those ideas. There were to be more of them.

Soon a seaweed factory by Breiðafjörður also became a great interest of mine. I furthermore wanted to increase the services the people of the Westfjords provided to the Icelandic fleet and to strengthen workshops and ship repairs to that end. Tourism I considered an untapped source of income, and it seemed obvious to me that the bird cliffs and deserted coves held a magic that ought to be made known. Everywhere I saw projects and untapped opportunities that urgently needed attention. Most often my message was well received and various people had words of praise on their lips. There were, however, certainly exceptions to that. New ideas fall on soil of varying quality.

The Restoration government (Viðreisnarstjórnin) held on in the 1967 elections, though only barely. The government relied on 32 members of parliament out of 60, which was the minimum number needed to have a majority in both chambers of parliament. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) received 37.5 percent of the votes and 23 members of parliament. The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) 28.1 percent and 18 members. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) 17.6 percent and 10 members, and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkur) 15.7 percent and 9 members.

The Restoration government stood on shakier ground than these numbers suggest. The outcome was decided when Helgi Bergs, member of parliament for the Progressive Party in the South, lost to the candidate of the People's Alliance. Helgi had won election as the party's third member of parliament four years earlier by a very narrow margin. Number-crunchers worked out that Helgi would have kept his parliamentary seat, without the People's Alliance losing any members, if one hundred votes had shifted from the People's Alliance to the Progressive Party in the South constituency in the elecin

the year 1967. The reason was that the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) would have been credited with an equalization seat in another constituency at the expense of one of the government-coalition parties. With that, the government would have fallen.

In the Westfjords, however, the election results were better than most Progressive Party members had dared to hope. We received over 38.2 percent of the vote, which was more than two percentage points higher than four years earlier. The party's support had thus never been greater since the formation of the Westfjords constituency in 1959. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), which came next in 1967, received 34 percent of the vote.

Deep down I had nursed a faint hope of being elected to parliament. That did not happen. Yet even though I was not elected, I was satisfied with my own share. Party members and friends throughout the Westfjords felt the same. Many of them contacted me and wanted to thank my work in the campaign for this success of the party. I appreciated those greetings, though I knew full well that the victory was not thanks to me alone.
Oratory Learned from a Book

During the election campaign I gave speeches and talks in many places on the policies of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). For that I was well prepared after years of training. Speaking technique and orderly presentation, however, were far from innate to me. I gave my first real speech after being elected inspector scholae at the Reykjavík Gymnasium (Menntaskólinn í Reykjavík). I pored for a long time over this first effort of mine, which was to be delivered in the school assembly hall (Salur). I still remember how nervous I was. I showed my father the speech and confided my anxiety to him. "It is good that you are uneasy," he said. "You should only start worrying if the pre-match jitters desert you. Then you have begun not to care." This has proven true for my father. My best speeches I have delivered with a knot in my stomach.

Soon after I came to the United States I noticed that most of my schoolmates had received more training in presenting their case than we Icelanders had. Most of them knew how to express themselves. I was ill at ease not being their equal and bought myself books on public speaking. One book that proved especially useful to me is called "The Eloquence of Public Speaking", which might be translated as "Áhrifarík ræðumennska". I still own it. It says there, among other things, that if the reader feels confident sitting over a cup of coffee and convincing a friend of some particular position, he can just as well speak before a full hall. At first the notion seems extreme, but it proves correct when put to the test. The trick lies in good preparation.
The main principles are, first, that a speaker must have knowledge

of what he is speaking about. Otherwise it is better to stay silent. I have therefore taken care to acquaint myself, at every opportunity, with the issues under discussion. Second, it is necessary to begin a speech by kindling a spark in the audience. The main section should turn the spark into a blaze, and in the closing words one should hammer the iron and stress what is to live on in the listener's mind. On all these main parts of a speech the book gives good advice. If a speech is to be given in a new place, it is good to arrive somewhat early, familiarize oneself with local conditions and talk with the locals. The best way to catch people's attention is to open by discussing something close to the inhabitants' hearts. "He's not so stupid. He knows something about this place," the listeners then think, and they listen to the rest.

I followed this excellent book to the letter and immediately set myself the goal of being able to speak without notes once I had sufficient training. When I came to a new place during the election campaign, I studied the conditions and often opened by speaking about what seemed to me to be lacking in that particular place. As a result, I managed to be something other and more than an executive from Reykjavík in these remote settlements of the Westfjords. I never delivered my speeches from papers. That is invariably far less engaging to listen to. At first, though, I composed every speech word for word. That done, I wrote key words in the margin, and from there I transferred the main points, in short bullet form, onto special cards that I took with me to the podium. As time went on I hardly needed to glance at the cards.

I do, however, possess numerous fully written-out speeches and cards that fill boxes, and all of it is in the same format. Key words in the margins and cards from every meeting. It is not uncommon for the speeches to bear the note: "Delivered from cards, considerably altered."

I often found, when I had sat down after speaking without notes, that I had forgotten something of what I had intended to say. No one knew this but me, so it never did any harm. Rather, people expressed astonishment that at the start of an hour-long speech I could say that I would come back to something later — and then not forget it. In these matters I do not believe in coincidence or innate genius. The key is training and good organization. Nothing comes without effort.

After I began delivering my speeches mostly without notes, I nevertheless frequently spoke them onto tape from memory once I got home, or took the tape recorder with me to the podium. I then had them typed up and added them to my collection of speeches. I have always considered it important to keep track of what I put out into the world.

I followed the book and did so systematically. It would not occur to me to claim that I was any master orator. Sometimes, though, I think I gave good speeches, and the best ones were certainly all delivered

without notes. There have always been brilliant orators in Iceland, and many have no doubt taken less trouble over things than I did, and with better results. Many politicians, on the other hand, struck me as wooden and stumbling at the podium.

Gradually the craft of speechmaking became so natural to me that I did not set a single letter down on paper. If I was asked to speak at a meeting, I prepared myself almost involuntarily in my mind, even if there was plenty of time in hand. I gradually gathered material and got ideas while swimming, doing carpentry, skiing or up in the mountains. I composed my speeches wherever I found peace to think. One of my favorite places was Heiðmörk, or the sauna at home with Wagner at the stereo's highest volume. In good quiet it is good to think. When the moment came, the speech was fully formed; it had a beginning, a body and an end, and the delivery came as if of its own accord.

I had a beloved retreat in Heiðmörk where I composed many of my best political speeches. I would often walk the same beautiful path and take a seat on a stone in a dense clearing. From this spot on the slope, at the top of the forestry plantation, there is a beautiful view. On one occasion, as so often, I was sitting on the stone in the middle of the day when the end-of-session parliamentary debates (eldhúsdagsumræður) were to be held that evening. It was dead calm and the stillness such that the smallest sounds carried hundreds of meters. Nonni, the family dog, had come along, and I was making good progress shaping the evening's speech in my mind.

I had not been there long when I saw a young man and a girl step out of a car. I paid them little attention until I noticed that they had settled into a nearby hollow. There was no mistaking what hour had struck, and Nonni had become very excited. I had to hold tight to his collar to keep him from dashing off or barking. After a while, and much rustling, a loud moan rang out, followed by human voices. I let the dog loose at once and he shot straight toward the sound. I myself stayed firmly seated. I do not know whether the lovers were startled. My speech was inspired, and in the side halls of parliament I could not refrain from telling of the day's adventures. In the television broadcast, members of parliament could therefore be seen far and wide with smiles on their lips. The story is probably more memorable, both to them and to me, than my speech that evening.
I cannot possibly remember what I said there.
My Father's Retirement

My father longed for peace from the bustle of politics long before he parted ways with political work. Probably few suspect how early he had begun to think about leaving that arena. In the autumn of 1950 he still had 12 years ahead of him in the chairman's seat of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and many years in the seat of minister of agriculture and, later, prime minister. He wrote me these words at the time:

The party congress – of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) – has lasted a week and ended yesterday. – I was once again elected chairman with every vote. Before too long now I am going to stop this. I must remain involved in this a while yet, as long as you children need support at your backs. But when that is done, I am going to live life a little for myself – books, travel, cultivation, fishing, freedom, and so on. I have earned it.

Seventeen years passed before he made this dream of his a reality, and fate arranged things so that he never got to enjoy the peace and the pleasures of life that the bustle of his working career had prevented him from devoting himself to fully. He developed an illness that robbed him of his freedom, made him dependent on others, and finally brought him to his death.

My father was incredibly strong on foot until late in life. He leapt over brooks and hopped across rivers on stones as if he had never done anything else, and nowhere was he more content than in such surroundings, in the embrace of nature. On one occasion when we were hiking on Skálafell, probably around 1962, I noticed that he was stubbing his toes on stones and often close to falling. This was very unlike him, but I thought no more of it.

Around the elections of 1963 my father had begun to feel a rhythmic tremor at rest. A year later he went to Denmark and was diagnosed there with Parkinson's disease. The tremor in his hands worsened with the years and had come to trouble him greatly. He therefore went to Britain and underwent what was called a brain puncture. It consisted of severing certain pathways in the brain. The tremor on one side then improved. Around the same time new drugs for the disease appeared, the so-called L-dopa drugs. They are based on mimicking neurotransmitters in the brain that Parkinson's patients are believed to lack. The drugs helped keep the symptoms at bay for some time.

My father took care to stay entirely out of the fray in my first elections. His reputation among the voters was enough for me as it was, and at times I even found it a bit much, as mentioned earlier. He spent his time instead with my mother and the grandchildren. After my father left parliament in 1967, my parents stayed for long periods at Klettur in Borgarfjörður, where they had built the family a stately summer house. Nature was also close at hand there. The river Reykjadalsá flows past the house, and my father's forestry planting had begun to provide shelter from the wind.

My father had always taken delight in fishing, and one day we tried our luck casting for salmon in the Grímsá. He had always been a very good fly fisherman and cast both beautifully and far. I can still see him there as

he tried to get the fly out into the water; his concentration was total and he gave it everything he had, but all to no avail. The disease had gotten the better of him and the fly went nowhere. I watched Pabbi struggle before I helped him get back into the car. Only a little over a decade earlier, he had refused to stop practicing wrestling holds on the floor at Klettur when the Clausen brothers showed him a new technique for breaking free of a headlock. He took turns holding one of the brothers in the grip and freeing himself from their iron holds. These were such struggles that neck joints cracked and faces turned blue from lack of oxygen. This turned out to be the last fishing trip my father and I took together. He was silent the whole way home to Klettur. I had trouble falling asleep that night.

Despite the best medical treatment available, my father nevertheless gradually took on the characteristic appearance of Parkinson's patients. He walked with small steps, slightly stooped, and his face, which had once been marked by playfulness and mirth, became as if turned to stone, lifeless, with a rigid expression. Only the eyes were spared. They still radiated the life force that dwelt within my father even though his body refused to obey.
Chapter Two

During my years as a substitute member of parliament, 1967–1971, I seldom took a seat in the Althingi. Sigurvin and Bjarni rarely missed a session. I did not get my chance until December 1968. The Althingi of the Icelanders disappointed me. It was very far from being a modern workplace. Most members of parliament seemed to be yes-men of the party leadership, and it made no difference which party was involved. The working conditions of members of parliament in fact gave no indication that they were expected to work independently. The working facilities were practically nonexistent. I did not hold back my opinions on these matters in a newspaper interview conducted with me after I had sat in parliament for two weeks as a substitute:

The situation of members of parliament seems to me utterly deplorable. I have never encountered even the shabbiest office of a business enterprise with working facilities as poor as these. The office of the Althingi and the typing facilities are far too small. The right thing would be to reduce the number of members of parliament by at least a third, but to improve the working facilities correspondingly. Nor am I impressed by the party rule that prevails there. Everyone knows that members of the same party do not agree on every issue. I would consider it preferable for the members to act more as individuals and follow their own convictions.

At the parliament office one could obtain promissory-note forms from most of the banks and savings banks in the country. The work of members of parliament was to a large extent devoted to doing favors and providing guidance on the administrative system and the banks. Members of the Althingi were pastors and errand boys at once. It was the custom that they co-signed loans.
During my years as a substitute member I in effect served the constituency as an "errandboy

down south,“ as I had feared before I decided to run. When it came to it, I actually did not mind the role. I assisted the people of the Westfjords and smoothed their way in the capital as best I could. I did, however, follow my father's advice never to co-sign promissory notes for voters. A great many people asked me for such a favor, but I answered them all along the lines that if I signed a note for one person, I could hardly refuse others. People generally took that answer with understanding. I later learned, though, that there were men in parliament who turned few away. Some of them fared badly from such friendly favors. Both, fortunately, have largely disappeared: the promissory-note forms in the Althingi and requests for members' signatures.

My maiden speech in parliament was on fisheries affairs, and it appeared in full in Tíminn under the headline: "The government declares war on seamen." It is entirely conventional in form. A journalist at Tíminn noted on another occasion that winter, however, that I was considered to have figured "unusually prominently" in two matters that came before parliament in those weeks. On the one hand, I had introduced an amendment to the budget to the effect that funds should be allocated to mineral prospecting. It was passed without a vote against, which is unusual since I was in the opposition. On the other hand, it attracted attention that I did not support a proposal by another member of the opposition, Lúðvík Jósepsson. He wanted to reduce the appropriation for state automobiles from four million krónur to two.

I was the only member of the opposition who abstained when the proposal was put to a vote. The reasons for my position, I said, were that it seemed to me unwise to skimp on funds intended for the renewal of state-owned automobiles, and I added: "running an old automobile can be very costly." I actually had experience of that at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). I had tried to have the car that I had at my disposal there replaced because the maintenance costs were getting out of hand. No funds had been made available for it. The repair bills for this car were later to become notoriously famous in the so-called "green peas affair" (grænubaunamálið). It broke out a few days before I took a permanent seat in the Althingi for the first time in 1971.
The Restoration Government Runs Aground

Prosperity had followed in the wake of the economic measures of the Restoration government (viðreisnarstjórnin) in 1960 and lasted almost without pause for six years. Favorable external conditions weighed more heavily there than the measures themselves, and the greatly increased herring catch probably weighed heaviest. But the herring disappeared, and what remained were useless herring-processing stations and indebted ships. National income contracted by nearly one tenth. Unemployment inevitably followed in its wake, and the government's economic policy ran aground. Direct subsidies were introduced
for the export industries, and price subsidies were revived, in addition to which a price-freeze law was enacted. Finally the currency was devalued and the cost of living kept rising.

The Restoration government established a new state employment affairs committee (atvinnumálanefnd ríkisins) with wide-ranging activities in the effort to build up employment. There was as a rule one committee in each constituency, but the development effort was centrally directed by a nine-man committee chaired by Prime Minister Bjarni Benediktsson. The government's other representatives were the ministers Gylfi Þ. Gíslason and Jóhann Hafstein. Enormous sums were allocated by this committee, and the allocation of state funds has probably seldom been subject to such direct political control, since the government's principal ministers sat there. Nor was there any shortage of loans and grants for their political allies. I found the allocation of the assistance far too haphazard, and the work was carried out in a disorganized way.

Despite these obvious flaws, I supported these wide-ranging measures, no less than the abolition of the restrictions in 1960. I am not of the opinion that the state must never come anywhere near the economy. Indeed, the leaders of the Restoration government proved not to be of that opinion either, when it came to the test. All their earlier declarations about the free market and the necessity of state non-interference in the economy were forgotten, fortunately. Otherwise the industries would have run aground. Some free-market believers criticize state intervention of any kind. They consider it natural to endure a depression if external conditions are unfavorable, and that the authorities should look on idly at mass bankruptcies if it comes to that. It is in fact astonishing that such free-market believers often seem to regard the Restoration government as their darling.

The fact is that few governments have undertaken such extensive rescue operations; central direction has seldom been greater, and patronage considerations never carried more weight, since nearly all rules for allocation were lacking.

The employment situation landed on my desk at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) in connection with these measures, since one of its roles was to advise on new ways of creating employment. The state employment affairs committee had made Jónas Haralz one of its chief advisers, and Sveinn Guðmundsson also had a seat there — both good and loyal Independence Party men, though Jónas had actually been more than a little radical in his younger years. They both likewise had seats on the executive committee of the Research Council. In the first half of 1969, extensive meetings were convened with the directors of research institutes and various scientists engaged in applied research. This was done with the aim of putting more pillars under the economy than herring and fish.
The Research Council was assigned to carry out a study of promising industries that might be established, not least in the countryside, since unemployment was then rising sharply. There was a

thorough review of the visible possibilities for creating employment in fisheries, agriculture, construction, industry, and more. These turned out to be very informative meetings, even though they were not decisive to any significant degree for the building up of the economy.

I advocated planning-mindedness (skipulagshyggja) in investments at every opportunity toward the end of the Restoration years. I drew on technological progress and science and the Americans' first voyage to the moon, which aroused an intoxicated enthusiasm all over the world. In my mind it was "a testimony to the importance of planning, of systematic operation, in the free society of a democratic state." I believed the public sector had a substantial role to play in coordination and policy-making. That could go well together with the freedom of action of individuals, enterprises, and their associations, "which most of us Icelanders are determined shall prevail here," as I put it.

Planning-mindedness, as it was called, took a middle path between a planned economy and the free market. It was an attempt to improve the foundations of business operations by looking ahead and making long-term plans. It was closely tied to the idea that science, technology, and careful working methods held the solution to most problems. In that sense it was the answer to the uncontrolled and often erratic "free market," as it is called.

Planning-mindedness has long since vanished from the battles of politics and become a natural part of working methods both in public administration and in the running of private companies. Early on, however, the reaction of men of the right was often to look askance at all planning and policy-making in investments. The actions of the Restoration government in its last electoral term bore clear marks of this. I considered them characterized by aimlessness in investments. Its leaders refused to face the fact that the free-market path had failed and bore a large share of the blame for the very problems that had to be solved:

In practice, the shipwreck of the policy has in fact been acknowledged. We have established a great many funds. I doubt that anyone knows the names of them all. They all dispose of their capital according to the doctrines of egalitarianism, to assist those who are worst off. Thereby, of course, the central doctrine of free-market liberalism is flagrantly violated. But there has been no coordination of all this activity on the part of the public authorities. There seems to be no definite goal being pursued, unless it be solely to maintain free enterprise, whatever it costs and even if only in name.
The Restoration government's response to the economic difficulties convinced me

once and for all that when the shoe pinches, it can be sensible to spend considerable public funds to avert a bloodbath. Hardly anyone raised objections to this view at the end of the Restoration years. It was as if the air had suddenly been let out of those supporters of the government who had objected to all state intervention. This atmosphere laid the groundwork for its fall in 1971.
The Presidential Candidacy of Kristján Eldjárn

President Ásgeir Ásgeirsson declared in his New Year's address at the beginning of 1968 that he intended to step down from the presidency. It came as a surprise to few. Speculation about his successor was already in full flight. When Ásgeir announced his retirement, the candidacy of his son-in-law Gunnar Thoroddsen had long been in the air. Gunnar had long stood in the front rank of Independence Party men. He had sat in parliament, been mayor of Reykjavík, and a minister in the Restoration government. Gunnar had, however, withdrawn from politics for the time being and was sitting in peaceful repose as ambassador in Copenhagen. It seemed clear that it would be difficult to prevent his election. Without much noise, there was considerable discussion in the executive board of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) about whom the party should support.

Truth to tell, there was, to put it mildly, little support for Gunnar Thoroddsen at that meeting. The Progressives did not, however, want to commit the party openly in this matter, even though the constituency association of the East had passed a resolution calling on the party to put forward its own representative. It was considered more proper to look for a candidate who stood outside the parties but was at the same time from the social-minded wing of politics.

Within the Progressive Party, however, all discussions bore the mark that most wanted to avoid involving the political parties directly in the contest. The party had supported the Reverend Bjarni Jónsson against Ásgeir Ásgeirsson sixteen years earlier, with well-known results.

Jóhannes Elíasson, a director of the Fisheries Bank (Útvegsbankinn), was the first to mention Kristján Eldjárn, the national antiquarian, in connection with the presidential elections, as far as I know. That was as early as 1967. In the biography of Kristján Eldjárn his memoranda are cited, and what is written there seems to confirm that Jóhannes played perhaps the largest part in Kristján's agreeing to stand.

I was immediately in favor of that idea. I had not been personally acquainted with Kristján. In my eyes, however, he had many of the qualities that a president needed to possess. He was an undisputed man of learning and socially minded. He spoke exceptionally fine Icelandic and had a polished manner

that was friendly and warm at once. It did no harm that various people considered him in reality a Progressive, because he had taken a seat low on the party's list in Reykjavík in 1949. Last but not least, he was a promising candidate "against Gunnar Thoroddsen," as it was often put in the party's meeting minutes when the party's search for a presidential candidate was under discussion. The outcome was that Jóhannes Elíasson was sent forth to speak with Kristján in the autumn of 1967. They were close friends.

Jóhannes received a flat refusal from Kristján at first. We did not give up, however, and sounded out support more widely. It was easy to sense that Kristján's candidacy would find great resonance among the other social-minded parties. Stefán Jóhann Stefánsson, former prime minister and chairman of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), was among the staunch supporters, and it has even been claimed that he pressed Kristján hard in the autumn days of 1967. That may be true. What is documented is that around the same time the chairman of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was in talks with Stefán to bring the parties into harmony in the presidential elections. In those autumn days it actually came as more of a surprise to us that influential Independence Party men felt the same way about Kristján's candidacy.
Not least important was the support of Pétur Benediktsson, member of parliament, bank director, and brother of Prime Minister Bjarni.

At the end of February 1968, the Progressives were nevertheless pessimistic that Kristján could be persuaded to run. The party's central committee had resolved to entrust the executive board and the parliamentary group with finding a candidate "with the broadest possible agreement with other parties or groups of interested citizens." This was in accordance with the wishes of the Social Democratic Party and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), which had emphasized in talks with the Progressive Party leadership that the parties' ties to the prospective candidate should not be formal.

At a meeting of the executive board it is recorded from me in the minutes that a group of interested citizens needed to be formed as soon as possible, "though it would be natural for the party leadership to hold the reins." Baldur Óskarsson, representative of the young Progressives, declared support for this view of mine, and the same was true of others. Presidential elections are not discussed further in the party's minute books until after the elections were over.

To repeat the appeals to Kristján, a fairly large group went to meet him, and I was among them. After more meetings and long discussions he finally agreed to stand. By then it was into March and only three months until the elections. This period of deliberation bore clear witness to Kristján's calm and thoughtfulness. He had the temperate bearing of the scholar and never spoke emphatically about his own merits — quite the contrary. Some from the hardest core of supportsupporters
had even begun to doubt whether his will was determined enough to wage a hard election campaign. In me, Kristján inspired trust. He was a man of integrity.

Once Kristján had made up his mind, we had to get briskly to work, for the election was not far off. Everything indicated that it would be hard-fought. We felt certain that the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) would spare nothing for Gunnar's candidacy and that considerable funds would be put behind his wagon. Still, that was small change compared with what is now spent on a presidential campaign.

I was one of the seventeen who put their names to an address to the Icelanders on the front page of the first newspaper of Kristján's supporters. It bore the name 30. júní (June 30). In that group were, among others, the Progressives (framsóknarmenn) Karl Kristjánsson, Halldór E. Sigurðsson, and Jóhannes Elíasson, who has been mentioned before. There were also Guðmundur Hjartarson and Jónas Árnason from the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalag), and the Social Democratic Party leader (Alþýðuflokksforinginn) Stefán Jóhann Stefánsson. The address was also signed by Ragnar Jónsson of Smári, who was a kind of campaign manager for the effort. He became one of my most memorable colleagues in the election battle — entertaining, spirited, and colorful in manner. In all, five issues of "30.

júní" appeared, and among other things I conducted an interview with my father, which was published in one of them. There he stressed, as many others did, that the president needed to be able to unite the nation.

Individuals of good repute were recruited to write in these papers. An effort was made to keep the group broad. Among them were Pétur Benediktsson, Eysteinn Jónsson, Vilmundur Gylfason, Sigurður A. Magnússon, Guðmundur "jaki" Guðmundsson, and Adda Bára Sigfúsdóttir, to name just a few. The solidarity around Kristján in this heterogeneous group was incredible, and it is not unlikely that it in some measure gave rise to the loud voices that called for a united front of the left and of social-minded people in the wake of the election.
"One Interview Is More than Enough"

I was chosen for the campaign's executive committee, the so-called committee of 12. It supervised all operations and organization. Among other things, I drafted an organizational chart for the work, in addition to setting up trusted local contacts in every district in the Westfjords. The same methods were used in the other constituencies. Out west I took care to approach men from all parties, and I placed particular emphasis on Independence Party and Social Democratic Party men. The trusted contacts in the Westfjords came to number 53 in 24 districts and villages. They gathered declarations of support for the candidacy

and spoke for it among their neighbors. I kept in close contact with them all throughout the campaign, and this grew into an extensive operation. In my papers I still have a card index with the names of these trusted contacts; conversations with them are dated, and it is conscientiously recorded how many declarations of support each one had gathered. Kristján's supporters in the Westfjords also opened a campaign office in Ísafjörður.

The tailwind Kristján enjoyed in that election is unforgettable. At first we were not especially optimistic about the outcome, but it was as if some chord had been struck that found resonance in people's hearts all over the country. After that there was no turning back. It was as if a storm broke loose, and the enthusiasm kept building right up to election day. Wherever Kristján went, community halls and meeting places filled up. Frequently fewer got in than wanted to. I do not remember any enthusiasm like it.

I traveled with Kristján to the Westfjords and introduced him to various supporters whom we had managed to recruit out west. In Ísafjörður a campaign meeting was held in the Alþýðuhús. Kristján spoke there to a packed house. His meeting in Akureyri became even more famous. It is estimated that well over two thousand people attended it. It will probably be a long wait before that record is broken north of the mountains.

In Reykjavík, Kristján and I met regularly during the campaign to lay plans, sometimes in a larger group and sometimes one on one. The candidate's reticence was extraordinary. As an example, the magazine Vikan wanted to present him with an interview and photographs. Kristján, however, politely declined, saying that a detailed interview with him would appear in his own campaign paper — and that would be more than enough! It therefore often fell to me to spur him on to action. Among the things we debated was whether a large supporters' rally should be held in Laugardalshöll. I strongly urged it. Kristján, on the other hand, was doubtful. There was room for three thousand people in the arena, and he felt certain that that many would not be interested in hearing him. When it came to it, the place was packed beyond the doors.

Kristján won the election by an unexpected and unheard-of margin. He received nearly twice as many votes as his opponent, 67,544 votes against 35,428. Many interpreted these results as a defeat for the party system and the traditional political parties. Others spoke of a swing to the left. Both views doubtless had something to them. In a newspaper article I wrote in the wake of the election, I said I believed that in the presidential election a broad front of liberal-minded people had formed in the country, with young people at the forefront. To me it was a sign that young men and women wanted to have a far greater influence on the development of national affairs. At the same time I stressed that "voters did not let parties or politicians dictate to them" and

that they were choosing people, not parties. I was not, however, prepared to accept that the voters had been rejecting political parties as such; rather, I thought the results showed that single-member constituencies needed to be adopted for elections to the Althing (Alþingi). I had come to that view in the United States and had often corresponded with my father on the subject. On the occasion of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkur) and the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkur) having formed an electoral alliance in 1956, I put it this way in a letter to my father:

It is quite certain that the situation at home will not be remedied until one party gains a majority, as you point out. On the other hand, I am sorry that the Progressives have not taken up the fight for the one system of government that can bring such a thing about — an arrangement of single-member constituencies. I do not care at all even if the conservatives get a majority in the first election. It would inevitably lead to a union of all the left-wing parties and the center parties, with the result that a majority would be obtained. It seems to me that you ought to put emphasis on establishing single-member constituencies. There one might very much follow the example of the British.

My acquaintance with Kristján Eldjárn during the campaign became a good one, and we met frequently after he took office. He said he felt he lacked the contact with the general public that I had as a politician. I know that he sought opinions more widely, and Sigurður Líndal was among those he consulted, and doubtless many more.

Kristján Eldjárn died before his time on September 14, 1982, two years after he left office. He was buried on September 23. The day before, we Progressives had a parliamentary group meeting. When we had sat down, Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson approached me and said that a memorial article from me was being awaited at the editorial office of Tíminn. I was startled — to tell the truth, it had somehow slipped past me to write in Kristján's memory. I immediately began writing a short memorial article and finished it at the start of the meeting. It was sent by courier to be printed in the paper. In it I said, among other things, that Kristján had not considered himself above politics. On the contrary, he regarded it as his duty to follow those matters as closely as possible. The memorial article also says:

Kristján Eldjárn never grew conceited over his great election victory. On the contrary, he devoted himself to uniting the nation. He succeeded in doing so in an incredibly short time. Kristján Eldjárn combined an unassuming and down-to-earth manner with the dignity of the presidential office.
All the presidents of the republic have been good in their own way, but with full respect for them all, it seems to me that Kristján was the foremost among them.
Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson

Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson and I discussed national affairs and got to know each other well at our regular waffle meetings in the winter of 1965–66. In the autumn of 1967 he went to England for further study in political science. By then he had already become one of the leading figures of the radical wing of the young Progressives. He was elected to the board of SUF (the Young Progressives' Association) in 1966, and he had also managed to exert a shaping influence on the party work of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). His supporters held key positions among the young Progressives, and within the party Eysteinn Jónsson took him under his wing.

It is safe to say that political ferment was felt in society in those years. The Restoration government (Viðreisnarstjórnin) and foreign currents of youth revolution stirred up a swing to the left and fanned radicalism in Iceland, especially among young people. This development was not displeasing to Eysteinn Jónsson. He supported Ólafur Ragnar in many things, and also the wing of the young Progressives that was the most radical in various respects. He believed the Progressive Party ought to lead a new and powerful social-minded force in which the left-wing parties would unite — either all of them, or all except the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið).

The young men around Ólafur Ragnar took up a hard fight for this, along with increased democracy, decentralization of power, and social solidarity; they opposed the foreign military presence and heavy-industry schemes and large-scale enterprise in all its forms. They also argued with no less fervor for increased influence for young men within the party — that is, for themselves.

Ólafur Ragnar kept in good contact with various party members while he was in England. I have in my papers a copy of a letter I wrote to him in December 1967, the autumn he went abroad, and it testifies that we then considered ourselves allies in most of our views. The salutation was "Dear friend." The greatest space is devoted to describing the political situation in the country and disappointment with the work of the Progressive Party in opposition. I found the arguments of the leaders "often rather haphazard and not sufficiently responsible," and I was completely opposed to the Progressive Party entering into a national-unity government, as had been discussed at the initiative of the leaders of the Restoration government during the economic hardships:
I must admit that I am not pleased with the workings of the Progressive Party today. It seems to me there is now considerable stagnation, es-

pecially in the party's leadership. The party's policy is good, we may say. It is built on the same fundamental principles, timeless ones. We want an Icelandic party; a party that is not built on dogmas and isms, but that judges every policy with regard to what suits us, our distinctive economic life.

This passage describes very well my fundamental position at that time — and in many respects still today. It seemed to me that the leaders' positions were far too often based on habitual thinking and on "examining only the headlines of the issues," as I put it. I raised the coming shake-up in the party's leadership and said it was clear that Ólafur Jóhannesson would take over from Eysteinn before long. Various changes I considered right to make. Eysteinn and Ólafur would, however, doubtless be opposed to major reshuffles, and it would prove difficult "to rise against them":

It is another matter that some feel a more radical change of course is necessary in the party than the changes now under discussion promise. For my part, I can accept that, but I nevertheless oppose ill-considered actions in this area.

At the central committee meeting at the end of January 1968, the party chairmanship changed hands, as had been expected. Ólafur Jóhannesson took over from Eysteinn. Stability was in his blood. A less revolutionary man would be hard to find. That soon became apparent. By the same token, things heated up within the party.

Ólafur Ragnar long enjoyed being under Eysteinn's protective wing. At the central committee meeting he was elected to the editorial board of Tíminn, where he held a seat for years. In addition, a special organizational council of the party was established, on which Ólafur Ragnar was given a seat. Both were at Eysteinn's instigation. The organizational council was a great passion of Ólafur Ragnar's. It was to work at "strengthening the party's activities and at innovations," as well as running policy groups to prepare the formulation of positions.

Party operations fell within the purview of the party secretary, and some considered the establishment of the council a slight to Helgi Bergs, who held that post. He nevertheless led the organizational council. The meetings, however, dissolved into endless bickering between Helgi and Ólafur Ragnar. From Helgi one gathered that he was unsettled by the energy and assertiveness of Ólafur Ragnar, who was enormously productive and pushy. Ólafur wrote a large report on changes to the party and made numerous proposals for a shake-up. Party congresses were to become more frequent, primaries were to determine the ordering of candidate lists, and the share of the youth wing was to increase. The leadership was not pleased with all of them.

Ólafur Ragnar found it incredibly easy to get into quarrels with people both inside the party and out, and some felt he was systematically undermining the party leadership for his own advantage. We, however, never clashed, and I am not aware that he ever tried to undermine me. The same can be said of our dealings later in the Althing (Alþingi), and our cooperation in government was also good when it came to that. I did, though, sometimes find him unscrupulous and rather too sharp-tongued toward others.
Frenzy Politics

Shortly before the central committee meeting in January 1968, Ólafur Ragnar published a series of articles in Tíminn. It included two spirited pieces entitled "Óðapólitík" (Frenzy Politics) and "The New Generation." There he spoke harshly of the governing policies of all parties since the Second World War and called the politicians of that era "the war-years generation," which was afflicted with many faults, and he exempted no one in these writings. Not even Eysteinn, his mentor:

It is well worth putting forward the idea that the reason Icelanders have always been entangled in the vicious circle of the same problem, runaway inflation, may lie in the working methods and style of the politicians, in the system of government itself.

Ólafur said that nowhere did political parties have a greater hold on society than in this country, and that nothing was judged on its merits — neither men nor issues, creditworthiness nor profitability. Everything was measured by the yardstick of parties and party loyalty. Individual leaders also received their share of savage abuse, Prime Minister Bjarni Benediktsson most of all:

It is the clearest example of the underdevelopment of Icelandic politics and the dominance of frenzy politics in Iceland that on the throne of the government should sit a power-hungry Tom Thumb, who all his life has fought mercilessly for party interests and party-based judgment in all fields, and who wants, if possible, to beat literally everyone into obedience to his political will, whether they be members of parliament or poets, company directors or foreign travelers, scholars or office-hungry young politicians.
In fairness to Ólafur's choice of words, it must be noted that his radio programs Þjóðlíf had been banned the year before at the instigation of Independence Party men, particularly

the prime minister's. In the aftermath followed extensive writings by Bjarni in Morgunblaðið and articles in Tíminn in which the censorship was said to illustrate well the minister's arrogance of power. As a counterweight to these horrors of "frenzy politics," Ólafur Ragnar put forward "the knowledge generation":

From the young people, therefore, will come the effort that suffices to change the course of national affairs and bring it into a sensible modern form, in place of the anarchy and helplessness that have prevailed for a while.

In the wake of these articles began my first and probably only polemic with Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson. Looking back, one might perhaps say that the die had been cast. Our disagreement, however, was always more about how fast the shake-up should proceed than any dispute over where we should be heading. I called my article "Young Angry Men." I have often thought, both before and since, that Ólafur Ragnar's timely criticism and useful observations missed their mark because of careless argumentation. So it was on this occasion too:

The extremes are so great that the useful observations get lost. The abuse of the leaders of the Icelandic nation over the past decades is so enormous, and so affects the mind of the reader, that he sees no overall policy, only extremes.

With my article I began the endeavor of positioning myself between the party leadership and Ólafur Ragnar's followers in order to try to mediate and sheathe the weapons. I tried to soften the tone of the young members' rhetoric and to present their views in a more moderate way. I probably reaped little popularity with them as time went on, but that in itself was never my goal. They regularly counted me among Ólafur Jóhannesson's men and among the right wing of the party. With my article I also wanted to make clear that my views were not compatible with Ólafur Ragnar's writings. At the central committee meeting in question I nevertheless defined the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) as a liberal left-wing party. Despite everything, I did not want to be counted among the men of the right:
Of course the Progressive Party is a left-wing party, and it is completely wrong to suggest otherwise. It is a left-wing party in

the good old sense of that word — as a liberal party and even a radical party. An old man may have been a man of the left, but stagnated, and then he is no longer a man of the left. The Progressive Party must not stagnate. It must always be a liberal left-wing party.

I was in favor of a mixed economy in which the state guaranteed equal access to education and health care and was prepared to take on larger tasks that individuals or cooperatives could not manage. I emphasized liberalism and social solidarity rather than a radical left-wing course. Ólafur Ragnar, on the other hand, grew more radical as his years of study multiplied, and various others wanted to be angry and hot-headed. They believed they were playing a noble role and compared themselves to the student rioters in Paris and Prague. They were therefore surely about as pleased with the conclusion of my article as they disagreed with my proposals for more responsible argumentation:

In some places abroad a movement has formed that has been called "Angry Young Men." These men have criticized everything and everyone. They have tried to pit generation against generation. But they have been extremists and have accomplished little. I want to hope that Ólafur Ragnar does not prove to be merely yet another of that kind.

Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson quickly acquired a fairly large group of followers among the young Progressives. Many of them were among the most capable representatives of the young generation. From the beginning these young men put tremendous effort into forming a united front on the left under the leadership of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), and their positions were also radical in most respects. As said before, Eysteinn supported these plans early on, as did various radicals in the ranks of the older men.

Among those who stood shoulder to shoulder with Ólafur Ragnar among the young Progressives may be named Baldur Óskarsson; Már Pétursson, later a district court judge; and Elías Snæland Jónsson, current editor of Dagur — all of whom became chairmen of SUF in those years — as well as Eyjólfur Eysteinsson, son of Eysteinn Jónsson. Friðgeir Björnsson, later chief judge in Reykjavík, was a close collaborator of Már's and was also counted in the group, as were Jónatan Þórmundsson, professor of law, and Sólveig Ólafsdóttir, lawyer, Jónatan's wife. The last three largely withdrew from involvement in politics shortly after things boiled over, as will be related later.
From Eysteinn to Ólafur Jóhannesson

A sea change took place in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) when Ólafur Jóhannesson became its chairman in 1968. In economic matters the party moved to the right, support for Western cooperation gained greater weight, and the ties to the Federation of Icelandic Cooperative Societies (Samband íslenskra samvinnufélaga) were loosened. The effects of the change were felt not least in the party's internal work, where fierce clashes arose between Ólafur and the left wing of the party.

Ólafur Jóhannesson was the self-evident choice for the leadership role in the party when Eysteinn stepped aside. Ólafur was a professor of constitutional law at the University. The scholar's meticulousness and his sureness in examining every matter were without question his greatest strengths, along with unshakable honesty and integrity. He was, however, unlike Eysteinn in many ways, as became most apparent after he became prime minister.

On the question of the desirable relationship between the Progressive Party and the Federation, the difference in emphasis between Ólafur and Eysteinn was as conspicuous as it had been between Eysteinn and my father before. Eysteinn was for a long time chairman of the board of the Federation, and a more devoted cooperative man was hard to find. During his years as party chairman, my father felt that Vilhjálmur Þór, the Federation's director, sometimes expected too much of the Progressive Party. Eysteinn never thought so. Ólafur Jóhannesson had himself been a lawyer for the Federation, but nonetheless the party moved further away from the Federation during his chairmanship. Ólafur did not want SÍS to run the party and had little interest in running SÍS. In a small circle he even remarked that he had grown tired of the whining in the Federation.

Various people thought they could detect that Eysteinn was not entirely at peace with withdrawing, especially as time passed. In the 1950s Eysteinn was in step with Vilhjálmur Þór and the Federation on many issues and was considered to reflect the views of the right wing of the Progressive Party, while my father reflected those of its left. Clashes between them occurred time and again at closed party meetings, and tempers verged on rage when things were at their worst. In my hearing, though, my father never spoke an ill word of Eysteinn.

In the years of the Reconstruction government (Viðreisn) one may say that Eysteinn changed horses. He strove first and last to bring down the government and in many respects took up the rhetoric and banner of Jónas from Hrifla and my father. He criticized the government from the left and won a large group of new voters over to the party. Not least among them were young and radical people of the new era. Many capable individuals who carried the ideals of the left at heart joined the Progressives in those years. The reasons for this were simple.

The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) had led the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) captive in the Reconstruction coalition, and in the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) radical socialists had taken the upper hand, with the social order of the Soviet Union as their guiding light. Eysteinn preached to these young people that the Progressive Party should play the same role in Icelandic politics as the large social democratic parties do in the Nordic countries. The cornerstone of that vision was to be laid with the fall of the Reconstruction government in the elections of 1967. Eysteinn threw all his energy into those elections and had high hopes of victory. He took it very hard when this undertaking of his failed, and therefore considered it time to make way for a new man.

I had great respect for Eysteinn. He had held the office of party secretary for about two decades, under my father's chairmanship, and shaped the tradition that the party's organizational work fell within the secretary's domain. In that arena he was always at it, incredibly industrious. Eysteinn attended every meeting he had the chance to and nothing was beneath his notice. To get everything done, Eysteinn was invariably up before the crack of dawn. After I entered politics, he was apt to call between seven and eight if he had a new idea. He was wide awake to everything, never waited to be told, and got things done. At the party office he would go from person to person and talk with them. He wanted to follow closely what was being discussed and chatted about. That he had learned in order to keep pace with Jónas from Hrifla.

Eysteinn remained vigorous for a long time and attended party meetings long after he had retired from formal politics. After I had become chairman, he would sometimes pull me aside at such gatherings to lay out plans. We simply had to do this or that.

When Eysteinn stepped down as party chairman in 1968, however, he still had six years to serve in parliament before he retired. He could be extremely firm in his opinions and was not easily swayed. At meetings he spoke almost every time. He was an excellent speaker, logical and decisive, yet he also allowed himself to muse aloud over the matter at hand each time. In the early part of his chairmanship, Ólafur Jóhannesson felt it keenly whenever something displeased Eysteinn, not least within the parliamentary group. It was for the most part made up of men Eysteinn had worked with for decades. In that arena it was therefore hard to tell whether Eysteinn's words or Ólafur's carried more weight. After Ólafur became prime minister in 1971 this gradually changed, and Ólafur's word became law in the party.

I was in step with the leadership on most things after Ólafur was elected chairman in 1968. We were of a similar mind about argumentation in opposition, as we had both doubted Eysteinn's policy of finding fault with nearly everything that came from the government. In the parliamentary group Ólafur once broke a general silence when some of the members of parliament were
putting together a long and expensive wish list of projects they intended to lay before parliament: "How about it, gentlemen? Do you never intend to sit in government again?"
"A Petrified Party"

I felt the party had in many respects failed to use the years in opposition as well as was necessary. I traced this among other things to the one-sided negativity that seemed to me to strip the party of credibility. I did not feel as much changed in that regard with Ólafur's chairmanship as I had hoped. It also seemed to me that Ólafur sometimes had difficulty taking decisive action and setting out the party's policy in easily understood language so that people were carried along. The party seemed of two minds, and in consequence there arose the refrain that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was both for and against every issue. It was said to be "open at both ends." At a central committee meeting more than a year before the 1971 elections I described my concerns:

I have traveled widely, and everywhere I find an incredible listlessness even among the most committed party members. There is no enthusiasm. The party and its leadership are said to be stagnant and negative on all important issues. A petrified party, which feels no touch whatsoever of a new era, one young man declared to me a few days ago — a man who has nonetheless supported the party until now. You are bewildered and timid, say others. Morgunblaðið propaganda, someone will no doubt say. That is true, but such propaganda still needs soil in which to take root.

I proposed that the party's spokesmen talk first and foremost about the future and not speak of times past with nostalgia. Resolutions should be passed "with boldness and foresight about the future society we want." In these words of mine lay criticism of the party's leadership and its chairman. Moreover, I felt the chairman lacked decisiveness and authority, and I found he came across rather awkwardly on television. I therefore made the role of the party chairman a special topic of discussion at a central committee meeting before the elections:

On no one, however, rests a heavier burden than on our chairman. Everyone looks to him for leadership and guidance. It cannot be denied that this work has been difficult of late. The party has in various respects been hesitant. [. . .] Ólafur is not, either, the showman who achieves the great-
est momentary effects, for example on television. We who know Ólafur, on the other hand, are in no doubt about his great personal qualities.

I actually gave considerable thought to politicians' television appearances in those years. Few had the knack of speaking into a camera and getting their message across memorably and clearly. I maintained within the party that party members did not fully understand the importance of television. It was the medium of the future. The Progressives were by no means alone with this problem, however. It became famous that Bjarni Benediktsson was repeatedly seen grimacing terribly in the first broadcast of Icelandic television in 1966. He thought the camera was not pointed at him. To remedy this I proposed that the leaders of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) learn to "use the modern technology of mass media to the utmost":

With television a speaker enters, for a brief moment, the home of the viewer. Television is a medium of quick effects, which are achieved first and foremost with short answers or assertions that express, unmistakably, a definite opinion — one that is, however, seldom substantiated with words, but first and foremost with bearing, a relaxed but convincing manner. The question is really only whether it awakens trust in the man or suspicion.

It probably never occurred to any of the party's leaders in those years to take a course in public speaking and presentation, as I understand has long since become the rule. Few Icelanders could likely have taught them much in those years. I myself turned to my books from the United States, where I had sought advice on conduct in public settings. They became my bible in these matters, as in speechmaking before. I have always followed the basic rule found there: Anyone who wants to come across well on television must begin by forgetting that he is on television.
Youth Revolt and Internal Party Strife

Ólafur Jóhannesson, however, had other things to think about than his television appearances in the coming terms. Within the party, before anyone knew it, clashes broke out between him and the radical young members who had flocked to the party during Eysteinn's years as chairman. In those disputes some found him rather too inflexible and lacking in both political finesse and adroitness. Instead of Eysteinn's indulgence and encouragement, the young members met with the sternness and displeasure of Ólafur Jóhannesson.
He was never a man of compromises. The two namesakes, he and Ólafur Ragnar, did not get along, and their quarrels at party meetings were many in the years that followed.

The young people made loud demands for influence, and perhaps that was no wonder. Everywhere in society it was echoed that the most educated generation in Iceland's history was rising up, even though those who were older did not always find the course the young people took promising. An abyss seemed to separate the generations and their values. I felt I stood midway between them, tried to understand the disagreement, and wanted to bridge the gap. Perhaps it was not possible.

In the Union of Young Progressives (Samband ungra framsóknarmanna) the radicals were the most prominent. The right wing still existed, however, and sided with the party's new chairman. Yet the two factions had one thing in common. They both had at their disposal a large group of talented people who were already becoming conspicuous in public debate. These young Progressives certainly let their hair grow down over their ears, but they were nonetheless sharp dressers. What chiefly connected Ólafur Ragnar and Baldur Óskarsson to slogans about a flower revolution were the carnations they wore in the lapels of their suits with the bell-bottomed trousers. They were probably more dandies than hippies.

Some of these promising men in fact became known nationwide for their performance in the media in those years. They took up a critical discussion of the stagnant society of the Reconstruction years; corruption in the system of government, the political parties' overbearing control of the country's banking and funds system — they attacked the censorship of the media and every kind of extravagance. Tómas Karlsson wrote sharp moral-reform columns in Tíminn that attracted well-deserved attention, and even more prominent was Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, who ran his own television program. There he went hard at those "representatives of the system" who were his guests each time. The programs were enormously talked about, and opinions differed on their merits.
The First Primary

Throughout the 1967–71 parliamentary term I made a point of meeting voters on their home ground. I revived the old custom of holding annual district meetings (leiðarþing) in the spring and often traveled through individual parts of the constituency in the autumn and over the winter months as opportunity allowed. I also made an effort to attend þorrablót feasts and regional festivals. In this way I cultivated ties with a great number of Progressives and worked with the Progressive societies in the constituency. Among other things I advertised public-speaking courses, which were well attended. Once I got Atli Freyr Guðmundsson from Akranes to assist me. In the evening we journeyed

to a þorrablót feast in Ísafjörður and enjoyed ourselves until nearly morning. Atli tells the story that I bet him I would ski down the top slope at Seljalandsdalur, first of anyone that morning, and all the way down to the shore. He is fond of describing in grand terms how I dragged myself out of bed before daybreak so he could witness the ski run. I won a bottle of whisky off him for it.

I quickly came to the view that a primary election should decide the composition of the list in the Westfjords (Vestfirðir) at the next elections. A proposal to that effect was approved in the constituency council as early as 1968. The primary was held at the end of November a year later, nearly a year and a half before the end of the parliamentary term, and was open only to party members and those who declared their support for the party. It attracted considerable attention, however, because it was one of the first primaries or opinion polls held ahead of parliamentary elections. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) had, to be sure, held so-called trial elections earlier in the century and had regularly used this method to compose lists for the Reykjavík city council elections.

Young Progressives had argued within the party for lists to be composed by primaries, among other things on the grounds that renewal in the party's parliamentary ranks would then presumably be greater. In the Westfjords there was reasonable agreement about this method, though there were also those who thought the third seat could be won if I remained there and worked as hard as before. I answered that such a thing was out of the question. I was aiming for the top seat on the list. That is where I wanted to be, and I knew moreover that I could not put as much into the election campaign as I had done in 1967.

I proposed that the candidates travel together around the constituency before the primary and hold meetings. This was thought too radical and no consensus was reached on it. I therefore made such a trip on my own, but benefited first and foremost from the work I had carried out before the 1967 elections. My political activity after them had been limited by my ever-growing work at the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins). Still, I was probably no less often on the road than those members of parliament who had a fixed residence in the west.

The result of the primary was that I received the most votes for first place, Bjarni Guðbjörnsson for second, and Halldór Kristjánsson for third. Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson received the most votes for fourth place. Naturally, Bjarni and Halldór had many staunch supporters who voted for them for the first seat. Bjarni in particular received support, and that did not surprise me. I was in France at a meeting of the Council of Europe's science committee when the votes were counted. Edda sent me the results in a letter.
In the reply I sent her, I expressed some disappointment with the outcome. I was especially sorry that Ólafur Þórðarson had not received

support for a higher seat. I wanted more renewal and to make the list younger. I had far from anything against Halldór from Kirkjuból, for whom I had always borne great respect because of his strong social ideals. I considered it clear, however, that he would draw little new support to the party.

It came to pass that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) as a whole followed the example of the Westfjorders and held primaries in all the country's constituencies before the 1971 parliamentary elections. In them the representatives of the factions to the right and left tested their strength against each other, and many of the party's leaders from the older ranks went surprisingly unhesitatingly to the support of the right wing's representatives. Thus Tómas Karlsson, editor of Tíminn, took the third seat in Reykjavík and shot Baldur Óskarsson, Ólafur Ragnar's right hand, down below himself on the list. For that he enjoyed the support of the party's members of parliament. The left wing considered all renewal in the party branded with the same mark: only those who enjoyed the favor of Ólafur Jóhannesson would rise to prominence.

Around the time the results were in from the Westfjords, the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) resolved at its 1969 national convention to follow our example and arranged open primaries almost everywhere. The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) arranged a primary in only one constituency, Reykjanes, and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) nowhere.
A Congress of Compromises

Within the Progressive Party I was counted among the moderate right-wingers. I had certainly done a thing or two to deserve that in the debate on heavy industry, foreign investment, and economic affairs. Also counted among the "right-wingers" were Tómas Karlsson, editor of Tíminn, Kristinn Finnbogason, later managing director of Tíminn, Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson, the party's city councilman, and Alfreð Þorsteinsson, director of the Sales Commission for Defense Force Property (Sölunefnd varnarliðseigna). They were in constant conflict with the left wing.

I was not counted among the fiercest opponents of the radical young members, and many from the ranks of the older party members considered me first and foremost part of the young generation in the party even though I was past forty. I thus stood somewhat between the factions. That without doubt played its part in my being chosen to serve as the party's secretary when Helgi Bergs stepped down from that post in 1971.

It had long been in the air that Helgi was on his way out of politics. He had lost his seat in the 1967 elections after one term in parliament, and most people knew he was not contemplating running again. Helgi was appointed temporarily to the position of a director of Landsbankinn for half a year in 1969, and in the spring of 1971 he departed en-

gone off to those duties. At the same time he stepped down from the office of party secretary. To those in the know it was clear that Ólafur Ragnar was seeking the secretary's position. Indeed, it is not unlikely that Eysteinn had encouraged that ambition early on. In a memorial article about Eysteinn, Ólafur Ragnar wrote that Eysteinn had spoken as early as 1967 of how it would probably be sensible to "enlist" the two of us along with Ólafur Jóhannesson in a new party leadership. Ólafur Ragnar adds that he was to be given the office of secretary and I that of treasurer.

In those years Ólafur Ragnar's ambition within the party showed itself not least in the way he aimed his spears very much at Helgi Bergs and his work as secretary. Helgi recalls that early in Ólafur Jóhannesson's chairmanship, a delegation of the youth wing, headed by Ólafur Ragnar, Baldur Óskarsson, and Eyjólfur Eysteinsson, came to meet him and put to him the request that he resign and support Ólafur Ragnar to take over. Helgi felt sure that Eysteinn favored this, but he refused for his own part.

Ólafur Jóhannesson worked resolutely against the ideas that Ólafur Ragnar should become party secretary. He supported me for the position. When the time approached for Helgi Bergs to step down from the secretaryship in 1971, Helgi and Ólafur led the group that supported me. My candidacy also enjoyed the support of Þráinn Valdimarsson, the executive director, who was perhaps the one who worked hardest for it.

There was no clash at the central committee meeting where the secretary was elected. It was held immediately following the 15th party congress in April 1971. Before the vote was taken, Ólafur Ragnar and Jóhannes Elíasson, a bank director who had been serving as deputy secretary, specifically declared that they would not stand. Eysteinn's mind I never knew. The only ones who, as I understand it, worked against my election were a few representatives of the rural districts led by Stefán Valgeirsson. They said it was unacceptable to elect to this office a city child who had no understanding of the interests of the scattered rural settlements. I received the great majority of the votes, 67 out of 80.

The radical young members could in fact be well pleased with the results of the preceding party congress, which was called the congress of compromises in the media. They carried great weight in all the debates and resolutions. Ólafur Ragnar set the tone and wanted to define the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) as the "chief opposition party" to the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). This fell on fertile ground, though a few men had doubts about the young men's fervor. Thus Ólafur Ólafsson from Seyðisfjörður remarked that he wanted to "invite these young lads out into the countryside to take part in the people's work, since he considered it of little use to speak finely if experience was lacking. People should beware of talking about right and left and instead unite in a single

front," to quote the minutes of the party congress. It could nevertheless be seen as an attempt at reconciliation within the party that Ólafur Ragnar received a good vote in the election to the executive committee, coming next after Eysteinn in number of votes with a total of 70.

Those who knew the situation best, however, knew that compromise and reconciliation were not uppermost in Ólafur Jóhannesson's mind. At the party congress a delegation of Southerners went to see him and requested that he give his blessing to Ólafur Ragnar taking third place on the party's list in the constituency. The party chairman, however, rejected this outright and flatly refused. He could not bear the thought of Ólafur Ragnar gaining further influence in the party and was not willing to meet halfway on that matter. I considered this to show little shrewdness, unless Ólafur's direct intention was to drive Ólafur Ragnar and the radicals out of the party.
The Progressives and the Unification of the Left

Even though the young men did not attain the influence they had aimed for, they had various reasons to celebrate after the 1971 party congress. A resolution was passed calling for a united front of the left under the leadership of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). It was put forward after a fierce battle over wording and substance, and read as follows:
During the coming electoral term, the Progressive Party will work toward shaping a common political force of all those who embrace the ideals of equality, cooperation, and democracy.

The resolution attracted great attention. It may be said that once it had been passed, the leadership was practically duty-bound to aim for the formation of a left-wing government after the elections. The radicals considered that they had won a great victory in one of their main causes. That was not far from the truth, for the party congress's resolution was closely related to a similar resolution that the SUF had passed at its national convention in August 1970. The history of the Progressive Party states that at that meeting, radical and left-leaning youth members had the upper hand and that Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson was their principal leader. That is certainly correct.

During the last electoral term of the Restoration government (viðreisnarstjórnin), there indeed seemed to be considerable movement on the question of unifying the parties. In those years it occurred to few people that the Progressive Party was anything other than a left-wing party, or that Progressives did not have much in common with the supporters of other left-wing parties. In 1968, talks had taken place between Eysteinn and Ólafur Jóhannesson of the Progressive Party and Hannibal Valdimarsson and Björn Jónsson,

who had split off from the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). In these talks it was discussed, among other things, that they might join the Progressives' parliamentary group. I thought very poorly of that idea. I believed that Hannibal's entry into the party would not do us any good. It may be that the memory of his part in the fall of the left-wing government in 1958 played some role in that. I believed then, and still believe, that there would have been little peace around Hannibal, as was invariably the case wherever he was involved.
