Added to this was the fact that I faced an election campaign in the Westfjords, where it was by no means ruled out that Hannibal would stand, as later proved to be the case, though for a long time it was thought most likely that he would run in Reykjavík.

I found it a strange thought to have him at meetings of the parliamentary group with such a prospect looming. I therefore worked against these ideas within the central committee and the party's executive committee. Nevertheless, it was decided to enter into further talks with those comrades. They petered out when they founded the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna), or the Union (Samtökin) as it was often called. Its declared purpose was to unite all left-wing people in a single party. Talks between the parties were suspended for the time being.

In 1970 the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) began pushing for unification talks between the Social Democrats, the People's Alliance, and the Union. This could perhaps be traced to the Social Democrats' fear of elections after eleven years of participation in the Restoration coalition. The Progressive Party's parliamentary group rejected a proposal from the youth members to take part in these talks. At the end of the same year, the Union of Liberals and Leftists approached the Association of Young Progressives (Samband ungra framsóknarmanna) about similar talks, and the youth members entered into them despite the party's resolutions. These led, among other things, to a joint declaration with 14 numbered objectives concerning "cooperation with labor movements and cooperative movements" and "joint actions" after the elections.

The outcome of the talks was splashed across the Union's party organ with a banner headline, and they were said to mark "a turning point in Icelandic political life." Ólafur Jóhannesson called these talks "a mistake" in his opening address at the 1971 party congress, and those remarks provoked sharp reactions in the camp of the young. Morgunblaðið also made much of them and in an editorial urged the youth members to revolt. It may be said that these exchanges of fire were the beginning of their conflict with the party leadership in the public arena. The aforementioned talks had in fact been broken off by the young Progressives when the Union sought the formation of an electoral alliance.

All these talks nevertheless had one thing in common: the socially minded parties never all came to the same table. The Social Democratic Party had rejected the participation of the Progressive Party, and the People's Alliance members wanted the Social Democrats to break off the Restorationcoalition

partnership before going any further in talks with them. At meetings of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), however, considerable support was repeatedly expressed for cooperation talks among all the socially minded parties, though the men in charge did not want such talks under way when an election was at hand. When the fall of the Restoration government came into view, the party in effect split in two. Many hoped that renewed energy would flow into the unification ideas, while others had growing doubts. Myself among them.
The Restoration government out of power!

In the 1971 election campaign I traveled widely around the constituency, though it came nowhere near the grand circuit of four years earlier. For that I had no time. Among the reasons was a considerable workload at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). I was nevertheless forced to take leave from work for a while because of the election campaign. I stayed a good deal in Ísafjörður and traveled from there to other places. The campaign meetings were much as before, except that now I occupied the first place on the party's list and led the party without exception. I therefore always delivered the opening speech at the meetings I attended and had the closing words. Among the Independence Party men, Matthías Bjarnason took over the leadership. Our fencing did not diminish because of that.

The new Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) was led by Hannibal Valdimarsson. His candidacy attracted great attention, since he was taking part in an election campaign in the Westfjords after an eight-year pause. He had run on a separate list in Reykjavík four years earlier. I knew from my own experience what Hannibal was capable of, for I had watched him at election meetings in 1963. At a meeting in Bolungarvík he gave a heartfelt speech about his fight for the working people and the labor movement of the Westfjords. He recounted how he had once been carried out of Bolungarvík in bonds because employers had not tolerated his forthright conduct. Some indeed say that he was stuffed into a sack, which was tied shut, before he was carried to the ship. I sat near the back of the hall and heard the woman beside me begin to weep aloud.
Hannibal reached the people.

Hannibal still touched chords in the people of the Westfjords even though he was beginning to age. No one doubted that here was a strong politician. He always kept his boyish appearance and youthful fervor. Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson sometimes recalled that at one campaign meeting Matthías attacked Hannibal on account of his age. I was sitting between them at the head table. My eyes fell on Hannibal's childlike cheeks on the one hand and Matthías's stone-gray hair on the other, and I blurted out: "Now, what matters most is not
how old men are but how men age." It took the meeting chairman a long time to restore calm in the hall, so great was the laughter.

Opposition to the Restoration government had intensified greatly in the four years that had passed since the last elections. The current ran to the left because of economic turmoil and youth revolt. The lines of conflict in Icelandic politics were sharpened still further by the herring collapse and the depression of 1968 and 1969. The rescue measures of the Restoration government confirmed, in the minds of many, that the government's policy was bankrupt no less than the businesses around the country. I considered the policy of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) the right answer out of this impasse, and I was not alone in that.

In the election campaign the Progressive Party emphasized "the other way," as it was called: the organized building-up of the country's economy, with the government putting its hand to the plow instead of the disorder of the unrestrained market. In economic affairs the party spoke for the triumph of planning. I supported this policy wholeheartedly and put the thought this way in my speech at a central committee meeting a year before the elections:

The next elections are therefore the first of a new era – an era that demands radically changed ways of working. Things can no longer be allowed to drift, if this nation wishes to keep its self-determination. Foresight and forward thinking – the planning approach – have always been a matter of course; now such systematic methods are a vital necessity for Icelandic national life.

The other main issue of the election campaign was the extension of the fishing limits to 50 miles. On that issue the opposition parties had reached complete unity in the Alþingi under the leadership of Ólafur Jóhannesson, Lúðvík Jósepsson, and Hannibal Valdimarsson. I agreed with the party's policy on the fishing limits issue, took an active part in shaping it, and supported it within the party's central committee and executive committee. In the fishing limits issue crystallized the disagreement with the government parties, which wanted to move more slowly on the extension for fear of opposition from our allies in NATO.

I had trouble with only one issue in this election campaign. That was the Progressive Party's position on the European Free Trade Association, EFTA, which had come before the Alþingi in the last year of the Restoration government. I considered EFTA a good option for us Icelanders and found the case made by the Progressives in parliament unconvincing. They wanted to dismiss the matter and in the end abstained when it came to a vote. This I considered a wrong policy and a clear example of the tendency of opposition parties to be against whatever the government advocated. Eysteinn's refrain was always to "take no responsibility for the government'

s policy." I thought it self-evident and right to establish cooperation in the field of trade and commerce, to lower tariffs through reciprocal agreements, and to increase freedom in these areas. Sovereignty is never threatened by pure trade agreements.

The arguments of us Progressives found a broad echo in the Westfjords. It soon became apparent, however, that the main thing in the minds of young voters was to remove the Restoration government from power. Although we had a good following wind in the Westfjords and Strandir, it immediately became clear to me that we would not reach the support we had had four years earlier. Hannibal's candidacy was the main reason. He had a large personal following in the Westfjords from earlier times, and moreover many reasoned that only by voting for Hannibal could the Restoration government be brought down. No one believed, understandably enough, that we Progressives would get three men into parliament.
Third chapter

I was deep in the election campaign out west in June 1971. Morgunblaðið came off the press in Reykjavík early in the morning, as was its custom. Five days remained until election day. I was preparing for the day's tasks over a hearty breakfast when I was called to the telephone. "It's Tómas Karlsson, editor of Tíminn. He said it was urgent." I could not imagine what the matter might be.

Tómas was unusually short of breath when he told me the news. In the middle of Morgunblaðið a harshly worded attack piece had appeared across a full two-page spread, in which I was accused of bearing responsibility for extensive disorder in the finances of the State Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins), where I was executive director. The author was Þorsteinn Sæmundsson, astronomer. I asked Tómas to go through the content of the article for me. I had to content myself with jotting down a few points. I was badly shaken and hardly knew what should be done. The piece came at the worst possible time for me, so shortly before the elections, and it seemed exactly as if the publication date had been chosen so that I would find it difficult to mount a defense.

It appeared obvious to me that I could not clear myself except through an official investigation, and that would never be completed before election day. I nevertheless requested such an investigation that very day. It was hopeless, though, to be able to refute the accusation before the elections were over. That weighed heavily on me.

The course I took was to turn to Matthías Johannessen, editor of Morgunblaðið. I went over the facts of the case for him and sought advice. After long and frank discussions he decided "to give me space in the paper," as it was called. Two days after Þorsteinn's article appeared, Morgunblaðið

followed it up with a back-page news item reporting that I had requested an official investigation of the matter and had sent the state prosecutor a telegram to that effect. The paper also published a statement from the insurance company that the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) did business with, in which the part of Þorsteinn's accusations concerning it was refuted. This was an act of friendship and testifies to Matthías's integrity. In those years it was almost unheard of to publish the defenses of political opponents in party newspapers without distortions. I know, in fact, that various Independence Party men were angry with Matthías over this.

They felt that he had thereby given me the chance "to glue my head back on once it had already been severed from the body." The Morgunblaðið news item stated that all the points Þorsteinn had blown up in his article had previously been examined by the National Audit Office (Ríkisendurskoðun). It also said that following that examination the Ministry of Education had seen no reason for further action.

Þorsteinn's accusations have in later times commonly gone under the name of the green peas affair (grænubaunamálið), both in conversation and in the media. Most people, however, have long since forgotten what it was about, and few indeed seem to care to know. The green peas became famous across the country because some cartoonist published a picture of me pouring from a can of peas into a gasoline tank. I was chairman of the Surtsey Society (Surtseyjarfélagið) and had bought provisions on good terms from the cannery in Bíldudalur, chiefly peas and meatballs in cans. The scientists at Pálsbær on Surtsey polished these off. The green peas were paid for by the Surtsey Society. The invoice to the Surtsey Society, however, had been wrongly entered under the Research Council's automobile account. Numerous bookkeeping errors of this kind had been found at the Research Council every year.

The National Audit Office did nothing but correct the entries, since the mistakes were innocent. There was never so much as a hint of embezzlement until Þorsteinn's writings. Many, however, seem to remember only the accusations and not the outcome of the case.
Frictions in the Research Council

After I began to be increasingly involved in politics, a certain distrust toward me began to make itself felt within the Research Council, especially as my term as substitute member of parliament wore on. This was never noticeable, however, in the council's executive committee. That was a kind of governing committee of the Research Council itself, which was a much larger assembly. In the executive committee the cooperation was always excellent, even though staunch Independence Party men had seats on it. In the Research Council, on the other hand, the waters grew rougher as time went on. In addition to members of parliament, who saw everything in a political light, seats had by then been taken in
the council by young and conservative scientists. Among them were Ragnar Ingimarsson, associate professor, and Þorvaldur Búason, physicist.

In 1969 the astronomer Þorsteinn Sæmundsson took a seat on the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). In March 1970 he came to a meeting with me and sought various kinds of information about the council's activities and finances. I found this interest gratifying and told Þorsteinn so. Following that, I let him have the council's payment overview along with other information. He did not consider this sufficient, however. Two weeks later I therefore sent him photocopies of all the council's ledger cards, and copies of the travel expense invoices shortly after that. All these dealings were entirely amicable, but with the words that, as a member of the council, he was obliged to show responsibility in his handling of the information.

Around the same time, in April 1970, two anonymous articles about the Research Council appeared in the newspapers. In the first, a question was posed in the headline: "Does the Research Council pay for Steingrímur's propaganda trips?" It appeared in the paper Ný útsýn, which was published by the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). The second article was in the paper Nýtt land – Frjáls þjóð, the organ of the newly founded Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna), where the executive director of the Research Council and its executive committee were attacked under the headline: "The Research Council: An expensive but idle propaganda nest?" The information in the article was attributed to a "young scientist." These writings were discussed at a meeting of the Research Council's executive committee on April 17.

The minutes state that it was decided that the executive director should reply to the article with reference to the discussions that took place at the meeting. It was considered especially necessary to correct a gross misstatement about the travel costs of the chairman and the executive director and a misunderstanding about the annual report, and to explain high automobile costs. The minutes state verbatim:

The executive director also called on the executive committee to state its position on the paper's assertion that he devotes up to three months a year to political work in the Westfjords, since it would be incumbent on the executive committee to make objections to his work if that were the case. The members of the executive committee present at the meeting said they saw no reason to suppose that the executive director was neglecting his duties on account of other engagements.

More than half a year after this, in November 1970, Þorsteinn Sæmundsson telephoned, this time wanting access to all the supporting documents of the Research Council. I said that went without saying but mentioned at the same time that those records were in the hands of the National Audit Office (Ríkisendurskoðun). I therefore asked him to wait until their processing there was finished. The next I heard, however, was of the astronomer's movements as he

sat in the offices of the National Audit Office (Ríkisendurskoðun) together with his female assistant from the Institute of Natural Sciences (Raunvísindastofnun), examining all the supporting documents. He had said he was working on examining them with my knowledge and consent, for a special project for the council. Both claims were far from the truth.

A special meeting was held between us, also attended by Magnús Magnússon, chairman of the council's executive committee, and the office manager, Pálmi Pétursson. At this meeting Þorsteinn put forward all manner of accusations, directed not only at me but no less at Pálmi and other staff of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð), whom he accused of charging various personal expenses to the council's accounts. I tried my utmost to answer Þorsteinn's questions, but I will freely admit that I found it hard to contain myself. What stung me most was that the accusations against my colleagues were put forward without being supported by any evidence. The points that concerned me personally were also open to question.

In the wake of this meeting, Þorsteinn submitted comments on the Research Council's accounts for the year 1969. On the basis of these, I felt there was reason to ask the National Audit Office to go over the council's accounts more thoroughly than usual, and the approval of the Minister of Education was obtained for this. It was remarked that no more detailed examination of an institution's accounts had been carried out in Iceland up to that time.
The National Audit Office's comments on the Research Council's annual accounts were discussed at a meeting of the executive committee on 24 March 1971. The minutes state, among other things:

Those present agreed that the detailed examination which has been made of the annual accounts of the National Research Council has shown that there is no question of misconduct in the finances of the Research Council.

It was noted, however, that there was a lack of formal rigor at the bookkeeping office, where an unusually large number of errors occurred, and the ministry's approval did not appear to have been sought in various cases as it should have been. The main finding was that payments relating to entertainment, travel and the like were somewhat generous.
"A Christmas Present for Jankovic"

In its detailed examination, the National Audit Office made comments of many kinds, about fifty in all. Entries had been recorded incorrectly in the books even though they had been correctly labeled by me. No suspicion arose, however, that the bookkeeper had embezzled funds, let alone I. On the other hand, various items were considered questionable. Three spare parts for my own car had been

paid for by the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) by mistake. The National Audit Office (Ríkisendurskoðun) pointed this out. Secondly, the National Audit Office considered that I had not been sufficiently careful in distinguishing telephone calls made for my own purposes from calls made on behalf of the Research Council. Thirdly, the National Audit Office did not accept that the Research Council should pay me rent for the use of my car for transporting salt on behalf of the Research Council in connection with the Sea Chemicals Plant (Sjóefnavinnslan) on Reykjanes. I had lent it because no car could be hired for this filthy job. I had accepted the car-rental rate for this loan, and I had decided on that arrangement in consultation with the office manager. The National Audit Office, however, held that payment should be made according to the state's per-kilometer rate.

I considered that absurd in this case, since the car was used to move the salt only about a hundred meters, so that the use cost far more in wear and tear — among other things because of salt corrosion — than the kilometers driven would indicate.

It was nothing new for the National Audit Office to go carefully over accounts. Pálmi Pétursson had for many years been at once office manager, treasurer and bookkeeper of the Research Council. He was a conscientious man but prone to mistakes. It was therefore common at the Research Council for there to be errors in the bookkeeping. This was one of the first things I ran into when I began working there in 1957. At first I made numerous comments on every single annual account. As time went on, however, my oversight diminished. There were two main reasons for this. In the first place, no suspicion ever arose that any embezzlement was taking place, and in the second place the National Audit Office always went carefully over the accounts. It would often make numerous comments and corrections with great conscientiousness.

In the years 1969–70 I was moreover deeply immersed in other projects of the Research Council, which had greatly expanded its activities, in addition to which I devoted considerable time to the hurly-burly of politics. I cannot deny that this took its toll on my supervisory role as the council's director.

On the basis of the National Audit Office's comments, I repaid to the Research Council everything about which there was not full agreement or which was considered objectionable. I decided not to argue over individual items, neither the car rental nor anything else, and paid in full everything that had been criticized. The amount was in fact insignificant, 23,294 krónur in all. Nor did I make any fuss about the fact that I had myself borne various costs for travel, telephone communications and for guests of the Research Council at my home, none of which I had been reimbursed for. With this I considered the matter closed. I also went carefully over the bookkeeping for the next financial year, 1970, to set it right in light of the National Audit Office's observations.
There I applied the same rule of caution: if I saw the slightest reason to think that suspicious minds could find fault with entries, they were corrected.

Þorsteinn Sæmundsson, however, was by no means content to let the matter rest. His first writings appeared a month before the parliamentary elections of 1971. The article spread onto a third page in Morgunblaðið. There he recounted the course of events in the case in the minutest detail. He claimed that the examinations by the National Audit Office (Ríkisendurskoðun), the executive committee's handling of the matter and the calling of a meeting by the Minister of Education, who was chairman of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð), had been delayed far beyond all reason. This article of Þorsteinn's appeared the same day the matter was taken up in the Research Council.

There the Minister of Education announced that the conclusion of the auditor general, which had received thorough consideration in the ministry, would "of course be acted upon, and the matter was thereby closed on the part of the Ministry of Education." Following the meeting and the newspaper writings, the executive committee of the Research Council issued a statement and sent it to the media together with a summary of the National Audit Office's report. At the same time I set out my side of the matter in a separate statement. With that I thought the matter was finally over and done with, and I went off to hold meetings in the election campaign in the Westfjords, which was at its height.

Þorsteinn Sæmundsson ended his long article with the words that "the purpose of this article [was] not to pass any final judgment on the finances of the Research Council." His verdict, however, was not long in coming. He chose to publish it five days before the parliamentary elections, as mentioned earlier. His article bore the headline: "A Christmas Present for Jankovic." It was drawn from one of the bookkeeping errors that had occurred. Shirt buttons made of Icelandic stones, which had been bought as a Christmas present for the prospector Jankovic, had been entered under the accounting code: "other services related to mineral exploration." The invoice for the green peas was another example of the same kind.

Þorsteinn called such bookkeeping mistakes "innocent disorder." He used harsher words, however, about high car and gasoline costs, insurance matters, telephone bills, foreign business contracts, travel costs and entertainment expenses, the working methods used in budgeting, improvements to the premises and, finally, my corrections to the accounts for the year 1970, which he seemed to want left unchanged despite the National Audit Office's observations.

I could freely admit that certain aspects of the Research Council's finances were not all they might have been. For example, I was entitled to the use of a car under my employment contract. By 1968 the car was getting on in years, and I proposed that a new one be bought in view of impending maintenance costs. This was rejected by the Ministry of Education. The maintenance, however, was not long in coming. While repairs were under way, it was agreed between me and Pálmi the treasurer that it would be best for me to lend my own car while the workshop repairs lasted and receive either a per-kilometer

charge or buy gasoline and minor maintenance for it with funds from the council. Þorsteinn made no fuss about the fact that a new car had not been purchased; instead he cast suspicion on the fact that gasoline had been bought for my own car at the council's expense. It was characteristic of his accusations — whether they concerned insurance, telephone bills, travel costs or improvements to the premises of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) — that he not only listed the items the National Audit Office (Ríkisendurskoðun) had found objectionable but also brought up much of what the auditor general had considered to have natural explanations. In every point he saw grounds for suspicion; everywhere he found reason to cry: "Wolf, wolf!"
Green Peas on the Car

I do not know whether the "green peas affair" (grænubaunamálið) had an effect on the elections out west. Most people, I think, regarded it as a bitter political attack, while others made fun of it. Progressive Party people (Framsóknarmenn) freely compared it to the eider-duck-killing affair (kollubanamálið), which became notorious before my father's first elections. I doubt that our opponents profited from it, at least not the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), for many remarked that it summed up the conservatives perfectly. Matthías Bjarnason was at pains to deny that these attacks originated with the Independence Party. Perhaps that gives an indication of the affair's effect in the constituency. Hannibal and the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) also decided not to say a word about these accusations in the election campaign.
Their campaign committee considered the matter trivial and did not want to risk that discussion of it might create sympathy for me.

The people of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and Þjóðviljinn showed the greatest interest in this matter, and the same was true out west. The party's candidates in Reykjavík, however, directed their spears no less at Tómas Karlsson, editor of Tíminn, who had made a name for himself by criticizing questionable handling of public funds. Tómas wrote in my defense in this matter, and the Þjóðviljinn men took that badly. The physicist Þorsteinn Vilhjálmsson wrote two articles about the affair in which he attacked Tómas and said he was wrong that this was an election bombshell — Þorsteinn Sæmundsson's "battle saga" bore witness to that. Þorsteinn then wrote at length to argue that people's positions on the matter did not follow party lines. Among other things, he reached the curious conclusion that the position of Gylfi Þ.
Gíslason, the Minister of Education, was "in fact one of the most astonishing things in this whole affair." Þorsteinn said, verbatim:

Everyone knows that the Minister of Education is no political ally of Steingrímur Hermannsson; some would sooner have considered them rivals for a ministerial seat. Nevertheless, the minister leaves nothing untried to shield the director in this matter.

I felt Gylfi behaved honorably in connection with these matters. We were on good terms and discussed them thoroughly. He assured me that there would be no further repercussions on the ministry's part if I made a clean breast of things vis-à-vis the National Audit Office (Ríkisendurskoðun).

I did not suspect that various Independence Party men are said to have pressed the Minister of Education hard during those weeks to remove me from office. All I knew was that the Independence Party men in the Westfjords disclaimed any part in the accusations against me, and that the executive committee of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) stood behind me. From where I stood, I enjoyed the support of those who knew the case best, whatever party they belonged to. This was in fact also a source of astonishment to Þorsteinn Vilhjálmsson.

He pointed out in his later article that the chairman of the executive committee was "a declared Independence Party man," and of the other members of the executive committee he said that they "generally backed Steingrímur," even though he was not aware that they had been "associated with the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn)." Þorsteinn did not take this as particular evidence that there were any mitigating circumstances in my favor, or that his namesake Sæmundsson had gone too far; instead he drew the conclusion that this was "in other words one branch of that generational divide which is very noticeable in Icelandic society these days." He then added:
I permit myself, for example, to assert that virtually the entire younger generation of scientists stands behind Þorsteinn Sæmundsson.

Writings of this kind, I believe, took their color from the election campaign rather than from the merits of the case. Þorsteinn Vilhjálmsson in fact wrote about the matter yet again ten days after the elections, urging on the public prosecutor in an article under the heading "The Joint Liability of Officials" (Samábyrgð embættismanna). Þjóðviljinn largely lost interest as the elections receded, and if anything it seemed to me that certain men in the Progressive Party did not lament that word should get around that not everything had been quite as it should.

The public investigation took quite some time, and as far as I know it was thoroughly carried out. The public prosecutor and the Reykjavík Criminal Court (sakadómur Reykjavíkur) saw no reason for further action. In the whole affair only one item came to light that did not seem to have any natural explanation. This was an invoice

for a large hinge which was said to be for a Scout vehicle — and that was the make of car I owned. I paid this invoice with my own money even though I did not know where it had come from, since no such hinge had ever been replaced on the car.

Nevertheless, it may be said that this affair never fully faded from memory. The "green peas affair" (grænubaunamálið) has popped up from time to time throughout my entire career, and most often those who have discussed it have not known a single thing about the facts of the case. Critics tend to look sheepish when they are asked to explain what they know about the circumstances. But to fight such corrections on every front is a hopeless task. I therefore soon came to the conclusion that there was nothing for it but to laugh at the whole thing.

Although the inaccuracy of the bookkeeper at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) unfortunately meant that "green peas" have followed me through my career, it has never occurred to me to blame him; indeed, it may be said that I could have prevented errors with stricter oversight. Þorsteinn Sæmundsson, on the other hand, is one of the few men with whom I have chosen to have as little to do as possible. I am of the opinion that right should be right, but I strongly doubt that this alone was what motivated Þorsteinn. If he let himself be used in a game of political chess, that was stooping low.

Nearly ten years after Þorsteinn Sæmundsson wrote "A Christmas Present for Jankovic," he published an article he called "From Keflavík to Bessastaðir." In it he dealt with the presidential candidate Vigdís Finnbogadóttir. The article was considered so crude and unscrupulous that people flocked to support Vigdís's candidacy. Many believe that with his slander Þorsteinn managed to float the candidate most of the way to Bessastaðir. Perhaps he considered me no less dangerous a communist than Vigdís. Þorsteinn Sæmundsson seems to have the peculiar quality of hardly being able to attack anyone in his writings without the person targeted rising to the highest honors as a result.
Research and the Utilization of Natural Resources

My involvement in politics unfortunately took its toll on my work at the Research Council, not least while an election campaign was under way. This applied to the years 1967 and 1971 and in fact to every election until I left the position of director of the Research Council and took up ministerial office in 1978. I was, it is true, constantly rushing to and from Reykjavík and thus managed to attend to my most pressing duties. My mind, however, was very much on the elections. Every weekend was taken up, whether I was in Reykjavík or out west.

After it became clear that I would not get into parliament in 1967, however, I set to work in earnest, and it was far from being "an expensive and unproductive nest of propaganda," to use my critics' wording. The Research Council went from

to strength in these years, even though appropriations grew slowly. The staff increased, and at the end of 1967 I received permission to hire Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson, a newly graduated doctor of chemical engineering. This was a turning point in the whole operation, for Vilhjálmur was a great asset. He is energetic, thoroughly educated and knowledgeable. Our collaboration was excellent, as our views coincided, and our interests as well. Vilhjálmur is a lover of nature, and as time went on we traveled and went fishing together a great deal. After I became a minister, however, that diminished considerably.

Vilhjálmur worked at first mainly on studies of the utilization of the country's natural resources but gradually became involved in more matters. A few years later, the engineer Reynir Hugason and the business economist Gunnar Björn Jónsson were hired by the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). Gunnar Björn dealt not least with the study of funding for research and experiments and handled those matters admirably. Reynir led various of the studies of the development of research and the utilization of natural resources that the Research Council had in hand, not least after Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson left for other work. Although Reynir was an enthusiastic and good employee, losing Vilhjálmur was a great loss.

Studies of the utilization of the country's natural resources grew rapidly, and a special appropriation was obtained for them. Among the large projects may be mentioned the idea of sea-chemical processing on Reykjanes. Baldur Líndal led that work together with Vilhjálmur, but I was also somewhat involved in those matters. Considerable funds were devoted to that research. Test wells were drilled, and foreign specialists were engaged for market surveys. Support for these matters was obtained, among other sources, from the United Nations development organization, UNIDO. In that connection I visited that institution. Its specialist considered the idea very promising. Foreign companies also showed interest in the project; the Swiss at Alusuisse were among that group, along with American parties.

A plan was drawn up for the construction of a 250,000-ton salt plant on Reykjanes. For a long time the plans looked very good, but then the price of salt fell sharply and the bottom unfortunately dropped out of these ideas. Later, in fact, a smaller salt plant was built in this area, and it had a hard time of it. It was too small to make it possible to extract from seawater various other substances, which were important for a plant of this kind to have a viable operating basis. The ideas for a magnesium plant that are now on the agenda can be traced to this research.

The sea-chemicals project was among the joint projects of the Research Council and the geothermal division of the National Energy Authority (Orkustofnun), which had previously come under the Director of Electricity

Affairs (raforkumálastjóri). Baldur Líndal was the moving spirit in everything there. Baldur and I worked together a great deal and became good friends. He was a quiet man but incredibly imaginative and resourceful. I think he is one of the deepest-thinking men I have ever known. He was like a geyser. Sometimes he would sit without stirring for long stretches until suddenly the ideas came streaming forth. Besides the sea-chemicals ideas, Baldur also played a substantial part in the diatomite research of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) together with the geologist Tómas Tryggvason. That research led to the founding of the Kísiliðjan diatomite plant at Mývatn.

Research on kelp in Breiðafjörður was supported by the Research Council and began in these years in cooperation with the Director of Energy Affairs (orkumálastjóri). The chemical engineer Sigurður V. Hallsson worked chiefly on it. The cost of these studies far exceeded estimates, and for a time it was uncertain whether they could be completed. Sigurður's results ultimately led to the construction of the seaweed processing plant on Breiðafjörður, which had a rather bumpy ride at first but has now become a robust company. The plant has largely passed into foreign ownership.
Oil Exploration and Gold Fever

When the Norwegians found oil in the North Sea, great interest arose in searching for it on the Icelandic continental shelf. To that end, the Research Council promoted the establishment of a so-called continental shelf committee (landgrunnsnefnd). Magnetic surveys were made of the seabed, with foreign ships engaged for the purpose. At the same time, one or two foreign companies received permits for surveys north of the country. None of these studies, however, led to a positive result. Little was found of sedimentary strata that could bear oil. The continental shelf of Iceland is probably too young for that.

Numerous other ideas for innovation in the economy were under consideration, including heavy-water production, geothermal greenhouse cultivation and more. They were generally smaller in scale. Mention may be made, though, of the first systematic mineral exploration ever carried out in Iceland. It took place in the East Fjords, especially in the Lón area, in the years 1968 and 1969. In that connection I visited the United Nations and managed to obtain a grant for a foreign specialist, Dr. Jankovic, from Yugoslavia. He stayed here those two summers and worked very systematically in the area considered most likely to hold some valuable metals. Some amounts of most of the valuable metals were found, but in such small quantities that extraction was not considered profitable. This survey attracted considerable attention, abroad as well.

The directors of Alusuisse, among others, declared their interest in financing mineral exploration in return for receiving a priority right to exploit any metals that might be found. It was not considered feasible to accept this, and indeed

the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) would not have had the authority to issue such a mining permit. Now, nearly thirty years later, some gold-prospecting company is in fact trying its luck in the same area, but I would be surprised if it achieved better results in its search for gold than the Yugoslav.

The Surtsey Society (Surtseyjarfélagið) had been founded after the eruption that began in the sea in 1963. The society carried out extensive work and was given oversight of Surtsey, which has been a protected nature reserve from the beginning. Numerous scientists from countless countries worked on the most varied research on the island in the fields of geology, geochemistry, geophysics, and biology. Some of this research is still ongoing. Careful attention has been paid to how life and nature developed on Surtsey. In this way, invaluable knowledge has been gained about the formation of Iceland. The Surtsey Society regularly publishes reports on the progress of this research and still organizes scientific expeditions to the island. The Coast Guard (Landhelgisgæslan) has been an invaluable ally of the society on those trips.

It would take too long to list all those who have worked on the Surtsey research, but one can name men such as Sturla Friðriksson, Sveinn Jakobsson, Eyþór Einarsson, and Aðalsteinn Sigurðsson, who have all sat on the society's board along with me. These scientists are among the many who have done invaluable work on Surtsey.

One of the most gratifying consequences of the Surtsey eruption was that scientific cooperation with the United States grew rapidly. Among other things, this brought cooperation in the field of sea-ice research. At the end of the 1960s there was considerable sea ice off the coast and hard times throughout the country. The Research Council then pushed for the establishment of sea-ice research at the Icelandic Meteorological Office (Veðurstofa Íslands). The council also pushed for an international conference on sea ice. My friend, Professor Þorbjörn Karlsson, took on its preparation and visited UNESCO, among others, for that purpose. He succeeded in arousing considerable interest abroad. The sea-ice conference was held in 1970 and was very successful.
In connection with this work, great interest arose in cooperation on international research in the northern seas, which is now finally being established.

My trips abroad in these years were quite numerous, and that part of the director's job grew steadily, among other things in connection with the Nordic cooperation in research matters, Nordforsk, the OECD science committee, and a committee on higher education and science under the auspices of the Council of Europe. On these trips I often took the opportunity to visit institutions with which I thought it sensible to establish contacts, such as the United Nations Development Organization in Vienna and UNESCO in Paris. I also visited a number of companies in Europe and the United States in connection with ideas about utilizing the natural resources
of the country. On these trips of mine I often met in equal measure with representatives of companies and research institutions.

The role of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) in gathering information and preparing reports also grew gradually. Around 1970, a great deal of information about the country's natural resources and the possibilities for new heavy industry had accumulated at the council, which had been assigned a role in those matters by the 1965 law on its operations. The contribution of Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson and other staff members was of no small importance in that regard. In August 1970, the Research Council published a work by Vilhjálmur and me on the possibilities for new heavy industry in this country. The publication was in English and summarized the results of most of the studies that have already been mentioned.

As a sign of the Icelandic government's interest in this matter, we heard at some point that for years hardly a business meeting with Icelandic participation had been held at which this document was not distributed.
The Russians Are Coming! The Russians Are Coming!

As the voices calling for the departure of the military grew louder, the writings of various conservatives became all the more vitriolic toward everything connected with opponents of the military base, the Soviet Union, or their supporters. There, Morgunblaðið was at the forefront. Everything that argued against the departure of the military was played up and turned into major news. The Cold War was stoked and suspicion sown at the slightest provocation.

As an example of how far the Cold War delirium could go, one may note that considerable jitters arose among the staunchest supporters of the Americans when Russian scientists were granted permission to conduct research in this country at the beginning of the 1970s. They were led by a world-famous Russian scientist, the geophysicist V. V. Beloussov. The research was intended to disprove the so-called continental drift theory, which Beloussov opposed.

The Russians' research was carried out with the permission of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (utanríkisráðuneytið) and the Ministry of Education (menntamálaráðuneytið). It went on for several years. At its conclusion, the Russians gave us various instruments that had been used here in Iceland. Among them were six Russian mountain vehicles that the Research Council was tasked with allocating. Guðmundur Pálmason and I were invited to Russia in 1973 in connection with this research, and it was a most informative trip. There we were given access to the Russians' research data and became convinced of its scientific purpose.
On this trip, Guðmundur and I were invited to Tiblis in Georgia. There we

we were received by a member of the academy of sciences who was also the vice president of Georgia. In the evening we were invited to a banquet at a restaurant up in the mountains. We had the place to ourselves. Our interpreter had warned us that it was customary to toast all evening long, and our host did not fail to live up to that. We toasted practically everything between heaven and earth. There was a toast to me and a toast to Guðmundur. There were toasts to Iceland and to wives and children and grandfathers and grandmothers. All evening there was toasting, and with each toast everyone had to empty his glass. Anything else was considered a gross insult to the host. After each toast the glass was turned upside down, and it was said that the number of drops that fell onto the tablecloth equaled the number of enemies of the one drinking.
It was considered natural to have a few ill-wishers, but bad if their number got out of hand.

In the end everyone had risen from the table except me and our host. Someone had become unwell and gone out. Guðmundur was sensible enough to know his stomach's limits, but this group of six had by then emptied twelve bottles of white wine. The host was still in the best of spirits and had begun drinking a toast to peace in Europe, in addition to which mistresses were shown the honor of having their toast drunk. According to the interpreter's instructions, I was to conclude the banquet by toasting our host. I said a few words of thanks and knocked back my glass. For some reason I then squeezed it vigorously, and as luck would have it, it shattered with a loud bang. The host sprang from his seat in sincere admiration, and I explained at length that this was in the Viking manner. He ordered another bottle and began struggling to toast and squeeze, but nothing happened.

When he asked me to repeat the trick, I had the presence of mind to recall the important rule that it brought misfortune to break two glasses, and in fact one was not allowed to drink any more after this age-old ceremony. He gave up on the glass-squeezing when he had finished drinking the thirteenth bottle, but I have never tried this again.

We were driven home to the hotel when the banquet was over. I woke up on the sofa the next morning, not having made it into bed. We were picked up early in the morning for a sightseeing trip and were rather rusty. When we came to a beautiful mountain lake, a married couple arrived there. The woman was a veritable babushka and at least three times my girth. She goes for a swim in the lake even though the weather was cold and biting. I felt I could not be any less of a man. I have never been in colder water.

The Georgians showed us a great palace they had built in honor of the art of chess and the chess masters of the Soviet Union, who are held in high esteem in that country. The building was constructed like a boxing arena with a main hall in the middle, but

countless side rooms where one could sit down to a game of chess. They showed us pictures of their greatest heroes, Tal and Petrosjan and others. At nearly every picture I could say that Guðmundur had in fact drawn against the person in question, because it was true. He was a very good chess player and a superbly good drawing player. It was impossible to beat Guðmundur if he played for a draw. Our escorts were so astonished that they began stepping several paces backwards to get a better look at Guðmundur.

At the 250th anniversary of the Russian academy of sciences in 1975, Edda and I accepted the Russians' invitation to attend the festivities held for the occasion. This was a great pageant, and it was obvious that the Soviets were proud of their scientists. There I became acquainted with, among others, the famous scientist Linus Pauling, who later came to Iceland and was a guest in our home. He is famous not least for vitamin C, which he was the first person to isolate.

When he and his wife came to Iceland, we invited them to our home for lunch together with Sturla Friðriksson and his wife Sigrún Laxdal. We served fish with a good white wine. When I was pouring it, Pauling asked instead for beer. I said that it was, unfortunately, forbidden to sell it in Iceland. Then Pauling looked at me in astonishment: "You don't allow beer?" he said thoughtfully. "But do you then allow Coca-Cola?" I said yes. He then said: "That is strange. Coke is far unhealthier than beer could ever be." Then he took out an enormous vitamin C tablet and crunched it. He had boundless faith in the supplement and took some 18 grams a day. That is surely a generous weekly dose. I take only 2–3 grams. Pauling must have done something right, though, for he reached a great age and was 93 years old when he died in 1994.

On this trip to Russia, Edda and I were invited to the home of Beloussov, which was very unusual on official visits in Russia. He picked us up at the hotel in his own car. When we arrived at his home, he took the windshield wipers off the car. I asked him what this was about, and he told me that otherwise they would be stolen. Windshield wipers were worth their weight in gold on the black market. This world-renowned scientist lived in a reasonably spacious apartment in a large block of flats. The entrance hall and stairwell did not strike us as grand. We could not see the walls of the apartment, for every inch of them was covered with books. I have hardly seen anything like it in my life. We dined with the couple, and they were very agreeable. It turned out, in fact, that Beloussov was viewed with suspicion in the academy of sciences.
He was looked at askance by the leadership of the Communist Party.

On this visit to Russia we traveled on an ornate train from the imperial era from Moscow to Leningrad, which is the cradle of Russian scientific work. We then visited Georgia and the Black Sea at the invitation of the academy of sciences. It was a most instructive journey. On the first morning, eight locals

were sitting at the next table. At first I thought they were also having breakfast like us. However, they seemed to me louder than most breakfast guests, and it turned out that they were drinking champagne and having a fine time. These were Georgian farmers celebrating a good sale of their produce.
Chapter Four

The people of the Westfjords gave Hannibal Valdimarsson a feast in the parliamentary elections of 1971. When he set out, he did not know whether he would lay his political bones to rest in a humiliating rout, but the outcome was a landslide victory. Hannibal received 24.7 percent of the vote and took Karvel Pálmason, the second man on his list, with him into parliament. His organization received nearly double the support the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) had won four years earlier. All other parties lost support, the People's Alliance proportionally the most. Yet Hannibal's showing was probably most fateful for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). The firm base of social democratic support, which had been solid through the years, came loose. The Social Democratic Party in the Westfjords has never been the same since.

Hannibal also cut great gaps in the ranks of us Progressives. His supporters energetically claimed that his election hung by a thread and that his organization was therefore unlikely to get anyone into parliament. Their votes across the whole country would then have fallen dead, and the "Restoration" coalition would probably have held its ground. The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), on the other hand, was said to be certain of two members of parliament in the Westfjords but unlikely to gain a third. With this propaganda, the Hannibalists won considerable support among the Progressive Party's voters.

One of those who suffered inner turmoil over whom to vote for was my friend Kristján from Garðsstaðir. He voted for Hannibal and wrote me a letter in which he underlined in red how important it was to get him into parliament in order to bring down the government. On election night, Kristján is said to have listened to the results with his nationally famous fervor. It is said that he sprang from his seat when Hannibal had received enough votes to get into parliament and kept adding to his tally. For the rest of
the evening, Kristján paced the floor, chanting both aloud and under his breath: "No more, Hannibal, no more. That's enough! That's enough!"

The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was nevertheless the largest party in the constituency, though by a narrow margin. We received 30.3 percent of the vote, down from 38.2 four years earlier. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) came next with 30.1 percent, but it had received 34 percent in the 1967 elections. The election results in many parts of the country were a disappointment to the Progressive Party. Its overall support fell from 28.1 to 25.3 percent, and the party's members of parliament decreased by one. The other results for the country as a whole were that the Independence Party received 36.2 percent of the vote, the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalag) 17.1, and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkur) 10.5.
Hannibal's support in the Westfjords was unique, for the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) received only 8.9 percent of the vote in the country as a whole.

I believed that more than Hannibal's candidacy explained the Progressive Party's loss of support since four years earlier. In my opinion, the party had completely failed to renew itself. This was most evident in its parliamentary contingent, and so it had in fact long been. As early as 1956 I had written to my father that renewal had long since become necessary in the parliamentary party. I proposed that young men be recruited to run in the battleground seats on the party's lists throughout the country, since in that way new voters could be reached. Many had foreseen the danger this stagnation posed to the party, and various people believed that primaries for choosing the lists would change much in that regard. In a speech I delivered at the general meeting of the party's central committee in April 1970, I tried to spur the party to answer the call of a new era.
After speaking words of appreciation for the work of the party's members of parliament ever since the Depression years, I urged renewal:

I have not concealed my opinion before, that it is a vital necessity for the party to substantially renew its parliamentary contingent. This is not aimed against anyone in particular. The honorable men who sit in parliament must examine their own minds. It is our most urgent necessity now that a group of younger men and women join the parliamentary party — people who have been shaped in the present, who understand and are unafraid of the future, yet have strong roots in the national heritage. There are many such people in our ranks. Our fine men in parliament would raise for themselves the most magnificent monument if they exert themselves and encourage such people to take up their standard right away.
The signs of old age in the parliamentary party were in fact so conspicuous that its renewal became one of the chief causes of young Progressives. In that matter, Ólafur

Ragnar and I were in step, and this often came out in party forums. Young Progressives calculated that by the end of the electoral term the average age of the parliamentary party would be 59.8 years, or more than six years higher than the average age of the parliamentary party of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), which came next, and more than ten years higher than the parliamentary party of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), which was lowest.
Old men and a party without women

The parliamentary party of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was of course convened immediately after the elections. When I looked over the group, it seemed obvious to me that the party had not met the demands of the new era. It may be said that seldom has a parliamentary party borne such thorough marks of this as the Progressives did that term. It was not only that I was the sole newcomer. No woman had held a seat in parliament for the Progressive Party since 1956, when Rannveig Þorsteinsdóttir left parliament. So it still was, and in fact it did not change for the next sixteen years.

The party's primaries, which had been held in all constituencies, did nothing to improve matters. It seemed to me confirmed yet again that older men tend to cling to their parliamentary seats longer than is reasonable. Twelve of the Progressive Party's seventeen members of parliament in the autumn of 1971 had held seats there during the first term of the "Restoration" government twelve years earlier. The young men from that time, Ingvar Gíslason and Jón Skaftason, were still the youngest, with me alone excepted, in the summer of 1971. Eysteinn Jónsson was taking part in his fifteenth elections. The young man, me, had just turned 43. Six of the party's members of parliament were born in the first decade of the century and twelve of the party's members were born in 1915 or earlier.

I had strong feelings for these old leaders of the Progressive Party and still do. They were great idealists but worked in the spirit of their time. They were rural men heart and soul, and that shaped their position on most issues.

Some of the members of parliament who sat beside me in the parliamentary party room I had first come to know as a child in my father's house, for they had served in parliament since my father's first years as prime minister in 1934. Although no one could fail to see that they were both reliable and honest, they seemed to me exceedingly conservative.

Gísli Guðmundsson had sat in parliament ever since the Depression years. He is one of the worthiest men I have met. Gísli, however, did not share my faith in the modern age but distrusted it and much that came with it. Everything centered on the worthy idea of preserving what was good even though it was old. Björn of Löngumýri,

Páll Þorsteinsson, Ágúst Þorvaldsson, Björn Fr. Björnsson and other members of parliament all had it in common that they were sterling, noble men. The development of society, however, was moving far too fast for them to find their footing. They gravely doubted that the changes were for the better. Nevertheless, they were among the most popular of men in their home districts, and perhaps that is no wonder. They were honest in their positions and shared them with many of their neighbors. To the credit of most of these long-established members of parliament, it can also be said that they were usually open to reasoned argument, though they would not budge from their fundamental convictions.

The older men were strongly marked by the ideas of Jónas from Hrifla. Farms and homesteads were to be many, and equality was to reign in smallness. They accepted new farming methods only grudgingly if these meant that machines would replace people. The greater part of the nation was to live in the countryside and support itself by farming. Heavy industry was of the devil if it disrupted the settlement of the country by drawing people to the towns. I was at odds with them on all of these matters.

I felt the older generation went too far in its ideas about balance in the settlement of the country. Every croft that fell into abandonment was sorely mourned. I repeatedly raised objections to this and argued that with changing times and new farming methods it must inevitably follow that farms would become fewer and larger. At the same time I considered it important that population centers should form as widely as possible around the country, because only in that way would it be possible to provide the services that people demanded in a modern society. I spoke openly for these views but nevertheless quickly realized that within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) I would have to steer between rock and wave. I must not take on more than I could carry. That I knew very well.

I worked with the older men no less as secretary of the party than as a member of parliament, and it was not least in that role that their life experience and sound advice proved valuable. It fell to me to draft various proposals and resolutions of the party. I remember well an exchange with Karl Kristjánsson after I had written "shall ensure" again and again in drafts of party resolutions. Karl retired from parliament the same year as my father, 1967. He came to speak with me, cocked his head and gazed into the air as was his habit, and finally said: "But Steingrímur, how do you intend to ensure this?" Karl knew from his long experience that nothing is ensured in this life. He therefore wanted the Progressive Party to promise only to "promote" and "aim for" its causes. One should always have solid ground beneath one when fording a river.

Gísli Guðmundsson did not like it when I wrote "out in the country." Then he narrowed his eyes, sharpened his voice and said rather sternly: "We inhabitants of the rural areas are no outcasts left to graze outdoors." He wanted to say "in the countryside."
Cramped Quarters in Parliament

The working conditions of members of parliament had not changed at all since I took a seat in the Althing (Alþingi) as an alternate member in 1968. The members' offices were scattered among four or five buildings in the vicinity of the parliament house. There was no rule that members of the same party should be located near one another. This was extremely inconvenient, since there were only one or two secretaries in each building. When a member made use of a secretary's services, he could expect members from other parties to read his letters over the secretary's shoulder. I found this intolerable and decided not to accept an office from parliament. I therefore attended to all my work from the director's office at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð), where I continued in a part-time position, or from home.

I discussed these facility matters with, among others, the president of parliament, but conservatism stood in the way of reform. When I passed through the offices of the Althing in preparing this book, however, I saw to my great pleasure that the members of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) have finally all been given accommodations in Kirkjuhvoll. This is certainly a great improvement, even though it took 25 years of waiting.

Many rural members of parliament lived in cramped circumstances in Reykjavík, especially at the beginning of their parliamentary careers. Some of them had no other recourse than to settle into inhospitable hotels and guesthouses. Several rural members lived at Hótel Borg, and Matthías Bjarnason lived in a little cubbyhole at the City Hótel on Ránargata during his first years in parliament. I do not even know whether he had a desk during that time.

The situation of the rural members was, however, improved somewhat when they received a special payment to cover the cost of maintaining two homes, one in their home district and the other in the capital area. Soon, however, it began to emerge that various rural members were registered in their constituencies only for form's sake, apparently in order to receive these payments. Progressive Party members were unfortunately no exception in this regard, and this disgrace has persisted to this day, as far as I know.

Among the new members elected to parliament were heavyweights with whom I would later have extensive dealings in governments. The presidential candidate Gunnar Thoroddsen had resigned his office as a Supreme Court justice and was elected to parliament after some absence from that arena. Geir Hallgrímsson had won a splendid victory in the city council elections the year before and was clearly one of the brightest hopes of the Independence Party members, and for the East Iceland constituency Sverrir Hermannsson was elected to parliament, quick-tongued and competitive.

From the Independence Party members in the Westfjords, Þorvaldur Garðar Kristjánsson returned to parliament. We quickly became good acquaintances. Þorvaldur has many fine qualities and was a hardworking member of parliament. Among other things, he had the advantage over Matthías Bjarnason of being diligent about traveling around the constituency. We were the only ones who went from farm to farm in Árneshreppur and called on the local people. Þorvaldur visited, for example, Guðmundur at Bær and others in those parts, without having the slightest hope of their support in elections.
The Formation of the Left-Wing Government

The formation of a government precedes a government's taking power. According to the constitution, governments serve on the mandate of the President of Iceland. Government formation and coalition talks therefore take place under his guidance. Kristján Eldjárn always followed the practice during his presidency of granting one of the political leaders a "mandate to form a government" and otherwise involving himself little in the course of the talks. In the summer of 1971 it was not obvious who should receive the mandate first.

After the parliamentary elections, word spread from the camp of the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) that Hannibal's supporters believed he should lead the next government. His party had won a splendid election victory. To tell the truth, I thought it absurd that Hannibal should preside over a new government. I respected Hannibal, but knew full well that keeping his troops together and directing the work was not one of his many virtues. Nor is he said to have advanced these ideas himself, but was reported to be thinking mostly about isolating the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), even by forming a government with the participation of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). That does not seem to have found much resonance within the Union's ranks, as was to be expected.

The president's conclusion was that Ólafur Jóhannesson received the mandate to form a government. The reasoning was that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was the largest of the parties that had brought down the sitting government. Ólafur immediately declared that it would be most natural to form a government of the parties that had been in opposition. That was also a logical continuation of the parties' cooperation and unity on the territorial waters issue. Within the executive committee of the Progressive Party there was broad agreement on this step, though voices were heard from the young members' representatives that it would be desirable for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) to take part in the government as well. The conclusion was nevertheless to request talks only with the People's Alliance and the Union of Liberals and Leftists in the first round.
The Union, however, proved to be of the same mind as the young Progressives

and wanted the participation of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). That should have come as no surprise. They had recently split off from the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and had been founded with the goal of uniting the social democrats. Advocates of such a merger, whatever party they belonged to, feared that the gulf that tends to form between parties in government and in opposition would prevent the parties from uniting. That fear was well founded.

The Social Democratic Party's participation in government in fact also enjoyed broad support at the central committee meeting of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) held at the start of the coalition talks. Helgi Bergs and Ólafur Jóhannesson both spoke to that effect. Ólafur, however, made the important reservation that the Social Democratic Party would have to declare its support for the other parties' policy on the territorial waters issue. The young men, on the other hand, placed their main emphasis on the merger question, and Már Pétursson, who by then had become chairman of the SUF, put forward a proposal to that end. The party chairman wanted to postpone taking a position on the merging of parties and wanted to refer that discussion to the party's executive committee. As a result he reaped protests from Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson and Baldur Óskarsson.

Baldur poured further oil on the fire with an unequivocal proposal for the departure of the military from Keflavík airport. Eysteinn Jónsson and other older men who sympathized with the vision of a merger mostly declared that forming a government had to take precedence, with unification to follow afterward. The chairman's motion to set the matter aside was therefore approved without dissenting votes. Subsequently the Social Democratic Party was invited to coalition talks, on the condition of agreement on the territorial waters issue.
The Social Democratic Party sent the Progressive Party the reply that it believed that "attempts to unite the social democrats [should] precede talks on forming a government":

The Social Democratic Party considers, in light of the election results, that it is not feasible to enter negotiations on forming a government without serious attempts having first been made to unite the social democrats.

These words were probably intended more for the Union than for the Progressive Party. At the very least they were not calculated to speed up the formation of a government, for they further stated that the Social Democratic Party could not agree to support the "questionable" methods that were to be adopted in the territorial waters issue. There the party was referring to the plan to annul the Viðreisn government's pledge to submit the extension of the fisheries jurisdiction to the International Court of Justice in The Hague. These answers were probably influenced in part by the fact that the Social Democratic Party was licking its wounds after a crushing defeat in the elections. Its support had
collapsed from 15.7 to 10.5 percent of the vote, and its members of parliament had fallen from nine to six.

For a time it seemed that this move by the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) would delay the coalition talks, for the Union responded with a letter proposing that a "unification council" of the Social Democratic Party, the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the Union be formed at once, in which representatives of "both the younger and older movements of the parties" would have seats. In the end, however, the Social Democratic Party's position on the territorial waters issue led Hannibal to accept that a government of the opposition parties was the only realistic outcome.

For the coalition talks, the Progressive Party chose, in addition to the party chairman, Halldór E. Sigurðsson and Einar Ágústsson, the party's vice-chairman. Eysteinn Jónsson was also in the group, though it was known that he did not intend to take a seat in the government. The talks lasted nearly the whole month of July. There were often hard clashes over individual points. When agreement had finally been reached, the new prime minister, Ólafur Jóhannesson, is said to have remarked that he doubted this would have succeeded "if the television had not been on summer vacation." As is well known, there was no television broadcasting in the month of July until 1982.

When the government was formed, Ólafur proposed Halldór and Einar as his fellow ministers, and this was approved in the parliamentary group without a struggle. Halldór received the finance ministry along with agricultural affairs, while Einar got foreign affairs. I harbored no illusions about a minister's chair. It was clear to me that many of the older men in the parliamentary group had long been hungering for ministerial office after years of wandering in the wilderness of opposition, and considered themselves entitled to the chairs. I also found Ólafur Jóhannesson's choice natural, although some believed Þórarinn Þórarinsson was better suited to the office of foreign minister because of his tireless work on the territorial waters issue and his shaping of policy on it before the elections.

He had also long been the party's spokesman on foreign affairs and was exceptionally well versed in that field. I would myself have supported Þórarinn on those grounds, but it never came to a vote. Einar was more of a man of the world and in many ways a more polished politician. He was considered better able to advance matters in international arenas. No doubt it was true that such qualities mattered greatly.

For the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), Lúðvík Jósepsson became minister of fisheries and commerce, and Magnús Kjartansson took charge of industrial affairs and health and social insurance matters. Magnús Torfi Ólafsson became minister of education for the Union and served the entire term. Hannibal Valdimarsson, who was minister of social affairs and transport, and Björn Jónsson, however, made an agreement to divide the term between them. Hannibal held the minister's
chair for the first part of it. One thing was noted: among the seven ministers there was not one who had been born or raised in Reykjavík. This was the government of the countryside.

I supported this government's formation from the beginning. I had my doubts, however, about various things in the coalition agreement. I thought it unwise to promise the great increase in purchasing power that was pledged there. I doubted that the economic conditions for it existed, and I also thought it more natural for wage policy to be set in collective bargaining agreements.

Morgunblaðið hammered away at the government's inexperience on the day it took office, and there was certainly something to that. Only Hannibal and Lúðvík had previously held seats in a government. Anything else would in fact have been strange after the new governing parties' 12 years in opposition. Ólafur Jóhannesson, however, quickly shook off any reputation for weakness. He grew greatly in office and proved determined and tough in political disputes.
"The Horror Story"

The left-wing government took over the economy in a state of complete disarray. Toward the end of the electoral term, the Viðreisn government had resorted to desperate measures to increase its popularity and had approved a shortening of the working hours of state employees. When the left-wing government took over, most labor unions had open contracts. A price freeze was in effect, but a large price increase was expected as soon as it ended.

The situation was perhaps best described in a famous speech by Ólafur Björnsson, professor of economics and member of parliament for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), in the election winter of 1971. He said it was a "horror story" (hrollvekja) to contemplate the problems that lay ahead. I agreed wholeheartedly with the economics professor's assessment and used his arguments freely in the election campaign.

No less important to me was that Ólafur rejected both laissez-faire liberalism and Marxist planned economy in his speech, saying that both "trace their roots to ideologies that belong to a past century, not to modern society." Those who sang the praises of enterprise, freedom and individualism he said were possessed by the doctrine "that selfishness is man's most desirable spur to achievement and that everyone is permitted to push his own snout forward, so long as it does not directly violate the criminal law." Ólafur then dispatched laissez-faire liberalism with these words:

This could apply in those times when each man lived off his own, like Bjartur of Sumarhús, and one's livelihood depended on the success of man's struggle against the forces of nature. But it does not apply in the same measure,
when people begin to live together in community. Then collectivism is, at least to a certain degree, unavoidable.

I did not know Ólafur Björnsson at all, but I came to hold him in high regard after this speech and admired the philosophy of caution it embodied. It hardly needs saying that I agreed wholeheartedly with Ólafur in this assessment, and indeed I find it thought-provoking how certain advocates of unbridled laissez-faire liberalism in this country have painted a distorted picture of his sensible reasoning. Progressives all over the country naturally welcomed Ólafur's testimony and used it as proof of the merit of "the other way" that the party championed in the elections before the formation of the left-wing government.

With the collective bargaining agreements of September 1971, labor peace was secured for two years. The government worked there, among other things, for the shortening of the work week in the general labor market to forty hours per week, in addition to which vacation time was lengthened by law. In debates in the Althing (Alþingi) I expressed doubts about the premises of the agreements. I considered it highly doubtful that productivity would grow enough to sustain the government's economic policy. I was of course aware that much of this was welcome and some of it was certainly necessary and right. I feared, however, that the national economy could not withstand as large and rapid an increase in purchasing power as had been promised, and that this would fuel inflation.

The labor peace came at a high price. The labor leadership took the improvements in wages and benefits provided for in the coalition agreement as given, but wanted more.
