It would have been far wiser to let the wage-earners' organizations pursue the improvements there was room for through collective bargaining, instead of handing them over on a silver platter. The government was overeager to take credit for the increase in purchasing power. Even though economic growth was greater during the left-wing government's time in power than in any other three-year period in the nation's history, the wage increases were nevertheless greater than the economy could sustain.

As early as July 1972, a new price freeze had to be imposed, and the currency was devalued shortly thereafter. In 1973, by contrast, the exchange rate was raised in an attempt to curb price increases. That was done at the proposal of the Central Bank of Iceland (Seðlabanki Íslands). To tell the truth, these economic measures seemed to me rather haphazard and lacking in long-term vision. The horror story had in reality only been postponed.
The Cod War Near the Shores of Africa

The territorial waters issue was uppermost in Ólafur Jóhannesson's mind when he took over the keys of power in the Prime Minister's Office. One of the government's first acts was to begin preparations for the extension of the fisheries jurisdiction. A committee was appointed with the participation of all the parties in the Althing (Alþingi), and talks were opened with the governments of West Germany and Britain. Foreign Minister Einar Ágústsson dashed around the world to speak for the Icelanders' cause, and in Geneva, meanwhile, meetings were under way in the preparatory committee of the so-called Law of the Sea Conference, which later put forward an international treaty on the utilization of the oceans. There Ambassador Hans G. Andersen spoke for the nation's cause.
In the Althing, vigorous efforts were made in those autumn days to win the opposition over to supporting the extension, and compromise was eagerly sought.

Among the many whom the foreign minister met were ministers and leaders of the Organization of African Unity (Einingarsamtök Afríkuríkja). A large delegation of theirs came on a visit to Iceland in October 1971. The Organization had been founded by 41 states to create stronger solidarity among African countries and shape their policy toward the outside world. As such they were influential on the continent and doubtless still are. It emerged during the visit that the organization's scientific committee intended to take up seabed and territorial waters matters for special discussion at a meeting in Nigeria at the beginning of November, and the Icelandic government was invited to send its representative there. Einar Ágústsson contacted me and I said I was willing to make the trip. Assisting me on the journey was Ambassador Hannes Jónsson, who was then the government's press officer.

The meeting was held in an old, English, fenced-off university district in the city of Ibadan, in the middle of Nigeria. We later learned that Ibadan was called the largest village in Africa. About one million people lived there! It struck me how well-informed the countries' representatives were and how substantive the discussions. Many of the meeting's participants indeed held doctorates from Oxford, Cambridge and Harvard. Some misunderstanding, however, prevailed about important points. They believed that international law limited fisheries jurisdiction to 12 nautical miles plus a 12-nautical-mile zone of control beyond that. I gave a speech at this meeting in which this was corrected. I also explained our fight for a 50-mile territorial limit and the Icelanders' long-term policy of a 200-mile fisheries jurisdiction.

The speech was extremely well received. It did no harm that we were a small nation at odds with old colonial powers. The participants were all very alert to oppression at the hands of great powers, and they knew numerous examples of the plundering of resources off the coasts of their countries. We were told that Hannes and I were the first Europeans to have attended a meeting of the council.

Hannes rose after me when the applause died down and delivered a speech three times longer about an information booklet we had distributed earlier. His speech was certainly informative and everything in it was correct. I believe, however, that half the guests had walked out by the time he finished. If I did not know it before, I became convinced there once and for all that long speeches are dangerous, however good a cause the speaker otherwise has.

After excellent discussions it was unanimously approved to recommend to the ministerial meeting of the Organization of African Unity (Einingarsamtökin) that African states extend their fisheries jurisdiction to 200 miles and that full support be declared for us Icelanders in our struggle. Hannes and I were of course overjoyed at this great support and gratifying result. It came to pass that the African states gave us loyal support in the territorial waters dispute. The countries of the third world played no small part in the recognition of the 200-mile economic zone at the third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea in Caracas in 1974. The Organization of African Unity was at the forefront there.

This was my first visit to Africa, and though it was short I was considerably affected by my acquaintance with Nigeria. There was a glaring difference between the university buildings and the other dwellings that met the eye. The university was modern and its buildings recalled Finnish architecture. The professors lived well and clearly had good incomes. In central Ibadan, on the other hand, there were only a handful of modern buildings. Most of the houses were some sort of clay huts, with sheets of corrugated iron laid on top of them to form roofs. The streets were generally dirt tracks, and sewage and other waste ran in open ditches alongside them. The crowds were larger than I had ever before seen gathered in so small an area.

The streets swarmed with old cars, carts drawn by oxen or by men, and women carrying the most incredible burdens on their heads, often with a child strapped to their back as well. In a newspaper interview with me that appeared in Tíminn after my return home, I say that despite these conditions "everyone seemed to have enough to eat and the people were cheerful and friendly, for they hardly know anything else." On the other hand, I said I could not predict that the peace the people seemed to possess would be lasting:

It seems to me, however, that the question must arise: what happens when the children who are now growing up out of the street learn to read and write and come to realize the enormous difference in living standards that prevails in the country, and no less in comparison with Western nations. I fear that things could then become rather turbulent.

To this it should be added that somewhat later I went again to Africa on behalf of the Althing (Alþingi). I attended a meeting in Nairobi in Kenya at an institution run by the United Nations. There too I spoke about the extension of the fisheries jurisdiction, or "the protection of the fish stocks" as we invariably called our struggle in international forums.
Parliamentary Work and Nationalization Ghosts

The Althing was divided into an upper and a lower chamber. The nation's sixty members of parliament were divided so that twenty sat in the upper chamber and forty in the lower. I took a seat in the upper chamber, which was considered quieter, since the decisive debates on most matters took place in the lower chamber. Most of the government's ministers, the party chairmen, and those members who enjoyed fencing at the podium therefore usually sat in the lower chamber. I, however, liked sitting in the upper chamber. There the meetings were fewer and shorter and the debates more focused.

Each chamber elected standing committees in all the main policy areas, of which there were nine. Each was composed of seven members of parliament. The government supporters in the upper chamber numbered twelve and had to fill 36 committee seats in order to have a majority on every committee. Each government member therefore had to serve on three fronts. I was elected to serve on the two committees of parliament that I had sought. These were the education committee, because of my interest in research and reforms in school affairs, and the industry committee, because of my interest in heavy industry and the vision that industry would play a key role in increasing the diversity of the country's economy. I also took a seat on the fisheries committee.

I was no less pleased with that, since I believed that countless unused opportunities lay in building up the fleet and in the full processing of marine products. I served as chairman of the industry committee and was happy with my lot. In addition I was elected to serve on the social affairs committee in 1972.

I spoke on a good many matters in parliament and exerted myself considerably in what fell under my committees. I also introduced quite a few proposals concerning the interests of the Vestfirðir and the building up of industry there. I sparred somewhat with members of the opposition, as one does. But I found the most relish in my exchanges of views with Magnús Jónsson from Melur. We were seatmates in parliament. Magnús had, among other things, been Minister of Finance in the Restoration Government (viðreisnarstjórnin) and was one of the more respected members of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). He was composed and sensible, though I found him conservative in his views. Magnús never distorted the truth and was precise with facts. I remember well that he went through the mail faster than anyone

in parliament and generally threw away half the letters, unopened. When I asked him why this was, he replied that he knew exactly what was in those letters. "And there is nothing to be gained from it."

In the parliamentary group of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) I was not always of the same opinion as the government, and perhaps especially the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). I found it incredibly common for old nationalization ghosts to stir in its rhetoric. It may be said with some truth that the Progressive Party stood guard over private ownership in this government, just as my father had done in the Government of the Working Classes nearly forty years earlier. When the regional energy utilities were discussed, I held that local people might well own a majority in such enterprises. Magnús Kjartansson, the Minister of Industry, on the other hand, placed chief emphasis on the majority being in the hands of the state. Similar disputes arose within a committee on the canning industry that Magnús established.

I sat on it together with Ragnar Arnalds and Ólafur Hannibalsson. The premise of the committee's work was that canning companies were generally small and had difficulty bringing their products to market. Agreement was therefore reached on founding an organization that was given the name the Marketing Institute of the Canned Goods Industry (Sölustofnun lagmetisiðnaðarins), modeled on the Marketing Center of the Freezing Plants (Sölumiðstöð hraðfrystihúsanna). Disagreement arose, however, over who should hold the majority on the board. I thought it natural that representatives of the industry should be in the majority there, but Magnús Kjartansson and Ragnar Arnalds thought it right that the state should be in charge. The compromise was that the state would hold the majority for five years, after which the organization would take over.

Otherwise I liked working with Magnús Kjartansson. He was razor-sharp and quick to grasp things. Few were cleverer with the pen, and his articles in Þjóðviljinn were often priceless. Although Magnús and I were sometimes on opposite sides, it did not linger with either of us, and our priorities often coincided. I supported, for example, the health services law that he had passed during the left-wing government's time. It provided for the building up of the health system, the construction of health clinics and hospitals, far into the future. This was legislation in the spirit of planning. The chief drawback of these far-sighted plans was that they were not revised, which is just as necessary as making plans in the first place. They were followed almost unchanged to the end. Improved transportation, meanwhile, shortened travel between places and changed the premises of the original law.
The result was that there are too many large health institutions.

In general debates in parliament the same story held. Sometimes I differed with the members of the People's Alliance. More often, though, I was on the attack and the defense against the assaults of opposition members. When major issues were on the agenda, however, it fell chiefly to the ministers to respond. In such matters

night sessions were not uncommon, and they were much more frequent than now. Certain stories circulated among people that during night sessions Einar Ágústsson, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, and I would withdraw and play bridge in a side room of the upper chamber. These stories were true, for ordinary members from the government side took little part in the debates while these bouts went on. The foreign minister also had peaceful nights, since the spears were seldom aimed at him. All of us, however, had to be in the building to vote when it came to that. Speechmaking on our part was frowned upon, for the ministers concerned would then think we were prolonging the debates. In fact, the opposition was usually quite capable of that on its own.

Members would even stand silent at the podium for a long time while waiting for some particular minister to come into the chamber to be present for the debate. During my time as minister I felt such tricks keenly. Some members made a practice of having me called into the chamber, especially if I had gone home. Halldór Blöndal, a member of parliament for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), more than once had me roused from bed in the middle of the night to listen to some tedious droning of his from the podium. I found this tiresome and owed him little thanks for it.
The Beginning of an Organized Regional Policy

One of the most contested matters of the first parliament was the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun). It was established in 1972. It was founded in the spirit of planning. It was intended to carry out the government's policy in regional affairs. The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) had fought for an institution that would work toward balance in the country's settlement for more than ten years. Regional policy was especially prominent in the 1971 election campaign, where all the parties in fact wanted to make it their own.

Morgunblaðið wrote an editorial under the headline "Regional Policy" which said that "under the leadership of Independence Party men in government a new offensive has been launched, which will contribute to the strengthening of the countryside and more even regional development." Even young Independence Party members, who otherwise marched under the slogan "away with the bureaucratic monster!" went on a meeting campaign around the whole country to present their resolutions on the "paramount necessity that in the coming years and decades a massive effort be made to strengthen viable communities throughout the country." It had even come to the point that Tíminn saw special reason to emphasize that the Progressive Party had taken the greatest initiative in shaping regional policy, and made a detailed survey of the Restoration parties' opposition to the proposals of Progressive members in the Althing (Alþingi).
I supported the regional policy wholeheartedly but did not consider the bill on the Development Institute flawless. I had grave doubts that it would be sensible

for a three-man executive council to head the institution, with each of the government parties having its own representative there. This arrangement was later called "the commissar system," because experience of course proved that the three men looked after the interests of their parties no less than the goals the institution was supposed to pursue. I likewise had doubts that the board of the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun) should be politically elected. I put forward an amendment in the parliamentary group to the effect that the institution should have only one director, who would be hired by the board. Jón Skaftason and Björn of Löngumýri supported this proposal, and Björn said that when appointments were political, hardly any experts would be chosen for the job. He then added:
It would of course be best if the ministers had so much sense in their heads that they did not need to borrow much of it. But if they did need to, then that sense had better be good.

A more entertaining ally in debate than Björn of Löngumýri would probably be hard to find. He was also mischievous and contrary, and supported every opinion put forward in defiance of the party leadership's policy. In this respect Björn was unique where the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was concerned. Ólafur Jóhannesson, however, was not amused; he said he disagreed with us on this point and considered it "very ill-advised" to place the institution under a single director. He stressed that this was a political institution and "that people must not be too afraid of politics." The question, though, was whether a member of the opposition should be brought into the executive council. That, however, foundered on the fact that there were three government parties.
Ólafur believed that agreement on the Development Institute could not be reached within the government unless all the government parties had a direct part in its top management.

Magnús Torfi Ólafsson, who was Minister of Education for the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna), has related that his party put forward similar views about the commissar system but was defeated in clashes with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and the Progressive Party. The same story applied to me. We three were overpowered in the parliamentary group, where the party chairman's arguments enjoyed overwhelming support. I did not express myself on the matter outside parliamentary group meetings.

I had ambitions on behalf of the Development Institute no less than for myself, and declared an interest in the chairmanship of the institution's board. I raised this with Ólafur Jóhannesson. He made clear to me that it was out of the question if peace was to be achieved over the institution. The People's Alliance placed great

emphasis on getting the chairmanship of the board, since the institution came under the prime minister, who was a Progressive. The outcome was that Ragnar Arnalds became chairman of the board and I vice-chairman. We consulted closely on all major decisions. It was good to work with Ragnar.

I came to value Ragnar highly after my collaboration with him. Despite his young age he was quite an experienced member of parliament and had already become chairman of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). Our collaboration was to become extensive in the years that followed. Ragnar Arnalds is a man one cannot help but like. He is a gentleman to his fingertips, and this shows both in his speech and in his manner. I do not recall him ever speaking ill of a named person in my hearing. He is imposing in appearance, with a sharp nose and a determined expression. At the same time he has the gentle eyes of an artist. After he left ministerial office in the government of Gunnar Thoroddsen he has, it seems, sat in parliament to get good peace and quiet for writing, so much has his mind seemed to me bound to literature, playwriting, and the arts.
When he retired from parliament last spring, it was surely more than a decade since he had spoken with fervor for a cause in the Althing (Alþingi).

With the arrival of the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun) the administrative system was considerably simplified. Three institutions merged into it under a single management. They had attended to tasks similar to those intended for the Development Institute, but without coordination or an overall vision — "haphazardly," as it was put in Tíminn. The main change the Development Institute brought about, however, did not lie in administrative reorganization. What mattered most was that large sums of money were placed in its funds so that the goals in regional affairs could be achieved. These great financial resources were its greatest strength, but at the same time they brought out the biggest flaws of the commissar system.
Ambitious Development

The policy of the Development Institute was, in my judgment, marked by integrity. It is important to bear in mind that the institution's goals of strengthening settlement and industries were always kept as a guiding light, even though there was a tug-of-war over funds between constituencies. So that the work could be well prepared from the start, Ragnar Arnalds and I and others went on a study trip to Scotland, Norway, and Sweden in 1972 and acquainted ourselves with regional affairs in those countries. This was an extremely instructive journey and gave us a great deal of information on which we based much of our work.
The biggest tasks during the left-wing government's time concerned the renewal of the fishing fleet, which was in decay after decades of stagnation, and a similar story

applied to the quick-freezing industry. The ambition in these fields went hand in hand with the extension of the territorial waters to 50 miles. As matters stood in 1971, I doubt that the Icelandic fleet would have been capable of drawing from the sea the fish that were to be had there. By the end of the electoral term in 1974, however, investments had been made in 55 stern trawlers, which were distributed to communities all around the country.

Trawlerization began as soon as the government came to power, and the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun) took over the task after it was established. In hindsight one may ask whether it was prudent to proceed as fast as was done. We certainly overshot the mark regarding the number of ships. There is no doubt about that. When the trawlers arrived, things began to go well, and it was plain that the purchases were paying off, it was simply as if the devil were loose everywhere around the country. Every remote cove wanted a trawler. They were the great salvation.

A freezing-plant program was also urgent, since new times brought increased demands for hygiene and the finishing of exported foodstuffs. Some of the old buildings were so dilapidated that it was considered more economical to build new ones than to renovate them. In many places machinery for fish processing was also lacking, and many of the older machines were worn out and made poor use of the raw material.

The intention was not to undertake investments except after careful planning. But eagerness simply overpowered this foresight. Regular work on a fishing-vessel plan within the institution did not begin until the end of 1974, when fifty-odd stern trawlers had already been bought with the institution's support.

The 1970s have sometimes been named after the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), and in many respects rightly so. The Progressive Decade is invoked by opponents chiefly in connection with runaway inflation and mismanagement of the economy. I make no secret of the fact that both charges have some basis. Yet the decade is no less rightly called a decade of foresight, enterprise, and progress in Iceland. Economic growth has never been greater since the end of the war. The 1990s, now drawing to a close and considered one of the longest periods of prosperity in Icelandic history, pale in that comparison. Society was nourished by the optimism that was kindled at the fall of the Restoration Government (viðreisnarstjórnin) and grew still stronger with the territorial waters dispute. The optimism lasted most of the time despite difficulties in managing the economy.

The Development Institute was only one element in this building-up effort, and its benefits were felt not least in the scattered settlements of the country. There were enormous undertakings in road construction, where the opening of the Ring Road set the tone. In energy and district-heating matters such great strides were taken that it may be considered astonishing. In the wake of the oil crisis the nation abandoned the practice of the industrial nations of

heating most of their houses with oil, and instead piped hot water through mains and radiators. The electrification of rural areas surged forward. As an example, of the roughly 930 farms that had been left out under the Restoration Government (viðreisnarstjórnin), the connection of 765 was completed during the left-wing government's time, and a plan was made for the remainder. A similar story could be told of the television distribution network and the laying of automatic telephone lines.

In the Reykjavík of my youth, dirt and gravel streets were the rule, and for a long time not a shower could fall in the city without people having to put on rubber boots, for everything turned to mud where paved sidewalks were widely lacking. The most consequential revolutions of this century have taken place in people's immediate surroundings, and they have all been quiet ones. Road building, gardening and sidewalks, running water, sewer systems, and electric lighting are the most notable monuments of the 20th century. The nation also accomplished an incredible feat in environmental matters, which is seldom mentioned, when oil heating was almost entirely abolished within a short time.

I have often thought about how parliamentary matters that seem small can have great effects. Ragnar Arnalds and I jointly introduced a proposal in parliament that a portion of the road funds be allocated to paved surfaces in populated areas. Various people were doubtful about this and thought it questionable to draw this from tightly rationed funds. It was nonetheless carried through, and the improvements were incredible. Not only did rain puddles disappear from the streets, but no less important was binding the dust that otherwise blew everywhere when it was dry. In the wake of this, the residents themselves took to beautifying their surroundings and cultivating their gardens. Now the villages have in many places become beautiful. Paved surfaces in the villages and towns of the country are one of the greatest environmental revolutions I have witnessed in my entire political career.
Patronage Politics

I made it a rule to travel around the constituency in spring and autumn. In most places I arranged meetings in the party associations, and at times I brought with me a lecturer from Reykjavík. What was most valuable to me, though, was that on these visits some people were always added to the large group of good folk I came to know in the Vestfirðir. There is no way to mention everyone who would deserve it.

About my travels I quite often kept notes and even whole reports on individual matters, which I constantly made use of in my parliamentary work and errand-running. Through close acquaintance with the voters I got a clear picture of their wishes and a good idea of what was most pressing in each community. A considerable part of my work also concerned, as before, errands and chores for voters in the constituency and projects connected with the building up of employment

in the west. As a member of parliament I took on a role that all MPs from the countryside had had. I assisted a great number of people from Strandir and the Westfjords with favors and errands in Reykjavík. Many needed to get documents through the proper channels, to seek loans, guarantees, the approval of the right authorities, or import licenses and customs papers.

Much had changed, however, since my father became MP for the people of Strandir. In those days it was taken for granted that voters would show up unannounced at the MP's home, and many of them gladly stayed the night when they were in town. That disappeared after Hótel Saga could offer farmers on a trip to town bargain rates, and many had relatives they could turn to. Still, it was considered that to deal with various kinds of errands it was good to turn to political representatives in parliament. I gladly took on such tasks for my supporters. After all, it was endemic that little got done if no one was there to follow matters up. For this reason I was engaged in extensive correspondence with the west. No less time went into running the errands, following them up, and complying with the many and varied requests of my constituents. In this way I gained many of my most loyal allies.

Voters greatly appreciated being able to have direct dealings with their members of parliament. On my travels in the west I often got to hear stories of the obligingness and helpfulness of other candidates or of the MPs who had represented the areas before. Stories about my father were a regular feature, but there had hardly ever been an MP so wretched that there was not some cycle of tales about him. Nor did the people of the Westfjords lack storytellers.

Gísli Jónsson had been an MP for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) during the first half of the Reconstruction years. He was exceptionally obliging and ended every visit by asking the household whether there wasn't something they needed. The story goes that at one farm the household assured Gísli that they lacked nothing. At those very words he dropped his coffee cup from his hands so that it shattered to pieces. He was devastated by this. Shortly afterwards, a complete coffee service arrived for the householders with greetings from the MP. The wags said that Gísli had surely broken the cup on purpose.

At another farm Gísli is said to have received the same answer, that the household needed nothing at all. The farmer, however, is said to have added in jest that if he had any means of providing them with an heir, he would in fact accept that. When Gísli was about to leave, he surprised them by asking the farmer to fetch his horse from the paddock, a short distance from the farm. Nine months later the couple had a most handsome baby boy.
My favors were of a different kind and indeed changed over the years. After the telephone came to most farms, simple errand-running such as

helping them obtain forms or information became less common. People instead phoned the relevant institutions themselves. Improved transportation also mattered a great deal, and it became more common for people of the Westfjords to make the trip south to run their own errands. Those who were in business, however, often sought good advice and help in obtaining grants and loans. I showed them the way as best I could and spoke on their behalf at meetings at the Development Agency (Framkvæmdastofnun) or with bank directors.

Hörður Guðmundsson, who ran the airline Ernir in Ísafjörður, describes one such visit very well in his memoirs, Þá flugu Ernir. I went with him to a meeting with Helgi Bergs, a director of Landsbankinn. I directed most of my clients to Helgi. He is sensible and resourceful and told every story as it was. On top of that, he was regarded as "the Progressive Party's bank director." Hörður was evidently surprised that we had to sit in the bank director's waiting room like any other customers. It never occurred to me to expect otherwise. In his book, however, Hörður says that after our good meeting with Helgi it was considerably easier going to obtain assistance from Landsbankinn. I am convinced that both parties profited from those dealings. Hörður Guðmundsson the pilot soon became a good acquaintance of mine. I flew a great deal with him, and some of those trips were adventurous.
I supported him in every way I could. I considered the airline Ernir to be an important link in the region's transportation, especially in ambulance flights.

Favors of this kind are still practiced today, and certainly a strong case can be made that in the long run they are unfortunate and thereby unnatural. Improved transportation, professional perspectives, and effective administration should have replaced them with new and better working methods. In the 1970s, however, loan facilitation was interwoven with the political system even more than it is now, and it could prove difficult for business operators to stand outside it. I therefore tried to back those Westfjorders whom I believed in and who needed assistance.

In the Westfjords I encouraged in many places increased cooperation between the fjords and the merging and enlarging of operating units, but as said before, this was not particularly well received. Often a merger or consolidation did not happen until things had come to a dead end and expensive loans had long since crushed the operation. Most industry in the Westfjords was and is connected to the fisheries. This was not unnatural. I made a point of visiting the workshops, familiarizing myself with their activities, and helping young men as best I could to set up such services. I visited Marzellíus's shipyard in Ísafjörður more than once and thought it a shame that funding could not be obtained to enlarge it and thus increase the service to the Westfjords fleet.

In Strandir it grieved me to see the driftwood chopped into fence posts. I got the engineer Svavar Jónatansson to make cost calculations on the feasibility of a sawmill to be located in Árneshreppur. I wanted to get the farmers to join together in that processing. The idea was well received but foundered on the fact that the farmers wanted to keep what was theirs and felt they got something for their labor by using the driftwood for posts.

To demonstrate that good timber was being treated badly, I got Guðjón Magnússon of Kjörvogur to select for me some fifteen large driftwood logs. I sawed them into boards myself and then paneled the basement at home in Mávanes with the sawn wood. Most or all who have seen that paneling have praised the wood highly. Now, at last, driftwood processing has begun in Strandir, and individual farmers have taken the lead in it.
The Cold Menace at Arnarnes

We were the third family to move to Arnarnes in 1966. In the following months and years, however, the area's population grew rapidly. One might say that these first residents were a kind of settlers, for no agreement had been reached with the district (hreppur) about any services or works in the new neighborhood. The lots at Arnarnes are freehold lots and subject to various covenants concerning construction, distance from the street, height of houses, and much more. We who moved there thus had many kinds of common interests to look after. I therefore worked for the founding of a lot-owners' association and became its chairman. I was, however, probably the only Progressive Party man in the group and the one most socially minded. For some reason it fell to me to a considerable extent to drive this work forward.

The lot-owners' association negotiated with the district about road construction, utility lines, garbage collection, and a great deal more. Then, in May 1963, all the lot owners on the streets Mávanes and Blikanes, which were the streets built first, agreed to set up a shared heating station and district heating system. This was done because we had no access to a utility network, and house builders in the area would otherwise each have had to have a boiler station in his own house.

We laid hot-water pipes in the streets and set up a small temporary heating station where the road runs down into Mávanes. The pipes all conformed to the strictest requirements and standards of Reykjavík District Heating (Hitaveita Reykjavíkur), because we expected to be connected to it later. The heating station, however, was imperfect at first. We bought a small oil boiler, and I looked after its operation. The snag was that if the electricity cut out, the heating station died and did not start up again on its own. Before long there was

then cold in the houses of the neighborhood, and telephone calls to my home began. I therefore kept a cold-weather suit hanging by the bedpost. I would throw it on over my pajamas when the heat had gone out of the houses and the station had to be started up again. I soon acquired the nickname "kuldaboli" (the cold menace) in the neighborhood.

Besides the night trips, one had to see to it that there was always enough oil. My trips out to that corner were thus not few in those first years, and the errands connected with the duties of district-heating manager were more than can be counted. In 1968 we built a proper heating station where the streets branch at the top of the Arnarnes hill. Following that we hired an excellent machinist from Kópavogur, Kristján Þorkelsson, to look after the operation, and with that my nighttime wanderings blessedly came to an end. After Reykjavík District Heating (Hitaveita Reykjavíkur) reached Garðahreppur, we sold it all the pipes in the street and also got a good price for the boiler. In this way we could pay off the debts we had incurred and came out of this district-heating adventure without financial setbacks. In addition, we saved ourselves the construction of boiler rooms in the houses.
Without doubt this was therefore an excellent undertaking. I believe there was general satisfaction with it.

In those years the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) had no one on the municipal council in Garðahreppur. In the wake of my projects at Arnarnes, various party members pressed me hard to stand for the municipal council, and I complied in the elections of 1970. There I placed the greatest emphasis on planning matters and a clear vision of the future, as well as the need for prudence and foresight in financial management. Outdoor recreation areas needed to be defined and a policy for building up employment laid out, along with providing the obvious services in health care and schools. I believed residents should be able to enjoy outdoor life, quiet, and tranquility in an unpolluted environment. The Progressive Party's support increased considerably and I was elected.

I suspect that various Independence Party supporters from Arnarnes voted for me in those municipal elections and regarded me as the representative of the settlement there. I strove to look after our interests as best I could, but many of our fellow parishioners looked askance at Arnarnes and considered it a rich man's enclave. Perhaps there was something to that.

The work on the municipal council was in many ways instructive. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) had an outright majority and thus decided whatever it wished. Ólafur G. Einarsson, later a member of parliament, government minister, and Speaker of the Althing, was municipal manager and then council chairman. He made an effort to reach consensus with us in the minority. Our proposals were therefore considered with more goodwill than our share of the vote warranted, and most were in fact approved. My main criticism was that the resolutions were not followed up with action and that the Independence Party men were reluctant to make plans ahead of time, both as regards works and finances. I advocated systematic planning in these matters.

I also criticized the Independence Party for neglecting the operation and construction of schools and daycare centers, and I said that Independence Party men "seem to have an exceedingly hard time accepting a social solution to the municipality's service tasks."
Two Families in Two Countries

I was loaded with work when I took my seat in the Althing. I continued my duties at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). For that I accepted 60% pay, though in reality I put in full-time work. I could not, however, attend to it as much as I had done before. Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson took over the management of the larger part of the operation, which grew ever more extensive. I also had a seat on the district council. That had to give way. I stood for only one term, although in many ways I had enjoyed that work. Politics took enough time as it was. Among other things came the added bustle that accompanied the office of secretary of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). In that I took Eysteinn Jónsson as my model.

I made every effort to attend all the meetings I possibly could and went to constituency conventions all over the country, in addition to other meetings of the party associations. I regularly delivered a survey speech on the party's work and the political outlook at these gatherings. I therefore traveled a great deal around the country and got to know a great many party members.

My first wife, Dolly, lived with her second husband in the United States with our three children. In 1971 John Bryan had turned twenty, Ellen Herdís was 16, and Neil fourteen. They took turns staying with Edda and me in the summers. No sooner had I been elected to parliament than I was served with a summons demanding an increase in the child support. The reasoning was that my salary would rise substantially since I had become a "senator." Instead of a total of 120 dollars in monthly support, Dolly demanded 150 dollars for each child. This would have meant nearly a quadrupling of my support payments. The premise of the lawsuit was that I received a salary equal to that of United States senators.

In my eyes this was only one case in a long series. Dolly had again and again shown the same sort of maneuvers in the ten years that had passed since our divorce. I was not able to attend the court proceedings but sent a letter in which I set out my side of the case. It stated that after taxes had been deducted, I paid about a fifth of my total salary in support for my three children in the United States. In addition, I paid various costs for the children, among them Jón's schooling at MIT's engineering school, which by itself equaled the support payments. I found Dolly's demands utterly unfair and expected nothing other than that they would be
dismissed. It was probably a mistake, though, to let the letter suffice instead of hiring a lawyer to argue my case.

I had, however, long since had enough of my former wife's litigation. Shortly before, she had made an attempt to have me detained at the airport in New York over alleged debts to her. She did not get her way in that. The judge, however, went a long way toward meeting her demands for increased child support. I was ordered to pay 200 dollars a month for the children and 150 dollars in addition for Jón's school fees. I was astonished at this ruling and wrote to the court and to the Icelandic embassy in the United States, besides consulting an American lawyer. The lawyer found the entire ruling incredible. Our conclusion, however, was that it would be expensive to have the case reopened and the outcome entirely uncertain.

Following the ruling there was no avoiding sending the dollars every month if I was to be allowed to come to the United States and have the children visit in the summers. I therefore paid everything in full, and more besides, as before. As regards the school fees, it was fortunate that the children had Icelandic citizenship and thereby the right to loans from the Icelandic Student Loan Fund (Lánasjóður íslenskra námsmanna). That eased matters. Undeniably, the remittances to the United States took their toll on the finances at Mávanes, especially after Edda stopped working outside the home. According to the ruling, I was obliged to let nearly half of my regular disposable income from my parliamentary seat and my work at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) go to my children abroad.

I had a better salary than members of parliament generally because of my work at the Research Council. I also received pay for sitting on the board of the Development Agency (Framkvæmdastofnun), on the district council, on the heavy-industry committee, and on other temporary committees, in addition to my fixed salary. Though these were not large sums, they made a difference. The per diem allowances I received on my travels abroad also weighed heavily. If I traveled on behalf of the Research Council, I had to pay for hotels and other costs out of my per diem, and it went entirely to expenses if one was not careful. On the trips of the heavy-industry committee it was another matter. Then we were very often invited out to meals, and that made a substantial difference counted in money. I could therefore use the per diems to buy various things for Edda and the kids.
That also mattered, because the price difference between countries was great. Most often I also managed to save some part of the per diems.
"Don't These People Know You Have Children?"

While the litigation with Dolly was going on, Edda was expecting our third child, Guðmundur. She worked as a secretary at the Supreme Court (Hæstiréttur) until he was born and had previously been at the Management Association (Stjórnunarfélagið). She had taken the position at the Supreme Court after Hlíf, our second child, turned one and the oldest boy, Hermann, three. At that point we took in an excellent Norwegian girl, Inger by name, who helped look after the children. Edda was experienced in secretarial work and considered very capable at her job. She had been private secretary to the director of electric power affairs when we met, and some time after the wedding she became private secretary to Eiríkur Briem, director of the State Electricity Authority. There she took over from a girl who was with child.

But no sooner had Edda sat down in the secretary's chair than she too was pregnant with our first child. When Eiríkur heard the news he is said to have remarked: "It must be the chair." He could probably have offered childless couples access to it for a fee.

While Edda worked outside the home, there were constant difficulties getting our children looked after, especially after the Norwegian girl went back home. We tried hard to get them places in preschools. There was nothing to be had in Garðahreppur, even though I pressed hard for improvements on the district council. We finally sought help from Elín Torfadóttir at Tjarnarborg, almost directly opposite my parents' house on Tjarnargata. The location suited us particularly well because of the proximity to my parents and to both of our workplaces, which were downtown. When three weeks had passed, this arrangement was the subject of a complaint, since we did not live in Reykjavík.

We therefore had to find other solutions. Elín was distraught over this outcome. She soon left Tjarnarborg and founded her own daycare center in Breiðholt. Hlíf got a place there and was happy, while Hermann started school a year earlier than was customary. Elín is an exceptionally kind woman with a warm manner. She was the wife of the labor leader Guðmundur J. Guðmundsson, and this was our first acquaintance with that couple. Although a good solution was found there for the time being, matters became complicated with the birth of Guðmundur, our third child. Then Edda turned entirely to the home and the raising of the children. I am certain that this was a great blessing for our children.

In those first years of my parliamentary service I was also finishing fitting out the basement of our home in Mávanes. I would thus regularly disappear down there right after dinner, and I also spent there those weekends when I was not traveling around the country, whether on party business or fishing or other outdoor pursuits. I paneled the basement with driftwood from Strandir,

as mentioned before. I kept it for five years in the basement to allow it to dry. At about the same time as our son Guðmundur was getting ready to come into the world, I was working these logs, as the driftwood is called. I sawed them into boards with a large saw that I had access to at the Agricultural Research Institute (Rannsóknastofnun landbúnaðarins) at Keldnaholt.

When Edda went into labor, I drove her to the maternity ward. This was shortly after midday on October 28, 1972. There was no question of my being present at the birth, as has now become the rule, and since the midwives thought it was a long way off, I went to attend to the sawing. I called the maternity ward regularly, and between six and seven o'clock I got the news that all was still quiet; I should stay calm. I was alone at my labors, in full swing with that big saw, and had worked up a sweat from hauling the timber. When I called again between nine and ten, I was more than a little surprised. Guðmundur had then been born two hours earlier. The midwife said she had tried repeatedly to call, but the saw must have drowned out the telephone. I rushed down there to see my sixth child. He first met his father out of breath and panting, covered in sawdust from head to toe.

The bustle for Edda did not lessen even though she stopped working outside the home. As my political work grew more extensive, the strain on the household increased as well. We entertained a great deal at our home, colleagues as well as other groups, from within the party and outside it. We were likewise often invited out. I also made a point of keeping well informed, "showing myself and seeing others," as the saying goes. We went to most opening nights at the National Theatre (Þjóðleikhúsið) and seldom missed a symphony concert. One week we were out five evenings in a row. Then Hlíf had to hold on to her little brother, who stood in the doorway with tears streaming down his childish cheeks. The last thing we heard before we slammed the car doors behind us was Guðmundur crying out with a sob in his throat: "Don't these people know you have children?"
My Father's Illness and My Mother's Feats

My father's Parkinson's disease worsened greatly in these years. Late in 1971 he had become too infirm to be able to stay in Borgarfjörður as he would have most preferred. After that he was very nearly bedridden. The muscles for swallowing failed him, and an operation was performed so that he could breathe through an opening in his windpipe. He also had to have a special device fitted to his throat in order to make himself understood. This was very sad. Sometimes one could not tell how he was feeling except by his eyes. For example, I read to
ir a verse I had composed about Stefán Jónsson for some parliamentary banquet. He teared up at it, and I took that as a sign that the verses were to his liking.

When the illness had reached this stage he suffered repeated lung infections. Because of this he frequently lay in the National Hospital (Landspítalinn), where he received treatment with antibiotics. In 1974 the infections became ever more frequent. I am convinced that my father himself wanted, above all else, to be allowed to go. The body, however, would not give way, even though he could not move at all. One of the doctors who cared for my father said that he probably would not have lived so long if his heart had not been as strong as it proved to be. Thanks to it, the lungs cleared in a remarkable way despite repeated infections.

As soon as my father's condition improved, my mother would hear of nothing but that he come home again. There she cared for him mostly alone all those years. I will never understand how she managed. More than once I came upon her as she was helping him out of bed. I of course lent a hand, but had my hands full getting him into the bathroom, and I am at a loss to understand how this slightly built woman could so much as budge my father. He was still of great bulk. I worried about my mother because of this, but was met with an iron will where she was concerned. She was not going to leave my father in the care of strangers. She drew strength from her faith and from a love of many years.
After my mother's death I found in her nightstand drawer a little notebook in which she had recorded my father's medical history. At the front she had written this prayer:
May my works, Lord, be pleasing to you; grant that they go well for me. May my labor be fruitful. May your blessing rest upon me.

My mother pushed herself very hard during these years. When my father lay in the National Hospital she walked there from Tjarnargata, without exception, twice a day to keep him company. We siblings also tried to come every day. Once, when Pabbi had been admitted because of an infection, my mother let it slip that she was in agony from pains in her side and stomach. I took her straight to a doctor, who diagnosed her with gallstones.

She had concealed her suffering for a long time so that she would not have to leave my father's sickbed. She was immediately admitted for surgery and the gallstones were removed. When she woke from the anesthesia, her first thought was how my father was doing and whether she would be fully recovered in time to receive him when he came home again.
Fifth chapter

The formation of the left-wing government in 1971 was a setback for the unification of the left in Iceland, as strange as that may sound. The reason was that the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) remained outside the government. Indeed, its interest in cooperation with other parties only grew once it landed in opposition. Within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), this gave the skeptics of the unification dream a pretext to attack the Social Democratic Party. It was frequently emphasized in those writings that the Social Democratic Party had declined to take part in the left-wing government.

The young men in the Progressive Party were, however, by no means giving up. They were tireless in pushing the unification issue forward within the party's executive committee. They were most likely in constant contact with their acquaintances from the other parties, making plans with them. As before, their dream was that the Progressive Party would lead a united party of the entire left — those who embraced the ideals of "equality, cooperation, and democracy."

After agreement had been reached on forming the left-wing government in August 1971, the executive committee of the Progressive Party took up the proposal from the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) which had arrived while the government was being formed, as mentioned earlier. It called for talks on "the unification of democratically minded leftists" and proposed the establishment of a "unification council." Participation by the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) was not envisaged — only the Progressive Party, the Social Democratic Party, and the Union.
The executive committee of the Progressive Party passed a resolution along similar lines but with the change that the People's Alliance would also be invited
to the talks. I was chosen for the party's negotiating committee along with Eysteinn Jónsson, Þórarinn Þórarinsson, Már Pétursson, and Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson.

From the very beginning I placed strong emphasis on ensuring that these talks must in no way damage the government coalition. In this I sided with Eysteinn. He was the chairman of the negotiating committee. It was our view that little would come of left-wing cooperation in any case if the coalition broke apart. Before long, things began knocking against each other in these talks. The Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) wanted to keep the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) out of them, and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) was of the same mind. This position also enjoyed the support of Már Pétursson and Ólafur Ragnar, the representatives of the young men.

They nevertheless drew inspiration from the talks, and the Federation of Young Progressives (Samband ungra framsóknarmanna) held meetings on "the unification issue" all around the country, often in cooperation with associations from other parties. The youth organizations of the Social Democratic Party, the Union, and the Progressive Party also issued joint resolutions and policy statements.

So that no distrust would arise between the coalition parties because of the talks, Eysteinn took great pains to keep the representatives of the coalition parties informed of how matters were progressing. Particular care was taken that Ragnar Arnalds, chairman of the People's Alliance, received all information. The talks, however, dragged on. Our negotiating committee met with representatives of each party separately, but when all was said and done, the story from the previous electoral term repeated itself. The four parties never came to one and the same table. Before it was over, things had boiled over yet again.
Things Heat Up

The leadership of the young Progressives had long since grown weary of the slow pace of the unification talks among the left-wing parties. They passed numerous resolutions at their meetings to push the matter along and advance its progress. Gradually, however, it became clear that in this matter they faced the opposition of the party chairman, Ólafur Jóhannesson. His patience with the radicals had perhaps never been great, but it was long exhausted by the time 1972 arrived. He longed for peace within the party but was at the same time unwilling to depart from his policy to accommodate the disgruntled group. Ólafur also earned the ill will of the young by defining the Progressive Party as a centrist party that could work either to the right or to the left. Such a declaration would have been unthinkable during the Viðreisn years, and in the minds of the young it still was.
This disagreement led to fierce clashes within the party, which became especially visible in two matters: the unification issue and the position on the milibase
of the Americans at Keflavík Airport. Both were matters close to the hearts of the leaders of the young Progressives.

In the unification talks mentioned earlier, a serious rift began to open between the party leadership and the representatives of the SUF. Within the negotiating committee there was, for the first time, serious disagreement between Eysteinn and the young men. In the autumn of 1972 the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) decided to begin talks between themselves on merging the parties, and late in the year the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was invited to take part in them. Around the same time, the State Broadcasting Service (Ríkisútvarpið) interviewed Eysteinn Jónsson, as recounted in his biography.

In his closing words in the interview, Eysteinn said that he "could not imagine dissolving the Progressive Party." The next day he received a telegram from Ólafur Ragnar containing only these words: "There you went and ruined the whole thing!"

The military issue was no less difficult for the Progressive Party. The platform of the left-wing government stated that the defense agreement would be taken "up for review or termination with the aim of having the defense force leave Iceland in stages." This was to happen within the electoral term, in the spirit of the resolutions of the party congresses of 1967 and 1971. A sizable group of party members was nevertheless opposed to the withdrawal of the military. Jón Skaftason, member of parliament for Reykjanes, declared already in the first months of the left-wing government that he was against the ideas of the military's departure. The SUF board reacted strongly to all such declarations and devoted a special SUF page in Tíminn to reminding people of the party's policy and of the duty of those elected to positions of trust to carry it out.

In the early part of the left-wing government's term, the military issue otherwise received little attention, since there was unanimity that the territorial waters issue had absolute priority. Young Progressives were nevertheless prominent in the ranks of the opponents of the military bases. Elías Snæland Jónsson spoke at a large outdoor rally in June 1972, and 4 of the 25 representatives on the central committee of the Campaign Against Military Bases (Samtök herstöðvaandstæðinga) came from the ranks of the SUF.

Toward the end of 1972 the opponents of the occupation began to grow restless, as there then seemed little to suggest that the military's withdrawal was on the agenda. Supporters of the defense force, however, were also stirring. Alfreð Þorsteinsson, an alternate city councilman for the party and director of the Sales Commission for Defense Force Property (Sölunefnd varnarliðseigna), wrote an article at the beginning of 1973 in which he proposed that a national referendum be held on the matter. It may be said that this piece marked the beginning of the emergence of two wings among the young Progressives in the public debate on defense matters. Morgunblaðið published an editorial in support of Alfreð. That did nothing to soften the reaction of the SUF board. It published a full-page article in Tíminn in which Alfreð was styled a sports correspondent and
"a representative of the right wing." The author of the article, who did not sign his name, had no doubt about what Alfreð was up to:

The purpose of Alfreð Þorsteinsson and his associates is precisely to try to delay the handling of the military issue so that there will be no time to bring it to completion within the electoral term. They are then counting on the present government falling in the next elections and the conservatives regaining their former position. Then, they know, the military will not be touched.
It was probably true that Alfreð wanted to sidetrack the matter.

Defense matters did not weigh on me as heavily as they seemed to on many others. I did, however, consider far too strong emotions to be interwoven with the stance of a large part of the nation, both among the supporters and the opponents of the military. For that reason a national referendum would be unfortunate. It would probably have led to great bitterness, and the wounds would have been slow to heal.

I also found it hard to see what should be asked in such an election. Should one ask whether the outlook for peace in the world was good? Or should one ask: Are you for or against a military? Within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), as elsewhere, there were individuals who were against the military no matter what, and others who supported it come what may. It soon became clear that a clash over these matters and others was brewing at a central committee meeting called for April 1973. The volleys between the factions in the party grew ever harsher in tone. In mid-March, the members of parliament Jón Skaftason and Björn Pálsson of Löngumýri declared at a meeting that they were in favor of the military, and for their trouble earned the honorary title "self-appointed petty dictators" on the SUF page in Tíminn.
A Battle Without End

I suspect the young members had no inkling of how heavy the mood was in the party leadership by that point. At the central committee meeting, matters were brought to a head. Eysteinn delivered a report there on the unification talks. He said in plain words that there were no grounds for participating in further merger talks with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the Union (Samtökin), but that it would nonetheless be right to continue talks with all the left-wing parties, each separately. Following this, a motion was put forward by Jón Skaftason that the central committee resolve that there was no basis for talks on the founding of "a new political party, a party merger, an electoral alliance, or talks aiming at such a goal." Twenty-five central committee members signed the motion. Among them were Guðmundur G.
Þórarinsson, Tómas Karlsson, and Kristinn Finnbogason, all of whom had been

very close to me. I did not sign it, but I did express support for it in personal conversations. The same was true of Ólafur Jóhannesson. The young members considered the motion tantamount to ending the unification talks. Before it came to a vote it was withdrawn, but — to the bitter disappointment of the young men — it was resolved not to enter into talks with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the Union (Samtökin) about a joint candidacy.

At the central committee meeting, no less attention was drawn by Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson defeating Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson in the elections to the executive committee by a margin of one vote. Everyone knew that Guðmundur had been put forward at the instigation of Ólafur Jóhannesson, who also had the greatest influence on the outcome of the election. This proved fateful. Following Ólafur Ragnar's defeat, the SUF representatives declined election as full or alternate members of the party's committees and councils in protest. For the next year the party therefore operated largely without the direct participation of the young people.

The imbalance of power revealed in the executive committee election became even more evident in the other elections at the central committee meeting. The landscape seemed utterly changed from the "congress of compromises" only two years earlier. The party chairman now exerted himself forcefully, and the radical young members enjoyed the support of few among the older men, many of whom were loyal to the leader above almost all else. The left wing thus had little sway in the handling of matters. SUF spokesmen considered the party to have rejected their policy in nearly all essentials. Not least important was that their motion on the departure of the military failed to pass. It was in the spirit of the party congress resolutions of 1967 and 1971 but was defeated by 40 votes to 23.

In its place it was resolved that "the review of the defense agreement shall begin shortly, in accordance with the provisions of the [government's] policy agreement." This wording went nowhere near as far as the earlier resolutions on the military issue.

The Federation of Young Progressives (Samband ungra framsóknarmanna) had amended its bylaws in 1970 to the effect that, instead of the SUF's main role being to present the party's policy to young people, the role of the SUF would be to present the policy of the young Progressives both within the party and outside it. After the clashes in the spring of 1973, the young Progressives increasingly operated like an independent political party. They were a party within the party.

It was Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson who played the role of unseating Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson from the executive committee. His history within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) is a stormy one. It began when Guðmundur walked into the party office sometime in 1969 and asked for information about the party. He studied it carefully and decided to join the Progressives. He immediately received a place on the candidate list for the city council elections in

Reykjavík in 1970, after a primary in which he took third place. In that contest Guðmundur formed alliances both to the left and to the right within the youth movement and enjoyed broad support in the ranks of young people. He also performed well in the primary, being organized in all his work, as befits an engineer.

Guðmundur became a city councilman following the party's electoral victory, which I believe was won not least through his own energetic efforts and those of other young members. Shortly afterwards, however, Guðmundur G. swung over to the side of Kristinn Finnbogason and his men. Together they mounted an assault on the leftists in the SUF in the so-called "Saturday revolution" within the Association of Young Progressives in Reykjavík (Félag ungra framsóknarmanna í Reykjavík) in the autumn of 1971. There the left wing was evicted from all positions of influence. In the aftermath, the atmosphere in the party was poisoned, and for a time the young Progressives operated in two associations in the city. They also waged a nearly ceaseless war with each other, with constant complaints about the legality of meetings and of elections to positions of influence.

These skirmishes ended with an injunction and a court case! It is hardly an exaggeration to say that few things took up more space in the discussions of the party's executive committee in those years than rulings and disputes arising from the young members' clashes.

It says something about the party leadership's position in the disputes that despite this endless infighting and the clashes that followed, Guðmundur G. was considered the obvious representative of Ólafur Jóhannesson against Ólafur Ragnar in the elections to the executive committee. I myself supported Guðmundur, being of the opinion that he was one of the more promising younger men of the party.
Events Come to a Head

Cracks began to appear in the government coalition in 1973. There were difficulties in the economy, the Vestmannaeyjar eruption left enormous destruction in its wake, and inflation was getting out of hand. Bjarni Guðnason, my sworn friend from secondary school and one of the members of parliament for the Union (Samtökin), had withdrawn his support for the government, which therefore rested on as slim a parliamentary majority as a majority government can.

Magnús Torfi Ólafsson has expressed the view that the measures to fund the reconstruction of Vestmannaeyjar were the decisive factor in the fate of the left-wing government. It is probably more accurate, however, to say that they came on top of a series of questionable decisions and an imprudent exchange-rate policy. Ólafur Jóhannesson made the magnanimous decision that the settlement on Heimaey should be rebuilt. It was undoubtedly right. The expenditures for the reconstruction work, on the other hand, were a great drain and came at a difficult time, for a large oil price increase had occurred in

world market and dealt all industrialized nations a heavy blow. Added to this, the coalition parties could not reach agreement on a way to finance the reconstruction effort. Björn Jónsson, president of the ASÍ (Icelandic Confederation of Labour), had by this point taken a seat in the government in place of Hannibal Valdimarsson, in accordance with their agreement at the formation of the government. Björn was in fact ill and confined to a sickbed, and the parliamentary group meetings of the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtökin) were therefore frequently held in his hospital room. At the last moment, Björn turned against the plan whereby funds that were to go toward wage increases under the collective agreements would instead go to the reconstruction effort in the Westman Islands. Björn's opposition proved decisive despite the support of others who backed the government.

In the aftermath, that plan was abandoned and a special sales tax was imposed instead. The wage increases thus went through, and inflation shot up and instantly nullified them. There was no foundation for increased purchasing power.

Few predicted a long life for the government, and various people thought they sensed that Ólafur Jóhannesson would not flinch from working with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) if the coalition were to break up. It was obvious that this would put an end to all ideas of the departure of the defense force and the unification of the left, and this served to increase still further the unrest within the left wing of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Many in that group therefore felt there was strong reason to stand back to back and lay plans. In August, a group drawn from the ranks of radical Progressives met — youth-wing members and a handful of party members from the countryside. The group was not a formal association but took the name the Möðruvellir Movement (Möðruvallahreyfingin).

The name was derived from one of the teaching buildings of the Akureyri Junior College where the group met. The idea for the meeting had come from Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, but Kristján Ingólfsson, a school principal, deserved the credit for the name. The Möðruvellir Movement became known nationwide the same evening its founding meeting was held. Even though the gathering was supposed to be shrouded in secrecy, news of it "leaked" to the radio news desk and was read in the evening news broadcast shortly afterward.
The Clashes with the Möðruvellingar

Whether the Möðruvellir Movement was meant to prevent the Progressive Party from entering into a coalition with the conservatives, or was first and foremost conceived as a personal power instrument for Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson and his men, the association began to make itself felt as autumn 1973 arrived. News of these young men's initiative was in fact mostly to be found in Þjóðviljinn, which followed it with approval and splashed it on the front page when the Möðruvellingar published their platform. On the editorial board of Tíminn, however, where I held a seat, it was decided by eight votes to one not to publish the platform statement.

In the aftermath, Ólafur Ragnar took up battle with the editorial board and wanted to publish an article a page and a half long recounting 22 examples of the editorial board's abuse of power against the SUF (the Progressive Party's youth federation). The article was rejected and its publication delayed by a fortnight, until Ólafur Ragnar agreed to have it published on the SUF page. Tómas Karlsson did not hold back in his editorial writing about the Möðruvellingar, saying among other things that "weeds" were thriving within the party.

While these disputes were going on, the Progressive Party's local officers all over the country received an unsigned letter with the heading "policy address of the Möðruvellir Association." In it the group's causes were enumerated, and it also contained harsh attacks on the party leadership, the executive director, and the editorial board. Tíminn called it a "smear letter" in a strongly worded editorial.

Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson had become a lecturer in political science at the University. Shortly after Tíminn's articles he gave a talk on the State Radio (Ríkisútvarpið) in which he recounted a substantial portion of the policy address. There he said, among other things, that the leadership of the Progressive Party had abandoned the core of its policy and that in recent years "a small group of men has steadily gained power within the party, men who care little for the fundamental policy and appear in practice to be directly opposed to some elements of it." Ólafur Ragnar also said:

This group considers itself in reality little bound by the core elements of the party's policy. It considers private enterprise superior to cooperative endeavor. It regards regional policy first and foremost as empty promise-making, not as a radical social undertaking. It nurtures dubious profit-making and financial speculation in numerous fields. It views the Progressive Party not as a party of social solidarity, but as a centre party that chooses its partners according to the power interests of any given time.

This obviously referred to Ólafur Jóhannesson, the party chairman, and his other leading men, and I was doubtless not excluded. We were accused of betrayal in the unification matter, and this "small group of men" was said to want to "tie Iceland as long as possible to a foreign military power."

Ólafur Jóhannesson did not care to grapple with these young men in the public arena and called on me for that work. He asked me to go to meetings and speak there for the leadership, saying that this campaign could not be left unanswered on the party's behalf. I was sorry to have to engage in this work, though I admitted that one could hardly let

the criticism go unanswered. A week after Ólafur Ragnar had presented the Möðruvellingar's case on the radio, I delivered the party's rebuttal in the same forum and at the same time called for public debate meetings where I could speak for the leadership.

In my radio address I first raised the point that I considered the size of the "so-called Möðruvellir Movement" to be exaggerated, but that I had nonetheless thought it right to accept the invitation to appear on the program "even though most people feel this movement has already been given more prominence than it deserves." I also said that the party's governing board had considered very carefully the criticism associated with the Möðruvellir Movement, and that it all sprang from the same roots. "It is difficult to discern any deep-seated disagreement on substance," I said, citing examples from regional affairs, foreign affairs, and cooperative affairs. I did confirm, however, that there was disagreement in attitudes toward private enterprise, which the party leadership placed strong emphasis on supporting and did not consider to be in conflict with the cooperative ideal.

There was also disagreement over the unification matter, where "a large majority of the central committee saw no basis for [. . .] dissolving the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and merging everyone [. . .] together into one party."

At the end of my address I said that opinions in a political party built on broad freedom of opinion were bound always to be divided "both about men and about issues," and I aimed my barbs at Ólafur Ragnar, whom I liked to call the professor, and at other spokesmen of the Möðruvellingar, though none of them was mentioned by name:

Some people take it badly when they do not get their way in everything. For such men, however, dissatisfaction with the leadership is often the fundamental motive. They consider others, perhaps themselves, better suited to lead. Everyone is of course free to think this, and there is nothing to be said about it. But it is petty to hide such things behind a disagreement over substance.

The debate meetings were held in the name of the Progressive Party and advertised in Tíminn. Around the turn of November-December 1973, five meetings were held in North Iceland, and Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson took part in them along with me, while Ólafur Ragnar and Elías Snæland Jónsson spoke for the SUF and the Möðruvellingar. The meetings became lively and at times harsh. It was above all Ólafur Ragnar and Guðmundur G. who clashed fiercely. I tried to keep the discussion on the issues and not drag the dissidents' persons into the matter. I emphasized that gradual evolution in a political party was far more beneficial than revolution. I defined the Progressive Party as a gradualist party of social solidarity and praised the SUF for its extensive activity. I also strongly endorsed the view that before the next election it was necessary

that considerable renewal take place within the party, and I expressed my firm hope that it would prove possible to reconcile the viewpoints. Throughout everything I said, I strove to dampen the fervor of the Möðruvellingar and get them to weigh their outcries more carefully. The goal was to reconcile them with the party and its resolutions. It did not succeed.
Iceland in NATO but the Army Out

The second debate meeting in North Iceland was held at Siglufjörður on Sovereignty Day, 1 December 1973. Shortly before the meeting, Tíminn arrived up north, and in an editorial there Tómas Karlsson declared that the electoral term would obviously not suffice for the army to leave the country, and that it would therefore have to be enough to draw up a plan for its withdrawal. Opponents of the military base all over the country reacted furiously to this message. I had my hands full assuring the meeting attendees that little separated me from the Möðruvellingar in defense matters. That was nonetheless in accordance with the truth.
