The ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) used strong words about Tíminn's editorial, calling it "an undisguised attack on the prime minister and foreign minister of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn)." Sixty "well-known Icelanders" signed a petition for the departure of the army, which was delivered to the prime minister a few days later. Defense matters were once again at the focal point of the national debate.

At the debate meetings I strongly emphasized that I held views similar to those of the Möðruvellingar in defense matters. The same views could be read in the party's resolutions. This line of argument naturally found its way straight into the ranks of the base opponents. Shortly after I came south from the meeting tour, I was therefore asked to describe my views at a meeting of the Campaign Against the Military Base (Samtök herstöðvaandstæðinga). I complied with that request, but I do not know what the meeting's organizers expected.

Some years earlier I had joined the Association for Western Cooperation (Félag um vestræna samvinnu). By doing so I wanted to underscore my support for it. Under its auspices I had, among other things, gone on a trip to the United States in a group of a good thirty members in 1963, shortly before John F. Kennedy was assassinated. There we visited, among other places, the Capitol, where the vice president of the United States, Johnson, met us. The vice president had been in Iceland some time before and had brought his daughter along. Some of us in the group had been entrusted with holding a banquet for her, which we did with pomp and splendor at Naustið. Johnson, however, seemed to have hardly any idea what group he was addressing. He said a few words in haste, and some could not understand him otherwise than that he thought we were businessmen from

Texas. I spoke for the group, since I was the most at home in English, and thanked him on our behalf in a few words. When I finished off by asking him to pass on greetings to his daughter, it was as if he did not know whether to say thank you or take offense. He left without further words.

We were received much better by Robert Kennedy, who was attorney general. He was quick to smile and lively in manner, and his surroundings bore clear witness to his joy in life. On the walls of his office were countless delightful pictures made by his many children. He gave us generously of his time despite being busy. Kennedy knew a fair amount about Iceland, welcomed us with well-chosen words, and everything he said was sensible. I formed a high opinion of this likable man.

Because of these association activities of mine, the opponents of the military base had little reason to suppose that I leaned toward their cause. They did not know that over the years the Association for Western Cooperation (Félag um vestræna samvinnu) had seemed to me increasingly favorable to an army in the country, which was not my ideal. I therefore ended my participation in it.

Svavar Gestsson was a journalist at Þjóðviljinn in those years and has described how, in that camp, I was not held in high regard when the meeting of the base opponents was called. I had been counted among the conservative arm of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and considered right-leaning on many major issues. After my speech on this occasion, however, that changed completely, and I was elevated to "sainthood," at least for a while. The Þjóðviljinn men felt that salvation had come from an unexpected direction, and Svavar wrote a front-page story across the full width of the page quoting my speech, and the paper's editorial was also devoted to it.

In my speech I recounted the resolutions of the Progressive Party that had called for the departure of the army ever since 1953. I then said that the provisions of the government's policy agreement were fully consistent with the party's policy, and that "the question was only how it would leave and over how long a time." If the coalition parties could reach a joint conclusion, I considered that little stood in the way of requiring the Americans to accept it — or else terminating the 1951 defense agreement. This should be done as soon as possible.

My position was built on the policy of neutrality that I had inherited from my father. I considered it right that there should be no army in Iceland in peacetime, and although it was often disputed when it was legitimate to speak of peacetime, I said in my speech that the prospects for peace in our part of the world were far better in 1973 than in 1949, when the North Atlantic Alliance (Atlantshafsbandalagið) considered it unnecessary to have an army here and the Americans gave Icelanders commitments that no military bases would be requested here unless war threatened. I set out in six numbered
points the arguments for why the state of the world had "greatly improved." My arguments were these:

1. The Vietnam War is over, at least the direct participation of the Americans. 2. Nowhere in the world is there now a serious armed conflict. 3. The great powers are now working jointly for a resolution of the dispute in the Middle East. 4. Relations between the Americans and the Russians, and between the Americans and the Chinese, have greatly improved, and this is evident in numerous areas. 5. Some progress is being made toward an agreement on limited disarmament. 6. The Iron Curtain has been lowered with increased trade between the two German states and the agreement between West Germany and Russia.

My position was also shaped by my fear that generations would grow up without ever knowing that the country could be free of an army. I feared that a military base in Iceland would become a natural part of existence. That, I believed, would dull the nation's consciousness of independence and our sense of being a nation. It was also uppermost in my mind that Icelanders were financially dependent on the military presence, and that considerations quite other than the army's defensive role would come to form the basis of discussion about its presence in this country. This, I believe, has unfortunately come to pass. Although the economic influence of the army is much smaller than before, it is more prominent in the debate than ever before that the army cannot be allowed to leave because of employment in Suðurnes. I felt this most clearly when I ran for election in Reykjanes in 1987.

My speech was certainly not well received everywhere. I nevertheless published it, little changed, as an article in Tíminn a month after the meeting, in mid-January 1974. At that time a committee was at work in the parliamentary group of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) that was to make proposals on this matter. They were presented and approved in the parliamentary group barely a week later and then in the party's executive board. The leadership's proposals were in two parts. On the one hand there was a plan for the withdrawal of the army, and on the other, provisions for the arrangement of defense matters after its departure. Withdrawal from the North Atlantic Alliance, NATO, was not envisaged. I was among those who recommended entering into talks with the other coalition parties on this basis.
Elías Snæland, chairman of the SUF, argued for a harder stance and for tighter time limits to be set regarding the withdrawal.

While defense matters were under consideration in the party's institutions, they were no less a topic of discussion among people generally. Supporters of the army founded the association "Varið land" (Defended Country). Opponents of the military base made much of the claim that half of the 800 attendees of "the troops" at the founding meeting at Hótel Saga had refused to support the message of "Varið land" and had instead signed a demand for the departure of the army. A few days later, the Student Council of the University of Iceland failed to get anyone from the ranks of the school's teachers or students to argue the case for the military base at a meeting that was to be held on the matter, even though speakers were solicited over the radio.

At the end of January, the Campaign Against the Military Base (Samtök herstöðvaandstæðinga) held a meeting at which "around or over 3000 people" crowded into Háskólabíó and urged the coalition parties to stand by the provisions of the coalition agreement. A great many had to be turned away.

Four days after this meeting, however, 32 "supporters of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn)" went to see Ólafur Jóhannesson and delivered a declaration urging caution in defense matters. It was signed by 170 party members from all over the country. Among them were Alfreð Þorsteinsson and Tómas Karlsson, editor of Tíminn. The SUF leadership reacted furiously to this initiative and aimed its barbs not least at Tómas and his editorial work, which they called "the occupation of Tíminn."

Probably neither of these groups was pleased with the party's resolution. On its basis, nonetheless, agreement was reached among the coalition parties on a framework for negotiations. The development of the territorial waters dispute had engendered an atmosphere in which the government had no choice but to work toward the withdrawal of the army. It is interesting to read about the Independence Party's (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) reactions to the government's policy. They show better than most things that even the staunchest supporters of the defense cooperation hardly dared to go against the demand for a country without an army. The Independence Party's resolution states, among other things, that it is proper:

That Icelanders keep the country's defense and security affairs under constant review and form their own independent assessment of necessary measures, take the initiative automatically as to what steps need to be taken at any given time and when it is safe for the entire defense force to depart from the country. Until then, the defense force should be at the minimum that is safe for security reasons, and care should be taken that its presence not have national, social, and financial effects that are harmful to the Icelandic nation and make it dependent on the defense force in one way or another, beyond the security role that it performs.

Following the government's resolutions, its policy was presented to the ambassador of the United States, and in April it was put forward at a formal negotiating meeting between the two countries. A reply from the United States government never came.
An Unavoidable Reckoning

Even though movement had come into the military question, an unbridgeable split had long since become a fact within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). It is hard to say which weighed more heavily in that regard, the role of the Möðruvellingar or that of Ólafur Jóhannesson. Following the meeting tour around the country, I had had conversations with various people from the ranks of the radicals. I thought I heard in them a conciliatory tone and a sincere desire to lay the disputes in the party to rest by agreement. The same voices were heard widely around the country. The party's constituency assemblies had, one after another, passed resolutions urging reconciliation. The people of the East Fjords led the way, and it is not unlikely that Eysteinn had arranged matters there. The central committee of the SUF had passed resolutions to the same effect.

At a meeting of the executive board of the Progressive Party on 1 March 1974, I put forward a proposal to send a special conciliation committee of the executive board to talks with the SUF leadership, as the constituency assemblies had urged. Eysteinn Jónsson spoke next and supported the proposal. Ólafur Jóhannesson, however, reacted in the worst possible way and declared the resolutions in the constituencies "a vote of no confidence in himself." He rejected outright the idea of a conciliation committee and said he had always been ready to talk with young Progressives "one or more." This harsh reaction surprised Eysteinn no less than me. He said it was clear that the chairman and the secretary had not coordinated their views, and declared his full confidence in Ólafur Jóhannesson. I withdrew my proposal.

When these events took place, a central committee meeting was close at hand. At it, all compromises were rejected. This surprised no one after the outcome of the meeting of 1 March. After that meeting, part of the Möðruvellingar had begun talks with other parties with cooperation or the formation of an electoral alliance as the goal. Among other things, they were in talks with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), where cooperation and a joint ticket in the 1974 local elections were discussed. The People's Alliance offered the Möðruvellingar the fourth seat on its list in Reykjavík and "possibly an addition to the People's Alliance's name in the presentation of the list." The offer was rejected. In fact, I learned during the preparation of this book that Ólafur Ragnar had already in 1972 held personal talks with Magnús Kjartansson, a minister of the People's Alliabout
Ólafur joining the party. Magnús, however, seems not to have been able to offer him sufficiently good terms in the new position.

The outcome in 1974 was that the Möðruvellir movement people (Möðruvellingar) and the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) came together in an electoral alliance which then negotiated with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) about running the J-list in the city council elections. Once this was settled, I put forward in the party's executive board a motion for a resolution stating that those Möðruvellingar who had entered into cooperation with other parties "were of no concern to the party." At the executive board's next meeting it was approved that these individuals should be regarded as having left the party and could therefore no longer "hold positions of trust on its behalf." Making this resolution known in the media was not a particularly pleasant task for me, though it was my duty.

The J-list of the Social Democratic Party, the Union of Liberals and Leftists, and the Möðruvellir movement suffered a crushing defeat in the 1974 city council elections and received only 3,034 votes. That was less than the Union and the Social Democratic Party had each received four years earlier. Their city councillors dropped from two to one. With Ólafur Ragnar and others who took seats on the J-list, a large group of talented young people disappeared from the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) — people who by rights ought to have been in the party's leadership ranks. At the same time, several radical farmers who had supported the Möðruvellingar resigned from the party. This group lacked neither ability nor good ideas, but rather, first and foremost, patience and greater prudence.

Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson joined the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) some time after these clashes, as is well known, and was elected to the Althing in 1978. Accompanying him were, among others, Baldur Óskarsson and Eyjólfur Eysteinsson. A certain group who counted themselves among the Möðruvellingar returned to the Progressive Party as time went by, for example Gunnlaugur Sigmundsson, former member of the Althing, and Már Pétursson. Elías Snæland Jónsson took up journalism, was for a long time at Tíminn and DV, and is now editor of Dagur. Like a great many others from this group, he largely withdrew from party politics.

Most Progressives were ready, during the Restoration-government years, to agree that the opponents of conservatism needed to be united. These voices were especially prominent after the 1967 elections, when hopes that the party would return to power had been dashed. After the formation of the left-wing government in 1971 this task was not as pressing in the eyes of a large group, but at the same time the fervor of the young men doubled. As a result, support for their views declined and the backing of many of the older members dwindled. Eysteinn and the others who had stood behind them suffered the most painful

disappointments when things boiled over. By then only the very most radical remained among the supporters of the Möðruvellingar — left-leaning farmers and hard-line opponents of the military base. The unification question was, to my mind, the one issue on which it was impossible to reach substantive consensus within the party. In truth, the split sprang from that. The struggles over defense matters sowed distrust and fanned the flames. In the end, though, it was probably the personal ambition of impatient individuals that proved decisive, along with Ólafur Jóhannesson's limited willingness to reconcile.

It is hard to guess how things would have gone if Ólafur Ragnar had continued working within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). I actually consider it very likely that he would have achieved considerable advancement — a seat in the Althing was just around the corner, and it is not unlikely that he would have become ministerial material for the party at about the same time as I did. He would, however, have had to transform himself to become party chairman. That goal he probably would not have reached, any more than in the SUF, where he was considered too impetuous for formal leadership. His rhetoric appalled a large share of the party members, radical and revolutionary as he was. He was careless in his choice of words and offended many, who then waited for a chance to pay him back in kind, with interest.

I myself long held out hopes that Ólafur Ragnar would continue to side with the Progressives, and I hoped he would settle down and mellow. I believed the best way to achieve that was to get him into the Althing, and the same was true of various comrades of his whose loss I regretted. But this could not be brought about. Ólafur Jóhannesson's opposition was far too firm for that, and the fervor of the young far too great. It fell to me to run the errands of the party leadership, both in bringing Ólafur Ragnar into the party at Eysteinn's request and, in the end, pushing him back out of it on Ólafur Jóhannesson's authority barely ten years later.
A Historic Government Collapse

By the middle of the left-wing government's term, the earnings of the industries were good and the employment situation excellent, in part because of the government's efforts. But although peace seemed to prevail in the labor market, things were seething beneath the surface. When the wage agreements expired in 1973, all hell broke loose. Negotiations went with difficulty and widespread strikes ensued. The government was hobbled in dealing with the labor movement, since the ministers of the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) were on one side of the table. Björn Jónsson had succeeded Hannibal Valdimarsson in the ministerial seat. Björn was president of the Icelandic Federation of Labour (ASÍ) and Hannibal its former president. It was mainly on the other labormovement'
s other leaders that one could tell they would rather wait for the government to legislate wages in the country than enter into normal negotiations with the employers.

Other ministers in the government exerted themselves greatly in these negotiations, most notably Lúðvík Jósepsson and Halldór E. Sigurðsson. They sat over the negotiators and "contributed helpfully," as it was called. Agreements were reached quickly and once again provided for far greater wage increases than the national economy could bear. To respond to the situation, Ólafur Jóhannesson presented in the cabinet a draft of measures to counter the foreseeable inflation. The measures were discussed thoroughly in the Progressive Party's parliamentary group and enjoyed general support there. The same, I believe, could be said of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). The proposals were therefore put into the form of a legislative bill to be laid before the Althing.

With the bill, the greater part of the negotiated wage increases was in effect withdrawn. The leadership of the Icelandic Federation of Labour (ASÍ) within the government naturally could not accept that. Magnús Torfi Ólafsson, the minister of education, was the only member of the Union's parliamentary group who I felt showed full responsibility. Björn Jónsson turned against the measures at the last moment, as recounted earlier. He subsequently parted ways with the government, and with that the majority was broken. Ólafur Jóhannesson reported at a parliamentary group meeting on May 6, 1974, that the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) had withdrawn its support for the government. Earlier that day the Union's parliamentary group had approved a call for the prime minister to resign.

Ólafur said there were only two options: to ask to be relieved of office and receive a mandate to form an all-party government, or to dissolve parliament and call elections. At the meeting it was approved to authorize Ólafur to attempt to form a government.

These were busy and eventful days. In every corner of the Althing building, members put their heads together and read the cards. We Progressives feared that a new Restoration-style coalition with Hannibal's participation was in the making. The prime minister, however, held all the trumps and kept them close to his chest. Ólafur immediately began talks with the chairmen of the other parties. The result was nil. The Independence Party members hemmed and hawed and said they needed more time. Gylfi Þ. Gíslason held that the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) lacked authorization from its members to form a government. Hannibal demanded that the government resign before the formation of a new government would be considered. That did nothing to reduce people's distrust.

Two days later Ólafur's conclusion was that there was no basis for forming a national unity government. The fear of a new Restoration coalition with the Union's support was real as well. Hannibal smiled to the right, and various people let it

be understood that such a government would not be far from their liking. Ólafur announced at a parliamentary group meeting on the afternoon of May 8 that he considered dissolving parliament to be the only feasible course. He also reported that he had already requested authorization for dissolution from the President of Iceland. The President had indeed granted that request. It was well into the night when an "announcement from the prime minister" was placed on the Althing's agenda. Just as it came up, a motion of no confidence in the government arrived, signed by 31 of the 60 members then sitting in the Althing. That motion was never taken up for consideration. The prime minister took the floor and dissolved parliament.
The Beginning of the "Progressive Decade"

In this storm of battle it seemed to me that the story of the 1958 left-wing government was repeating itself. The labor leaders and the labor movement are often their own worst enemy, unfortunately. The left-wing government was a labor-friendly government, but it was not treated fairly in the ranks of the labor leaders, who tried to serve two masters. The left-wing government's will to improve the conditions of workers and other wage earners was nonetheless unmistakable, and indeed so strong that the task was undertaken too quickly: devaluations followed on the heels of wage increases, and inflation ate up the gain in purchasing power. I was and remain of the opinion that slow and steady progress is the surest way to build up purchasing power — not upheavals.
Living standards were supposed to improve in step with the building up of the trawler fleet, industry, and other economic activity.

The improvements in living conditions that proved most lasting consisted not least in strengthened rights for wage earners and development in the fields of social affairs and public services. During the left-wing government's tenure a major push was made in education, and the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands) grew considerably. New student loan legislation was enacted, and health clinics and hospitals began to be built all around the country. The policy was resolutely pursued that the country's citizens should be entitled to the same services no matter where in the country they lived. We classified regional policy as a social matter, and of it we Progressives were proudest. Regional affairs were tackled firmly for the first time in those years.

I completely disagree with the view that the development that took place in the countryside in the 1970s was characterized first and foremost by waste. In those years, for the first and only time, we succeeded in slowing and halting the flight of people from the countryside. Conservatism had no comeback in these areas, except to a small degree.

The label "the Progressive Decade" originated with opponents of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), who wanted to associate inflation with the party. I often rose to the defense and said that the nation had built up its productive capacity in those years and that this had become the foundation of the prosperity of recent years in Iceland.

I think there is something to this. It does not occur to me, however, to belittle the negative effects of inflation. It brought not only waste; the sense of value grew dull and moral fiber in business dealings withered. Inflation was, unfortunately, often a companion of periods of boom and development in Iceland.

I do not mind that the 1970s are named after the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), even though various things could have gone better in the management of the economy and in relations between the government and the labor movement. In that decade Iceland saw some of the greatest economic growth of the century, 6.5% on average; unemployment was unknown, and the nation's fisheries jurisdiction expanded from 12 miles to 200. Capital formation was also enormous, and investments were made in much of the economy's essential infrastructure. Development of this kind had for the most part been held in fetters during the Restoration era.
Bjarni in the Bank

Because the 1974 elections came on so suddenly, there was no time to hold a primary in the Westfjords any more than elsewhere in the country. I did, however, go on campaign trips, and as usual the electoral rolls were carefully gone over in every settlement. We would sit down with the party's canvassers or men familiar with the locality and mark voters on each farm according to which party they were thought to vote for. Most important were the so-called "uncertain lambs," the floating vote that shifted between parties from one election to the next. I concentrated on that group, for there the most was to be gained.

When the candidate list was decided, I believe it was undisputed that I would run in first place. Changes occurred, on the other hand, in the next seats. Bjarni Guðbjörnsson decided to retire from the Althing. The second seat was filled by Gunnlaugur Finnsson, farmer and teacher, from Hvilft in Önundarfjörður. Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson filled the third seat. I was at peace with Bjarni's departure, though it was clear to me that his seat would be hard to fill. The party has probably never been as strong in Ísafjörður as in Bjarni's time. He was beloved by everyone. In 1967 I had in many ways preferred working with him over various others who were mentioned as possible candidates out west.

Bjarni's reluctance to travel and attend meetings weighed heavily as time went on. A certain tension had arisen between us in connection with the decision to call a primary in 1968. Bjarni was not particularly taken with it. Moreover, he could not be persuaded to hold meetings in the constituency before the primary. I brushed that aside and set out on my own. Once in the Althing,

Bjarni rarely felt he could get away from home. He was not much for going farm to farm and meeting voters, and I had no less trouble getting him to organize with me the necessary meetings in the constituency.

In the end I could not be bothered to wait, and in consultation with the local people I called meetings in the summer of 1973. Then Bjarni exploded. I particularly remember a telephone call in which I expressed the opinion that I found him rather lazy about traveling around the constituency and that I feared he kept little contact with the voters out west. Bjarni gave me small thanks for my candor. Our conversation ended with him slamming down the phone.
I was not used to having the phone slammed down on me, and I wrote him a letter so as not to give him the chance to repeat the performance.

In the letter I said there was little reason for suspicion even though I was in constant contact with my supporters in the constituency. That was something I had always made an effort to do. The local people, however, decided themselves when meetings were called, and they were rarely tailor-made to my needs. I may have been rather cross with Bjarni when the letter was written, and I was blunt in my choice of words:

To tell the truth, I think there would be few meetings and little party activity in the Westfjords constituency if we waited for you. Nor am I going to do so. I will try to hold my own as a member of the Althing and work as energetically for the constituency as I can, and keep as good contact with the voters as I possibly can, both through meetings and through conversations with individuals, without asking anyone's permission.
I do not know whether Bjarni had by then already decided to leave the Althing. I made it entirely clear to him, however, that in that matter he had my full support:

To tell the truth, I think you ought to think seriously about these matters and start showing some willingness to work in the constituency, if you have in mind to continue serving as its member of the Althing.

Discord of this kind was not unique in the Westfjords. Between Matthías Bjarnason and Þorvaldur Garðar there prevailed at best an armed truce, in between the fierce battles they fought over the ordering of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) list. Matthías describes Þorvaldur in only one place in his memoirs, and in these words: "Þorvaldur lacked a sense of humor, but he had a strong voice." Otherwise he is mentioned only in connection with bitter

disputes among the Independence Party men in the constituency over the ordering of lists and primaries. I, on the other hand, got along quite well with both of them, though Þorvaldur was perhaps more to my liking. We became good acquaintances. Þorvaldur and I, of course, clashed no less in debates. Unlike Matthías he was guarded in his words, and our exchanges of opinion were never ill-natured. The disagreement between Bjarni and me, however, ran nowhere near as deep as that between Þorvaldur and Matthías. We were in step on most things, for Bjarni was the greatest of gentlemen and ambitious on behalf of the constituency.
The Trials of the Social Democrats

In 1974 Sighvatur Björgvinsson and Vilmundur Gylfason held the top seats on the list of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) in the Westfjords. They were young and ambitious and intended to claim a large share in the elections. The story goes, however, that they were rather hasty on their first trip. They came driving from Reykjavík. In Gilsfjörður they saw a handsome farm and agreed to begin their canvassing tour there. The farmer of the place received them with every courtesy, and they launched into long speeches to convince him of the merit of their policies and the unquestionable virtues of the Social Democratic Party. They thought they were getting a good hearing, for the farmer was in the merriest of moods. When he said goodbye, it was likewise with great cordiality. He praised them for their presentation and said: "That was well done, boys.

The only pity is that the Westfjords constituency doesn't begin until beyond the brook." And then he laughed uproariously. This was Jóhannes, the farmer at Kleifar, and the story instantly flew around all the districts. I recounted it at more than one campaign meeting and cited it as evidence of how little those Social Democrats knew the constituency. Sighvatur took my jabs badly and spent a great deal of time explaining this incident, saying the Kleifar farmer was a good acquaintance of his whom he had not wanted to cheat of a visit. A large part of Sighvatur's speaking time went into this backpedaling, and my purpose was thereby of course achieved.

There was no more peace over the Social Democratic Party's list than in the other parties in the Westfjords. Despite the loyal support of his father, Björgvin Sighvatsson, Sighvatur did not enjoy undisputed confidence, according to what is said in the biography of Vilmundur Gylfason. In the wake of this, Vilmundur was called in from the south. He had by then already become known throughout the country for his television programs, and he agreed to stand. At the ordering of the list, however, Sighvatur is said to have shunted Vilmundur in behind himself by trickery. He refused to run unless he was in first place, and it is said that Vilmundur was heavy-hearted over it.
The campaign meetings were traditional, hard-fought and well attended, and much was let fly. Matthías was among the most hard-hitting of men, as so often before. He

enjoyed telling stories, and he did not think it any the worse if they were risqué. Sometimes, though, Matthías flagged as the meetings wore on. He was plagued by a persistent headache that came in bouts. I had come to know the symptoms, for when the pains were at their worst Matthías would sit holding his head between his hands. At the very worst he even had to step out of the building to let it pass. I sometimes looked in on him by the wall of the house when matters stood thus.

When I met Vilmundur Gylfason for the first time at a campaign meeting, I could of course not have suspected that I would one day balk at handing him the keys of a ministry at a change of government five years later. Before it came to that, a great deal had in fact happened. On first acquaintance Vilmundur struck me as a sharply intelligent man, well versed in most fields and one who argued his case firmly. I found him often eloquent and witty in his criticism, with which he was in fact unsparing. He often reminded me of his father Gylfi, both in determination and in intensity. He spoke rapidly, thought quickly, and the manner of speech was the same. No one could mistake that Vilmundur was an angry young man. I liked the lad, and I do not recall that we ever clashed badly.

The Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) again fielded candidates in the Westfjords in these elections. This time the candidacy was without Hannibal's backing, except that his son Jón Baldvin occupied the second seat on the list. The top man of the Union was Karvel Pálmason, who had followed Hannibal into the Althing three years earlier. Vilmundur and the Social Democrats' fourth man, Bárður Halldórsson, are in fact said to have played Jón Baldvin just as rough a trick as Sigurður Bjarnason once played on his father with the pencil. They constantly flung taunts and remarks at him while his speech was in progress, without the audience hearing. When this had gone on for a while, Jón Baldvin's patience ran out and he turned his speech upon the pair with a torrent of abuse.
The people at the meeting did not know what had hit them, any more than on the earlier occasion.

At the end of the election campaign out west it so happened that Vilmundur was nowhere to be seen, and he did not speak at the final meeting in Ísafjörður, where the top men of the lists otherwise all appeared. Malicious rumors about his nocturnal wanderings are said to have thrown him off balance. He wanted to trace them to a disgruntled faction within his own party. He was not accustomed to the Westfjords manner, and perhaps his reaction may be cited as testimony to the fierce temperament that dwelt within him.

In Vilmundur's place there spoke at the meeting the Social Democrats' fourth man, mentioned above. That was in fact Bárður Halldórsson, who has since become known for his work for the Association for National Ownership (Samtök um þjóðareign). I cannot possibly have
remembered what opinion I had of his conduct, if I ever had any view on it at all.
Bad Results but a Long-Awaited Renewal

The elections were a disappointment to us Progressives. We did, admittedly, keep an unchanged number of parliamentary seats and had 17 members elected. Everywhere, however, we lost support, with the sole exception of Reykjavík. There our support increased slightly. I had hoped that in the West Fjords we would win back the support that Hannibal had plucked from us three years earlier. Those hopes were dashed. Karvel and Jón Baldvin managed to hold on to a much larger share of it than we had expected; 14.2 percent, which was far above the national average of the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtökin), which was 4.6 percent. In the West Fjords constituency the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) fell from 30.3 to 28.6 percent of the vote.
The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) had thereby become the largest party of the constituency for the first time since the 1959 elections.

I was worried by this outcome and wrote a letter to fifty of the party's local officers in the constituency asking for their views on its causes. That letter was the beginning of my regular mailings to this group, in which I discussed the political outlook, individual issues and the affairs of the constituency. In this first letter I posed six numbered questions about everything from the Progressives' publicity and meeting practices to the Independence men's stranglehold on the West Fjords banking system, which some said was the reason for their gain in support. A great many replies came in, of all shades. The radicals lamented that the army had not been sent out of the country. Various of the older people said they had missed Halldór of Kirkjuból in the second seat.

Others thought that the split of the Möðruvellingar had damaged the party in the countryside, and that was doubtless correct. It was likewise clear to me that many had been disappointed that the left-wing government did not sit out the electoral term, and in economic matters the results aimed at when the government was formed had not been achieved. I felt we were paying dearly for the exuberance of promises in the coalition agreement.

Before the elections the party leadership made every effort to call new people to service. It was clear to everyone that renewal was urgently needed. Not least for that reason, I felt the loss keenly of the various people who had joined Ólafur Ragnar's company and left the party. I argued in closed meetings that an attempt should be made to win them back with good places on the Progressive Party's candidate lists. That was tried in some constituencies. This could, however, put some of these individuals in a peculiar position, as they were engaged in talks with other parties about their own candidacies. Már Pétursson has related that

it happened that individuals from their group received offers from the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) by telephone while they were sitting across from representatives of the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna) at negotiating meetings about their candidate lists.

When parliament convened, the transformation in the Progressive Party had become a fact. We kept seventeen members of parliament, and of those, seven were newcomers. Without doubt many of these seats would have fallen to those leaders of the Progressive Party youth movement (SUF) who had departed. Friðgeir Björnsson, Elías Snæland Jónsson, Már Pétursson and Baldur Óskarsson would all have acquitted themselves well as representatives of the party. Ólafur Ragnar indeed no less, though some had long thought it self-evident that he would move on to other fishing grounds.

The exodus of the Möðruvellingar has been called "political mass suicide." Perhaps it may be cited as a sign of the Möðruvellingar's mistake or impatience that four of the seven who took seats in parliament for the Progressive Party for the first time after these elections were to become government ministers. These were Halldór Ásgrímsson, Páll Pétursson, Jón Helgason and Tómas Árnason. Few of the four had been prominent in party work, and only Tómas in any way comparable to many of the Möðruvellingar. I considered these new recruits a great asset. Halldór and Tómas were examples of solid men who lived in Reykjavík but had roots reaching back to the countryside. The others were true rural men.

Halldór was fetched from the University, where he was a lecturer in business administration. He became the Progressive Party's third member of parliament for the East. It was immediately clear to us that Halldór would be a powerful spokesman and leadership material. He concentrated on tax matters and was very useful there. It took me some time, however, to get used to how often Halldór wears a heavy brow and how hard he finds it to take criticism.

Jón Helgason is brilliantly gifted and extraordinarily tireless. He has a high forehead and a sharp nose, a long face, and it is easy to picture him in a clergyman's vestments. He has a calm demeanor and is at the same time one of the most sincere and guileless men I have ever known, a true gentleman. Jón never promoted his own interests but spoke for the countryside and for agriculture in every matter. He was a mathematical genius in secondary school but decided to take over his parents' farm at Seglbúðir instead of pursuing university studies. This surprised many. At times I sensed a trace of wistfulness in Jón because of this. I know he would have made an outstanding professor.

Páll Pétursson always counted himself among the radical wing of the party. He shared common ground with the Möðruvellingar on many issues and to some extent came into parliament in place of his brother, who a few years earlier would have been considered

a more likely parliamentary prospect. I was not as radical as Páll, but a good understanding nonetheless quickly developed between us. For a time we were often on opposite sides, as I felt Páll marched at the head of the column of reactionaries in agricultural matters. Later I often supported Páll vigorously in the parliamentary group when various people had it in for him. Páll's eloquence unquestionably counts among his chief personal traits, and his tongue frequently loosens when he is in an unusually good or bad mood. Páll is never more serious in manner than when he has a witticism on his lips, and he then draws out his words in his own particular way.

Tómas Árnason I liked immediately, and our cooperation was always excellent. He was usually well turned out and nimble in his movements, having been a great sportsman all his life. He is an able golfer, and more than a few afternoon tasks had to yield to that noble sport when the weather favored the outdoors.

Tómas was not a politician of passion, but he got on well and was beloved by everyone. He is a reliable party man, a good comrade, and never ran off on his own. Tómas began as a field agent of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) in Akureyri. After he moved to Reykjavík he took an active part in party work there. He was one of those young men who grew up under Eysteinn's wing. Some believed Tómas was destined to checkmate me in the race for a leadership role in the party as time went on.

When Eysteinn stepped down as chairman in 1968 he was determined to make Tómas the party's treasurer. Sigurjón Guðmundsson had held the office for 22 years. Sigurjón was a gentleman of the old school and one of my father's closest colleagues and friends in the Progressive Party. When Sigurjón got wind of how the foxes were being skinned, he declared that he would not stand. He supported, however, Halldór E. Sigurðsson, member of parliament, against Tómas in his place. With his candidacy Halldór wished to show Sigurjón respect for his work, for he thought it worth some sacrifice "so that the man of honor Sigurjón would not have to depart with hurt feelings." Eysteinn worked resolutely for Tómas, and Halldór lost. There were no repercussions.

Tómas became the Progressive Party's "commissar" in the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun) in 1972 and continued in that job even though he took a seat in parliament. I do not remember whose idea that arrangement was, but in the party some remarked that Tómas owed his parliamentary seat to Eysteinn. Tómas took the party's second seat in the East. Kristján Ingólfsson, alternate member of parliament and school principal at Eskifjörður, had an explanation for it. He said that Eysteinn and Tómas had skied together a good deal. On one of these trips Eysteinn had fallen and broken his leg, and Tómas had carried him on his back down to the settlements. For that reason, he

been given the parliamentary seat. Whatever the truth of this, it is at least certain that Eysteinn had a great say in the composition of the list in the East. To this story it should be added that it is said that when Jónas of Hrifla heard it, he blurted out: "Oh, he might as well have left him lying there."

Tómas got the nickname Tommi on the Carpet when he was chairman of the Defense Affairs Committee (varnarmálanefnd), which I have mentioned before. It came about because he procured a splendid carpet for the floor of his office. This aroused both gossip and envy, since most things were rationed in Icelandic society. He thus got a reputation for holding firmly to his own. That quality of Tómas's served well when he became finance minister. He was, in my judgment, a very good finance minister — cautious, careful and thrifty. Indeed, Tómas comes by it honestly. He is of the Hánefsstaðir line.
Chapter Six

In the Althing (Alþingi) a stalemate arose after the elections of June 30, 1974. The governing parties had half of the members of parliament elected, thirty of sixty, and the government was considered fallen. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), on the other hand, was the unambiguous winner of the elections. Geir Hallgrímsson, chairman of the Independence Party, was therefore the first to receive the mandate to form a government, as was natural. His attempt failed.

In the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) there was a firm will to form a left-wing government with the participation of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). The Social Democrats, however, had only five members elected and thus did not improve their position after the drubbing of four years earlier. The Social Democratic Party seemed close to vanishing from the scene. On July 22 Ólafur Jóhannesson received the mandate to form a government. At a meeting of the parliamentary group the next day he proposed that the group's executive board assist him. It consisted of Einar Ágústsson, Halldór E. Sigurðsson and Þórarinn Þórarinsson. At the same time it was agreed to assign me, Tómas Árnason and Stefán Valgeirsson to examine "matters in connection with negotiations on forming a government," as it is phrased in the minutes of the parliamentary group.

Ólafur Jóhannesson at once began an attempt to form a left-wing government with the Social Democratic Party and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), along with the remnants of the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna). They had brought only two men into parliament. On August 7 Ólafur presented a framework for a policy agreement in the parliamentary group. He had drafted it entirely on his own and presented it in confidence. This was typical of his working methods. Afterwards, those of us on the policy committee received the draft for review and made various comments. I reported on them at a meeting of the parliamentary group two days later.
At the start of the left-wing talks, negotiations broke down that had

been going on in parliament over the election of the speaker of the united Althing. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) became isolated, while Ólafur Jóhannesson worked for an agreement among the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) on the election of Gylfi Þ. Gíslason. Such stirrings are often said to be a sign of a likely government formation. Ólafur's support for Gylfi need not have come as a surprise. Earlier in the summer, overtures had been made to the Social Democratic Party when the Progressives worked for Gylfi's election to preside over the ceremonial session held to commemorate 1100 years of settlement in Iceland. On that, too, all the parties came together except the Independence Party.

The Þingvellir session was held in glorious weather. I had a movie camera that I had recently acquired and tried to capture as much as possible on film. We members of parliament were, among other things, to march in procession down Almannagjá to the Althing's ceremonial session on the plains. I felt I had to get shots of the whole company, so I disobeyed the speaker's instructions and ran up onto a rock by one wall of the gorge. I could see that Gylfi was displeased when I could not be persuaded to join the group until I had filmed the entire procession on its march. The ceremonial session itself struck me as rather lacking in drama.

The People's Alliance dragged its feet for a long time before supporting Gylfi for speaker, voted for a Progressive in the first round and did not give way until the last moment. The Progressives found little conciliatory spirit in that. Many also felt that Lúðvík Jósepsson, chairman of the People's Alliance, showed indifference and disrespect toward the talks. He was salmon fishing east in Vopnafjörður for a large part of the time the talks lasted. Svava Jakobsdóttir sat in the negotiating meetings in his place.

At a meeting of the Progressive Party's parliamentary group on August 12, 1974, Ólafur Jóhannesson reported that his conclusion, after the left-wing parties' talks earlier that day, was that further attempts to form a government with them were pointless. This was a great disappointment to me. I did not doubt that Ólafur believed he had tried this route to the utmost. I would probably have tried longer, though. Ólafur, however, always had his own way of doing things and judged in private what possibilities the situation held. I had often heard him express the view that the People's Alliance and the Social Democratic Party could not work together. No doubt his assessment was correct, like so much else. Perhaps it showed most clearly in the parties' coalition in 1978 and 1979.

I think that in reality both of these parties were split in their attitude toward a left-wing government. Their disputes sometimes recalled the bickering and squabbling of a divorced couple, with those opposed to cooperation stoking the fire. After the break came, loud disputes erupted between them over which of the parties bore the heavier responsibility for the fact that no left-wing government was formed. Neither of them

wanted to bear responsibility for that outcome. So fierce did that dispute become that more than a year after the government formation was over and done with, Kjartan Ólafsson, member of parliament for the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) in the West Fjords, summoned me to an open meeting at Ísafjörður where his party was to be washed clean of the Social Democratic Party's (Alþýðuflokkurinn) mudslinging. I did not do so, however, but said:

While these attempts were under way, I had conversations with a great many men whom I know within the People's Alliance, among others with Kjartan Ólafsson. I am convinced that within the People's Alliance there were men who were prepared to go to great lengths to see a new left-wing government formed, but I also soon saw that within the Alliance there was a large group of men who did everything they could to prevent such a government from being formed.

In the west it was often remarked that Kjartan was a shade to the left of Stalin. Some indeed added that Stalin had nonetheless been somewhat more liberal. Such quips had their origin with Matthías Bjarnason. Kjartan was, on the contrary, one of those who detested Stalin. Kjartan wields a good pen and was a fair propagandist. Those talents of his, however, were no more put to use settling accounts with Stalinism in the pages of Þjóðviljinn, where he was editor, than within the People's Alliance. There, those who stood furthest to the left had the upper hand. The party's newly published platform stated clearly that its policy was social revolution. About the attitude of this part of the People's Alliance I put it this way:

The communists considered [sitting in government] incompatible with their future ideals of seizing power in this country. They realize that various measures would have to be taken which might perhaps be somewhat unpopular. That they did not want. They know no responsibility, no obligation, to work first and foremost for the interests of the nation. They value the party's advantage above the nation's advantage.

In the government-formation talks, this group within the People's Alliance put forward a non-negotiable demand for the departure of the army, which it knew full well the Social Democratic Party would not accept. I suspected that they did not trust themselves to tackle the economic difficulties that stared us in the face. This outcome seems to be an embarrassing subject within the People's Alliance. From the party's history, recorded by Óskar Guðmundsson, one is apparently to understand that no left-wing government came about in 1974 because the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the Independence men had already agreed on forming a government. That, I know, is not correct.

Of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), in truth, much the same story could be told from these talks. The party was still licking its wounds after the "Restoration" (viðreisn) rout and had only five members of parliament. It also mattered that there was little love lost between Ólafur Jóhannesson and Björn Jónsson. Björn had long stood close to the Social Democratic Party and joined its ranks before the elections. Many believed that the Social Democratic Party's most unyielding demands came from Björn. Among other things, it was demanded that there be close consultation with public employees and the Federation of Labour (Alþýðusambandið) about the coalition agreement. Björn was president of the Federation of Labour.

The experience of the left-wing government's demise at the Federation of Labour congress in 1958 meant that a clearer message could hardly have been sent to the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) leadership that there was no interest in cooperating in government. That government blew apart because the Federation (ASÍ) had a veto over its economic measures under provisions in the coalition agreement.

Ólafur Jóhannesson was not the sort to try to row past such a reef. He sought other fishing grounds. A coalition of the Progressive Party and the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) was the only option for forming a government that could hope for the support of a majority of the Althing (Alþingi).
Into Bed with the Conservatives

After acquainting himself with the state of affairs, Kristján Eldjárn gave Ólafur a continued mandate to form a government. Ólafur began talks with the Independence Party. After a week's work, a draft policy agreement had been produced and was laid before the parliamentary group. It had been prepared by Einar Ágústsson and Geir Hallgrímsson and was well received. Few, however, liked the idea that the party was heading into a coalition with the conservatives. The Progressive Party had regarded itself as the chief adversary of the Independence Party for eighteen years. Now the conservatives were the only option. At the meeting many took the floor, and all laid heavy emphasis on Ólafur Jóhannesson becoming prime minister in such a government. I spoke first and argued that anything else would be very difficult for the party.
I said I regretted that agreement had not been reached with the left-wing parties.

The policy agreement remained under discussion at daily meetings of the parliamentary group. In its final version it provided, among other things, for quite radical economic measures, the extension of the fisheries jurisdiction to 200 miles, and a massive strengthening of the Regional Development Fund (Byggðasjóður) of the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun). Rural members of parliament from both parties had come together on that. It was also clearly stipulated that the army was not on its way out of the country, though talks were envisaged on individual points of the defense agreement. Little of this caused real disputes in the parliamentary group. Defense matters were, however, discussed to some extent, and the parliamentary group issued a special
statement on their account when the government formation was otherwise complete. It said:

The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) states that the party's policy on defense matters is unchanged from the last government, but considers that, since the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) cannot accept any adjustments to defense matters other than those set out in the defense section of the coalition agreement, the Progressive Party must for the time being accept that its policy will not be carried through.
In hindsight it may be that Einar Ágústsson found it easy to negotiate the defense matters with the Independence Party and Geir Hallgrímsson. He was no zealot for the departure of the military.

More meetings of the parliamentary group were spent discussing the division of duties within the prospective government. On August 22 the parliamentary group once again placed heavy emphasis on the prime minister's seat. The next day Ólafur Jóhannesson reported orally on two proposals from the Independence Party. One provided for an equal division of ministries, with four ministers from each party. Under it, the Independence Party would head the government, while in return the president of the united parliament would come from the Progressive Party. The other proposal entailed the Progressive Party receiving the prime minister's office, but with the party's ministers numbering three against four ministers from the Independence Party. Furthermore, the party's ministries were to be five against seven falling to the Independence Party members.

In addition, the president of the united parliament would come from their ranks. There was no hesitation in the parliamentary group. We wanted the leadership of the government. At a special evening meeting the same day, a "working paper" from the Independence Party members was presented, setting out three options on the same basis but with different divisions of ministries between the parties. We resolved, with all votes cast, that the party must receive the prime minister's office for its share. Only Ólafur Jóhannesson himself abstained from the vote.

At half past midnight a meeting was called again, and there was then on the table one written offer from the Independence Party on the division of ministries between the parties. It provided that the Independence Party would receive the prime minister's office but that the ministers would be equal in number from each party. The parliamentary group rejected this. I spoke, among others, and emphasized that our earlier resolution should be followed, even if the party received fewer ministerial seats as a result.
The next day there was yet another meeting, and Ólafur then reported that the Independence Party had rejected the Progressive Party receiving the prime minister'

s office. He also proposed yielding on this point, with ministers equal in number from each party, and the ministries likewise. I was unhappy with this outcome and wanted to stand firm on our demands. In my mind it was Ólafur who, more than anyone else, made Geir Hallgrímsson prime minister, and I disliked that. Still, I did not vote against this government formation.

When it came to choosing our Progressive ministers, Ólafur Jóhannesson asked me to meet him at his home. There he met one member of parliament after another. He informed me there without preamble that he would not be proposing me for a ministerial seat. I, for my part, made no secret of my desire to take on a ministerial post. Ólafur was indeed shrewd and praised me to the skies for my work for the party and my extensive duties as secretary. He said he was reluctant to lose me from that arena. Finally Ólafur said that he believed my time for a ministerial seat had not yet come. He was certain it would come soon. I found Ólafur convincing and acknowledged that it was important for the party's work to flourish.

At eleven o'clock that morning a meeting was held in the parliamentary group. Before votes were cast on the ministerial candidates, the view was expressed that new men were needed to deal with new circumstances. The election, however, went as Ólafur had wanted. Besides him, Halldór E. Sigurðsson, Einar Ágústsson and Vilhjálmur Hjálmarsson were chosen. I received one vote. Where it came from I do not know. Ólafur had probably already spoken with all the members of parliament, and most of them had accepted his conclusion. Jón Skaftason was the only one who criticized the way things were done in the parliamentary group, saying he believed the ministerial team should be renewed since the party was entering into cooperation with the Independence Party. Perhaps he had hoped for a ministerial seat. Jón's claim to further honors in this arena was in various respects legitimate.
He had long done good work in parliament but had suffered for being in opposition to Eysteinn on various matters. Jón never became a minister.

I was restless when I came home after this meeting, and the family hurried up to Klettur. It is a good place to be when the mind starts racing. In my heart I was dissatisfied with the outcome of the ministerial selection. I was fond of Vilhjálmur Hjálmarsson. One could not be otherwise, for a finer gentleman is hard to find. Yet I felt that my time had come and that more combative men were needed to stand up to the conservatives.

Others were of the same mind, and a great many people contacted me and expressed disappointment that I did not become minister of education. I had been chairman of parliament's education committee and had a university degree and broad
experience from my work at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). Vilhjálmur was self-taught beyond his district-school examination and drew his greatest experience from political work.
The "Commissar System"

I kept my seat on the board of the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun) despite the change of government in 1974. The Independence Party members had not come away short-changed by the Development Institute during the left-government years, even though they were in opposition and part of their parliamentary group kept up resistance to the institution in parliament. The party's representatives on the board and most of its rural members of parliament turned to it for assistance and fought there for their causes with no less vigor than members of other parties. They often reaped the rewards of their labors, not least when they joined hands with government members from the constituency concerned. Indeed, most of the Independence Party members in the Althing came around to supporting the Development Institute once they were in government.
I never recall a single one of them mentioning so much as one word about the party's election promise to abolish the institution.

Although the Independence Party took the lead in the government of 1974, this did nothing to reduce the funds devoted to the Development Institute, road construction, industrial development and regional affairs, even though various signs were in the air that over-investment was looming in several areas. The Independence Party essentially adopted the left government's policy in most of the areas mentioned here when it took office in 1974. In that respect the change of government had very little effect.

The main change that the coalition with the Independence Party brought about within the Development Institute was that the Independence Party members placed strong emphasis on increasing their influence within the institution, not least in the allocation of funds. The law was slightly amended and the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun) was made an independent institution under the supervision of the prime minister's office. It is, however, a misunderstanding that the "commissar system" was abolished, as has sometimes been claimed. The institution's board did, admittedly, receive the power to appoint the "commissars".

The only real changes were that the "commissars" of the Union of Liberals and Leftists (Samtökin) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) on the executive board stepped down, and Sverrir Hermannsson, later minister and bank director, took a seat as "commissar" for the Independence Party.

According to Sverrir himself, his appointment was to reward him for supporting Geir Hallgrímsson in Geir's deputy-chairmanship contest with Gunnar Thoroddsen in 1971. Sverrir had been defeated in a battle with Ingólfur Jónsson

over the seat of chairman of the board of the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun). By becoming a "commissar" he considered himself to have "won the war even though he had lost the battle". This testimony perhaps says more than many words about the mindset that accompanied this party-political arrangement.

Sverrir and Tómas Árnason, who continued as "commissar" of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), swore what amounted to blood-brotherhood in those years, and their friendship has lasted as far as I know. Sverrir has in fact said that Geir Hallgrímsson and I used him and Tómas as a bridge between the parties after I became chairman. They are supposed to have been tasked with exploring the possibility of a coalition in 1979. I do not actually recall this being at my initiative or Geir's, though Sverrir and Tómas were both heavyweights in their parties and no doubt keen to work together.

The Development Institute long lay under harsh criticism. Some of it was justified, some not. I find it hard to point to specific examples of improper favoritism within it. I even doubt that what is open to criticism in its work deserves such labels. On the other hand, there is no concealing that allocations and lending were heavily shaped by the fact that representatives of the political parties sat on the institution's board and held the positions of "commissars". They looked after the interests of the parties, their members of parliament, the constituencies and party members around the country.

All matters that came to the institution were certainly assessed by its experts, and some did not survive that scrutiny. I doubt, however, that the staff always had strong enough backbones to withstand pressure from their superiors in particular cases. To keep the peace on the board and with the Althing, it proved necessary to maintain a balance between regions, constituencies and localities in lending. That often came at the expense of considerations of profitability.

I soon came to the view that it would be more sensible for the institution's board to be composed of professionals, at least in large part. I thus envisaged parliament electing three representatives to it, while four would come from the various institutions of the industries. I also grew firmer in the position that having a politically appointed executive board was untenable. Its drawbacks soon became apparent. However good the professionals and however upright the officials chosen for these positions, the arrangement encouraged lending and grants to obey the laws of politics rather than of profitability.

In my judgment this went too far. Members of parliament and party members all over the country considered themselves to have "their man" on the executive board who was supposed to attend to their needs and the party's. It was disputed, and partly with justification, that in

on the board we thought not least about "looking after our constituencies". When I went to meet voters I did not want it thrown in my face that I had done a poor job of advancing the interests of the West Fjords people. The applications from there were in fact mostly sound and from good companies. The occasional small-boat fishing operation I did champion even though I suspected it would be difficult to set it back on an even keel. For a politician it is hard to withstand pressure when it is applied insistently, and it is tempting to use the opportunities that the power of allocation offers. In those respects I was no exception. And when the "commissars" were also members of parliament, like Tómas and Sverrir, the outcome was perhaps hardly surprising.

Whether it is coincidence or not, the East Iceland constituency received the largest share of general loans and grants in those years, as can be seen when the allocations of the Regional Development Fund (Byggðasjóður) by constituency in the years 1972–1982 are examined. Sverrir and Tómas were both members of parliament for East Iceland. The people of the East Fjords were in fact distinctly worst off at the start of the period; almost no fish-processing machinery was available and freezing plants were few. In the East Fjords, therefore, no fewer than six new freezing plants were built.

The board chairmanship also seems to have had its effect. In the years when Ragnar Arnalds held that position, contributions to his constituency were a third higher as a proportion of the Regional Development Fund's total expenditures than they became after Ingólfur Jónsson, member of parliament for the South, took over the chairmanship. The South Iceland constituency's share then rose correspondingly by a fifth from what it had been before.

I advanced the interests of the West Fjords no less from the seat of deputy chairman of the board. Only East Iceland and the Northeast constituency received a larger share than the West Fjords constituency, which outfoxed the constituencies of both board chairmen.
Heavy Industry and Ferrosilicon

I was elected chairman of parliament's industry committee when it convened. In December 1974 a bill was introduced for a ferrosilicon plant at Grundartangi. It had been prepared by the heavy-industry committee that Magnús Kjartansson had appointed, on which I had sat. Now, however, it so happened that the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) opposed the matter fiercely, as only an opposition party can.

This struck various people as strange, since Magnús had been the party's minister. In his first weeks in office he had appointed a so-called negotiating committee on energy-intensive industry. Its members were Jóhannes

Nordal, governor of the Central Bank, Ingi R. Helgason, lawyer, and Ragnar Ólafsson, lawyer, in addition to me. Its work was a direct continuation of the heavy-industry committee of the Viðreisn years, on which Jóhannes and I had also sat and which I have recounted earlier in these pages.

From 1971 to 1974 as many as one hundred meetings were held in the committee, and by the time it was disbanded at the end of 1978 they had reached 170. Following the change of government in 1974, the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) received a representative on the committee. Ingólfur Jónsson, former minister, took a seat there. Ragnar Ólafsson, attorney, also left during its term. There were no other changes. Throughout the whole period Jóhannes Nordal held the chairmanship despite changes of ministers and governments; indeed he had a reputation for loyalty to his masters, in addition to being an outstanding negotiator and the most experienced of all Icelanders in those matters.

Although numerous options were examined and negotiations conducted on many of them, ideas about ferrosilicon soon became the most extensive part of the committee's work. For a long time Union Carbide was the most likely company. The negotiations with Union Carbide involved a great deal of travel. Some of the trips were very instructive. I recall, for example, a trip to the United States in January 1975 with Eyjólfur Sæmundsson, chemical engineer at the State Health Inspectorate (Heilbrigðiseftirlit ríkisins). I liked Eyjólfur. At some point I remarked at a meeting of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) in Hafnarfjörður that he was the most tolerable social democrat I knew.

Eyjólfur and I went to Union Carbide's factories in West Virginia to acquaint ourselves with pollution controls. To tell the truth, we were appalled by all the filth that came from the processing. The factories were located in a valley and I have seldom seen greater squalor. Black smoke rose from the chimneys and lay like a black crust over the entire surroundings. This experience had a great effect on me and strengthened me in the position that strict conditions on pollution controls should be imposed. On this trip we also visited the world-renowned environmental agency of the United States and had informative meetings there and received information about the requirements that were beginning to be made for pollution controls. We followed that model after we came home.

Environmental matters were not in the spotlight in those years, neither for me nor for others. Few suspected how enormous the effects of emissions of carbon dioxide and various kinds of toxic substances can have, and do have, on nature, as has become clear a quarter of a century later. Yet the little I had learned about environmental matters in those years was enough to convince me that great attention needed to be paid to these factors. So one may say that this was the beginning of my ever-growing involvement in and interest in environmental matters.
Many more projects were discussed at the meetings of the negotiating committee. Sea-chemicals processing was much discussed. Those plans were based on the work of Baldur Líndal

for the State Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins), mentioned earlier. That project looked promising for a time. An oil refinery was discussed, among others with Gulf Oil in the United States. Expansion of the aluminum smelter at Straumsvík was also discussed; there were grandiose ideas about large aluminum smelters and power plants in the East Fjords, which were called Alusuisse's "integral proposals". Ilmenite production was floated with the Russians, basalt production was discussed with a Czech company, and alumina production using geothermal heat was high on the agenda for a time. There was talk of siting such a plant near a geothermal area, for example on Reykjanes or in South Iceland. In alumina plants, bauxite is refined into alumina, from which aluminum is then produced by electrolysis. The refining uses caustic soda and great heat.

I discussed these ideas thoroughly with, among others, Baldur Líndal, whom I trusted more than anyone in these matters. The conclusion was that this would be a heavily polluting operation. We therefore opposed these ideas.

I do not recall other major projects that were opposed on environmental grounds. Few of the ideas became reality then, perhaps fortunately. Strange as it sounds, after the environmental debate of the past twenty years, the dust has nevertheless been blown off an astonishing number of them in recent years. It is close to the truth that no new idea has emerged in this arena in more than two decades. That does not testify to great richness of imagination. The problems of the present are once again to be solved with the solutions of yesterday.

The handling of the ferrosilicon matter in parliament's industry committee dragged on all the way into 1977. Numerous people were called before the committee and thorough discussion took place. What mattered most, however, was that we were waiting for the negotiations with Union Carbide. They had reached the final stage in the spring of 1976 when the company withdrew following major changes in its operations. Shortly afterwards it left ferrosilicon production altogether. At the same time, however, talks had been held with the Norwegian company Elkem, and that company took over the agreements in little-altered form. The result was the construction of a ferrosilicon plant at Grundartangi in Hvalfjörður. In parliament's handling of the matter I pushed, among other things, for firmer requirements on pollution controls.
Banquets, Salmon and Stiff-Tongued Politicians

Banquets and expensive meals invariably accompanied the negotiations. The Swiss were probably the most generous, in surroundings, food and drink alike. It happened that meetings were held at mountain hotels where one could go skiing between sessions. The Icelandic Aluminium Company (Íslenska álfélagið) long invited Jóhannes Nordal and me salmon fishing after
the aluminum smelter at Straumsvík began operations. The delicacies were no lesser on those occasions.

After Union Carbide dropped out of the picture and an agreement had been reached with the Norwegian company Elkem, the Norwegians invited us salmon fishing in Norway. It was a lavish invitation. Present were Gunnar Thoroddsen, minister of industry, Jóhannes Nordal, chairman of Iceland's negotiating committee, and I, together with our wives. We stayed at the mouth of the famous Lærdal river, which is the favorite fishing ground of Crown Prince Harald, who has now become king of Norway. We stayed in beautiful and well-equipped cabins. To support and assist us there was a certain guide, Olaf by name. He was known throughout Norway.

Olaf began the day by advising us to use a large Blue Charm fly. I cast it a few times but then switched and put on a smaller Icelandic fly called the Shrimp (rækja). Soon a fourteen-pound salmon took it. While I was contending with him, traffic came to a halt as far up the road as one could see. When I was about to land him, Olaf came up and drove a gaff into the fish. I was very much against that, being accustomed to landing my catch myself with a grip on the tail. He looked at the flies and shook his head. Before long, however, I had caught another salmon, and Olaf then began to grow rather restless. But when I had brought the third one to land, he examined the shrimp fly minutely, and then he brightened considerably. "Oh, this is the Icelandic fly that Crown Prince Harald has sometimes fished with," he said, and with that I had his approval of the catch.
Jóhannes also got a salmon, but the others nothing. I rose greatly in Olaf's esteem.

The trips abroad that accompanied the negotiations would have been enough to kill any man had it not been for the evenings. Then there was leisure to sit down with a drop of whisky over the next day's business or to discuss life and existence. Through the work on the negotiating committee I came to know Ingi R. Helgason and his wife Ragna Þorsteins quite well. Ingi is a likeable man, good to work with and a reliable companion. We became good acquaintances and our friendship has lasted to this day. Ingi was a hidden man in politics and did not seek advancement in that arena. On the other hand, it was easy to hear that he knew the inner workings of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) well.
