He was their chief financial strategist and was said to be behind many things, though quietly. Ingi is a sensible man of the left and our views coincided on many points.
He is a sincere believer in welfare, cautious in financial matters, and by no means possessed by revolutionary delusions.
I also came to value Ingólfur Jónsson more after I got to know him. I had considerable dealings with him on the board of the Development Institute (Framkvæmdastofnun) and no less in

contact with the heavy-industry matters. It was both good to work with Ingólfur and enjoyable to get to know him. He was a sincere champion of rural areas and in his attitudes reminded one in many ways of the old men of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Ingólfur was a meticulous, precise man. In the heavy-industry committee, however, it hampered him greatly that he was not a man of languages. He therefore could not take an active part in the committee's negotiation meetings abroad.

I actually believe that among politicians in those years there was a great shortcoming in men's ability to make themselves understood in international settings. This has tended to persist right up to recent years. When Davíð Oddsson's first government took office, no one who held a seat in that government had been educated abroad except the two Jóns, Baldvin and Sigurðsson. Other leaders of the nation appeared abroad with dignified silence. Indeed, Jón Baldvin was known to poke good-natured fun at Davíð and his command of English when he was in good spirits. Davíð, however, has improved greatly in his English.

When the Progressive Party entered the government in place of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) in 1995, the situation got worse again, if anything. Halldór Ásgrímsson was the only minister in that government who had lived abroad. He spent one year in Bergen studying accounting. Naturally, he spoke weak English when he started as foreign minister. Once I attended a banquet where Halldór addressed the guests in English. I was hanging my head rather low by the time he finished his speech. Just like Davíð, Halldór has fortunately made great strides in this area.
Ferrosilicon burning and biting

I was chairman of the industry committee of the upper chamber of the Althing, as I had also been during the left-wing government's time, and I directed its consideration of the heavy-industry matters when they came before parliament. Within the Progressive Party, however, there were men who had great doubts about the matter. Páll Pétursson, for example, immediately declared his opposition.

Among the members of the industry committee was the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) man Stefán Jónsson, who was often called "the reporter" because of his work at the State Broadcasting Service (Ríkisútvarpið). Stefán is, among others, the father of Hjörleifur the architect and Kári the physician at deCODE Genetics (Íslensk erfðagreining). He had been a Progressive in his younger years but had parted ways with the party over the question of the military base. He was nonetheless always very positively disposed toward my father, and they kept in good contact. I first got to know him when my father invited him up to Klettur for salmon fishing in Reykjadalsá, sometime around 1970. We became fishing companions and good friends from then on. Stefán was one of the fiercest opponents of heavy industry
in the parliament. The debates lasted into the night and we killed time by trading verses. I sent Stefán several quatrains, and this one is probably the least bad:
At Grundartangi yet rises great and strong a pillar for the nation's household store, and it will always testify to the work of those who proved the most far-sighted now.
Stefán was far superior to me in the art of poetry and answered promptly:
Ferrosilicon burning and biting, soon you'll get the same with aluminum. You were all out taking a crap, you who backed that cause.
There was a sting in those words. I, however, criticized Stefán sharply both in verse and in prose for misquoting me in the debates. He sent me an apology and was true to himself:
You will surely forgive me in the blink of an eye – but did I quote something from you that some other fool had said?

Stefán took a permanent seat in parliament for the first time in 1974 but had been the first alternate for the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) members elected at large since 1971. Our acquaintance grew ever deeper as the years passed. Stefán was in many ways a singular man. He delivered his arguments with great artistry in his velvet voice. All Icelanders had grown up with Stefán's news reading, and it was hard to resist the feeling that this agreeable voice must be telling the truth. Stefán was a great nationalist and a fighter for equality and equal standing, while also being a resolute advocate of the welfare system and mutual aid. Yet I found him far from being a radical socialist, and in fact he was well in step with most Progressives in his attitudes toward society.

During tedious debates Stefán often passed the time by composing verses which he sent me on little slips of paper that I collected and still have. I often had trouble not bursting out laughing when I received these missives. Þorvaldur Garðar was for a long time speaker of the upper chamber, and Stefán liked to hold him responsible for tedious sessions. Stefán composed the following verse beout
of boredom on some drab gray winter day. He called it Spring Longing:
I waited for green grass, a cuckoo from the south, an old friend, distance from toil and bickering and from Þorvaldur Garðar Kristjánsson.

The more tedious Stefán found things in parliament, the more he composed about salmon fishing and the outdoor life, comparing these different worlds. During some long-winded speech in the upper chamber he slipped me this quatrain:
When members flap their jaws so wide that thunder rolls across the air, then the rod bends and the line pulls taut and a salmon leaps in my mind.
Early bends the rod and hook

I got to know Stefán Jónsson not least on our fishing trips, which I delighted in no less than he did. I had grown up with salmon fishing from earliest childhood. When I was eight years old I caught my first salmon. My father at that time had the lower part of Grímsá on lease together with his companions. We often went there in the spring before I went off to the countryside. Under a bridge at the place called Fossatún is Hörgshylur pool. It is very deep and narrow at the top. A great deal of salmon often gathers there. Conditions, however, mean that they very rarely take. My father was casting for salmon at Lækjarfoss, which is a short way above the pool. I, meanwhile, eyed with longing the salmon lurking there. So Pabbi put a worm on a 16-foot fly rod and told me I could dangle my line from a rock at the top of the pool where he could see me well.

My father later told the story this way: suddenly he saw that I had disappeared. He was frightened, threw down his rod and rushed down along the river. There he found me just below the bridge. I was lying on the riverbank on top of a 10-pound salmon. It had taken at the top of the pool but shot off downstream without my being able to do anything about it. Pabbi, however, had not heard me over the roar of the river. So I scrambled with the rod after the salmon over rocks and rough ground. It is not easy terrain to cross there. I have experienced that since. At the bridge I saw that if the fish got any farther I would have lost it down a waterfall. So I threw down the rod and hauled it in on the line. I dragged

it ashore after a great struggle. Fortunately the line and leader were strong and the salmon had swallowed the hook deep. It was, however, unexhausted and thrashed tremendously. So I threw myself on top of it as soon as it came up onto the bank and lay there until my father arrived.

Nor was I old when I caught my first salmon on a fly — 12 years old. I was then traveling with my father on the way to the countryside in Skagafjörður. This was during the war years, and the Englishman Fortescue had Vatnsdalsá on lease. He was a good acquaintance of my father's. Because of the war he could not get to the country himself. He gave my father, however, permission to fish the river as he wished. So we stopped on the way north and my father cast for fish. Valtýr Blöndal, bank director and his fishing companion, was with us. My father was casting a fly in the so-called Hnausakvísl channel, and Valtýr was a bit farther upstream. Valtýr hooked a salmon and got into trouble landing it. So my father rushed to help and set his rod down. I took it and started dabbling it out in the water. When my father came back down I had landed a beautiful 12-pound fly-caught salmon.
It took a short way from shore — a Blue Charm no. 2, single hook. Large flies were used in those days.

Under Fortescue's contract, caught salmon were the property of the respective farmers. They therefore had to be handed over. I was very unhappy about that, and it ended with my father buying the salmon. Then I smiled my broadest and took the catch with me to the countryside.

I soon developed an unquenchable interest in fly fishing and often went with my father and his companions to Grímsá, especially in spring and autumn. They had it on lease for many years. My salmon fishing thus began long before it became a rich man's sport. Sveinbjörn Dagfinnsson, my brother-in-law, and I later leased part of Grímsá for a long time — from Múlakot, as it was put, for in those days the rivers were leased out from individual farms. For that we received as our share twelve days on the whole river, and we each got half. That was quite manageable for us even though we were by no means men of wealth. Then of course I also went fishing in various other rivers. I did not consider it a good trip if I did not get 10–12 salmon, and a poor summer if I did not land 60 to 70 salmon.

For a period I often sold a considerable part of the catch and thereby nearly covered the fishing permits. After Hótel Saga began operating I made an agreement with Konráð Guðmundsson, the hotel manager, and supplied salmon there. This came in handy for financing this hobby of mine. Probably no one could manage it the same way nowadays. The price of fishing permits has gone through the roof. With increased demand, the catch has at the same time diminished.
Edda caught her first salmon in 1959 in the waterfall in Reykjadalsá, which flows past the family's summer house at Klettur. There my children from my first

marriage — Jón, Ellen Herdís and Neil — also caught their first salmon. Ever since, Edda has taken great pleasure in fishing. The eldest son of Edda and myself, Hermann, caught his first salmon in Langá at 6 years old. On that occasion we landed 52 salmon in two and a half days. All 40 of mine were caught on Blue Charm flies nos. 8 and 10. My daughter Hlíf caught her first salmon at nearly thirty and showed little interest in fishing. The youngest son, Guðmundur, was of the same mind for a long time. He felt keenly for the fish. When I clubbed a salmon in his sight for the first time, he cried out in anguish and looked at me as if I had committed murder.

I have taught all my sons to cast a fly by first standing at their side and guiding the casting hand. When Guðmundur was around confirmation age he came with Edda and me to Miðfjarðará. He quickly got the knack of the casting stroke. In Miðfjarðará he stood a whole day in wild weather casting a fly to prove that he could do this too. There he got his first-ever salmon, and another besides, on a no. 10 fly. When we got home Guðmundur told his brother Hermann, who had already become a great fisherman, that this was really child's play.

Around the time I entered parliament, Reykjadalsá was a very good salmon river. Some two to three hundred salmon were caught there per year on two rods. The river was warm because of the Deildartunga hot spring, and the salmon took especially tiny flies that were drawn fast. The pool by the farm at Klettur was the best fishing spot in the river. Often when Stefán Jónsson and I were fishing there, together with our companions Jón Hjartarson, Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson and often Haukur Jónasson, we warmed ourselves by the fire in the evenings and read the poems of Einar Benediktsson, Stephan G. and other fine poets, and discussed national affairs with fervor, often over a glass of Irish coffee, which became a kind of house drink. I was considered skilled at making that drink. These trips became the source of poetic descriptions and high-flown literature that adorn the guest books at Klettur.
There one finds this verse, which Stefán composed on a trip when Edda was clearly sorely missed:
With pleasures aplenty, the spirit's magic dram and the scent of autumn's brushwood — but the nymph of this forest and the queen of your house remains far from us.
The territorial waters issue

Our Icelanders' struggle for the extension of the territorial waters took on various forms, and not all of them were peaceful. For most of the time, ministers of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) held the leadership in these matters. The territorial waters issue seldom came before rank-and-file members of parliament. At the beginning of 1976, however, the conduct of the British on the Icelandic fishing grounds went so far beyond all bounds that I could not hold my tongue in public. Warships were then trying to drive the patrol vessels Þór and Týr off the grounds by ramming. These were extremely dangerous tactics. In the wake of this, the Icelandic government threatened to break off diplomatic relations with the British, and an ambassador was dispatched to explain our position to the member nations of the North Atlantic Alliance (NATO).

On January 11, 1976, I published an article in Tíminn in which I opened by saying that I saw little reason to tiptoe around NATO. I put it this way: the government's actions are "commendable, as far as they go." I expressed my doubts, however, that results would be achieved until a harder line was taken. I proposed that not only should our ambassador in London be called home, but also the ambassador to NATO, if ramming were employed again by the British. At the same time, I said I wanted to notify NATO "that we would take our participation in the alliance under review, and likewise, of course, the presence of the defense force here in this country," if the British warships did not leave the Icelandic fishing grounds within a specified time. There were those who held that our participation in NATO was our chief weapon in the territorial waters issue.
To them I replied with these words: "Little strength lies in a weapon that may never be wielded."

The article bears witness to how appalled I was at the harshness of the British, and I was not alone in that view. This writing provoked strong reactions in many places and considerable attention. The reception within the party was also for the most part positive, and a quotation from the article is included in its history. Around the country I sensed among a great many party members that this hard-line position was very much to their liking. It made no difference what attitude the person in question otherwise had toward defense matters. Those who had made NATO an article of faith and regarded the military presence here as the cornerstone of Icelandic foreign policy grew uneasy, on the other hand. They wanted least of all to disturb the Cold War world order and insisted firmly that membership in NATO was valuable to us for the advancement of the cause.
At a meeting in Hveragerði on February 1, I took no less hard a stance than in the articles
I had written. I said that "we should apply political pressure." And then added:

Not by asking the North Atlantic Alliance (NATO) to mediate negotiations with the British, but by making clear to the alliance that our participation and the defense agreement with the Americans are placed in imminent danger if the British are allowed to get away with laying waste the economic foundation of the nation.

I had no further involvement in the territorial waters issue during those years beyond taking part in the party's and parliament's consideration of those matters. The extension of the territorial waters I consider to have been the greatest political victory of Icelanders since the founding of the republic.

In the territorial waters dispute with the British we enjoyed the support of countries in South America and Africa, and indeed of a great many other nations that were coming around to the view that the jurisdiction of coastal states worldwide should be extended to 200 miles. This mattered considerably, especially in the long run. Icelanders won the battle for a 200-mile jurisdiction because we had the world's sympathy in our struggle with the British, and not because of our participation in Western cooperation. To get our arguments across it was of course necessary to be able to reach the ears of the outside world, and not least of the most powerful states in the world. Our position within NATO secured us that. Goodwill toward small states, however, seldom carries much weight in their disputes with great powers when push comes to shove.

The goodwill of NATO countries did not weigh heavily compared with their fear that the disputes over the territorial waters would lead to Iceland's withdrawal from NATO and from the defense cooperation of the Western nations.

I believe that Ólafur Jóhannesson, more than anyone else, deserves credit for the fortunate outcome of the territorial waters issue in the 1970s, though he certainly did not act alone. When the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea was finally concluded in 1982, it so happened that Ólafur held the office of foreign minister. It thus fell within his purview to attend the signing of the convention, which took place in Jamaica. Ólafur, however, could not get away from home and called me, who was minister of fisheries. He said he considered it right, given the importance of the matter, that a minister from the government of Iceland be present, and asked me to go. I agreed.

When I arrived in Jamaica, Ambassador Hans G. Andersen, who was already there, was rather taken aback. He had not been notified of my arrival. He immediately turned to the foreign ministry and there received confirmation of

that we should both sign the convention on Iceland's behalf. I quickly sensed that Hans found this a bitter pill and felt that my ministerial rank cast a shadow over him at this historic milestone. It mattered greatly to him to sign before me, first on Iceland's behalf. So when Iceland's name was called out, Hans was not slow to spring from his seat and dash up to the stage. I did not mind at all; such formalities meant nothing to me. I understood the ambassador's feelings well. With no disrespect to other Icelanders, he was without question our foremost expert on the law of the sea and had worked on the Law of the Sea Convention from the very beginning. Hans placed no less emphasis on being allowed to deliver our Icelandic address at the signing. I was equally happy to oblige. I believe we parted from these dealings on good terms.
Vilmundur and the "Vísir Mafia"

When I spoke belligerently at the meeting in Hveragerði on February 1, 1976, the nation was, however, absorbed by other news. Vilmundur Gylfason had thrown out a "big bomb" that would come to overshadow nearly all other matters in Icelandic public life over the following seasons. Vilmundur was an emotional man and could be as erratic as he was brilliant. He was at the forefront of a group of young men who took their models from the United States, where journalists in their twenties had exposed Nixon and set in motion the Watergate affair, which before it was over led to the resignation of one of the most powerful men in the world. Here Vilmundur pressed hard in pointing out corruption and excess and sought to substantiate his unshakable conviction that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was the center and mecca of corruption in Icelandic society.

In the autumn of 1975, for example, he published an article in the afternoon paper Vísir in which he connected the finances of the restaurant Klúbburinn and the finances of the Progressive Party with the ruling of Ólafur Jóhannesson, Minister of Justice, in the establishment's affairs during the investigation of the so-called "spirits case." No one responded to the criticism on the party's behalf.

In the early hours of January 26, 1976, Magnús Leópoldsson, manager of Klúbburinn, was arrested in connection with the disappearance of Geirfinnur Einarsson, of whom nothing had been heard since the end of November 1974. Little was talked about more in the following days than the arrest of Magnús. On the front page of Dagblaðið two days after the arrest, rumors were reported that the disappearance was connected with "the purification or distillation of sea-mixed spirits, which had been transported illegally into the country." On Friday, January 30, Vísir published a front-page headline that some say was the largest in the paper's history:
Serious accusations against the Ministry of Justice: Accused of obstructing the investigation of the Geirfinnur case

In an article that Vilmundur wrote under this headline, the previously mentioned "spirits affair" from four years earlier was tied together with the Geirfinnur case, and the involvement of Ólafur Jóhannesson, Minister of Justice, in the investigation was made to look suspicious with the words that he had there committed conduct "which will hardly be forgotten in Icelandic legal history." Ólafur reacted sharply and called Vilmundur a plaything of the owners of Vísir, "the Vísir mafia."

The matter attracted enormous attention. Sighvatur Björgvinsson called for a debate outside the agenda in the Althing (Alþingi), and it was awaited with great anticipation. Nearly all the members of parliament were present and the spectator galleries were packed. Ólafur's defense in parliament was powerful and brilliant, and by the same token I thought Sighvatur made a humiliating showing at the podium. There he brought up various things from Vilmundur's writings, spiced them with a thorough misunderstanding of the prevailing laws on criminal investigations and a good dose of gossip, and stirred it all together with what appeared to be a fanatical antipathy toward Ólafur and the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Sighvatur has probably never had a worse day in parliament.
Ólafur indeed capped off his speech by saying that he couldn't be bothered to waste any more words on this meadow pipit. That phrase spread across the country at once.

I have never admired Ólafur more than on that day. He quoted laws and legal authorities verbatim and tore his opponent's argument to shreds. Usually he spoke methodically, calmly and gravely, but on this day he broke up his speech with powerful pauses and delivered heavy blows in every sentence. When he finished speaking, there was surely not a single person in the chamber who doubted his cause. Such was his effect on his listeners. Ólafur was one of the most irreproachable men I have ever known. He was certainly reserved and did not always speak his mind. His words, on the other hand, could be trusted without exception. If he got something wrong, it was only because he did not know better.

The afternoon papers were not of the same opinion. There Ólafur was said to want to "silence" Vilmundur, who in letters to the editor was called "the representative of the common people" and said to be "in the same class as those who exposed the scandal in the Watergate building." Þorsteinn Thorarensen, whom Vilmundur considered a "pioneer" of investigative journalism in Iceland, went about the furthest. After describing at length the degeneration that characterized the ideals and working methods of the Progressive Party and the cooperative movement, beneath a large portrait of Ólafur Jóhannesson, he reached the following conclusion:

This is ugly filth, and the reality will prove to be that such activity must sooner or later lead to serious crimes — that is simply the law of impermanence. A core of power that knows no restraints may think it has it within its grasp to conceal its dark deeds, but the time comes when they break out into the corruption of power [. . .] The most alarming thing about the events in the lava field and down by the coast is that when criminals resort to murder to silence people, experience in other countries tells us that more highly placed men in society have entered the game and are standing behind it. Ordinary petty thieves and small-time smugglers do not resort to such measures to save a small reputation. It is not until the honor at stake becomes greater in society that such desperate measures are taken.
At this point in these incredible writings, it is as though the author came to his senses, recalled the libel laws, and hastened to append to his piece:
But of course it should be clearly stated that I am not accusing the leader of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) of such things.

When the attacks began, Ólafur Jóhannesson had earned both the trust and the respect of the nation for his conduct in the territorial waters dispute. He was "the hard man" in the government, as it was sometimes put, and it soon became apparent that various Independence Party men bore a grudge against him. It was not only NATO they cared about. They were probably no less resentful that their members of parliament and ministers stood in the shadow of the Minister of Justice. Only one member of parliament from that party supported Ólafur through these ordeals. That was Gunnar Thoroddsen, Minister of Industry.

I do not doubt that Gunnar was sincere in his support of Ólafur, but this whole affair became strangely entangled in conflicts within the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and the battle between the two afternoon papers, Dagblaðið and Vísir, over readers and sales. Two mysterious disappearances weighed on the nation, and gossip and conspiracy theories took flight as never before. In Ólafur Jóhannesson's shadow stood the ministers of the government, who did not lift a finger in his support or defense. It was as if, deep down, some of them believed the accusations made against him, or for other reasons were not troubled that he found himself on the defensive. At least one of these ministers, Matthías Bjarnason, has called it a "disgrace" that they did not take up the gauntlet for Ólafur while the storm raged.
"The coarse type of person"

The afternoon papers allowed themselves no rest in pursuing the matter. Jónas Kristjánsson, editor of Dagblaðið, actually defended Ólafur Jóhannesson, saying he was among the "more trustworthy and respected" politicians, though he was not "an all-white knight." At the same time, he said Ólafur had made two mistakes. On the one hand, he had conflated Vilmundur with the Vísir mafia, and on the other he had "relied too much on men like Kristinn Finnbogason." And Jónas added:

The leaders of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) have been too relieved at not having to worry about the finances of the party and its newspaper, and have closed their eyes to the methods that have been employed . . .

Here the editor touched on what remained outstanding after Ólafur's speech in parliament: the question of whether there had been financial ties between the Progressive Party and those who ran the Klúbburinn nightclub. Ólafur had denied this. The truth was that the building fund of the Progressive associations in Reykjavík had made an agreement with the club's operator, Sigurbjörn Eiríksson, to write off an old debt the party owed him. This was done just a few days before Ólafur granted a request to reopen the establishment, despite the investigation of the "spirits affair." On February 11, Sigurbjörn was then taken into custody on suspicion of involvement in the Geirfinnur case. When word of that got out, some people needed no further proof. Klúbburinn was a den of crime that had thrived under the protection of the Progressive Party.
Instead of the storm blowing over, it raged as never before.

The ringleader in these dealings between the party and Klúbburinn was supposed to have been Kristinn Finnbogason. He was said to be the intermediary between Ólafur Jóhannesson and the club. In the mid-1970s Kristinn was perhaps more conspicuous than the fundraisers of other parties, and Vilmundur drew thorough attention to him. In October 1975 he published an article about the parties' fundraisers under the headline "The coarse type of person" and ran a huge photograph of Kristinn with it, even though he was in fact nowhere mentioned by name in the article. There Vilmundur first put forward the accusations that took flight three months later, in connection with the investigation of the Geirfinnur case.

At that time three innocent men were imprisoned, and I am convinced that the political attacks and the aggression of the media played their part in the fact that they were not released until after more than a hundred days of confinement.

The prisoners and their families went through a miserable ordeal over the following weeks, months and even years. The affair likewise laid a paralyzing hand on all the party work of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Members had all but stopped admitting to strangers that they supported the Progressives; well-known Progressive Party men were looked at as if they had committed a crime. In a speech I gave at a central committee meeting the following year, I recalled the atmosphere in these words:

These attacks left a heavy mark on the party's work. Party members were dispirited. Many felt they had no ready defense. This has now completely changed. An entirely different atmosphere prevails at our meetings. People hold their heads high once more.
What had changed was that the suspects had proved innocent and were released. A conspiracy had been formed to fabricate charges against them.

When the case took this new turn, Progressive Party members gradually regained their self-confidence. The afternoon papers nevertheless continued to assert that "most criminals in society were Progressives." Now, however, more people spoke up in response, myself among them. In the autumn of 1976 I wrote an article in which I said it had "long been clear that the most conservative forces in the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) are working systematically to spread slander about Progressive Party members." At the central committee meeting a good half year later, I struck a very similar note when I looked back on the preceding year and said it was memorable not least because "the leaders of the Progressive Party have been attacked unrestrainedly and systematically with slander and fabricated accusations." I added that I doubted anyone had ever stooped so low before.

The explanation, I said, was to be found in the fact that "the most conservative [forces] within the Independence Party and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn)" had felt that "the standing of the Progressive Party was too great in the coalition government under the leadership of Ólafur Jóhannesson." At this meeting, this difficult affair had become a reason for the party to beat its chest rather than hang its head in shame. I drove the point home by recalling the reactions the article had received within the party:

Some felt [that with the article] the blows fell too close to our coalition partners, and I received some reproach for it. I believe that today people are fairly convinced that it is precisely such a clique that has stood behind these attacks. In this way the aim was not only to strike a telling blow against the party's leaders, but of course against the party as a whole, so that it would never recover . . .

In the investigation and trials that took place in connection with the Geirfinnur case, I had the fullest confidence in Ólafur. I also know that he believed the police were working on the case in good faith, and he made every effort to secure funding and manpower for the task. I certainly had pause for thought when the Klúbburinn men were released. It was said among people that we did not live under the rule of law if innocent men could be kept locked up for over a hundred days without guilt being proven. I also felt I could sense that Ólafur regretted that things had gone this way. There was, however, no way for him to involve himself in the case after all that had gone before. Meanwhile, the pressure to solve these disappearances only increased.

In the aftermath, the investigation was placed in the hands of a German expert who came to the country at the instigation of the Minister of Justice. When the German said he had solved the case and new defendants had confessed to the crime, I had no doubt whatsoever that the case had been solved. The nation breathed a sigh of relief when the matter seemed to be over and done with. I was no exception. After the coverage of the investigation in recent years, this certainty has turned into deep-seated doubts. If it is true that confessions were extracted through harsh treatment and solitary confinement, that is a knockout blow to the Icelandic judicial system. To dispel the doubts, it is necessary to reopen the case.
The finances of the Progressive Party

One cannot leave the Geirfinnur case and the debate that followed it without giving an account of the finances of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the dealings between politicians and businesses in Iceland. In managing and financing the party, we Progressives emphasized separating the finances of the party's operations and political activity on the one hand from the finances of the party's real estate on the other. The party leadership, headed by the treasurer and the executive director, handled the financing of the party's political work. Kristinn Finnbogason, on the other hand, was the be-all and end-all of the party's building fund. This was among the reasons that Ólafur Jóhannesson was unaware of the ties between the building fund and Klúbburinn, as mentioned earlier.

Kristinn, among other things, played perhaps the largest role in establishing Glaumbær. The Progressive Party acquired the Íshúsið (Ice House) on Fríkirkjuvegur through a special purchase agreement with the Federation of Cooperatives (Sambandið). The purchase price of the Íshúsið was not unreasonable, but the loan terms were favorable, so the agreement amounted to a substantial subsidy to the party. In the building, the nightclub Glaumbær was established

which was to cover the costs of the party's work for the indefinite future. Unfortunately, the building burned down. The insurance was good, however, and a new property was bought on Rauðarárstígur, where Hótel Lind now stands, largely thanks to the diligence and energy of Kristinn Finnbogason. In connection with that purchase, Ólafur Jóhannesson said that Kristinn performed one or two miracles every day. From then on he was always called "the miracle worker" within the party.

Kristinn went about sorting out the finances of the building fund vigorously. He was, however, sometimes careless in his methods, and various stories about him grew in the telling. Not all of them were pretty. He pressed very hard if he believed he had been promised something. Then he would not let up until it had been honored. That was the kind of man he was. I do not know, however, whether Kristinn operated any differently from the fundraisers of other parties. The party leadership was pleased with his work.

I have never heard that Kristinn tried to take money from individuals or companies by trickery. He did, however, have a reputation for smoothing his friends' way through the machinery of government. He knew how to take the shortest route to a set goal. I cannot issue a blanket absolution for all of that activity. I do not know it well enough for that. I am nevertheless convinced that Kristinn was honest in his own forceful way, and he was dependable. He was helpful to the many who turned to him and was exceptionally obliging. Some compared him to Albert Guðmundsson, member of parliament and city councilman for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), who earned the nickname "friend of the little man." Kristinn was a patronage politician without office. He worked through others.

While Kristinn was a great friend to his friends, he was not shy about making those he disliked feel his displeasure harshly. Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson sometimes reaches for the following lines of verse by Páll Ólafsson when Kristinn comes up in conversation. They describe him well:
In him there is both gold and stone, he can do harm – and mend it too.

While I was secretary of the party, I had almost nothing to do with his fundraising and was frankly relieved, since begging has never suited me. I became more personally acquainted with the fundraising after I became party chairman and prime minister. Then the party's fundraisers would come to me with a list of companies they asked me to call. I remember, for example, that I called all the oil companies and said we would appreciate it if they contributed something. I also called Flugleiðir and Eimskip. Hörður Sigurgestsson

invited me on that occasion to coffee at his office. He said outright that they gave every party the same amount and mentioned some figure, three or four hundred thousand. Admittedly, someone later insisted to me that this was not correct, because the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) received more than all the other parties combined. Naturally, I also called the Federation companies. There I was always met with much complaining about hard times. Most of the companies of the Federation of Cooperatives (SÍS) were in financial difficulties. I found the Flugleiðir people stingy as well. There was little to be had from them.

Despite these personal fundraising expeditions, I have never experienced individuals or companies offering me money in exchange for advocating one thing or another. In fact, invitations to salmon fishing trips became fewer after I became a minister and attained a real position of power. I believe the same story can be told of other Icelandic politicians. Foreigners find this hard to believe.

This arrangement of political parties raising funds from companies is debatable. There are strong moral arguments that political parties should receive direct grants from the state treasury. This is an unpopular opinion in this country. Abroad it meets with much more understanding. If political parties receive funds from public coffers, they are less dependent on the financial support of companies, which have all sorts of interests to look after.
The Progressive Party and SÍS

The Federation of Icelandic Cooperative Societies (Samband íslenskra samvinnufélaga) and the party's ties to it are a chapter unto themselves. It is no secret that the cooperative societies and the Federation supported the party considerably in those years. Their managers considered it to serve their interests. Among other things, the Federation's companies bought the party's lottery tickets on a large scale, and most cooperative societies bought the calendars the party published, paying a generous markup. For a long period the cooperative societies collected subscriptions for Tíminn, and as mentioned before, a subscription to the paper was practically obligatory for those who did their business with the cooperative. This was discontinued in the 1970s as the ties gradually frayed.

When elections were at hand, the Federation paid some of its employees wages for working on preparations for the election campaign at the party office of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). It has sometimes been insinuated that the Federation handed over large sums of money. That has no basis in fact. By the time I began to be involved in the party's fundraising, what the Federation men could do for us had greatly diminished. There were instances of their having bought promissory notes, imported printing presses, and paid off Tíminn's debts on

years earlier. That era was past. Direct financial contributions from the Federation certainly still mattered. The amounts involved were not large, however, and did not come close to matching the favors that financially powerful companies did for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). Within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) it was also a common refrain that the financial support of SÍS for the party was trifling compared with what the party did for the Federation.

At the beginning of the 1970s, the dealings between the party and the Federation were considerable, though they had no doubt diminished somewhat from what they had once been. The parliamentary group of the Progressive Party met from time to time with the Federation's leadership. It happened there that spokesmen for the enterprise stressed that certain legal provisions should be changed or that matters should be arranged in a way that suited the Federation. Its representatives also approached the party's ministers directly at any given time, as is the way of things. It was considered an argument for a decision or a change in the law that it would benefit the Federation. On the other hand, I doubt that it was only the Federation's companies that had good access to those in power. That has always been true of Icelandic companies.
I think there is considerable truth in the words of Ólafur Björnsson, professor of economics, about the era of restrictions in Iceland. He said in a parliamentary speech in 1968:

SÍS is nevertheless not the only enterprise that has enjoyed privileges in this way under the shelter of political assistance, and Progressive Party members are not the only ones who have used their positions on allocation committees to advance the interests of companies and individuals that supported their party. This was a rule of the game that all parties followed.
I have no reason to believe that these rules of the game were abolished any earlier by other parties than by the Progressive Party, if indeed they were abolished at all.

When I became chairman of the Progressive Party, it was noted in the newspapers that I enjoyed the support of the Federation's leadership. Probably my personal friendship with Erlendur Einarsson, director of SÍS, mattered not least in that regard. I first got to know Erlendur when I worked for Vilhjálmur Þór, director of the Federation, in my younger years. We got along well right away. The acquaintance of Edda and me with Erlendur and his excellent wife Margrét Helgadóttir grew even closer later on.

After Erlendur became director of the Federation, he was elected to the executive board of the Progressive Party, as Vilhjálmur had been before him and as was customary. This was one of the party's unwritten rules. I often went to see Erlendur when I was secretary of the party and a member of parliament. My business, however, concerned the Federation's operations in the Westfjords more than party work. Like other members of parliament
from the rural districts, I looked on the Federation as a helping hand in advancing the interests of the settlements, since it had considerable operations in many places.

At these meetings I wanted to convey the viewpoints of the local people and urge action or improvements where things were tight. I visited some of these places in the west more often than the Federation's own managers did, and I was not always satisfied with the Federation's policy toward various places in the Westfjords. No doubt, though, it was shaped with the interests of the companies in mind. At the same time, I realized that in many of these places conditions would have been altogether different and worse if the Federation had not been there. On the other hand, it seemed to me that some of the companies were managed from Reykjavík without anyone really knowing how matters stood out west.
The Black Report

When the oil crisis struck the world at the beginning of the 1970s, it had a paralyzing effect on the economies of all Western countries. Around the same time, discussion of the limits of economic growth began to emerge among leading figures in business, science, and politics. In 1973 I attended a conference held by NATO on this subject. Numerous informative lectures were delivered there, presenting viewpoints and arguments based on the simple fact that the earth's resources are finite. Nearly thirty years later it is difficult to appreciate how novel this approach was at the time. Economic systems, business life, and government plans had until then completely ignored this.

In Iceland, the unrestrained spirit of expansion that had characterized business and politics throughout the century was one of the most obvious examples of this deep-rooted mindset. This was most visible in the affairs of the primary industries, as they were called — agriculture and fisheries. In me, and no doubt in many others, the idea took hold that in those areas we might be approaching dangerous limits. I was very keen for the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) to take these matters up. In 1973, therefore, preparations began there for drawing up a long-term plan and policy for the development of the industries.

Committees of experts were established to examine the development and future prospects of individual industries with a critical eye. Four such committees began work at the beginning of 1974, in the fields of construction, manufacturing, fisheries, and agriculture. In addition, a special report was published on the state of sheep farming. Individuals were chosen from the industry concerned, from the public sector, and from scientific institutions. Emphasis was placed on
that they were not representatives of institutions, industries, or interest groups but had full freedom and independence in their work.

In a publication of the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun) on the development of agriculture in the years 1945–1989, the report that dealt with agricultural matters is credited with containing, for the first time in the writings of public bodies, "a serious warning about the trouble that was looming with ever-increasing production." It hardly needs saying that most of the reports attracted undivided attention and set off an extensive debate. The fisheries report in particular provoked sharp reactions and earned the nickname "the black report," even though it actually had a light blue cover and looked quite innocent. In the report's very first paragraph the tone is set: the fundamental attitude of Icelanders toward the resource had to change. It says there:

The tendency of Icelanders to regard the Icelandic fishing grounds as the greatest and best fishing grounds in the world has shaped the whole attitude toward fishing operations and has been a guiding force in the fisheries.

"The black report," which came out in 1975, was one of the first attempts to change this attitude. The summary of its conclusions stated in plain words that continued improvidence in the affairs of the fisheries could in the worst case lead to economic collapse and in the best case to financial hardship. Overinvestment in both fishing and processing was sharply criticized, and a call was made for new instruments for fisheries management:

The methods now employed in the management of the fisheries are next to useless, and there is therefore a real danger of the collapse of the main commercial stocks in the same way as happened with the herring stock.

The committee's proposals on fisheries management were novel. One may say that they warned against management by fishing-effort limits, a scrap-day system with quotas, such as was adopted shortly afterward. The precondition for sensible utilization of the fish stocks was said to be "that the capacity of the fleet engaged in fishing be in line with the yield capacity of the fish stocks at which the fishing is directed." The committee believed that this goal could best be achieved through taxes or a fishing-license fee, as such ideas have later been called. The economist Bjarni Bragi Jónsson is said to have been the first Icelander to advocate that idea. Earlier in 1975, when "the black report" came out, he presented these ideas of his in a detailed exposition. Gylfi Þ. Gíslason, on the other
hand, was among the most energetic in keeping these ideas alive, and no less the contribution of the Research Council's fisheries report to the debate.

In "the black report" the development of the fisheries on the Icelandic grounds was reviewed in considerable detail, and an attempt was made to forecast five to six years ahead. A dark picture was painted of the situation, not least regarding the management of the fisheries, overinvestment, and overexploitation. In hindsight, the report came out at exactly the right time. In November 1975 it would not be long before Icelanders had sole control of their jurisdiction. The content of the report and the discussion about it marked the beginning of Icelanders' efforts to formulate a responsible overall policy on the management of fishing in Icelandic waters. In the wake of the four reports, it also became a substantial part of the Research Council's work to subject individual sectors of the economy to thorough examination. That has continued to this day.
The Passing of My Parents

My father died on 22 January 1976. He was then in the City Hospital (Borgarspítalinn). The doctors had made clear to us where things were heading. I had been sitting with him together with my mother all evening when a doctor came by. He said he thought it safe for us to go home and come back the next morning. Pabbi's condition had changed little. My mother wanted to stay on with him and got a cot to lie down on. I went home. She called toward morning. He was then fading. By the time I reached the hospital he had passed away. There is a calm about death when it has a long prelude of illness. Nevertheless, these were difficult days. There was considerable ceremony at the funeral, which was arranged by the government. Memorial addresses were given by Sigurbjörn Einarsson, Bishop of Iceland, and Árni Pálsson, my classmate. Police officers stood honor guard.

After my father's death, my mother lived alone in the house at Tjarnargata 42. She did, however, rent out a room in the basement. Various people dropped in on her and accepted coffee or other refreshments. I usually stopped by on my way home from work. I soon sensed that my mother was lonely, no matter how many visits she received. She felt she no longer had a role to fill.

In the autumn she rented the room to one of the leaders of Vaka, the Independence Party's (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) nursery at the University. She often invited the young man up for a cup of coffee and would then try to talk some political sense into him. One day in mid-October, I had no sooner sat down with her than she began telling me about the outrage that the Vaka men intended to get some dyed-in-the-wool conservative, whom she considered utterly beyond the pale, to give a speech at the students' celebration on Sovereignty Day, 1 December. She had

tried to change the young man's mind over coffee just before I arrived. She shook her head at the young people's lack of understanding, but then smiled at herself and said: "Anyway, why am I meddling in this?"

Shortly after I got home that same day, the telephone rang. It was my mother, and I could tell at once from her speech that something was wrong: "Denni," she said, "there's something so strange in my head. I feel as if I'm about to faint." She also said she was half powerless on one side. I immediately suspected a stroke. I told her to lie down and said I would call a doctor. I got hold right away of Sverrir Bergmann, who had been one of those who had cared for my father. I myself leapt into the car and drove at breakneck speed.

I arrived a few minutes ahead of Sverrir and found my mother lying on the sofa, as I had instructed. She was perfectly calm and tried to smile when I sat down on the sofa beside her. I took her hand and told her to rest until the doctor came. After examining her, Sverrir said that I was probably right that it was a stroke. My mother took it with equanimity, and it seemed to me that she was filled with an inner peace at the news. She looked into my eyes, squeezed my hand, and said: "Now I hope I will get to go to your pabbi." These were her last words in this world. Shortly afterward there was no way to communicate with her, and she never regained consciousness during the two weeks she had left to live. My mother passed away on 2 November 1976.

My daughter Herdís later remarked that she found a mystical connection between the dates of my parents' deaths, and perhaps there is something to it. My father died on 22. 1. and my mother on 2. 11. The digits are the same.

The division of the estate dragged on at great length because of disputes and disagreement between my sister and me. No doubt we both bore a considerable share of the blame. Those unpleasant matters were not fully resolved until nearly a decade later, after the mediation of lawyers and legally appointed assessors. There has been little contact between us since.
The Solstice Agreements of 1977

The oil crisis that broke out in 1973 with a tripling of oil prices was not temporary, as had been hoped. In its wake, economic growth slowed in many parts of the world. The effects were not long in reaching Iceland. The nation's terms of trade with other countries took a sharp turn for the worse, as a fall in the prices of our export products followed on the heels of the rise in the price of oil. The Vestmannaeyjar eruption of 1973 was also an enormous bloodletting. The country's largest fishing station was laid low

for a time. That alone meant a contraction of the national product by 1–2 percent. Exports shrank by 4–5 percent. Under these circumstances it was inevitable that purchasing power would be curtailed, and from that followed one of the main characteristics of the 1970s: bitter struggles over the division of the national income. They continued almost without pause until 1985 and brought with them more than six hundred strikes and labor disputes. By far the largest share of them took place in the years 1974–1978.

In 1975 the effects of the volcanic eruption and the oil crisis made themselves felt with full force. The National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun) forecast a contraction of the national product of 3.5 percent. At this news, remarkably, the labor movement proved both more responsible and more cooperative than it had been when its leaders were at the helm and had the greatest say in the turbulent end of the left-wing government in 1974.

Within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), most were determined to prevent a "Restoration-era situation" in employment matters. At a joint meeting of the parliamentary group and the executive board at the beginning of 1975, Eysteinn Jónsson argued that a tax should be levied on luxury goods and "that two things had to be avoided: sacrificing the regional policy, and unemployment here." Others stressed that development in the countryside must not come to a halt. It surprises me how similar my tone was to that of Eysteinn Jónsson in those years. At a meeting in Mosfellssveit in September 1975, I also argued for restricting the import of luxury goods and postponing the entry into force of the free-trade agreement on industrial goods from Europe. Neither of these ideas became a reality.

The government did not take the path of imposing import restrictions but resorted to a variety of measures, consisting chiefly of cuts in state construction projects, reduced lending by the investment funds, and the imposition of new taxes. In February 1975 the currency was devalued by 20 percent. There was broad agreement on this course in the parliamentary group. The labor movement also acknowledged the difficulties that had to be grappled with, and a wide-ranging consensus formed that the main goal of economic management was the fight against unemployment. This spirit of cooperation lasted until past the middle of the electoral term, when elections began to loom on the horizon.

These economic measures produced considerable results. Favorable external conditions also helped matters. Catches picked up and economic growth surged as terms of trade in foreign markets improved. With that, the labor movement's patience was at an end. Its first thought was to demand wage increases. This was explained by more than the economic recovery. Radicals within the Federation of Labor (Alþýðusambandið) were making themselves strongly felt

at its congress in 1976 and gained the upper hand in the central committee of the ASÍ with the support of the labor leadership of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). In the history of the People's Alliance it is in fact stated in no uncertain terms that "everyday political work" there was characterized by "party members trying to spur the labor leadership to resistance and confrontation with employers and the state." Conflicts in the labor market were not long in coming.

In 1977 an Icelandic record was set in strikes and labor disputes, one that I hope will not be broken for a long time. Close to three hundred strikes were recorded! In these struggles something had to give. The so-called solstice agreements were concluded in June 1977. Among other things, they provided for full indexation of wages and an increase in wage rates of 25–28 percent. Cost-of-living adjustments to wages were calculated quarterly, and wages rose accordingly each time, by varying amounts depending on the speed of inflation. The state's agreements with the Federation of State and Municipal Employees (Bandalag starfsmanna ríkis og bæja, BSRB), concluded in the autumn, were similar and contained the same provisions on wage indexation.

University-educated workers adopted the indexation provisions in their agreements shortly afterward, and with that the great majority of Icelandic wage earners had index-linked wages. These were pure-bred inflation agreements.

The solstice agreements wiped out the results the government had achieved in its struggle against inflation. The economy could in no way sustain these wage increases, and the consequences were easy to foresee. When such agreements are made, companies can resort to only two kinds of remedies: price increases or laying off staff. Since wages rose automatically because of the indexation provisions in the solstice agreements, they were in effect a voucher for layoffs and unemployment.

The labor movement and the employers were equally guilty in making these agreements. The wage-earners' movement paid no heed to the danger of unemployment and shifted the responsibility entirely onto the state. The employers, for their part, accepted demands they knew the economy could not support. Afterward, they called for state action to avert a collapse. Since there were indexation provisions in the agreements, however, the options were very limited. I think most people realized that desperate measures would have to be taken. In the election winter of 1977–78, the agreements were annulled by legislation from the Althing (Alþingi).
A Power Game in the Labor Movement

I had little involvement in wage matters and economic management in these years except in discussions in the parliamentary group and the governing bodies of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Party work was more my domain. Within it, however, there took place a littleknown

but interesting part of the history of the Icelandic labor movement. Within the Icelandic Federation of Labor (Alþýðusamband Íslands), the political parties strove hard to secure their influence. Before each Federation congress, the party office of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was given over to the struggle for power and influence within the ASÍ. No one worked harder at this than Þráinn Valdimarsson, the party's executive director. He had an incredible overview and remembered every name. When the occasion arose, Þráinn undoubtedly telephoned nearly every Progressive Party member who had anything to do with labor affairs to spur them to action. He himself introduced these working methods as early as 1947 and established trusted contacts in every trade union.

The emphasis on this labor work within the Progressive Party varied. It increased greatly in the wake of the government's collapse in 1958, in which the Federation of Labor played a key role. Þráinn's extensive card index of all the boards of the country's trade unions, in which each and every board member was marked with his political party, traced its origins to those struggles. Enormous work went into keeping these records up to date, and no less work went into trying to influence the elections to these boards.

The party leadership also held meetings with the party's delegates to the Federation of Labor congress. That was the labor committee of the Progressive Party. It was consulted whenever the party wanted news of the progress of wage negotiations. In the 1980s the balance of power gradually settled into place. At the end of that struggle, Progressive Party members held 2 of the 15 seats on the central committee of the ASÍ.

All four parties tried to secure and strengthen their own influence in the Federation of Labor. The Progressive Party schemed alternately with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) or the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) to secure its position. More often, though, the Progressive Party, the Independence Party, and the Social Democratic Party joined forces in opposition to the People's Alliance, since the struggle was for most of the time about preventing the People's Alliance from gaining an outright majority on the central committee of the Federation of Labor. The executive directors of the three parties even traveled around the country together to coordinate the parties' efforts. Strange as it may seem in light of the parties' policies, the Independence Party always had a strong position within the labor movement.
It was often second only to the People's Alliance in size. There it relied chiefly on seamen and shop workers, along with certain trade unions in the countryside.

The labor disputes before the parliamentary elections of 1978 showed me and others in black and white that there was every reason to resist total domination of the ASÍ by the People's Alliance. After those elections, the power struggle in the labor movement grew again. This work was not carried out in the open, however, and I am not sure that all the party's members of parliament knew about it.

The labor leaders never opposed these extensive ties between the political parties and the labor movement. On the contrary, most of them were influential figures on both battlefields. I believe they thought this would give the wage-earners' organizations strong advocates within the parties, and that in this way they could influence the parties' resolutions and policy-making. No doubt there was something to that. In the long run, however, I fear that the labor movement suffered from this factionalism. On that, Þráinn and I agree.
Chapter Seven

I stressed that the candidate list in the Westfjords should be settled early for the 1978 elections. It was ready in September of the year before and was unchanged as far as the top seats were concerned. Gunnlaugur Finnsson of Hvilft in Önundarfjörður was in second place and Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson in third. The reason I wanted the list finalized in good time was that I was preparing myself for a difficult election. The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) has without exception fared poorly after coalition government under the leadership of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). I sensed that left-leaning Westfjorders who had voted for the Progressive Party were especially disgruntled. Perhaps the dissatisfaction with the coalition showed itself most clearly in the emergence of a list calling itself the List of Independents (Listi óháðra). Karvel Pálmason headed it.
With Karvel were various good men whom I had counted as sympathetic to us.

The economic situation had likewise hit many people hard, even though the regional development policy had certainly absorbed the worst of the blow in the countryside. Added to this, the government had been forced to annul the inflation-driven wage agreements from the year before so that the ship of state would not founder. Yet I did not suspect how hard a blow the party would take in the elections. These turned out to be the most difficult elections I have ever taken part in.

The election campaign was fought in the middle of a labor dispute. At the beginning of 1978 the government had introduced a bill on economic measures which was, to put it mildly, poorly received by the labor movement. Perhaps that was not surprising, since with those measures the wage improvements of the "solstice agreements" were largely nullified. They had been built on wishful thinking and a lack of realism. The labor movement's protests were aimed above all at the fact that cost-of-living adjustments were in
various ways curtailed in the government's proposals. It made no difference that the criticism was met with amendments to the bill.

With the law on economic measures passed by the Althingi in February 1978, the payment of cost-of-living adjustments on wages was limited so that only half of them was paid out each time. The reaction was not long in coming. Across the whole country an overtime ban was imposed, and workers were in no hurry with their work. On March 1 and 2 the wage-earners' associations united in work stoppages in many parts of the country, and tens of thousands took part in these actions. In the wake of this, various guerrilla tactics were employed, and in mid-April a strike was launched against the loading of export goods onto ships. These were illegal actions.

The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) was in its element. Within its ranks were the scriptwriters, the directors, and the leading actors of this turmoil. The demands of the labor movement were its demands. At my meetings in the constituency that spring I therefore aimed my barbs especially at the People's Alliance, which I criticized for unrealistic proposals. I said it was obvious that it was using its influence in the labor movement for political purposes. Various people agreed with me on this. Nonetheless, I sensed that the labor movement's slogan, the demand that "the agreements be honored," had broad resonance.
A fateful turn

Parliamentary business concluded on May 6, 1978, and election day was set for June 25. It so happened that at the end of May there were municipal elections. They had an enormous effect on the election campaign. The governing parties were under attack in every single town in the country, without us members of parliament being able to mount a defense.

The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was on the defensive from the start of the campaign. My campaign speeches were defensive speeches. I invariably began my remarks by recalling that the Progressive Party had made a serious attempt to form a left-wing government in 1974. It had foundered on the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance. I also maintained that the most that could be said against the government was that it had not tackled the economy with sufficient firmness. "If consensus is not reached or the wage agreements get out of hand, the government must cut the knot." That was the message I served up to the voters.

If anything, I was strengthened by the adversity and thought the cause a good one. Along with the other candidates of the governing parties, I strove to show that the government's firmness stemmed from urgent necessity and that it would be unwise to
make concessions. Leniency would only come back to haunt us, for then inflation would spiral out of control.

In the middle of the campaign I heard on the news that the government had, by provisional legislation, relented and met the demands of the labor movement. This was May 24. Despite the provisions of the February laws halving the cost-of-living adjustments on wages, full indexation payments were to be paid from June 1, 1978, to those with the lowest wages. Others were to receive the same adjustment counted in krónur.

No one welcomed this legislation, neither the government's supporters nor its opponents. Employers held that the burdens placed on them would be more than they could bear, and the labor leaders felt it did not go far enough. My whole argument seemed to me to collapse like a house of cards. I was left standing weaponless and half ridiculous. The opponents, on the other hand, were emboldened twice over and pressed their advantage. The labor movement's demands, which we had earlier criticized, we could now hardly call irresponsible any longer. From the capitulation we gained no credit, only the scorn of those who said agreements would have been reached long ago if the government had come to its senses sooner.

Kjartan Ólafsson, the top candidate of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), was in full cry at the campaign meetings that followed, and the Social Democrats (Alþýðuflokkurinn) Sighvatur Björgvinsson and Jón Baldvin Hannibalsson were amused.

The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) suffered a rout in these elections, receiving barely 16.9 percent of the vote and only 12 members of parliament. Both the Social Democratic Party and the People's Alliance gained far more support, receiving 22 and 22.9 percent of the vote and 14 members each. The governing parties lost five members of parliament each. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) lost 10 percent of the vote, receiving 32.7 percent. A larger swing to the left had never occurred in an Icelandic election.

In the Westfjords the support of us Progressives shrank from 28.6 to 20.0 percent of the vote, or roughly by a quarter. Gunnlaugur Finnsson of Hvilft lost his seat, and we got only one man elected for the first time since the merger of the constituency in 1959. Karvel Pálmason's list received over 14 percent of the vote and came close to getting a man into parliament. The Independence Party remained the largest party in the constituency, though its second man came close to losing his seat.

The Progressive Party's loss was greatest in Reykjavík, where half of the support from the previous election was lost and Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson, second on the list, was not elected. In Reykjanes the party's only member of parliament there, Jón Skaftason, lost his seat. Halldór Ásgrímsson fell in the east and Ingi Tryggvason in the Northeast constituency. Only one member of parliament was added to the party's ranks, Alexander Stefánsson. He had taken over the leading

role of Ásgeir Bjarnason in the West constituency. Alexander was a vigorous and hardworking member of parliament. He had wide experience in municipal government and social affairs and quickly became one of the party's chief spokesmen in those fields. Alexander made his presence felt at once in debates in parliament, as he always did from then on.

Ólafur Jóhannesson cited many explanations for the loss of support. At the first meeting of the party's central committee he blamed the unpopular coalition for how things went. He also said that experience showed it was unpopular to be in government, and moreover that the party's ministers had perhaps "grown tired of their seats in government, and the nation perhaps tired of the ministers."

I agreed in many respects with these explanations, and in addition I felt that party members had underestimated the effect of the relentless smear campaign that had been kept up against the party and its leaders. In personal conversations, however, Ólafur sometimes let it be understood that the feebleness of individual party candidates was to blame. I myself do not put much stock in that. Ólafur was in no better position than other candidates. The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) lost considerable support in his constituency, Northwest Iceland, though no seat was lost there.

I was and remain convinced that the government's change of course in economic policy a month before the elections had a very negative effect. I have often pondered why the government gave way at the fateful hour, in the middle of the election campaign. I incline most to the view that the concession was a priority for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) because of the city council elections in Reykjavík, where their majority was thought to be hanging by a thread. The government's decision was announced four days before the municipal elections. The Independence Party men were more intent on holding the city than the reins of national government. The city of Reykjavík and its administration were the main stronghold of the Independence Party.

There the party strengthened its foundations with favors and privileges for party members, there was the nursery of the party's leaders, and there lay the centers of its financial power. It may be said that Ólafur Jóhannesson did the Independence Party's errand in the spring of 1978 with a concession at the eleventh hour.

The outcome was that both strongholds fell. The hasty measures had no less of an opposite effect in Reykjavík than in the country's other constituencies. Yet no one received a worse drubbing in the elections than the Progressive Party. It had been the country's second-largest political party for most of the century. In a single night it became fourth in line and the smallest party in parliament.
The prelude to "Ólafía"

It occurred to few that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) would lead the next government after the party's biggest defeat of the century. Nor did it enter anyone's mind that the incoming government would be called "Ólafía" after the prime minister, Ólafur Jóhannesson. Much water was still to flow to the sea before a government could be formed. Among the public, Vilmundur Gylfason was considered the victor of the elections. He had run on the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) list in Reykjavík and bore no small responsibility for the air of doom that hung over the Progressive Party in these elections. Vilmundur regarded the Progressives as the source of all the ills of Icelandic society.

The Social Democratic Party increased its support the most of all the parties; its members of parliament grew from five to fourteen. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) received just as many members even though it got noticeably more votes, and was thereby the largest of the opposition parties. The People's Alliance added three members of parliament compared with the 1974 elections. Geir Hallgrímsson asked to be relieved of office for his government, even though it still had a majority in parliament.

Three days after the elections the parliamentary group of the Progressive Party met. It was clear that the party's members of parliament anticipated leisurely coalition negotiations and did not expect the Progressive Party to be called on to take part in a government. The results had visibly affected Ólafur Jóhannesson, the party chairman, most of all. At the beginning of the meeting he put forward a motion which read:

In view of the election results, the meeting considers it inappropriate for the Progressive Party to take part in a government on this occasion. The parliamentary group is prepared to consider granting a government of the People's Alliance and the Social Democratic Party its neutrality and defending it against a vote of no confidence, once the policy agreement of these parties is available.

I endorsed the idea of neutrality, though I did not want to rule out participation in government. Some agreed with this view of mine, but many said it was obvious that the party should stay out of government. Neutrality toward a government of "the victors of the elections," however, was well received. Einar Ágústsson was nevertheless against passing a resolution, and Tómas Árnason made a reservation about neutrality until he had seen the economic proposals of the two labor parties.

I considered it unwise to close off the party's possibility of a seat in government. When Ólafur had offered to withdraw his motion, I put forward a proposal for a new resolution in which it was nowhere stated that it would be inappropriate for the party

should take a seat in government. It set out the same offer of neutrality, and the resolution stated furthermore that "it would be natural for the victors of the elections, the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), to be given the opportunity to form a government now and to carry out the promises they made before the elections regarding the solution of the economic problems." The resolution was adopted.
Talks to the left and right

The formation of a government proceeded very slowly. The president at first took a long time to talk with the party chairmen and thereby encouraged people to speak with one another informally. That, I believe, was rather shrewd. At a meeting of the Progressive parliamentary group on July 8, the People's Alliance's request for talks on forming a government was reported. By then the two labor parties had already held quite a few talks between themselves. Along with Ólafur Jóhannesson, Tómas Árnason and I were chosen for these talks, which took place on July 10.

At the start of the meeting Lúðvík Jósepsson gave a detailed account of the talks between the People's Alliance and the Social Democratic Party. I recorded the main points of his remarks in my notes and kept up that habit throughout all the government-formation talks, as I have done ever since. These notes show, among other things, that the People's Alliance was prepared to form a minority government together with the Social Democratic Party if the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) granted the government its neutrality. This, however, would be subject to the condition that the Progressive Party be "more or less responsible." Lúðvík mentioned the budget in particular in this connection.

The Social Democratic Party, on the other hand, was opposed to forming such a government but in favor of entering "New Deal talks" (nýsköpunarviðræður) together with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance. Those ideas, in turn, met with little enthusiasm in the People's Alliance. Furthermore, the Social Democrats wanted a devaluation route in economic policy, while the People's Alliance advocated a wage-and-price rollback. Both parties, however, laid heavy emphasis on the wage agreements coming fully back into force. The People's Alliance men also spoke frequently of the military base at Keflavík airport.

We, for our part, declared on behalf of the Progressive Party that since there was no consensus on a minority government with the support of the Progressive Party, the party was prepared for formal coalition negotiations. These, however, would have to be with both labor parties. After this meeting the Progressive Party did not figure in events until a week later.
Benedikt Gröndal, chairman of the Social Democratic Party, was the first to receive a formal mandate to form a government, on July 12, 1978. He wanted first to begin talks
