with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) about a "New Deal government." The People's Alliance, however, ruled out working with the Independence Party and refused to attend the talks.

Benedikt summoned Tómas Árnason and me to an informal meeting with him on July 17, 1978. Kjartan Jóhannsson, a member of parliament for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), was also present. Neither parliamentary group had discussed possible cooperation between the two parties. The Social Democratic Party had aimed its barbs very much at the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) during the election campaign, and on election night it had probably occurred to few that the parties would work together in a government. The talks between the parties therefore caused upheaval in both camps.

At this meeting Benedikt confirmed that his party had resolved a fortnight earlier that an attempt should be made to form a majority government. A minority government with the People's Alliance was therefore out of the picture as far as the Social Democrats were concerned. Benedikt wanted to find out whether the Progressive Party was prepared for three-party talks. Tómas and I were not entirely in step in our answers. I said the party would let the issues decide, while Tómas emphasized that various people were opposed to the party's participation in a new government.

Benedikt was content with our answers and sent the parliamentary group of the Progressive Party a formal request for talks among the left-wing parties: the Progressive Party, the Social Democratic Party, and the People's Alliance. These were taken up at a parliamentary group meeting the day after our conversation. A few members reacted badly to the fact that informal talks had taken place without consulting the parliamentary group and took a dim view of coalition with them. Ingvar Gíslason was foremost among them and criticized Tómas and me sharply for the conversations with the Social Democrats. Páll Pétursson took the same line. Most, however, were in favor of participating in government if the outcome of the negotiations proved acceptable. This attitude has always been predominant in the Progressive Party.

After Ólafur Jóhannesson had presented Benedikt's wishes at the parliamentary group meeting and the conclusion had been reached to enter the talks, he announced, to everyone's surprise, that he would not make himself available for the party's negotiating committee. I immediately urged him to reconsider that position. Ólafur said he was immovable, for the simple reason that a great part of the criticism the Social Democratic Party had put forward had been directed at him. He stood wholeheartedly behind the negotiating committee but did not want to be blamed if the talks broke down.

In addition to the points Ólafur mentioned at the meeting, I believe he also had limited faith in the leadership of the Social Democratic Party and its capacity to form a government. Perhaps what mattered most, though, was that there was no way of knowing who
would attend the talks on behalf of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). Ólafur could not bear the thought of sitting at the same table as Vilmundur Gylfason.

Jón Helgason took Ólafur's place on the negotiating committee after a vote in the parliamentary group. From the Social Democratic Party, Benedikt Gröndal, Kjartan Jóhannsson, and Karl Steinar Guðnason attended the talks, while Lúðvík Jósepsson, Ragnar Arnalds, and Svavar Gestsson came on behalf of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). Benedikt structured the talks so that they were to address economic affairs, foreign affairs, and thirdly "miscellaneous matters," as I have recorded in my notes. In all, eleven meetings were held in this round. Economic affairs were discussed above all, as it was obvious they would have to be tackled. Other matters fell completely into the shadows.

We Progressives thought it natural to hold back in the talks at first and instead state our position on the proposals that the other parties, the victors of the elections, put forward. I took the view that the party's economic policy had in effect been rejected in the elections and that the views behind "the agreements in force" had prevailed. I therefore declared the party ready to accommodate those demands if a feasible way could be found to do so. I pointed out, however, that those with the highest wages would benefit most, and it was agreed to consider responses to that. As time went on, the role of us Progressives in the talks increasingly consisted of mediating between the other parties.

From the beginning it was clear that the Social Democratic Party was wary of the People's Alliance's ideas on economic affairs, and the tension between the parties grew with every meeting. After two weeks and ten meetings it had long been clear to me that an abyssal chasm divided the two labor parties and there was little hope of a solution. We declared ourselves willing to accommodate the viewpoints of both parties. I became convinced, however, that the People's Alliance's ideas about economic measures were unrealistic.

The leadership of the People's Alliance, though, spoke with two tongues in its argumentation. I noticed that Lúðvík Jósepsson spoke of "devaluation as an accomplished fact" in small meetings, though he called it a great absurdity when he spoke among his own party members. Duplicity of this kind seemed to me especially conspicuous in the People's Alliance. On July 29 I informed the parliamentary group that "the talks had run aground because of the disagreement between the Social Democratic Party and the People's Alliance over economic measures." They were broken off the following day, at the twelfth meeting.
At the beginning of August, Geir Hallgrímsson, chairman of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), received the mandate to form a government. Yet his effort can hardly be called anybut

rather some kind of feelers. At first Geir explored the possibility of forming a national unity government in talks among the four party chairmen. Ólafur Jóhannesson called those talks "insubstantial" at a meeting of the parliamentary group, and most considered them a waste of time. The national-government talks did not last long. In their wake, Geir initiated talks with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), but the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) was not invited to take part. Ólafur Jóhannesson and I were chosen for those talks on behalf of the Progressive Party's parliamentary group.

Before the parliamentary group answered the request of the chairman of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) for talks, the party's central committee was convened. It was expected that party members would be opposed to continued cooperation with the Independence Party even though the Social Democratic Party would be the third wheel on the wagon. Tómas Árnason was one of the few who spoke in favor of such a government configuration. He considered the People's Alliance unfit for cooperation in economic matters after the exuberant declarations of its spokesmen during the election campaign. Tómas did not, however, get his wish.

At the third meeting of the three parties, amid rather rocky discussions, Benedikt Gröndal put it this way: from the discussion one might think that the previous government was still in office rather than that the formation of a new government with fresh ideas was at hand. I thought there was a good deal to that. The Social Democratic Party broke off the talks before long.
Lúðvík Gets the Mandate

A month and a half had passed since the elections and no government appeared in sight. A revival of the Restoration (Viðreisn) coalition seemed the only conceivable government configuration without the participation of the Progressives. That mattered. The Progressive Party's interest in government participation has always increased in direct proportion to the danger of a new Restoration government. In the parliamentary group, the voices of doubt that had spoken against government participation therefore fell silent. I also sensed that the further we got from the elections, the more the party's members of parliament regained their self-confidence, and soon the voters' cold greetings had become almost a side issue. Ólafur Jóhannesson was once again his old self.

The President of Iceland granted Lúðvík Jósepsson the mandate to form a government on August 16, 1978. He called for talks on a left-wing government. This time the negotiations among the People's Alliance, the Social Democratic Party and the Progressive Party went better than before. Already at the first meeting it emerged that the People's Alliance was prepared to yield somewhat on economic matters and accept a devaluation even though that was not their policy. The Social Democratic Party also said it could support a mixed solution of wage-scaledown and devaluation, and those were the two paths that had been most discussed as solutions to the economic problem.

Ólafur Jóhannesson now once again led the Progressives' negotiating committee. He was in a prickly mood about everything. He said the wage-scaledown went out to the farthest edge and that a devaluation was "a distasteful thought" and "worse than wage robbery." I wanted to be more positive and said that important milestones had been reached in the discussion of economic matters. I acknowledged that a devaluation was undesirable but at the same time I considered it unavoidable, and I proposed that the government aim at bringing down inflation in stages. These were not, however, fully formed ideas, and I believe the talks suffered from the fact that we Progressives did not really have a fully developed economic policy. It did not come into being until during the government's term. Bringing down inflation in stages was our main platform in the elections a year later.

In these government-formation talks, much work was done in preparatory committees between meetings. Lúðvík allowed himself only a short time to test fully whether there was a will to cooperate among the parties. Right at the outset he asked for the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) position on his leadership of the government. This was taken up at a parliamentary group meeting. The Progressive Party's parliamentary group was unanimous at its meeting on August 21 that attempts to form a government with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) should continue. Many, however, had doubts about whether the chairman of the People's Alliance should lead the government.
Tómas was, as before, the most adamant in his opposition to the People's Alliance, but few others wanted to let things founder on the question of who would hold the premiership.
The Last Shall Be First

The third government-formation meeting was held on August 22, 1978. The atmosphere immediately suggested that matters were coming to a head. The tension shone from Lúðvík's face at the end of the table. He opened the meeting by declaring that he considered there to be a strong likelihood that the parties could come together. No one said anything. It was obvious that something else was weighing on Lúðvík. After a short silence he continued his remarks. He said he had discussed with the party chairmen, Ólafur and Benedikt, whether their parties would support him as prime minister. Ólafur had said yes but Benedikt no. Lúðvík said he wished to return his mandate if that was where things stood. Everyone present looked at one another and no one knew what would happen next.

As if to buy time, representatives of both parties nevertheless took the floor and expressed satisfaction with the draft policy agreement that lay before them. The Social Democrats made no mention of the premiership. Ólafur Jóhannesson, on the other hand, did. He said that the Progressive Party was prepared to enter into cooperation under "anyone's leadership," though individual men in

the party held other views. The People's Alliance men all nodded as if in agreement, but the Social Democrats were visibly uneasy. Lúðvík pressed Benedikt and said he needed clear answers regarding the prime minister's chair. Ragnar Arnalds took the floor as soon as Lúðvík yielded it and said that if it were a "principle" on the part of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) that a People's Alliance man should not become prime minister, that seemed to him "not a friendly stance." Benedikt said he understood that, but put it in such a way that opinions were divided about the leadership within the Social Democratic Party. A central committee meeting called by the Social Democratic Party later that day would, however, settle those matters.

It was evident from everything that Lúðvík and the People's Alliance men were extremely eager to hold the premiership of the government. That does not surprise me. It would have marked a decisive turning point in the history of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). There had always been a tacit agreement among the other political parties that the People's Alliance would not handle foreign affairs because of its position on NATO (Atlantshafsbandalagið) and Western cooperation. The prime minister's chair, however, would have given the party even more far-reaching power, both at home and abroad. Ólafur Jóhannesson's positive stance therefore surprised many, not least the Social Democratic Party.

When word came from the Social Democrats' camp that Lúðvík did not enjoy their support, it was clear that the People's Alliance would be slow to support a Social Democrat in the prime minister's chair. The consequences were obvious. Suddenly we Progressives and Ólafur Jóhannesson held the palm of victory after the biggest electoral defeat in the party's history.

I do not know for certain whether Ólafur foresaw this course of events in the final stretch of the government-formation talks. Over the years, however, I have become convinced that he did. He worked for support for Lúðvík within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), since he was fully confident that things would founder on the Social Democratic Party. I myself had doubts about Lúðvík's leadership, and certainly others in the Progressive Party's leadership did as well. Tómas Árnason declared himself completely opposed to a People's Alliance premiership, and Eysteinn struck the same note. He did not, however, want to let things founder on the prime minister's chair. Nor did it come to that. The inescapable conclusion was that Lúðvík returned his mandate and pointed the president to Ólafur Jóhannesson. He set to work on August 25, 1978. Two months had then passed since election day.

In economic matters there were still unresolved knots when Ólafur received the mandate. Hanging over the talks was also the fact that on September 1 the price freeze would expire. It had been in force ever since the Restoration years and had been renewed regularly by all the governments that had held office. If that were not

done, it was expected that inflation would take off in a big way. The pressure for action was therefore great, and the country needed a government. Even those who had most doubted that a left-wing government should be considered spoke in favor of the coalition at this point. Tómas Árnason put it this way: the goal of forming a government was to "avert the imminent shutdown of businesses and thereby unemployment," and Eysteinn Jónsson said there was "a political state of emergency in the country."

In the talks that now got under way, Tómas and I took seats on a subcommittee on economic affairs and met intensively with parties from the fisheries and agriculture, and no less with the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) economic committee. It fell to me to draft a written proposal for the economic chapter of the coalition agreement. I put it together under the heading "substantive points of a coalition agreement," a typewritten document of seven pages. Svavar Gestsson made quite detailed amendment proposals to this text in fifteen points in all. At the same time, the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) made reservations conditioning important points on the approval of the labor organizations.

These documents were both presented on August 28, and on the same day there was a meeting with representatives of the Icelandic Confederation of Labour (ASÍ) and the Federation of State and Municipal Employees (BSRB). Their attitude toward the parties' ideas was positive, but there were disputes over particular points of implementation. The People's Alliance bided its time while the labor movement deliberated. Matters seemed to be at a standstill.
"We Set Out to Row, Though the Boat Is Leaky"

The day after these meetings, on August 29, Ólafur Jóhannesson was pessimistic about reaching agreement before the end of the month. He was gloomy over Svavar Gestsson's initiative in coming forward with countless comments on my text at the eleventh hour. Ólafur seemed to me tired and short on hope. I myself had been engaged in almost daily negotiations for weeks on end, in addition to the work that had to be done between meetings. I had had little time to be with my family, and so I mentioned to Ólafur whether it would be safe for me to slip away to our summer house at Klettur in Borgarfjörður now that there was a moment's respite between battles. He saw nothing standing in the way.

No sooner had the family arrived at its destination than a messenger came at full speed from the farmhouse at Klettur. A call had come there, and the household had been asked to pass on the message that Ólafur Jóhannesson requested that I come to Reykjavík at once. We loaded all the luggage back into the car and sped off. Below Úlfarsfell I was stopped by the police doing 110 kilometers per hour. I was fined on the spot.
On arriving in Reykjavík I went straight to see Ólafur. He had by then received a letter from ASÍ with positive responses to the main points

of the economic proposals. These were, however, all temporary measures. The conclusion had been that agreement on long-term measures should be reached after the government had taken office. Ólafur said that with this, things finally seemed to be coming together, and the draft coalition agreement that we had finalized the day before now seemed to enjoy the support of all the parties. We went over the text together once more, and I presented it at a parliamentary group meeting later that day. There we obtained the parliamentary group's approval for the formation of the government. That evening there was a meeting of the parties' negotiating committee. There Ólafur announced that he intended to call on the president the following morning and announce the formation of a government.

The parties' joint declaration of cooperation was dated August 31, 1978. Two days earlier, Ólafur had put it this way in the parliamentary group: it "carried with it the implication that what was impossible was to be done." He therefore said he was setting out on this swim with a great shudder. Páll Pétursson was not long in tossing off a verse after these words of the chairman:
We set out to row, though the boat is leaky and tedious toil lies ahead. Now we shall do all that's impossible but nothing of the rest, which is needed.

When the declaration of cooperation was under discussion, Ólafur also informed the parliamentary group that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) would in all likelihood receive the ministries of transport, agriculture and justice, in addition to the prime minister's office. No substantial objections were raised to this, any more than to the outcome of the parties' negotiations.

One of the biggest pieces of news in the declaration of cooperation was that this was the first left-wing government that did not have on its platform the departure of the military during the electoral term. Instead, the parties settled on a general statement on foreign affairs, and it was decided to establish a "committee for the examination of security matters."

I had presented our Progressives' idea of an "objective and impartial study" of the country's security matters in the parties' earlier talks under the leadership of Benedikt Gröndal. It immediately received positive responses from both of the A-parties. I had also said that the party did not consider there to be grounds for the departure of the Defense Force for the time being, and that the Progressives supported Western cooperation. The end of the left-wing government in 1974 and the Progressive Party's change of policy during the cooperation with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in 1974–78 were the main reasons for that. I said, on the other hand, that matters of peace were very close to

his party's heart. At this meeting Lúðvík remarked that agreement "could be reached on a general policy framework in the spirit of the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) resolutions." Benedikt had by then, for his part, rejected the People's Alliance's (Alþýðubandalagið) ideas of the departure of the military or the declaration of the North Atlantic as a peace zone.

The conclusion appeared in the coalition agreement under the heading: Committee for the Examination of Security Matters. I think it was clear to everyone involved in forming the government that a new chapter had begun. For the first time, the People's Alliance took a seat in a government without the departure of the military being stipulated. After this conclusion was reached in 1978, the departure of the military has never been seriously contested in government-formation talks in Iceland. The committee that was established later received the name Security Affairs Committee (öryggismálanefnd). Representatives of all political parties in parliament sat on it. Regarding its scope of work, the coalition agreement said, among other things:

The committee shall make a thorough assessment of the nation's security matters, the country's position in world conflicts, options for a security policy, the current arrangement of security matters and their effect on Icelandic national life, as well as the future of the military bases after the force leaves and defenses against groups of terrorists. The committee shall also address ideas of a peace-zone declaration, peacekeeping and surveillance in the North Atlantic, and shall have an overview prepared of the security arrangements of small states in the world, especially island states that have similar interests to safeguard as the Icelanders.
"Have You Lost Your Mind? I'm Just an Engineer"

On August 30, 1978, the parliamentary group chose the party's ministerial candidates in a secret ballot. Ólafur was of course the automatic choice for prime minister. In the vote on the other ministerial candidates I received 10 votes and Tómas Árnason eight. Others received far fewer votes. Ólafur called me to a meeting with him in Þórshamar before he made his proposal on which ministry I would head. By then the division of labor in the government had changed and the party had received finance instead of transport, which was of course a major addition. Ólafur said he intended for me to become minister of agriculture and of justice and ecclesiastical affairs. Tómas Árnason was to be put over finance. I asked whether he had lost his mind. "You expect me to become minister of justice?" I said. "I'm just an engineer." Ólafur answered without hesitation.
"Justice matters are on the one hand what concerns the laws and on the other what concerns the public," he said in his calm tone of voice. "You will be the ombudsman of the public
in justice matters." This came as much of a surprise to Tómas, the lawyer, as to me.

I found it remarkable to have become minister of justice, but amusing to be placed over ecclesiastical affairs. When I wrote to my son Jón in the United States and told him about these new duties of mine, I did not downplay having become the supreme head of the Icelandic church. I do not recall that anyone asked me whether I believed in God before I took up the office. That probably reflects the reality of Icelandic politics, in which religious views have, happily, never divided people into factions.

I have never been without faith, though Christianity has not played a key role in my life. But I have always had difficulty seeing the rationale for how people choose among different religions or split into bitter factions on their account. In my mind they are of equal standing and always have been. My position has been simple. Any faith that preaches good moral conduct is a good thing. I considered the Icelandic national church in no way superior to others in that respect.

In recent years I have in fact leaned ever more toward ideas of a higher power. I have applied myself to writings on the creation and evolution of the universe and come to the conclusion that this incredible story cannot have come about by chance alone. One of the most influential books I have read on this subject is by the religious philosopher Thomas Berry, Befriending the Earth. He presents arguments about the evolution of the world and the primal forces and powers that lie behind it. He in fact never mentions God in his theories, only an undefined higher power.

I agree with Berry that I find it hard to understand how a series of pure coincidences is supposed to have created this globe and the delicate balance that is the precondition of all life. That requires such a good engineer that the idea of God is probably the most obvious. Einstein was apparently of a similar opinion. He put it that God did not play dice. Previously I believed in God because I did not feel able to rule out that a higher power existed. With age I have moved closer to the idea of a creator, by whatever name he is called. When all is said and done, one might perhaps say that I have an engineer's attitude toward faith. It takes over where the explanations of science leave off.
The Parting from the Research Council

I stepped down as director of the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins) on September 25, 1978, since I had taken up a ministerial office. My last major undertaking was to organize the annual meeting, which was held in Háskólabíó. The meeting was well attended and was considered a great success. I permit myself to assert

that the meeting was better prepared technically than had previously been known here. Every presentation was carefully reviewed and timed. A Norwegian model was followed in the execution of the meeting, and a large number of people were invited to it. When I said my farewells, I had served as director for the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) for nearly twenty-one years. I was succeeded in my post by Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson, who had been associated with the council for a good many years but was at that time running an independent consulting firm.

The years at the Research Council were in many ways good. The work was enriching, and I found it extremely useful to get to know the great number of people who work in science in this country. During those years, research activity in Iceland strengthened considerably, no less than the Research Council itself, which moved from a cubbyhole by Vatnsmýrin into decent quarters at Laugavegur 13. Its operations grew no less than the research activity.

When I looked back, I was content with the state of affairs. The "new laws" that were enacted on research activity in 1965 had on the whole proved successful. Buildings had been erected for the industrial research institutes at Keldnaholt and for the Marine Research Institute (Hafrannsóknastofnun) at Skúlagata 4. Systematic studies of the development of research activity began, and studies of the utilization of the country's natural resources were greatly expanded. Even in politics the effects of these works could be seen in many places. The results of sea-chemicals research led to a salt factory and further dreams of sea-chemicals processing. Seaweed and kelp processing began at Breiðafjörður and diatomite processing at Mývatn.

International work and foreign relations increased greatly, and studies of unexplored fields of knowledge and new ideas became numerous. Research on the continental shelf began, studies of heavy-water production, of greenhouse cultivation, prospecting for metals, and the list could go on. On the foundation of what was done well, numerous other innovations took root: sea-ice research and avalanche studies began, and both received a worthy place at the Meteorological Office (Veðurstofan). An information service was set up at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands) at the initiative of the Research Council, and the first computer became the foundation of the University Computing Centre (Reiknistofnun Háskólans). Ties with research activity abroad and with international committees on science and higher education were built up practically from scratch. Much more could be enumerated.

Of course I did not deserve the credit for everything that happened during this time. Far from it. I was, however, involved in most things in some way, as an instigator, participant, observer, or in cooperation with the scientists and the executive committee of the Research Council. In my work in politics one can also see in many places the marks of my having been practically raised at the Research Council. In the Althing (Alþingi) I introduced quite a few measures whose idea had been sparked in the Research Council's arena, and in a great many others I drew arguments and experience from my years there.
This varied range of tasks and diverse experience was of great value to me, and indeed still is.
"The Hatless Generation"

One of my first acts in the Ministry of Justice (dómsmálaráðuneytið) was to visit the institutions that fell under it. At the Reykjavík police I was well received. When I greeted the staff at the front desk, I was handed a speeding ticket from the week before. I paid the fine on the spot, to the amusement of those present.

I later heard that the ministry staff had found the working styles of Ólafur Jóhannesson and myself utterly different. Ólafur had certainly never been caught speeding. He did not even have a driver's license. In his work he was calm and measured, just as he was in his bearing and speech. He was not one for arriving early at work; instead he took the number five bus once the morning was well under way and the worst of the rush was over. At midday he always went home, if there were no parliamentary group meetings, ate, and lay down for a nap after the meal. In the afternoon he rarely left the ministry later than five o'clock. In the library at his home on Aragata, however, he could sit late into the evening pondering the cards with a pipe in hand. Documents were rarely seen on his desk except briefly while he was signing them.

Ólafur used the telephone only out of pressing necessity, and visitors were a rare sight in his office. He was considered slow to make decisions, but he thought every matter through to the end. He kept his word without exception and was seldom budged. In my mind, Ólafur was a splendid representative of the old era.

A newspaper article put it this way: that I was the first representative of the "hatless generation" in a minister's chair. I immediately set about modernizing the ministry technologically, added telephone lines, and got the officials tape recorders to ease correspondence and secretarial work. I took pride in arriving first in the morning and stayed late into the evening when needed. More often, though, it was party matters or solutions to economic problems that held me up rather than the affairs of the ministry. The change involved more than that. The support staff in the ministry suddenly had to provide coffee and refreshments to all comers, for the waiting room was regularly full of people who had business with the ministry or whom I had summoned for consultation.

I also had a different working method in decision-making, which some of my colleagues at first found hard to grasp. They were unaccustomed to the minister testing his ideas on them instead of announcing his conclusion and an immovable decision. I listened closely to the viewpoints

of the staff. They no doubt thought me hasty as much as quick to decide, and found it unusual how ready I was to listen to arguments and change my mind. As time went on, however, cooperation within the ministries went superbly; the spirit was good and the output matched it.

Much in the Ministry of Justice (dómsmálaráðuneytið) was an inheritance from Ólafur's time as minister. Although I sometimes found his working methods old-fashioned, he had the open mind of a scholar and gave his support especially to those reform ideas that were novel and modern. Wide-ranging reforms of the court system had been launched in his time. The State Criminal Investigation Police (Rannsóknarlögregla ríkisins) was established, and the courts and the working practices of the offices under the ministry were subjected to a thorough review. When I came to this work, I often felt not enough had been done and wanted to approach these problems from new directions. Among other things, I brought in engineers to carry out an assessment of offices and institutions.
Such methods were without precedent in the administrative system, and many long-established officials regarded them as suspect at best.

In my work and policy-making I strove to respond to criticism of the slow pace of the court system. To that end I called for proposals from judges and their deputies on anything they thought would increase efficiency in the operation of the courts and could speed up the progress of court cases. Not everything was accomplished, however, by the courts working faster. I also saw how badly it could affect convicted men if there were delays before they served their sentences. Since the prisons were usually full, I came to the conclusion that it would be sensible to look for remedies other than imprisonment as punishment in criminal cases. Unfortunately, my tenure did not last long enough for me to put those ideas into practice.

In just over a year in office as Minister of Justice, I probably became most famous for "opening the bars," as it was called. I decided by regulation that alcohol could be served on Wednesdays, which had previously been "dry" days, and granted permission to sell drink after half past eleven on weekends. I saw no sense in the arrangement then in force. In those days there were scuffles outside the licensed establishments as the clock approached twelve and the patrons stormed in to stock up on drinks before the bar closed. After the changes, the bars could stay open until three o'clock on weekends. On weekdays I permitted the sale of alcohol until one o'clock. To me these were natural steps toward modern times. The teetotalers and templars in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), however, were about to hit the roof.
A Glimpse into Another World

The justice portfolio proved instructive for me. What Ólafur had said turned out to be true: the human element in these matters counts for more than might appear at first. During my open office hours a great number of women came to plead the cases of their husbands, the fathers of their children, or their sons, who were in prison for various offenses. They all had their stories to tell — of longing and love, difficult family circumstances, lack of money, drunkenness, and human degradation. Through their accounts I gained insight into corners of society I had not encountered before. I was often asked to pardon men, postpone the serving of sentences, or shorten their punishments. I could grant only a fraction of those requests. When all else failed, the women would call my home in tears at night.

The Minister of Justice did not decide these matters alone. A so-called sentence-enforcement review board (fullnustumatsnefnd), headed by law professor Jónatan Þórmundsson, gave its opinion on all requests concerning pardons and reductions of sentences. This board had been established by Ólafur Jóhannesson. I rarely went against its rulings or advice. It also served me very well that Ólafur Jóhannesson had set rules on the handling of certain matters. For example, the Minister of Justice's authority to lift penalties for drunk driving had been abolished. I often thought warmly of Ólafur for this, because cases connected with alcohol use were often thorny. More often than not I felt sympathy for those who came to me and would have preferred to do everything in my power to grant their wishes. Nevertheless, it was clear to me that concessions and exemptions sometimes did them no favor.
I understood that quickly.

I particularly remember that an acquaintance of mine in the Westfjords (Vestfirðir) was facing a prison term. He was the head of a financial institution but was convicted of embezzlement, lost his position, and was to serve three months. He was a staunch Independence Party man, but we knew each other well. By the time I became minister he had once had his sentence postponed. He came to me wanting another postponement. I said I could perhaps arrange it. But then he would still have the prison term hanging over his head, and the time would come when he would be forced to take his seat in the dock. I suggested he choose a convenient time, sooner rather than later, and offered to arrange for him to serve his sentence at Akureyri, which was considered one of the best places.

I telephoned north and was told that a place would be free there shortly. My acquaintance took this hard and said his wife was distraught at seeing him go to prison. He nevertheless followed my advice, and I believe I managed to get the sentence somewhat shortened. After serving it he soon got a job again, and the future lay open before him and his family.
I have rarely received as warm a greeting as when we next met.

In the Ministry of Justice I enjoyed capable colleagues and good advisers. Baldur Möller was permanent secretary. He is a singular man. When one entered his office, everything seemed to be in disarray. Papers overflowed from corner to corner and everything was covered in documents and stacks of files — desk, chairs, and floor. Yet if anything was needed, Baldur could find his way through the piles blindfolded. There his chess talents showed themselves, along with an incredible memory.
Eiríkur Tómasson, a lawyer and son of Tómas Árnason, had been Ólafur Jóhannesson's assistant in the ministry. He agreed to stay on and work for me. I also had unofficial advisers.

The Supreme Court (Hæstiréttur) was on the other side of the wall from my office. Among those serving there as justices were Ármann Snævarr and Benedikt Sigurjónsson. I knew them both of old. Ármann and I had sat together on the Council of Europe's committee on education and science in Strasbourg and got to know each other well there. Our friendship has lasted to this day without a shadow falling on it. Benedikt I had known since I was young. He was a staunch Progressive and I had often sought his advice on legal matters. Ármann and Benedikt soon became my chief advisers in everything concerning the justice portfolio. I went over difficult pending cases with them, and they proved sound counselors to me in each and every thing.

They accepted no payment for it, and to tell the truth I saw nothing objectionable in these two branches of state power, the judiciary and the executive, working closely together. Perhaps, though, this advisory relationship was more questionable than I realized.

Eiríkur Tómasson was a first-rate assistant, conscientious and meticulous. He was also chairman of the Federation of Young Progressives (Samband ungra framsóknarmanna), and I found it good to be in close touch with the currents stirring there. Eiríkur had obtained postgraduate training in constitutional law. Some of the older party men thought him too bookish in that field and, by the same token, too little of a party man. That thought was far from my mind. He was my loyal assistant, had previously worked energetically for Ólafur Jóhannesson, his father was Minister of Finance, and he himself had occupied third place on the party's list in the 1978 city council elections. Eiríkur often had firm ideas on sensitive matters and did not keep them to himself within the party.

For instance, few others spoke up for equalizing the voting rights of the country's citizens at meetings of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). I often found Eiríkur's working methods and attitudes exemplary and took considerable account of his views.
Church affairs were free of conflict and not a large part of the ministry's work. One

man handled them. In my work on church affairs I became acquainted, among others, with Sigurbjörn Einarsson, who was then bishop. Our acquaintance has lasted ever since, and my regard for him has grown the closer it has become. I count him among the finer Icelanders now living. He is an inspired thinker and a fervent man of faith.

As Minister of Ecclesiastical Affairs I attended the Church Assembly (kirkjuþing). This highest gathering of the national church struck me as a rather conservative congregation. As far as I could see, faith and human destinies there fell entirely into the shadow of routine worldly busywork. I also feared it would be difficult to change if the clergy alone were left in charge. It seemed to me there was a pressing need to open up the Church Assembly and introduce more modern attitudes and working practices. I did not, however, consider it within the remit of the Minister of Ecclesiastical Affairs to intervene in such matters.
An Obsolete Agricultural System

Ever since political struggle in Iceland began to be about something more than independence from the Danes, it had been the shared ambition of the country's political parties to increase production at sea and in the countryside. The spirit of development was drawn from the words and deeds of the turn-of-the-century generation, and the build-up in agriculture and fisheries continued unbroken until near the end of the 1970s. By then it had become clear that the page had to be turned, and the first attempts were made to do so. When I came to the Ministry of Agriculture (landbúnaðarráðuneytið), the hardest struggle was that the economic statistics said one thing but the prevailing mindset another. Changing that was no small undertaking.

Agricultural affairs were difficult and took a great deal of time. One of the most pressing tasks was a review of the export subsidy system. It had been established during the first term of the Reconstruction Government (viðreisnarstjórnin), and the legislation on it was named after the ministers Ingólfur and Gylfi. Its aim was to increase production in order to meet domestic demand for agricultural products. It may be said that the legislation quickly and effectively achieved that goal. By the time I took the chair of Minister of Agriculture, however, overproduction had been persistent for more than a decade.

At first the recourse had been to export the production that the nation could not consume. Often no acceptable price could be obtained for the goods abroad because of market conditions or tariff walls. Export subsidies were therefore resorted to in order to "secure farmers' incomes" and ensure that they received "full price" for their production. By 1978 the export subsidies on the lamb that was exported had reached up to 70 percent of the domestic wholesale price and were heading higher. To me this made no sense at all.

I realized nevertheless that the system had become entrenched. A whole generation of farmers hardly knew anything else, and most of them had long since become dependent on the income they had from exports and subsidies. One of my first tasks was to respond to the news that the Norwegians announced they would buy no more meat from Iceland. I went to Norway and spoke there with, among others, the minister of agriculture. He was very frank and said that we Icelanders would never be competitive with the Australians and New Zealanders. There, sheep grazed on their own all year round and there was no need to build expensive sheep sheds. Our production was doomed to be more expensive, just like Norway's. The Norwegian minister of agriculture added that he thought Icelandic lamb tasted better.
I managed to negotiate that the Norwegians would buy an unchanged quantity of Icelandic meat for one more year. I knew it was only a stay of execution.

This was only one example of many. Price developments in foreign markets had gradually squeezed the export subsidy system, and it had become clear to most people that exports would shrink greatly or cease. The domestic market was obviously not large enough to absorb all the production. It had to be cut back. This had in fact been known for several years. My predecessor in the Ministry of Agriculture (landbúnaðarráðuneytið), Halldór E. Sigurðsson, had raised the question of changes to the export subsidy system during his time as minister. To work on the matter he appointed a so-called committee of seven (sjömannanefnd). Representatives of the farmers sat on it together with the social partners of the labor market. The committee gathered a great deal of data, but its proposals were slow to appear. I am not sure that displeased Halldór.
In his memoirs he does not mention this review work by name but puts it this way:
It was [...] not my role to work toward contraction in agriculture. [...] It was [...] a decision of a later time to change this policy so as to reduce agricultural production.

I picked up the thread that Halldór had spun but wanted to go about the work more briskly. The foundation I had to build on was the resolutions of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) from the party congress of 1978. There the party had resolved, after considerable struggle, to abandon the "development policy" that had been pursued in agriculture. It took an insider, though, to spot the change of policy. Only slight nuances in the congress resolution hinted at it. The most honest course would have been to say outright that production should be for the domestic market only and exports stopped altogether. Instead,

the wording used was that farm products "[should be] produced to earn foreign currency insofar as it is considered economical." The resolution nevertheless contained the germ of the change of policy that I championed.

The work of the Ministry of Agriculture (landbúnaðarráðuneytið) was directed by Sveinbjörn Dagfinnsson, my brother-in-law, with great conscientiousness. To manage the important policy-making I felt was needed, I hired Hákon Sigurgrímsson into the Ministry of Agriculture. He had been an employee of the Agricultural Production Board (Framleiðsluráð landbúnaðarins) and was at the Farmers' Union (Stéttarsamband bænda) when I sought his services. He was a true godsend. Hákon had been prominent among the reformers within the party and was at the forefront of those who supported policy changes in agriculture. He became, in effect, my political assistant. Since I was authorized to have only one assistant, he was given the job title of adviser (ráðunautur).

Hákon bore, among other things, the brunt of the work on a parliamentary resolution on policy-making in agriculture. It summarized the development of agriculture throughout this century and the situation as it stood in 1978. An enormously large group was contacted and consulted in drafting the resolution, which together with its explanatory report ran to well over a hundred pages in all.

The parliamentary resolution stipulated for the first time that the production of agricultural products in Iceland should be first and foremost for the domestic market. Goals were set for production management, along with a plan to abolish the export subsidy system over a few years. Farm production was to be managed on the basis of a consumption plan, and the nation was to be given nutritional goals and a policy on wholesome food. It was also an innovation that the resolution stated that these stated goals should be achieved through direct agreements between the state and the farmers.

Our idea was to lay the groundwork for reducing sheep farming and milk production, since overproduction was a fact. At the same time, however, a path would be charted toward new and more profitable forms of farming. Emphasis was placed on the contraction happening in stages. A five-year plan was drawn up. In that time, overproduction was to be reduced substantially, export subsidies largely abolished, and part of the money saved by lowering the subsidies channeled into innovation. In this way the worst blow of the unavoidable contraction would be softened. The new branches of agriculture under discussion were poultry and pig farming, fur farming, fish farming, tourism, forestry, and greenhouse cultivation. The parliamentary resolution never received formal approval in the Althing (Alþingi).
Nevertheless, it may be said that it charted the policy that was followed in broad outline for the next twenty years and is in many respects followed still.
The Election Promissory Note Falls Due

When I run my eyes over the minutes of this first government of my ministerial career, I cannot help thinking how greatly the tasks of governments and politicians changed in the twenty-odd years that I was involved in governing the country. The first matter the prime minister raised when his government convened concerned the fact that "Kristján Jósefsson's animal collection" on Skólavörðustígur was to be sold at auction because of arrears in public dues. Nothing less would do than that two ministers were assigned to consider whether it would not be right to "do something to save the matter."

The smallest matters landed on the government's table, in keeping with the working methods, spirit, and economic system of the time. In the inflation society, the labor movement strove to maintain the purchasing power of wages, and a complicated indexation system was set up to further that. At the same time, efforts were made to hold down the price of goods. To that end a price freeze was applied, which had been in force since the last term of the Reconstruction Government (viðreisnarstjórnin), and a vigorous price-control regime was established to monitor compliance with the ban. In the end it regularly fell to the government to set the prices of various necessities and services. Naturally, fish prices and oil prices came up for decision, and these were often fought over.

The government also set the prices of domestic airfares and of agricultural and industrial goods, butter, ale, and soft drinks, not to mention the price of cinema tickets. Day-care fees in individual municipalities and tariff changes throughout society also had to receive government approval, and I laid my proposals for pardons of individual convicts before my fellow ministers. We released civil servants from their posts on account of age by special resolutions, and at one meeting we even decided, on the proposal of the Minister of Education, how many musicians there should be in the Iceland Symphony Orchestra (Sinfóníuhljómsveit Íslands). It is sometimes hard to suppress a smile when reading these old minutes.

Economic affairs, however, took up by far the most time in the government. One of its first acts was to issue provisional legislation on September 8, 1978. This was only a short-term solution, and everyone knew it. The currency was devalued by 15 percent, the price freeze extended, and various accompanying measures taken. What mattered most, though, was that the provisions of the summer-solstice agreements (sólstöðusamningar) were "put into effect" as of December 1, 1978. With that, the economy was in effect back in the same position as at the beginning of the year, when the government had been forced to halve the cost-of-living supplements on wages.

It was clear to everyone that these measures would not hold for long. The coalition parties had agreed to settle for reaching consensus on these first actions while the government was being formed, and to work on a long-term program in economic affairs after the government had taken office. In hindsight, this was an ill-fated decision. Inflation did not decrease. It remained in the range of 40–50 percent. The indexation of wages ensured that when employers responded to increased labor costs with price increases, wages rose correspondingly. This story repeated itself over and over and was called the interplay of wages and prices in the language of economists, but the inflation spiral or vicious circle in plain speech. Savings, however, were not indexed and burned up on the inflation bonfire in the banks. Interest rates on loans were negative. The banks bemoaned their lot.
It paid to be in debt.
A Stormy Coalition

At the government's meetings there was little peace, and a long-term program in economic affairs seemed nowhere in sight. The disagreement over economic matters affected the entire coalition; there were fierce disputes and accusations flew between people. Each minister is his own master. However, the approval of the entire cabinet is required if a bill is to be introduced in the Althing in the government's name. It follows that ministers can hold each other's bills "hostage" in the government by refusing to let them through. This is frequently employed, often to bargain for support on other matters than those being blocked. When hostage-taking gets out of hand, the government can become virtually unable to function.

Sometimes the disputes were so fierce that the prime minister took matters off the agenda before they had been fully discussed. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) members considered the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) to be standing in the way of most of their initiatives, and there was some truth to that. Nor was it far off that they were answered in the same coin. When the winter was well advanced, more than a dozen matters had piled up unresolved. Some of them had been brought up repeatedly for discussion. These were chiefly matters that fell under the purview of the Social Democratic Party or the People's Alliance. Between the two parties the rivalry that traced its roots to the internecine feuds all the way back to 1958 was alive and well. Throughout that whole time the parties had been more or less in opposition to each other, fighting over the same voters.

Neither party was willing to bury the hatchet, and this affected all the government's work. The disputes over the leadership of the government during its formation had naturally not helped the old grievances fade.
The ministers of the People's Alliance were Svavar Gestsson, who handled trade affairs, Ragnar Arnalds, who was Minister of Education, and Hjörleifur Guttormsson

was Minister of Industry. Svavar made his presence strongly felt and could be ferocious. He had a fine head of hair in those years, and the dark rims around his eyes gave him a striking look when he launched into long speeches through his intellectual's beard. Hjörleifur Guttormsson did not hold back in debates if he felt a matter concerned him. He is not the most flexible negotiator I have known. No minister read the minutes and documents of the government as carefully as Hjörleifur. He was tireless in recording protests and comments on how his position was entered into the record.

For the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), the ministers in the government were Benedikt Gröndal, who served as Minister for Foreign Affairs, Magnús H. Magnússon, who handled the ministries of health, social insurance, and social affairs, and Kjartan Jóhannsson, who was Minister of Fisheries. Kjartan was the one among the Social Democrats who most often spoke on their behalf. Benedikt Gröndal kept more to the background even though he was the party's chairman. He also faced an uphill battle in his own parliamentary group. There Vilmundur Gylfason and Sighvatur Björgvinsson held sway. Benedikt's courtesy and polished manner bore witness to fine gifts but seemed to serve him little when dealing with Vilmundur and Sighvatur. They wanted the government dead from the outset and had voted against its formation in the Social Democratic parliamentary group.
Benedikt's stamina was running out as time went on.

Magnús H. Magnússon and Ragnar Arnalds were moderate in all their conduct, and I felt they contributed much that was sensible. They largely stayed out of the sharpest disputes. From our Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) ranks, it was most often Tómas who fought the hard battles, chiefly with the ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). Tómas was Minister of Finance, fought for a deficit-free budget, and got his way. Tómas's achievements tend to be forgotten when the work of the left-wing government is tallied up. For a long while I stayed out of the conflicts within the government and spoke for compromise and reconciliation. As the winter wore on, however, things came to a head between me and the Social Democratic ministers over agricultural matters.

Björn Bjarnason, currently a minister for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), was responsible for writing the minutes of the government's meetings. He had been hired to the Prime Minister's Office in the days of Geir Hallgrímsson and was doubtless one of the most sworn opponents of the left-wing government. He was always considered one of Geir's closest advisers. Ólafur Jóhannesson nevertheless let Björn keep his job even though he had been hired as a kind of assistant to Geir. Björn was even himself of two minds about whether it was proper for him to continue in this position.
I sometimes found myself thinking how different they were in character

Ólafur and Björn when the latter deemed Helgi Jónsson, the television news director, unfit to carry out his duties before the 1998 city council elections. In his writings, Björn put forward as proof of this unfitness that Helga Jónsdóttir, Helgi's wife, had been hired as city clerk by the leaders of the Reykjavík List (Reykjavíkurlistinn). Björn showed neither Helga nor the news director, her husband, the basic respect of treating them as public servants who were carrying out their duties with sincerity and dedication. Ólafur Jóhannesson, by contrast, paid no heed to the political views of his civil servants, let alone their marriages. Björn's official duties in the Prime Minister's Office did not change at all from Geir's time until Björn himself decided to move on to other work.

After contentious cabinet meetings, the journalists of Dagblaðið seemed to be the first people some of the ministers talked to. The paper practically made a habit of reserving its front page for some sensational story leaked from cabinet meetings. In the aftermath, the party under attack would then have to respond, and thus one petty matter after another snowballed. I do not know who talked to the papers. No one would admit to it. What I do know is that this fed suspicion and disunity between the parties. In this respect, it was one of the worst governments I ever sat in.

Early in the winter, Ólafur Jóhannesson seemed to handle the situation well. He enjoyed more respect than any other Icelandic politician and had in fact stood head and shoulders above everyone else ever since he established himself as prime minister of the left-wing government in 1971. This coalition, however, was a tighter dance than any he had been in before. He leaned alternately on the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) or the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and thus got matters through by tenacity, if nothing else. Tómas and I followed him closely and supported his position almost without exception. If hard knots formed, ministerial committees with representatives of each party were often appointed. In this way it proved possible to reach agreement on important matters without cabinet meetings having to erupt over them.
An Attempt at Reconciliation
It is rather tiresome to serve in a government that seems on the verge of blowing apart every other day. It is like Valhalla in the old days. Men fell in the evening and rose up again in the morning.
So I put it when the first autumn session of the left-wing government was well advanced. The occasion was singular. The president of the upper chamber of parliament, the Social Democrat

Bragi Sigurjónsson, had resigned his office with great commotion out of dissatisfaction with the conduct of the coalition parties in matters of inflation. Bragi said the parties' disputes were such that he wanted "not to be a symbol of cooperation in such a game and such working methods." Later that same winter, Bragi delivered a no less memorable speech when he described the atmosphere in the government by expounding on how he could not make the old refrain, Oh, What a Lovely War, his own:

Certainly there has been a war, an almost continuous war, but it has not been lovely; it has been sorrowful, for in truth brothers have turned their spears against one another ... Though one fire is waded through to an agreement, another seems to take its place. One might say that the fire we are now trying to wade through toward solving the nation's problems is the third or fourth in the series since the current government was formed.

The fires Bragi referred to mostly blazed over economic matters. It proved costly to the coalition to have postponed agreement on long-term economic measures to a better time when the government's platform was drawn up. It was not least the Social Democrats who grew restless as time went on.

At the end of 1978, the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) had prepared a draft bill on economic measures. The proposals were disputed within the government, and the Social Democratic parliamentary group resorted to setting conditions and deadlines for agreement on the matter. This became a settled habit of the Social Democrats and did not make the cooperation easier. Few of the deadlines held, and thereby a homemade problem had come into being. To tackle the economic situation, it was agreed that a ministerial committee should be appointed to reach an accord. It was established in the first days of 1979. I was chosen for it along with Kjartan Jóhannsson from the Social Democratic Party and Ragnar Arnalds from the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). Hallgrímur Snorrason, an employee of the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun), assisted us.
He is now the head of Statistics Iceland (Hagstofa Íslands). This group worked hard and well together, and the meetings often lasted long into the evening. We had a month for the task.

We took turns hosting the meetings in our ministerial offices. Each party put forward its ideas, which we went over carefully together. Then they were pieced together as agreement was reached — in the fullest sense of the phrase. Hallgrímur Snorrason sat with the scissors and showed exceptional skill in cutting approved sentences out of the parties' typewritten proposals and gluing them onto a blank sheet. As the work progressed, ever more
was added to Hallgrímur's sheets. It was invaluable to have him along. Hallgrímur is one of the most conscientious workers I have ever known.

The government's difficulties crystallized in the work of the economic committee. The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) each struggled with internal problems, though of different kinds. The Social Democratic ministers were weak in their own parliamentary group and never seemed to have their base in order. It was therefore risky to rely on their agreements until the parliamentary group had approved them. I liked Kjartan Jóhannsson and found it good to work with him. He was exceptionally conscientious and allowed himself no rest. Kjartan chain-smoked at meetings and drank ink-strong coffee. He already had a receding hairline and often sat with his hand on his forehead as he pored over our calculations or proposals.

As Kjartan was more and more often sent back empty-handed from the parliamentary group, where Vilmundur and Sighvatur sat finding fault with everything, it seemed to me that Kjartan had an ever harder time keeping his composure. His wife was very worried about his health, and not without reason. Kjartan became unable to sleep, was visibly worn down, and grew sickly in appearance. In the end he very nearly broke down. It was painful to watch. Kjartan finally fell ill from excessive strain. When things calmed down, however, he made a full recovery.

The People's Alliance's problem was of a different nature but no easier to deal with. Everything the People's Alliance ministers approved in the field of economic affairs had to go before the party's labor council. It was large and temperamental. It rarely occurred to the party's leadership, however, to go against its will. If one wanted to make a deal with the People's Alliance, one had to reach agreement with the labor council. Ragnar Arnalds, the Minister of Education, sat on the government's economic committee. He has remarked, half in jest and half in earnest, that it is probably unique in the history of the republic that most of the time of the man in charge of the schools went into economic affairs.
It seemed to me that Ragnar and the People's Alliance ministers came back no less weary from their labor meetings than the Social Democratic ministers from meetings of their own parliamentary group.
A Solo Performance at the Kitchen Table

Despite these difficulties, the economic committee largely reached agreement in the end, and within the time allotted to us. That could be credited to the mutual trust and confidence that developed among the three of us. I was proud of this outcome and considered it quite a feat. That same day I went to see Ólafur Jóhannesson with what was called "Substantive points for a bill

and resolutions." This was January 31, 1979. The committee's agreement was presented to the cabinet at its meeting the next day. There Ólafur said he intended to draft a bill on its basis. Something else came to light, however. Ólafur had already prepared a detailed bill on the same subject "at the kitchen table at home," as he put it. In it, various things the committee had agreed on were left out and other things added. Among what Ólafur put forward were points that the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) had rejected outright but which, on the other hand, were more to the liking of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn).

Ten days passed from the time Ólafur received the economic committee's opinion until he presented his bill in the cabinet. During this time, two parliamentary group meetings were held and just as many cabinet meetings. I had gone regularly to see Ólafur while the ministerial committee was at work to inform him of how things were going, and I knew he was pondering these matters. However, I had not suspected that Ólafur was working on a bill of his own, let alone that he intended to depart in fundamental respects from the agreement in the ministerial committee.

Ólafur did not call Tómas and me to a single meeting with him during this coalition, neither to prepare this matter nor any other. When he presented his bill in the cabinet, it took us as much by surprise as the ministers of the other parties. I felt like a botched piece of work after having stood behind an agreement with my fellow ministers. Tómas and I were deeply hurt by this and talked about it between ourselves. We effectively faced the choice of quarreling with the chairman or supporting his cause. We took the party line, and I kept a low profile in the cabinet. Everything there blew sky-high, as was to be expected. It stung me no less that I could not place full trust in Ólafur. A breach of confidence arose between us, though I did not parade it in public. I had long known that he was solitary and heavy-tempered and rarely sought the advice of others.
This was, however, the first time I felt he had gone behind my back.

I was absent when Ólafur presented his proposal in the cabinet and the parliamentary group on February 12, 1979. Perhaps it was just as well. The ministers of the People's Alliance seemed ready to walk out of the government on the spot. They immediately declared their opposition and said that if the bill were introduced, it would seriously delay a resolution of the government's disagreement over economic affairs. A state of near-warfare prevailed when I arrived at the next meeting the following day. The People's Alliance ministers submitted a five-page formal entry with harsh protests and detailed comments. They rose up in their seats as they delivered their arguments, such heavy emphasis did they place on their case. The Social Democratic Party

on the other hand, supported much of what appeared in the bill, and its parliamentary group proposed that it be laid before parliament unchanged as a government bill. Kjartan Jóhannsson did not attend cabinet meetings for a fortnight.

Rumors soon began circulating that Jón Sigurðsson, the director of the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun), had taken part in drafting the prime minister's bill while Hallgrímur Snorrason, his subordinate, participated in the work of the ministerial committee that was under way at the same time. Ólafur never mentioned it to us, his colleagues. In the writing of this book, however, I have received confirmation that these rumors were well founded. The National Economic Institute worked on both at the same time.
Singular Methods

The prime minister's economic bill was taken up for thorough discussion in the parliamentary group of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Most of the party's members of parliament received the matter well and did not raise major objections. The party's ministers were charged with achieving consensus on the matter in the cabinet. Ólafur let the matter rest for a while and did not answer the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) members' formal entry until a cabinet meeting ten days later, with a four-page memorandum. By the end of February, the government had received the comments of the organizations of wage earners and employers, and in their wake Ólafur presented his bill in somewhat altered form. The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) expressed disappointment with the changes, but the People's Alliance considered them an improvement.

Ólafur subsequently tried to reach agreement with the chairmen of the other coalition parties, Lúðvík and Benedikt, so that the matter could be introduced as a government bill. The People's Alliance was most sensitive about points that touched on index calculations and oil prices.

Ólafur spoke for unity within the government. From the beginning, however, it was clear that he would not stretch to meet every point of view. A few days after he presented the bill in altered form, he declared at a parliamentary group meeting that he would introduce the bill in his own name if consensus could not be reached. In the following days the cabinet sat in daily meetings. I, however, was absent.

When agreement was coming together in the government's economic committee, I expected to be able to enjoy some quiet days and planned a ski trip with the family to Switzerland. When the disputes flared up within the government, I seriously considered canceling the trip. I decided not to and was away for two weeks. I was not averse to standing apart from the disputes that Ólafur had stirred up.

When I came back, agreement had still not been reached between the coalition parties in the negotiations of the three chairmen. At a meeting of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) parliamentary group on March 12, it was resolved that the prime minister had the group's support to introduce the matter as a private member's bill if consensus on it could not be reached in the government. That evening another attempt was made to reconcile the ministers, and at the parliamentary group's meeting the next day the prime minister reported that the disagreement chiefly concerned the bill's indexation chapter. In the middle of the meeting he was called out for talks with Lúðvík Jósepsson, chairman of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið).

Following those talks, the parliamentary group agreed to meet the demands to drop the provisions on oil matters from the bill and likewise to accommodate the criticism of the indexation chapter. At a cabinet meeting, after talks with the People's Alliance ministers shortly before, Ólafur nevertheless stated it as his conclusion that he "saw no possibility of agreement on the bill's cost-of-living compensation chapter."

The prime minister informed our partner parties in the government first through the media that he would introduce the bill in his own name as a private member's bill. The parliamentary group had by then known of this plan for over a week and had approved its support for it. Ólafur never mentioned any such thing at cabinet meetings. He probably did not consider it fitting to make threats.

The reactions were not long in coming. The People's Alliance ministers recorded harshly worded protests at a cabinet meeting in which they said the handling of the matter was a blow to the coalition, and that could certainly be said with justice. They said the prime minister's methods were unprecedented and sharply criticized his handling of the matter within the government. They also protested in particular the "impudent assertions of fellow ministers" about the People's Alliance's position, which they said had been misrepresented in the media. They said the partner parties had "in an unyielding manner ganged up against the third coalition party with the introduction of this bill." They declared that if the bill were passed unchanged in the Althing against their opposition, they would "of course" resign their ministerial posts.

Provisions on the indexation of wages were the most sensitive in the eyes of the People's Alliance. Such provisions had not been in law since 1968, when they were repealed. In the years 1968–1979, indexation was therefore anchored only in collective wage agreements. As mentioned before, those provisions were strengthened considerably in the "solstice agreements" of 1977. The bill provided for some curtailment relative to the wage agreements then in force, and it was this above all that provoked the opposition of the People's Alliance.
Ólafslög

Ólafur would not be dissuaded and introduced the bill. Discussions continued among the leaders of the coalition parties about minor changes to the text of the bill. In parliament, Jón Helgason took part in these negotiations on the party's behalf, not least after the bill had been introduced. He was chairman of the economic and trade committee of the upper chamber. Jón sat in long meetings with Ágúst Einarsson of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), who were the coalition partners' representatives on the committee. It soon became clear in parliament that the bill, unchanged, had the support of a majority of members, and few really seemed to have serious worries that the People's Alliance would break up the coalition. Ólafur would have driven the matter through against its opposition.
It did not come to that, however. The three men on the committee reached agreement at the eleventh hour. In the media the laws were given the name Ólafslög — "Ólafur's Laws."

After what had gone before, I believe Ólafur felt he had few options other than to introduce a bill in his own name and thus cut the knot in the coalition parties' disputes over economic measures. I freely admit that it was necessary to reach a conclusion on those matters. Ólafur's handling of the matter during those weeks, on the other hand, struck me as most peculiar. The prime minister had, of course, every right to be dissatisfied with the conclusion of the ministerial committee. I often found myself in that position during my own time as prime minister. It never occurred to me, however, to play a solo game from such a position. It is much more natural to take such matters up with the leaders of the coalition parties and bring them to a conclusion jointly. Ólafur and I probably differed in temperament in this respect.

Some said Ólafur had grown overconfident. I shall say nothing about that. Others remarked that he had made fools of us, his fellow ministers, to show who was in charge when push came to shove. I never wanted to echo such voices. This working method of the prime minister, however, unquestionably caused cracks in the coalition that it could not withstand. With tact and skill it could have been prevented.

The Ólafslög broke new ground in many ways. They laid down the main policy in economic affairs and made an attempt to bring to the management of the economy a formal discipline that had long been lacking. For the first time it was written into law that a national economic plan should be laid before the Althing (Alþingi) at the start of each parliamentary session, and that the budget should be accompanied by a three-year policy program for public finances. It was stipulated that investment and credit plans should be laid before the Althing, and provision was made for regular consultation and cooperation
between the authorities and the organizations of wage earners, fishermen, farmers, and employers in labor and economic matters. These provisions of the laws I supported wholeheartedly.

The best-known feature of the Ólafslög was the provision on the indexation of capital, which was to be introduced in stages before the end of 1980. Indexation of savings had not existed before. It was clear to me that the nation's savings had burned up in inflation throughout the 1970s and would have continued to do so if nothing had been done. This undermined banking in the country. I feared, on the other hand, that indexing capital on top of the indexation of wages would further accelerate inflation and make it nearly impossible for the government to bring it under control. I would much rather have abolished all indexation in the country by scaling back the indexation of wages. I long hoped that this path would prove passable in cooperation with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) despite its ties to the labor movement.

I did not feel it had been fully tried, the way things developed that spring of 1979, and I blamed Ólafur Jóhannesson for that outcome rather than the obstinacy of the People's Alliance members of parliament. Perhaps that was a wrong assessment.
Chapter Eight

My chairmanship of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) came about of its own accord, so to speak. I engaged in no backroom scheming to tie things up. When a meeting of the Progressive Party's central committee was called at the beginning of April 1979, it had been under discussion all winter whether Ólafur Jóhannesson would step down as chairman before long. He had suffered a deep disappointment in the 1978 elections.

The first reports of the change of chairman appeared about a week before the meeting. I was immediately named the likeliest successor. As the time drew near, Ólafur informed me of his decision at a private meeting of ours. He said it was his wish that I take on the chairmanship.
