I never doubted that I would seek the chairmanship when Ólafur withdrew, and I was prepared to face anyone in an election for it. I do not recall that anyone else expressed interest in the office. On the other hand, various people wanted Ólafur to stay on.

Reports appeared in the opposition papers that Ólafur was under great pressure to keep the chairmanship. Various leading men in the party were said to be in favor of that. On the other hand, it was said that the heads of the Federation of Icelandic Cooperatives (Sambandið), with Erlendur Einarsson at their head, were keen that Ólafur withdraw. Halldór Ásgrímsson was said to be able to imagine taking the chairmanship, and the people of the East Fjords were said to support Ólafur's continued tenure until Halldór regained a seat in parliament. Tómas Árnason was variously considered my chief ally or a supporter of Ólafur's continued chairmanship. Einar Ágústsson and Halldór E. Sigurðsson were said to want Ólafur to continue. Perhaps there was something to these speculations. I did not make much of them. Both Vísir and Morgunblaðið, however, carried reports that I was being strongly
pressed to urge Ólafur not to quit. No one mentioned it to me. That much is certain. I doubt, moreover, that I would have complied.

Various explanations were offered by people outside the party as to why I was the self-evident choice for the chairmanship. Dagblaðið said I had "risen in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) [first and foremost] on my own merits, inherited and earned," and cited both my father and my "unusual industriousness." I was also said to have managed "to get along with the older men of the party with sufficient tact to become the self-evident choice," and it was added that "such a thing is not easy in an old and weary party." Perhaps there was something to all these explanations, and the affair of the Möðruvellingar proved the last point.

In the media some surprise was expressed that there had not been more of a struggle over the leadership of the party. Tómas Árnason and Einar Ágústsson had both been named as possible candidates for chairman. Tómas did not seek the chairmanship but moved from the post of party treasurer to that of secretary. He left the party's finances in very good order, as was to be expected of a careful man of money. Einar had been vice-chairman of the party during Ólafur's chairmanship, and many said that for a long time he could have imagined taking over. As his ministerial career in Geir Hallgrímsson's government of 1974–1978 wore on, however, it was as if all the wind had gone out of him. Some wanted to trace that to the change of policy in defense matters in 1974. Others said that Ólafur Jóhannesson had pushed Einar around in the government and had not been shy about showing his power over him.

Einar was a good and agreeable man, but also sensitive and not one for harsh disputes. It was Ólafur's doing that he did not become a minister when the government was formed in 1978. When Einar was asked whether he was seeking the chairmanship he answered: "I consider it offered too late, if this is Ólafur's decision, for I have become too worn out by politics to take on that job." I thought that well put. It was agreed that Einar would continue in the post of vice-chairman. Barely a year later he left parliament and was subsequently appointed ambassador.

Once it was clear that I would stand for the chairmanship, word of it spread quickly to central committee members all around the country. Some said Þráinn Valdimarsson, the party's executive director, had spread the news quickly and well. It does not surprise me that Þráinn would have been anything but opposed to my becoming chairman of the Progressive Party. He was the great arbiter of fate in my political career. Þráinn played perhaps the largest part in my joining the party and did his bit to make me its secretary. Nor would it surprise me if Ólafur Jóhannesson had told Þráinn his mind before he
spoke to me about becoming his successor, and if Þráinn had already taken matters into his own hands. He was always at it.

I do not know, though, how much introduction I really needed. I had traveled all over the country in my work as secretary and had become acquainted with most of the party's central committee members and many others besides. Many of them had already mentioned to me that I was the natural chairman whenever Ólafur chose to step down. At the central committee meeting I received 88 votes in the chairmanship election. Einar Ágústsson received two, Tómas Árnason and Ólafur Jóhannesson one each. Four ballots were blank. Tómas was next elected secretary with 64 votes. Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson received 56 votes for the post of treasurer and Jón Helgason 31 votes. Einar Ágústsson received 87 votes for the office of vice-chairman. My honors within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) are among the things in my life that I have not had to fight for.
Others decided, almost without consulting me, that I would become the party's secretary, and the chairmanship fell into my lap just as effortlessly.
"The Madam Changes Her Style"

The change of chairman was seen as marking something of a turning point and heralding changes in the Progressive Party, if the writings of the media are anything to go by. Helgarpósturinn published an article under the headline "The Madam Changes Her Style" and Jónas Kristjánsson, editor of Dagblaðið, called me "a man of technology, urban areas, and industry, not of the countryside and agriculture" in his leading article. He said that with the party's new economic proposals my men and I had changed "the party's economic policy [...] from the archaic to the modern." Of my work as a minister Jónas said:

As minister of agriculture for a little over half a year, Steingrímur has introduced a tiny measure of good sense, namely, that overproduction shall be abolished. This is not a big step as such, but a big one nonetheless for a man from the party of agriculture and the Federation of Icelandic Cooperatives (Samband íslenzkra samvinnufélaga).

Suffice it to say that Tíminn reacted furiously to this leading article and called the piece "party-transformation drivel" in which everything was wrong, "the beginning, the middle, and the end." The leader-writer of that fine organ of the Progressive Party took particular exception to Jónas's sentence that I would try "to change the party from being the party of one class and one company." The fact is, however, that I believed it was vital for the party to

strengthen its support in the urban areas. Jónas thus came rather close to my view that the party had long placed too much emphasis on the farmers and the rural districts of the country in its message. This attitude of mine can be found in my letters as far back as 1956. That year I wrote to my father, the prime minister, following his New Year's address:

Progressives must not place far too much emphasis on being the party of farmers [and] on the two issues you have put at the forefront being first and foremost the affairs of the countryside. It hampers the party considerably, that "country-folk brand." It should first and foremost be the party of farmers and of the working classes in general, on land and at sea.
In interviews following my election I took up Ólafur Jóhannesson's banner and defined the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) as the center party of Icelandic politics. But I added:

That, however, is another matter: I believe that the Progressive Party, if I may use these old concepts like right and left — it is unquestionably to the left in the sense that it is a liberal party, it is a reform party, it does not want a stagnant society.

I was eager to make the party more modern, both in reality and in the public mind. I wanted to introduce new working methods into party operations and election preparations and to call more people to the work. The Progressive Party was to become a mass party. I had already set about this task in my work as secretary, with the loyal assistance of Þráinn, the executive director, at the party office. I often explained these ideas of mine by saying that Ólafur Jóhannesson, in his chairmanship and his leadership in governments, had "stood head and shoulders above the rest," and that this had undeniably left its mark on policy-making.
For my part, I believe that in the future we must build much more on numbers, call many more people in to the making of policy.

In my closing words at the central committee meeting I announced the founding of new policy groups to prepare the party's policy positions in as many fields as possible. At the meeting I had taken the lead on proposals to amend the party's rules. They all aimed at the goal of making the Progressive Party a mass party. The weight of the party congresses was increased, and it was laid down that they should

be held every other year instead of every four years. I also proposed the change that the party's chairman and governing board should be elected by the party congress rather than the central committee. To increase the role of young people it was proposed that at least two of the nine members of the executive board elected by the central committee should come from the ranks of the younger members. Some of these proposals had come forward in the days of the Möðruvellingar, only to be smothered in committees or put to a vote and defeated. Now they were all approved.

I also wanted to open up the party and make it more receptive to new ideas and new thinking. To that end I considered it sensible to affiliate with the international association of liberal parties. International currents and influences had long been taboo in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), which had prided itself on being "the most Icelandic of all political parties," as I and other party members had tirelessly proclaimed. I had nonetheless gathered considerable information on these matters in my work as party secretary. Ólafur had not been particularly keen on this, and I moved slowly on all changes at first after taking over the chairmanship.
The Struggle with the Agricultural Reactionaries

Receiving praise from the opponents' camp could cut both ways. Tíminn's sensitivity to Dagblaðið's writings proves it. Perhaps these positive reactions from Dagblaðið also served to harden the interest groups in their opposition to the changes in agricultural policy that I had announced. A great many within the farmers' organizations regarded Dagblaðið as an emissary of the devil.

Some of my ideas met with fierce opposition. Among other things, I thought it right that growth areas should be designated where conditions for a given type of farming were better than elsewhere. There seemed to me less reason to cut back sheep farming where the vegetation was not endangered by overgrazing, and I often cited Strandasýsla and the Þingeyjarsýslur as examples. In return, farmers in the South could, for instance, concentrate on dairy production. I thought it important that such considerations be heeded as production was scaled back, and I proposed among other things that subsidies per sheep or dairy cow be paid at different rates according to region.

The farmers' organizations would not hear of it. It was as if the future of the nation depended on large-scale dairy farmers also getting to potter about with a hundred ewes on the side. Support was to be distributed evenly and without conditions to all, no matter where they were located. To me this made no sense whatsoever.

The main battle, however, was over my proposals for cutting production. To follow them up I introduced a bill on the Agricultural Production Board (Framleiðsluráð landbúnaðarins), which was to strengthen production management and reduce the overproduction of farm goods. The chief instruments of production management were quotas on the one hand and a feed levy on the other. Revenue from the feed levy was intended to go to those farmers who reduced their production. The most radical part of the proposals, though, was that export subsidies in their existing form would be phased out over five years. After that they would be a matter for negotiation between the state and the farmers.

To present this policy I held fifteen open meetings with farmers all around the country. The subject was a new agricultural policy. This was an absolute novelty in policy-making and attracted great attention. Probably well over two thousand people attended these gatherings. The first meeting was at Hvolsvöllur. I believe close to four hundred people attended that meeting. Among them was a sizable group that Eggert Haukdal, member of parliament for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in the South, had gathered. Eggert moved a resolution that ran directly counter to my policy. The meeting was long and hard and did not end until it was going on three in the morning. I was frankly growing uneasy, for it seemed to me that Eggert's men were sitting tighter in the hall than the others as the evening and the night wore on.
The outcome was nevertheless that my policy won the support of a large majority of those at the meeting.

Farmers are some of the greatest meeting-goers I have ever known. Almost without exception many took the floor at each meeting, and every one of them seemed thoroughly practiced at putting his thoughts into words. There were often hard clashes, no lack of that, but people kept to the issues. A memorable meeting took place at Egilsstaðir. It, too, lasted six hours. Sveinn Jónsson, a local chieftain at Egilsstaðir, stood up and delivered an hour-long speech on the incompetence of the exporters of sheep products. He said they were damned wretches for not being able to get a decent price abroad for the best lamb in the world. If that were put right, there would be no reason to worry about the future of agriculture in Iceland. I half expected him to manage to kill the meeting with this rigmarole. Fortunately that did not happen.

Fear of change marked the attitude of the farmers' organizations. Perhaps that was no wonder. In their leadership were men who had put their soul and their life's work into the building up of agriculture that had continued almost without interruption since the last war. This applied not least to the three chief leaders of the farmers. Gunnar Guðbjartsson had been chairman of the Farmers' Union (Stéttarsamband bænda) since 1963, Halldór Pálsson at the Agricultural Society (Búnaðarfélagið) had become a consultant in the 1940s, and Sveinn Tryggvason, executive director of the Production-

Council of agriculture since 1947. These were all good acquaintances of mine and the most worthy of men. On the other hand, it was as though the heart were being torn out of them to discuss contraction in the branches of agriculture. From the produce division of the Federation (Sambandið) and the South Iceland Slaughterhouse Cooperative (Sláturfélag Suðurlands) came a similar tone. They had to have everything squared away and did not want to take any chances. To them, the export subsidies were a sacred matter. They were crucial to their operations. It seemed to matter nothing that everyone involved acknowledged the problem.

Like other bills, the Production Council bill was first presented in the government and in the parliamentary groups of the governing parties in order to gather support for it being laid before parliament as a government bill. When the farmers' organizations and the licensed slaughterhouses set themselves against changes, the matter became heavy going in the parliamentary group of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Those who considered themselves spokesmen for the farmers fell into incessant grumbling, as so often when changes in agricultural affairs came up for discussion. Foremost among them were Stefán Valgeirsson and Páll Pétursson. When matters concerning farmers came up for debate, it was not uncommon for them to get their way in making progress depend on the support of the Farmers' Association of Iceland (Stéttarsamband bænda) being secured first.

With that, legislative power effectively moved out of parliament. In my opinion, members of parliament thereby ran away from their responsibility. Through the years this applied equally to the Progressive Party, the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið).

The farmers' organizations could hold parliamentary groups hostage if they cared to — except for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). It simply had no support to lose in the countryside. The members of parliament of the Social Democratic Party, however, were not prepared to enter into an alliance to unwind the agricultural system. To them all compromises in that area seemed impassable. So they were of little help to me.

The interest groups knew as well as I did that changes were unavoidable. But they lacked the courage to take the necessary steps to meet changed times. They defended the system to the bitter end, faithfully supported by the most reactionary members of parliament from all parties. What my father once said to me proved true: farmers and their organizations are slow to change their minds. In the end I got nowhere at all and saw no other way forward than to accommodate these viewpoints.

I introduced only part of the original bill on the Production Council (Framleiðsluráð), the part concerning direct agreements with farmers. The export subsidy system thus survived in its essentials, and I introduced a bill to meet its financial needs through borrowing. The agriculture committee of the lower house of parliament was in fact persuaded to sponsor that bill. That was considered more expedient politically. The Social Democratic Party, however, refused all cooperation on the passage of the matter, and truth be told I was not at all satisfied with the outcome. The newspaper Dagblaðið criticized it strongly and said I was in retreat on the issue. There was a good deal of truth in that.

I had reconciled myself to the view that changes could only be brought about in small steps, and I achieved only a fraction of the reforms I had wished for. I had come to know the agricultural reactionaries from personal experience.

In parliament (Alþingi), the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) raged against my borrowing bill. Svavar Gestsson and the other ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), on the other hand, were in step with me on the matter, and we issued joint declarations in the government. In parliament I chose to appeal to the Independence Party members for support for the bill. It was all to no avail; only two opposition members voted for it. In those last days of the parliamentary session, the old "Restoration" coalition parties (viðreisnarflokkarnir) came together again, on this matter and perhaps others. They marched out of the parliamentary chamber in formation and thereby blocked the passage of the bill.

I was vexed at this outcome and criticized the Independence Party members harshly for sacrificing the interests of farmers for dubious political gain. They answered at the top of their lungs and tried to shift the blame onto me. Geir Hallgrímsson stumbled badly in this skirmish. He proved to be poorly informed and turned the farm leadership against himself. As a result, I received the support of the farmers' organizations and of numerous farmers all over the country. I had to hope that the next session of parliament would be more fruitful.
Salmon farming and fur animals

Building up is always more popular than cutting back, not least in parliament. The greatest consensus proved to be around the innovations and new ventures in agriculture that I introduced, which were meant to soften the impact of the cutbacks and take the place of the traditional farm sectors. Of the ideas that came forward, we emphasized two that seemed to us the most promising and attracted the most attention: fur farming and fish farming. To prepare for the buildup, a committee on fur farming was appointed, among other things. Jón Helgason was its chairman. In my opinion it delivered a well-crafted report. The committee benefited, among other things, from the advice of Scots who put forward sensible plans. On a trial basis, four farmers were to be assisted in switching over to fur farming. That was done.

The Scots strongly emphasized that price fluctuations were large and said it would be wise to follow their example and establish a stabilization fund. I stressed this in my remarks wherever I discussed these ideas for innovation in agriculture. They were quite well received. Pelt prices, however, leapt upward at the same time and seemed set to break all records. Out in the wide world, everyone wanted to wear furs. At the same time, all the Scottish caveats about price fluctuations and price equalization were forgotten. Before anyone knew it, some seventy farmers had taken up fur farming.

I do not recall a single politician expressing doubts about the fur-farming adventure while pelt prices were good. When the crash came, however, many were quick to say it had been damned foolishness. I can agree that this buildup proceeded far too quickly. Most of those involved in the matter agreed that fur farming was an ideal way to reduce traditional agriculture, if things were handled properly. Many members of parliament did not spare their words of encouragement and exhortations to farmers. In fact, words of urging were not needed, for farmers themselves saw great hope of profit in the high pelt prices. The Regional Development Fund (Byggðasjóður), the Land Cultivation Fund (Jarðræktarsjóður), and the Agricultural Loan Department (Stofnlánadeild landbúnaðarins) vied with one another to lend to fur farming.
The banks followed suit — and perhaps no wonder, since all the profitability assessments showed good results.

This great and rapid growth in fur farming came after my time in the chair of Minister of Agriculture. It would never occur to me, however, to claim that I opposed the buildup. Far from it. In important respects, though, there was a departure from the policy framework I had left behind in the Ministry of Agriculture. I had emphasized that the farms should be located in particular areas where professional expertise would be good and it would be economical to produce feed. This was part of my policy of defining growth areas and of having different parts of the country make use of their advantages according to their circumstances. Words of caution that one should proceed carefully at first were likewise ignored, and a stabilization fund was never established.

The same attitudes that prevailed regarding sheep and dairy farming unfortunately also governed the position of the farm leadership when the buildup of fur farming began. Everyone was to have equal rights, no matter where in the countryside they were located. It was regarded almost as a human right of farmers to receive support for investments in fur farming. The consequence was that fur farms were scattered everywhere, up into the mountains and into the innermost valleys. Unfortunately, it was also not required that farmers acquire education or knowledge of this new farm sector.

Fish farming seemed no less promising a sector. When I took the chair of Minister of Agriculture, six salmon farms were operating in the country. Ocean ranching had been carried out experimentally in Kollafjörður. In our policy framework, strong emphasis was placed on the need for generous funding of experiments and research that "should point the way toward economical and effective methods in fish cultivation and fish farming." It was likewise recommended that activities in these fields receive greatly increased financial support. However, no momentum developed in fish farming during my time as Minister of Agriculture, neither in buildup nor in research.

It has proven true in fish farming, no less than in fur farming, that it is wisest to build up new industries slowly. In both sectors the Icelandic temperament showed itself. Work was undertaken briskly and with great commotion. Those who saw money beat their chests, and those waiting for loans grew impatient in equal measure. We politicians, however, certainly pulled the wagon. Everyone lent everyone else a hand in stoking the hopes.
The clash with Ólafur

On 25 April 1979 a strike of officers on merchant ships began. Shortly afterward, the dairy technicians also launched a struggle over their pay. The reasonable peace that had prevailed over wage matters in the latter part of the winter seemed broken, and unrest in the labor market was growing. One of the government's economic measures had been to place a so-called index ceiling on wages. This meant that the highest wages rose proportionally less in step with price increases than the lowest ones. At the same time, taxes were lowered on those with the lowest wages. This led to a considerable narrowing of the gap between those with the highest and lowest wages. The dispute with the merchant-ship officers was an example of an attempt by high earners to lift this index ceiling off themselves.

I was of the opinion that the government should unquestionably take up the matter, and said "that it was utterly unacceptable that those who after all had the highest wages should break the solidarity that had been achieved on wage matters." I made those remarks in a newspaper interview at the end of April. Weeks passed, however, before the necessary measures were taken. During that time, sparks flew once again between me and Ólafur Jóhannesson.

By mid-May I had grown impatient for a resolution of the matter, which I believed could put the country's entire labor market in jeopardy. The Progressive Party members and the ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) put forward proposals in the government, and we waited for ideas from the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). Once again, recourse was taken to appointing a committee of three ministers to reach a common conclusion on the matter. I was appointed to it along with Svavar Gestsson and Magnús H. Magnússon. I sensed that Svavar was hesitant to intervene in the labor dispute with radical measures. When there is no consensus within a government, or in politics generally, statements in the media are often intended for one's coalition partners no less than for the public.

I declared after the first meeting of the ministerial committee that if the government did not deal with matters firmly, it had no reason to remain in office. Svavar got the message. However, it came to

the turn of the month without a conclusion being reached in the ministerial committee. We spoke with the parties to the dispute on both sides of the table, and I met frequently with the Progressive Party's representatives within the labor movement.

The battle lines were clear. The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) proposed that wage terms be fixed by law. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) wanted to raise wages and place a new index ceiling on the high-earning groups, while the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) preferred that a settlement take place through negotiations between wage earners and employers. The main discussion was about imposing provisional legislation on the dispute, which had begun to endanger all labor peace in the country. Such legislation was anathema to the People's Alliance.

The ministerial committee finally came together, and we presented the agreement to the government at its meeting of 28 May. I credited Svavar's adroitness for this achievement, since I knew the matter was sensitive within the People's Alliance. The proposal called for provisional legislation on the labor dispute. Maximum cost-of-living adjustments to wages were to be enacted into law, and subsidies on farm product prices were to be changed to save money for the treasury. I was pleased to have achieved this landing. Svavar had had to force the matter through the People's Alliance's large labor committee, and that was no easy task.

The Prime Minister sat silent as the proposal was presented. When the reading was finished, he shook his head and said it was absurd to suggest that the proposals fulfilled the constitution's provisions on provisional legislation. Ólafur spoke with commanding expertise where the constitution and the law were concerned. He halted our plans with those few sentences. As far as I could see, some of the Social Democratic ministers smirked at this outcome. Magnús H., however, did not smile. He is both a worthy man and a good one. Magnús is honest as well, and enjoyed respect for his personal qualities. On the other hand, he was no heavyweight in his own party. For the Prime Minister to be in a position to issue provisional legislation, he had to make certain that all the government's members of parliament supported it.

It may be that Ólafur believed Magnús had not taken sufficient care to secure his backing in the Social Democratic parliamentary group. It was no less sensitive for the Social Democratic Party than for the People's Alliance to take part in legislating on labor disputes.

I had little to say at the meeting when Ólafur swept our proposals off the table. Magnús was likewise guarded in his words. Svavar was the only one of us who kept up a protest. The next day, Þjóðviljinn reported that the Prime Minister had seriously rebuked me, and it recounted the People's Alliance's proposals for wage increases point by point. Nowhere was the agreement on legislating the labor dispute mentioned. For my part, I made every effort to adopt the Prime Minister's arguments as my own and to be the first to present in the media the government's conclusion that
provisional legislation would not be enacted for the time being. At the same time, I denied reports of disagreement between me and Ólafur.
"A battle of chieftains in the Progressive Party"

I nonetheless thought there were strong arguments for provisional legislation. They grew stronger still when the unions of subordinate crew members on merchant ships began a strike on 3 June 1979. The seamen's strike brought about a halt to all imports to the country, including feed concentrate and other animal feed. I called a meeting of the executive board of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) to discuss the situation and other matters on the party's agenda. Ólafur Jóhannesson was in Manitoba, where he was being awarded an honorary doctorate, and was therefore not present. Some maintained that I had used the opportunity to call the meeting.

At the meeting my ideas were approved, and afterward the party leadership held a press conference where the necessity of provisional legislation was argued. In my view Ólafur's arguments no longer applied. Tómas Árnason, Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson and I fielded questions about the party's policy, together with Þráinn Valdimarsson, its executive director, beneath a large painting of Hermann Jónasson, my father. At the meeting I said I "wished to correct the misunderstanding, which some have tried to insinuate into people's minds, that the Progressive Party does not want to take part in provisional legislation, for that is entirely wrong."

When a government meeting was held after Ólafur's return home, however, he still considered it out of the question to issue provisional legislation on so small a matter. The media had begun publishing reports of clashes between me and Ólafur, and Dagblaðið quoted an unnamed People's Alliance member of parliament on its front page saying that a "power struggle in the Progressive Party" was delaying action. For a while longer I tried to play down these reports. Þjóðviljinn published an article in which Tómas and I were likened to Eysteinn and my father in their fight with Jónas from Hrifla in their day. There it was again said that Ólafur got whatever he wanted within the Progressive Party, while I had grown restless because of his rigidity in carrying out the party's resolutions. That was probably fairly close to the mark. Between me and Ólafur a tension arose that grew day by day.

The opposition newspapers published editorial after editorial about the "battle of chieftains in the Progressive Party" and "the companions Ólafur and Steingrímur," in which we were pitted against each other. Helgarpósturinn did not hold back either, telling stories of a government meeting at which Ólafur was said to have leaned back in his seat with a smirk, looked at me and said very slowly: "What does the Progressive Party say about
this?" whenever some contentious question was under discussion. I do not remember this incident, but the story does not sound improbable.

I pressed hard over the following week and argued wherever I went for the enactment of provisional legislation. The seamen's dispute was escalating, and the employers announced a lockout effective 18 June. At a government meeting on 12 June, the Prime Minister finally proposed that he be given a mandate to prepare a bill of provisional legislation, and he directed the ministers of all the parties to seek their parliamentary groups' approval of it. Ólafur nonetheless still maintained his earlier position in the media and said on the television news that same evening that it was premature to intervene in the seamen's dispute. Morgunblaðið published a report that the Prime Minister was in opposition to me on the matter. I had stopped denying such reports.

The employers postponed their lockout by a week until a conclusion could be reached on the government's actions. At its meeting on 19 June, the representatives of all the coalition parties reported their parliamentary groups' mandate to issue provisional legislation. The strikes were halted, as were the lockout measures, and representatives of all the government parties expressed their satisfaction that labor peace thereby seemed secured for a year and a half. After that, reports of clashes between me and Ólafur ceased to appear.

During those weeks it occurred to only one journalist that the friction between us might appear greater than it really was. In the middle of the month, Björn Vignir Sigurpálsson at Helgarpósturinn sought to argue that it suited the party's interests well for Tómas and me to pursue a hard interventionist line in the seamen's dispute, one that was in accord with the will of the nation. Ólafur, on the other hand, was doing his utmost to hold the government together and had wanted to wait for the coalition parties' written approval of support for the legislation. My rhetoric had also served to increase the pressure on the seamen's representatives in the negotiations. Björn Vignir wrote, among other things, that in support of this interpretation one could note that the disagreement between me and Ólafur had never been great at government meetings.

The truth is that I was displeased with Ólafur's position after I believed I had achieved the significant result of getting the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) to approve provisional legislation. I of course acknowledged Ólafur's argument that national necessity is required to issue provisional legislation. That necessity I considered to be growing day by day. I also grew bolder in my argumentation because I sensed that it enjoyed broad support, both in the ranks of the Progressive Party members and among the public.

The fact is that it always creates difficulties when two men are on the bridge. Eysteinn continued to hold firm opinions on the governance of national affairs when Ólafur succeeded him in 1968, and he followed his convictions closely

afterward when he and Ólafur disagreed. Eysteinn felt that Ólafur did not always set policy in the "right spirit." My father must surely have felt much the same when Eysteinn succeeded him, though he never showed it, and one hardly needs to mention the disagreements those two had with Jónas frá Hriflu, who was long the party's chairman during my father's time as prime minister. Perhaps it was not least because of this experience that my father took no part in the running of the party after Eysteinn took over the chairmanship. It is a good rule that once the old man has left the bridge he should not be loitering there. That rule is hard to keep, however, when the person in question is prime minister. Ólafur Jóhannesson found it difficult to let go of the party entirely.

If I am to sum up the relationship between Ólafur and myself, I cannot say other than that it was good on the whole. At the same time it was in many ways difficult. It irritated me how secretive Ólafur was and how little he consulted us, his colleagues. Unfortunately that did not change at all when I took over the chairmanship of the party. With more consultation, the clashes would certainly have been fewer. Yet I never had the feeling that Ólafur created discord on unprincipled grounds. I did, however, find it hard to predict Ólafur and felt it a bad thing not to be able to count on his support. Ólafur was unafraid of disagreement. He went his own way.
Deceptive Calm

After the uproar over the Ólafur's Laws (Ólafslög) late in the winter, an air of doom hung over the government for some time. Before the end of the parliamentary session, many thought the government's fate uncertain as the battle over agricultural matters was fought. The clashes over the provisional legislation further strengthened the feeling that the government did not have long to live. In wage matters the prime minister contended above all with the leadership of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), while over agriculture the fight was between me and the members of parliament of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). I know that these battles took a heavy toll on Ólafur, and it was often a weary man I encountered when I brought some matter to him. At the worst moments he would remark in private conversations that this was no longer workable.
"There is no working with these men," he would say, shaking his head. "This is hopeless." These squalls eventually cleared, however, and as the summer wore on it was as if a calm settled over things.

In late summer the government worked at making ends meet in the state finances. Tómas Árnason put all his effort into having the budget passed without a deficit. The government also faced the fact that a "hole" that had formed in the current year's budget had to be financed. After some haggling, the government therefore agreed that taxes and duties would be raised to respond to the situa-

-istry. In particular, the consent of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) had to be secured in this matter. After the provisional legislation was enacted and calm settled over the labour market, I for the first time became confident that the government would remain functional through the end of the electoral term, and I worked energetically on my tasks in both ministries.

In the Ministry of Justice (dómsmálaráðuneytið), bills on administrative procedure law and legislation on the Ombudsman of the Althing were among the matters in preparation. In the spring of 1979 I had also introduced a bill on the duty of public authorities to disclose information. These met with strong opposition in parliament, and no less among civil servants, for the deep-rooted view prevailed that it should be left to the authorities' own discretion what information they provided. These major matters were unfortunately delayed for more than a decade because of the events that followed.

The law on the Ombudsman of the Althing I did not manage to get passed until my last term as prime minister. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) was then still balking at approving the administrative procedure law. In the negotiations over which matters would go through parliament in 1991, they made it a point of principle that the administrative procedure law would not be passed. I found this position utterly astonishing. I was no less amazed when Davíð Oddsson tried to make political capital out of the passage of this same administrative procedure law, with minor changes, in his first months in the prime minister's office. In my eyes it did him no credit.

In the arena of the Ministry of Agriculture (landbúnaðarráðuneytið), I devoted my energies chiefly to presenting ways of extricating the industry from the deadlock in which it found itself. I inclined most to the view that this could only be done through direct negotiations between the state and the farmers, and I advocated that course within the government. I had also set up a committee to work on implementing the agricultural policy and to promote unity between the coalition parties. In the ministry, work was pursued no less vigorously on ideas for new branches of farming. A great many of the matters that were in the melting pot during those autumn days have become reality in the time that has since passed. Most of them, however, were delayed by years and decades.
An Absence Turned to Advantage

One of the innovation ideas I had brought with me from the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) was to establish greenhouse cultivation on a larger scale in Iceland. Various people contributed good ideas to this. Árni Kristjánsson, a most excellent man, was one of them. He was the consul of the Netherlands in Iceland. Árni arranged for me to be invited on an official visit to the Netherlands at the beginning of October 1979. That trip was instructive in many ways, not least in what concerned greenhouse cultivation. During the visit to the Netherlands I spoke among others with the Dutch minister of agriculture and received extremely
very good responses to my ideas. It seemed to me ideal, for example, to grow cuttings for export, since in Iceland the soil was clean and unpolluted.

After the Netherlands trip, Edda and I went to Portugal, where we intended to spend a few days on holiday. We were greatly looking forward to it. The hotel, the Estoril, was excellent, the swimming pool beautiful and the beach within arm's reach. I rejoiced at being able to rest there for three days before the bustle resumed. We ate a good meal at a fine restaurant that first evening. When we returned to the hotel, however, it was not long before the telephone rang. It was the radio news service. The government had collapsed.

The late-summer calm in politics had proved to be the lull before the storm. The restless faction in the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) had seen its opportunity while the party's chairman, Benedikt Gröndal, was at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Vilmundur and Sighvatur won Kjartan Jóhannsson over to their side, and the parliamentary group resolved to end the coalition. Benedikt was faced with a fait accompli on his return home and was offered only one option: to present the proposal himself at a cabinet meeting held shortly afterwards. Otherwise others would do it. There was little dignity in this way of proceeding.

I was thunderstruck to receive this news. It was no less astonishing that a radio reporter should be the first to bring it to me. I therefore telephoned Ólafur, the prime minister. He confirmed the news. I was the chairman of one of the governing parties, with a government crisis brewing, so there was nothing for it but to return home. That proved easier said than done. At the airport I was told that there were no flights that evening. The next morning, moreover, everything was fully booked.

Edda and I refused to give up; we checked out of the hotel early the next morning and went out to the airport. The only way to get home was to fly through London. I appealed to the managers of British Airways and they took pity on us. I got a seat intended for the flight attendants up by the cockpit, and Edda sat in a folding seat by the aisle. When we arrived in London we met Tómas Árnason at Heathrow. He had been there on some errand or other. So we flew home on the same plane.

When I look back, it seems to me that the government had in fact been doomed from the start. The tension within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was child's play compared with what prevailed in the coalition partners. Throughout the government's entire term it seemed on the verge of falling — except when it actually fell. Then it took everyone by surprise.
The ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) had been the most restless at cabinet meetings and the hardest for the prime minister to keep in check. He had repeatedly in-

-clined toward the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) in order to reach conclusions in difficult matters. This was all the more remarkable in light of the party's history and the accusations he had suffered in the Geirfinnur affair and everything connected with it. Ólafur therefore felt badly betrayed by the breakup of the coalition, and he bore a grudge against the Social Democratic Party as a result. Everyone understood why, and Benedikt looked rather sheepish when he presented his party's declaration in the cabinet on Tuesday, 9 October 1979. The prime minister did not put it on the agenda until the cabinet had gone through a communication from the secretary of the Danish Social Democratic Party, one from the federation of women in Reykjavík, and a letter from the federation of Icelandic taxi drivers.

The atmosphere at this last cabinet meeting was electric, though the ministers strove to show restraint for a good while at first. There was no shortage of harsh criticism of the Social Democratic Party's position and its irresponsibility. It was very far from true that every avenue toward unity on economic policy had been exhausted, as the party's resolution claimed. The party's ministers knew the fault was their own.

The leaders of the Social Democratic Party also got themselves into the greatest difficulties over the resignation itself. Along with their request to be relieved of office, they submitted a demand for the dissolution of parliament and elections. The general rule, however, is that the entire government remains in office through the elections if elections are indeed called. The prime minister said he wished to know whether the ministers did not intend to follow that practice if the president approved a proposal to dissolve parliament. It would be unique in history for a governing party to desert the ranks after a dissolution had been approved. The Social Democratic Party had evidently assumed that the dissolution demand would be rejected, for Benedikt began to waver. Ólafur Jóhannesson smirked.

Benedikt shifted in his seat, and once the worst of his hesitation had passed, he said he would have to put the question to the parliamentary group if the dissolution demand were granted. Ólafur grinned even more broadly, but then said, grave of expression and with some weight, that he would then take this to mean that he would not be blamed if he delayed processing the ministers' resignation request while a conclusion on the dissolution was being sought.

The ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) pressed the Social Democratic ministers hard and demanded answers as to whether they were resigning or not. Svavar called this a "hold me back, let me go" stance in the media. Benedikt had to admit that if they were relieved of their duties before a position was taken on the dissolution demand, they could no longer influence how the matter was handled. He would therefore have to trust the prime minister to manage it. The chairman of the Social Democratic Party was in truth to be pitied, and I could tell from Ólafur that he thought Benedikt's party colleagues had treated their chairman badly. It was a stormy meeting. A journalist of Dagblaðið put it this way:
when we left the meeting, Svavar and I had seemed to him "hot under the collar," while Kjartan Jóhannsson earned the description of being "anything but sure of himself."

The cabinet meeting was held the day before the opening of the Althing, so the work of parliament was in complete disarray. The wits, however, cast their worries aside and speculated whether the senior member presiding over parliament would commemorate the government at the opening of the session, as it is customary to commemorate those who have passed away since parliament last convened. The parliamentary group of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) met after the opening ceremony. There it was resolved to reject the Social Democratic Party's (Alþýðuflokkurinn) demand for dissolution. Ólafur Jóhannesson also proposed that he request dismissal for himself and his cabinet. The party was unanimous that it was most natural for the Social Democratic Party to shoulder full responsibility for its actions, and people were likewise of one mind that elections were undesirable.
The Progressive Party did not, however, intend to stand in the way of those who wanted a dissolution getting elections as soon as possible. I declared this to the media right at the outset.

The Social Democratic Party, however, kept springing surprises and appeared to have put on its Viðreisn trousers. Word reached our parliamentary group meeting that the Social Democrats no longer stood by the coalition parties' agreement on the election of the speakers of parliament, which had been presented to the parliamentary group the day before. Instead, the chairmen of the parliamentary groups of the Social Democratic Party and the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) had decided to cooperate on the election of the speakers. The heavy blows came in quick succession in those October days.
The Social Democrats Provoked

It was considered likely that the Independence Party and the Social Democratic Party would use their parliamentary strength to force elections before the end of 1979. The Progressive Party seemed to have had difficulty getting its policy across to the voters. On the same day the cabinet took up the Social Democratic ministers' resignation request, an opinion poll appeared in Vísir in which the Progressive Party's support had fallen below ten percent, and the Independence Party was predicted to win a majority of parliamentary seats. It was clear to us Progressives that we needed to turn the game to our advantage and begin election preparations in earnest. In an interview about the opinion poll, I immediately floated the idea that the Independence Party and the Social Democratic Party should take over the reins of government until elections, which could be held in December at the earliest.
Geir Hallgrímsson, chairman of the Independence Party, replied at once that he was not prepared to enter a coalition government without prior

elections, neither with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) nor with others. He did not, however, rule out protecting a Social Democratic minority government from falling until the elections. That was the ideal situation for us Progressives. In that way the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) could be made to take responsibility for the Social Democrats' recklessness and for the difficulties besetting the economy. Left-wing people in the country would likewise see at once that a new Viðreisn partnership was imminent and abandon their support of the Social Democratic Party in large numbers.

The Independence Party approved the dissolution of parliament and winter elections on the very first day of the session. Within the party, on the other hand, there was disagreement over whether it should form a minority government until the elections or grant a Social Democratic minority government its neutrality. Geir, the chairman, favoured the latter option, but Gunnar Thoroddsen declared his total opposition to those ideas and said the Independence Party ought to lead such a government. It was nothing new for Gunnar and Geir to be at odds. Most Independence Party members, however, appear to have agreed with their chairman not to form a coalition government without prior elections.

The Social Democratic Party moved first and requested the Independence Party members' neutrality. Geir supported that idea, and so did the majority of the parliamentary group. Gunnar Thoroddsen soon began campaigning for a non-parliamentary government to take over until the elections. He spoke among others with Jóhannes Nordal in that connection, and it was known that the president of Iceland, Kristján Eldjárn, was prepared to entrust the reins of government to Jóhannes. Geir got his way in the Independence Party. On 15 October it was announced that a Social Democratic minority government had taken over the reins of power. Elections were called for 2 and 3 December.
Vilmundur as Minister of Justice

Various Social Democrats cherished a dream of a new Viðreisn. Indeed, they made much of the parallel with the course of events in 1958 and 1959. At a meeting of the Reykjavík Students' Society (Stúdentafélag Reykjavíkur), Vilmundur Gylfason compared the Social Democratic Party's breakup of the coalition to my father's decision to dissolve the left-wing government and dissolve parliament in 1958. "Vilmundur said that Hermann's decision had shown his manliness in difficult times, and that such a thing deserved respect," says Morgunblaðið in its account of the meeting. I was next at the podium and began my speech with these words: "I hope those present will forgive me for being in a heavy mood when Vilmundur Gylfason compares himself to Hermann Jónasson.

— Hermann Jónasson never played the clown in the halls of the Althing." The Morgunblaðið journalist adds that my words were followed by great applause from the audience, while Vilmundur sat silent under it.

We Progressives aimed our spears not least at Vilmundur after the Social Democratic Party's (Alþýðuflokkurinn) minority government took over. He had played no small part in the breakup of the coalition and had himself risen to prominence through his criticism of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and of the country's judicial system. To the Progressive Party's vexation, he was made minister of justice. Yet no one took this harder than the outgoing prime minister.

Ólafur Jóhannesson remarked to Morgunblaðið that he had thought it could never happen that "that fine 'scribbler' Vilmundur Gylfason would become minister of justice." Ólafur said he did not envy "our beloved president, Kristján Eldjárn," having to sign such a letter. In Tíminn, Ólafur spoke in stronger terms still and attacked the president over this official act. I know of no other instance, in fact, of a politician making comparable remarks about an official act of the president of Iceland. Ólafur called it "completely inappropriate and indefensible in my judgment — and it will be an everlasting disgrace — to have issued a letter of appointment to such a man to be the supreme head of judicial affairs."

Ólafur was very far from having forgiven Vilmundur anything. The tension between them was such that they could hardly be in the same room. Ólafur needed only to put on an expression and say "the right honourable minister of justice" when Vilmundur walked into the chamber of the Althing for the assembled members of parliament to fall about laughing. I could not do that to Ólafur Jóhannesson — to show Vilmundur the honour of handing him the keys to the Ministry of Justice when he took over the ministerial office there from me. So I left that to the permanent secretary. This was highly unusual and attracted considerable attention from the media.

Vilmundur did not have time for great feats in his ministerial work during the weeks he served, any more than was to be expected. Vilmundur was, however, constantly making high-flown declarations about how he was going to take the "paper-pushers" in the system to task, and when he "took matters into his own hands," his recklessness and haste were his undoing. Vilmundur held a press conference at which he presented the "opening of the judicial system" with pomp and circumstance. He had sent the country's judges a letter requesting that they grant the public an audience once a week. The next day all the newspapers were full of interviews with judges who declared they saw no reason to cut back this service to the public. The city court judge in Reykjavík said he received callers every morning, with his chief deputy doing so in his absence.

In addition, there was staffing every day to receive inquiries from the public. He did not see how it would be possible to make do with the single hour a week that Vilmundur's proposals envisaged. When Vilmundur announced reforms in the handling of tax matters, things went no better. He had to ac-

-knowledge that the reforms had lain fully prepared on his desk when he came to work in the ministry. I had appointed a working group on the matter, and on the basis of the work done there a bill had been drafted. Vísir, which had long been one of Vilmundur's chief supporting newspapers, gave his "reforms" the verdict "failed advertisements."
A New Progressive Party for Progress

In the wake of the drubbing the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) suffered in the 1978 elections, there was considerable discussion within the party about its position and policy. Party members urged one another to strengthen the party's work, and young Progressives put forward proposals to establish policy groups that would chart the course. I was very enthusiastic about these plans and worked at them energetically as secretary of the party. It was a particular priority of mine to engage young people in the work, for I believed a new generation needed to grow up to sustain the renewal of the party that I considered necessary. The work of the young Progressives therefore interested me. I attended the board meetings of the Union of Young Progressives (SUF) while I was party secretary and could thus convey their viewpoints directly within the party. That was an innovation.

This review of the party's work extended to its entire organization. I led the work of a special organizational committee of the party, which presented detailed proposals for changes to the party's work and its reorganization at the central committee meeting where I was elected chairman. It may be said that my first acts as chairman were to put those resolutions into effect. At the first meeting of the party's executive board during my chairmanship, I put the party's policy work on the agenda. Working groups were set up with the task of shaping forward-looking policy in clearly defined fields. Some of these groups built on foundations that had been laid in the preceding years. Back then, as secretary, I had taken the initiative in having individual spheres of national life examined and a vision for the future and goals formulated for the party in each field.

In that work we made every effort to call in people from far and wide for the task, even looking beyond the party, and Þráinn Valdimarsson in particular carried much of the burden of this work. Teachers were brought in from the University, and leading figures from business and the institutions of public administration. Most of those who were not already Progressives moved closer to the party, and some joined it. We also got key people to come to meetings and discuss matters on which they had special expertise. This activity became quite vigorous and the meetings were well attended.

In this policy work, young intellectuals again became prominent in the party's activities for the first time since the days of the Möðruvellir movement (Möðruvellingar). Especially notable was a group in

around Eiríkur Tómasson. Those men viewed society with a critical eye, and many had grown up under the wing of Ólafur Ragnar in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) but had parted ways with Ólafur. They also agreed with Vilmundur Gylfason and his like-minded allies in their criticism of much that could be improved in the country's public administration and constitutional order. This group believed, however, that the Progressive Party was a more promising vehicle than the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) for bringing about positive changes in Icelandic society.

In this group were the lawyers Gestur Jónsson and Jón Sveinsson, who later became my assistant in the prime minister's office; Hermann Sveinbjörnsson, my sister's son and director of the State Environmental and Food Agency (Hollustuvernd ríkisins), who was my campaign manager in Reykjanes in 1987; Georg Ólafsson, director of the Competition Authority (Samkeppnisstofnun); Þorsteinn Ólafsson, who later became my economic adviser for a time; Bjarni Einarsson the economist and his brother Guðmundur, who are kinsmen of mine; Björn Líndal, who is now an executive director at the National Bank of Iceland (Landsbanki Íslands); and Kristján Þórarinsson, businessman and brother of Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson — not forgetting Gunnlaugur Sigmundsson, former member of parliament, whom I later supported in becoming managing director of the Development Corporation of Iceland (Þróunarfélag Íslands).
Many of these men became my closest advisers for years.

This became some of the most enjoyable policy-making work I have ever taken part in. A great many people put their hand to the plough. Ólafur Jóhannesson had previously had the habit of thinking matters over by himself, over his pipe at home in his sitting room, and then coming to the meeting and there announcing the conclusion, on his own behalf and the party's. In place of this, strong groups were established for each policy area. Ólafur did not work in these groups, yet he was not entirely left out in the cold. I visited him at home when the work was well under way and went over the policy aims and political problems together with him. I could sense that he was pleased with that.
Ólafur's Comeback

After the Progressive Party's drubbing in the 1978 elections, the party had only one member of parliament in the southwest corner of the country, Einar Ágústsson. It was clear to most people that the time was approaching when he would withdraw from politics. Before those elections an open primary had been held in Reykjavík. There Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson had sought one of the top seats. He worked methodically and well at preparing his candidacy and managed to take the second seat, while Einar Ágústsson came first. In doing so, Guðmundur bumped Þórarinn Þórarinsson, editor of Tíminn, from first place on the list down to third. Tall tales circulated about this victory and about the hard-driving group that backed Guðmundur's caurumors.
It did nothing to quell this gossip that 6,227 people voted in the primary, but only 4,116 voters cast their ballots for the list in the elections that followed!

In the aftermath there was some unpleasantness, and some long-standing Progressives were hurt on behalf of Tími-Tóti, as Þórarinn was often called. A veteran group around Kristinn Finnbogason, Alfreð Þorsteinsson, and Jón Aðalsteinn Jónasson was also displeased with Guðmundur's advancement. These were men well seasoned in internal party battles. Among other things, they had pitted Guðmundur G. against Ólafur Ragnar at the central committee meeting in 1973. As time went on, however, they felt Guðmundur showed them coldness and unhelpfulness during his time on the city council. He made no effort to cultivate his relationship with these men, and they viewed his group of supporters as a threat to their own position within the party.

Many party members had long discussed the need for strong men to run in Reykjavík once Einar Ágústsson departed from the political scene. Several of them bore a grudge against Guðmundur G. and could not stomach the idea of him taking over the first seat. Because the elections came on so suddenly, there was no prospect of holding a new primary. Little, therefore, seemed able to prevent Guðmundur from moving up into the first seat, since Einar intended to give up his parliamentary seat.

I cultivated my relationship with Kristinn Finnbogason and his men as best I could in those years, though I was never really counted among their group. Kristinn urged me insistently to leave the Vestfirðir and run in the capital, since I was the party chairman. I considered that out of the question. Kristinn and his associates, however, loudly maintained that Guðmundur G. was an unsuitable candidate, and when I gave my refusal, they soon began working to bring Ólafur Jóhannesson south from the Norðurland West constituency. They said Ólafur was the only candidate likely to bridge the split the party was facing in Reykjavík. That was probably right.

At first I had little faith that Ólafur could be persuaded to run. In the media I likewise denied all reports of Ólafur's candidacy. He had declared repeatedly within the party that he intended to retire, and it was unlike him to waver from such a decision. I was in fact also content for Guðmundur to lead the list in Reykjavík and trusted him fully to do so. I considered him among the most promising men in the party. I was well aware, however, that he was something of a loner in politics and considerably inclined to go his own way. On the other hand, everyone recognized the strength of Ólafur Jóhannesson and the respect he enjoyed. I therefore soon declared myself
in favor of Ólafur running in the capital if he could be persuaded to do so. Ólafur gave in, changed his mind about quitting, and Guðmundur G. accepted the second seat without much deliberation.
A vigorous election campaign

The day after I stepped down as minister, I opened an office in the party's premises on Rauðarárstígur. I was chairman of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) full-time. The election campaign had begun. We were little troubled even though opinion polls seemed to show the party's support dwindling to almost nothing. It spurred us to action.

I placed great emphasis on adopting new and more organized working methods in the election campaign. Tasks were distributed and the work was organized by a small campaign committee. Three groups were appointed to oversee the campaign work. One handled policy preparation, another had the role of organizing publishing activities and the traditional election campaign, and a special group was to draft the party's messaging in the media. This bore fruit. I myself sat on the policy committee; Hákon Sigurgrímsson, my right hand from the Ministry of Agriculture (landbúnaðarráðuneytið), headed the media committee, and Eiríkur Tómasson the election committee. They went straight from their duties in the ministries to preparing the election campaign on behalf of the party. Better campaign managers could hardly be imagined.

The election campaign began with a loud bang when the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) presented its election platform under a war headline on the front page of Morgunblaðið: "Blitzkrieg against inflation" ("Leiftursókn gegn verðbólgu"). Þjóðviljinn, which came out the same day, printed this same platform in no smaller type with the slogan: "Blitzkrieg against living standards" ("Leiftursókn gegn lífskjörum"). This twist instantly became a catchphrase throughout the country. The opponents of the Independence Party united in their criticism of its policy, and Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson even went down to Lækjartorg and handed out Morgunblaðið to passersby! The Independence Party's candidates were everywhere on the defensive over this policy of theirs, which proclaimed that the nation would have to accept a "moderate" level of unemployment in order to defeat inflation.

No one profited more from the "blitzkrieg" than the Progressive Party. I called it "the conservatives' revenant," which was "an unadulterated depression policy" consisting in the Independence Party men wanting to wage war on the entire public through confrontations in the labor market. We Progressives went into the elections well prepared, full of self-confidence, and with a clear policy. It called for bringing down inflation while maintaining full employment. We called it "counting down inflation in stages" ("niðurtalning verðbólgunnar í áföngum"). Occasionally it was called "the Norwegian way."

It was acknowledged, even by hardened opponents, as the only alternative to the blitzkrieg. The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkur) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalag) put forward no tenable solutions to the inflation problem, any more than before.

In our advertisements we emphasized reliable leadership and put forward the trio of ministers: Ólafur, Tómas, and me. I believe this presentation was well received. Ólafur in fact got a new lease on life in the election campaign in Reykjavík. At first the intention had been to spare him the hectic round of meetings, workplace visits, and the various things that differed between the capital and Skagafjörður and Húnavatnssýsla, where Ólafur had always been a candidate. When it came to it, however, he was unstoppable at meetings, was in top form, and seemed more inspired and enthusiastic than he had been in years. Ólafur attracted attention and respect wherever he went.

Because of the chairmanship I had to attend to the election campaign throughout the country, not only in my own constituency. I attended meetings as widely as possible to give the party's candidates support where it was needed or requested. To get between places, I often took rides in small single-engine airplanes. Edda did not care for this mode of travel, and others remarked that I must have gone mad to trust these little machines with my life when any kind of weather could be expected. I made it a rule to choose reliable pilots who knew the country. That is what matters most. Out west to the fjords, and between places there, I flew a great deal with Hörður Guðmundsson of the airline Ernir, mentioned earlier. He was a good friend and supporter of mine.

Once Hörður flew me from Reykjavík to a meeting in Patreksfjörður. A thick fog lay over Patreksfjörður when we arrived, and getting down to the airfield was out of the question. Hörður resorted to flying out to Látrabjarg and over the lighthouse there, where he began to descend. When he had come down to 200 feet, it was not safe to go lower, and the ground still could not be seen through the thick fog. So we decided to fly in to Ísafjörður. Over Ísafjarðardjúp, however, there was a similar bank of clouds. Hörður tried the same trick again and began descending by the lighthouse at Ögur. Suddenly we hit a downdraft there, and the plane fell uncontrollably. It seemed to me we would never stop plunging, and it was little comfort to see Hörður growing ever paler in the seat beside me. Just as we caught sight of the ground, the plane caught the air and we were saved.

We were pressed down into our seats. It was as if the reins had been yanked hard to save us. Perhaps that is what happened. We did not say a word until we had landed at Ísafjörður, and a long time passed before I told my wife Edda this story. I have seldom been so close to meeting my fate.
On another occasion, all the airlines had canceled flights from the Vestfirðir because of weather.

I had to get to Reykjavík, however, and from there back to Akureyri, where I was due to attend a meeting. So I called Helgi Jónsson, who still runs a flight school and charter service with great distinction. I owe him much from my travels. He flew me practically anywhere in the country when the stakes were high, and it was him I called when I needed to get away from Klettur in Borgarfjörður in a hurry. One week, when one crisis after another struck in the government, he picked me up there three times. On this occasion, however, Helgi said conditions were impassable and he did not dare come get me. But I had to get through.

So I called Þórólfur Magnússon, a man from Strandir, who is a very good pilot. I asked him whether he felt up to the trip. He said he would look into it, and an hour later his plane came down out of the clouds. Þórólfur said he had examined the conditions carefully and found that there was a hole in the cloud cover over Faxaflói and Breiðafjörður. There he had dived down and crept over Kleifaheiði into Patreksfjörður.

Þórólfur and I then set off. When we came over Breiðafjörður, however, the cloud cover had closed the hole. Þórólfur therefore tried to creep under the clouds from Breiðafjörður south over Heydalur and thus into Faxaflói. When we got to the innermost point on the Breiðafjörður side, it was completely closed off and we had to turn back. There was nothing to do but climb up out of the clouds in the hope that there was still a hole over Faxaflói. We would not have had many options if that had not been the case, for the plane's fuel supply was running low. We breathed a sigh of relief when we caught a glimpse of the sea through the clouds over Faxaflói, and from there we glided in to the airport in Reykjavík.
A spring in the step

The tailwind in these elections was among the strongest I have ever felt. I sensed that all over the country the party members' spirits were surging, and there was tremendous fighting spirit among Progressives wherever I went. The same was true out west. I spent most of my time in the final week on travels and meetings there. Everywhere the going seemed lighter than just a year earlier. I also sensed in many places that the people of the Vestfirðir were pleased with my chairmanship of the party. They felt they were regaining influence.

Television presentations and debates mattered more and more in politics, and I felt this keenly. I benefited from having taken to heart instruction in television presence. I made a point of wearing a blue shirt rather than a white one, avoided clothes that would cause flickering in the television picture, and

trained myself to speak briefly, clearly, and into the camera. As always, though, I strove first and foremost to be natural, as if I were sitting in the viewers' living room rather than on a meeting platform. There is a world of difference between the two.

The party's media group had among its members Magnús Bjarnfreðsson, a television news reporter. Because of his job, however, this was never made public. Before the most important interviews and debates I took part in during the campaign, I held meetings with him and my assistants, Eiríkur and Hákon, where they pelted me with questions. The purpose was that nothing should be able to take me by surprise when the moment came. This paid off. The reporters' questions and the opponents' jabs were nothing compared to the assaults of those three.

Perhaps I benefited no less, however, from standing out among the party chairmen when we were called together for debates. Benedikt Gröndal had grown tired. Lúðvík Jósepsson was forceful and made a good impression. Everyone knew, however, that he was retiring from politics. Geir Hallgrímsson was no less worn out from the bitter feuds within his own party. He was also slow to find his words, spoke slowly and stiffly with that cracked voice which was long a favorite of impressionists. I felt very much at ease in the television debates. I managed to forget where I was and could concentrate on the message.

Although the election campaign was novel in many ways, some things did not change. The campaign meetings in the Vestfirðir constituency were the same as ever, and the same could be said of the competitors. Matthías Bjarnason, however, never really hit his stride in these elections. I think he did not care for much of what the "blitzkrieg" entailed. Matthías was of course a hardline Independence Party man, but perhaps first and foremost a spokesman for the rural districts and the people of the Vestfirðir. Nor did he hold back his views on the fecklessness of the leaders in Reykjavík when the occasion arose. It became famous when he described them as "dreadful money-grubbers" ("óttalegum gróðapungum").

Besides the economic issues, Matthías seemed to have the greatest difficulty responding to the ideas I had put forward about innovation in agriculture. He hardly spoke of them except in mockery. He seized on a sentence from the 110-page parliamentary resolution on agricultural affairs in which the cost of setting up a mink farm was calculated, and which was worded such that a little over one and a half square meters were needed "for one female mink along with space for part of a male and for the pups." He confronted me meeting after meeting, wanting to know which part of the male was supposed to be in the cage with the female. Matthías thought this brilliantly clever.

At one meeting I decided to reply in kind. I said I lamented that Matthías was so envious of the fur animals, and that it was obvious that a longing for a harem of his own slumbered within him. But since he was carrying on like this about the poor male minks, what did he have to say about the rams that were often given forty ewes to attend to? It so happened that Ómar Ragnarsson was present with a television camera at this meeting. He managed to make it look as though the campaign meetings out west were mainly about mounting and smut. Ómar even managed to edit the remarks of Sigurlaug Bjarnadóttir, the Independence Party candidate, so that they seemed the worst kind of obscenities. This scandalized various people, who felt that this showed politicians in their true colors.
Victory! Victory!

That election night I was at home in Mávanes, for once. I had to break with my custom of awaiting the results among supporters in the constituency, since I had been summoned to a discussion in the television studio along with the other party chairmen on election night. So I drove south on election day. In the early evening I followed the election returns with excitement, together with Edda and the children. As they began to come in, more and more people kept arriving to offer us their congratulations. Before long, it was standing room only in the basement at Mávanes.

The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) increased its support across the whole country, gaining 8 percentage points and five members of parliament. The support totaled 24.9 percent and the MPs became 17. In relative terms the increase was greatest in Reykjavík, where the party rose from 8.3 to 14.8 percent. The increase, however, was around and above 10 percentage points in nearly all the rural constituencies, which was more than in the capital area. In the Vestfirðir, support grew from 21 to 30.6 percent of the vote. I was overjoyed at this result and the victory won in the elections. To me it represented a vindication of the work we had done in preparing for the elections and of the performance of the party's spokesmen in the campaign and in the television debate programs, which attracted no small attention.

The guests left us toward morning, and Edda and I went to bed showered in congratulations from all sides. I did not fall asleep right away. Countless thoughts ran through my mind. I was the chairman of a political party that had won its greatest victory in many years. I had accomplished my mission. Yet one could probably have seen the victorious smile give way to a more determined expression the longer I thought. I was resolved to prepare myself well for the increased responsibility the results had laid on my shoulders.
Chapter Nine

The government formation following the elections in the winter of 1979 became one of the most historic of the century. The course of events was exciting, complicated, and at times even like a thriller. The country's largest political party, the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), split, and the disputes that arose from it are among the most intense in the nation's political history.
