Their effects were felt for a long time afterward. Individual aspects of this story have been disputed and no doubt will be for a long time yet. Now that some time has passed, however, there is perhaps for the first time an opportunity to lift the veil on much of what happened in those days and weeks leading up to the formation of Gunnar Thoroddsen's government.

When the ballot boxes had been counted in the early hours of Tuesday, December 4, 1979, probably no one foresaw the events of the coming weeks. In my mind, the most important results of the elections were that a landslide victory for the Independence Party had been averted, and that the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) gained nothing from having blown up the left-wing government. Quite the contrary. The Independence Party added one member of parliament and the Social Democratic Party lost four. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) lost three MPs, and Eggert Haukdal won election from a special list in Suðurland. After these results it was hard to see what the pattern of government would be. Little seemed obvious except the fact that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was the unequivocal victor of the elections.

Kristján Eldjárn summoned the chairmen of the political parties to meet with him one by one the day after the elections. I had often been a guest of Kristján's at Bessastaðir. We had regularly met at informal meetings where we went over the state of national affairs. This had been so since he was elected. These visits became less frequent after I became chairman of the Progressive Party. To Kristján, however, I had never come on formal business.

We had a fine meeting at which the president sought my views on the election results and the outlook in national affairs. I do not think it fitting to recount what passed between us, since such meetings with the president are generally confidential. I believe, however, that the chairmen of all the parties were agreed that I should be the first to receive the mandate to form a government.

Before Kristján Eldjárn's time in the presidential seat, the concept of a "government-formation mandate" ("stjórnarmyndunarumboð") did not have the meaning it has since acquired. Kristján played the largest part in shaping it through his working methods in the formation of governments. Previously, politicians had talked with each other through informal channels while the president followed closely all attempts to assemble a workable parliamentary majority. Instead, Kristján entrusted one of the party leaders with making an attempt to form a government, and it was then said that the person in question held "the president's mandate to form a government."

Earlier presidents had intervened considerably in the course of events on the political stage, having themselves had experience in that arena. Some believed, for example, that Ásgeir Ásgeirsson had arranged matters behind the scenes when the Social Democratic Party's (Alþýðuflokkurinn) minority government took power in 1959, and the Viðreisn government that followed it. Kristján Eldjárn wanted to avoid such interference. I consider that in many ways a healthy attitude. He therefore only entered the story by granting someone the mandate.

Kristján Eldjárn also shaped an informal rule about the order in which the political leaders received the government-formation mandate. The victor of the elections would usually receive the mandate first. If he failed, the representative of the largest party received the mandate, then the representative of the second-largest party, and so on down the line. This arrangement meant that the president in no way interfered with the outcome of the government-formation negotiations. That was probably the goal foremost in Kristján's mind.

Politicians naturally caught on to this predetermined order. Those waiting further back in line had no great stake in the current attempt succeeding. The pecking order, if one may call it that, also meant that leaders of parties with little or no likelihood of being able to form a government received the president's mandate to make such an attempt. Another drawback of one particular politician holding the president's mandate is that others become in effect inactive in government-formation talks unless they are invited to formal negotiations. Other conversations between individuals, which can obviously be a necessary prelude to forming a government, take on the appearance of "secret talks" and scheming.
These emphases of Kristján's in government formation were never criticized except in hushed tones, in conversations between individuals. I knew nothing other

from my career, and his way of working seemed to me good testimony to his respect for impartiality. Kristján's approach, however, also played a large part in why government formations often dragged on. This way of working was ill suited to the turmoil and instability of politics in the 1970s, and even less so at the beginning of the 1980s. The run-up to the formation of Gunnar Thoroddsen's government in the winter of 1979–1980 was perhaps one of the clearest examples of this.
Talks on a left-wing government

The President gave me the mandate to form a government on 5 December 1979. I was in no doubt about where my mind was headed. I was aiming for a left-wing government. I had declared that intention already on election night. The reasons were simple. In my mind, the "lightning offensive" (leiftursókn) ruled out any possibility of forming a government with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). I was certain it would lead to unmanageable conflicts and greater difficulties in governing the country than the outgoing left-wing government had grappled with.

I knew the task would not be simple. Not least, I feared intransigence from the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), which was still on the defensive over the break-up of the government. Jón Baldvin Hannibalsson, editor of Alþýðublaðið and one of the party's most influential men, wrote in an editorial on the day I received the mandate to form a government that he found it hard to see what part the Social Democratic Party could play in my attempt to form a government. He said experience showed that the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), on its unchanged course, was "a party unfit to govern".

The People's Alliance's lack of realism in economic matters was in fact also a worry of mine. Lúðvík Jósepsson, its chairman, had dismissed the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) economic proposals during the elections on the grounds that there was no economic problem to contend with. That was his style in politics. Lúðvík had earlier remarked that there was no problem in agriculture either — "people should just eat more meat". I went into the talks moderately optimistic. I feared deep-rooted animosity between the two labour parties (the A-parties) more than that policy disagreements would trip up the negotiations.

Various people criticized my left-wing dreams and considered them unrealistic. In my heart, however, I believed that Ólafur Jóhannesson had not exerted himself as was necessary to hold his government together. He was never much for compromises and never called the disputing parties together outside formal meetings to reach a settlement. On the other hand, I have always been an optimist where cooperation between people is concerned, and I trusted myself to lead such a government. My ambition was set on the prime minister's chair.

I got the parliamentary group's approval for my policy. A left-wing government it should be. At Ólafur Jóhannesson's suggestion it was also agreed that I would choose my own collaborators for the talks. He probably wanted to make things easier for me. Ólafur did not seek to take part in the government-formation talks. I then wrote letters to the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) inviting them to talks on a left-wing government, and set up a negotiating committee of Progressives consisting of Tómas Árnason, Jón Helgason, Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson, Halldór Ásgrímsson and Alexander Stefánsson, in addition to myself. This group met regularly between the parties' negotiating sessions. The first meeting, on 7 December 1979, was attended only by the party chairmen.

At other meetings Tómas was usually with me while the others on the negotiating committee took turns. Most often, though, Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson was chosen as the companion for Tómas and me, and I cannot see from my papers that Halldór Ásgrímsson attended any of these negotiating sessions.

I declared at the outset that I intended to take two to three weeks to determine whether there was any likelihood of cooperation between the parties. Lúðvík Jósepsson said he doubted a conclusion would be reached before Christmas, but said what mattered most was that the parties be prepared to stand or fall by the agreement that would be made. Disputes after the fact were to be avoided as far as possible. We all agreed that economic affairs would be the main subject of the talks and that the media would be kept out of them. The latter failed completely.

At the third meeting I presented the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) economic proposals in detail on five typewritten pages. They provided for a two-year working programme whose main objectives were job security, a phased reduction of inflation, and improved conditions for the lowest paid. The purchasing power of disposable income was to remain unchanged, external trade was to be in balance, and increased production was to be the aim in 1980 and 1981. The objectives were to be achieved without raising taxes. On the other hand, pay-as-you-earn taxation was to be introduced, and the Progressive Party's economic committee also stressed that a value-added tax should replace the sales-tax system.

The Treasury was to be run without a deficit, a ceiling was to be set on total investment in society, and a plan drawn up for price increases such that inflation, which at the time was heading for 60 per cent, would be down to 30 per cent in 1980 and 18 per cent in 1981. Agreement was then to be reached with the labour unions on these objectives. The fundamental point in that regard was that there would be no basic wage increases during the period.

The People's Alliance put forward its own ideas on economic affairs. They were much more general in all their wording than our proposals. Those proposals were nevertheless considerably in tune with the Progressive Party's policy. The People's Alliance

(Alþýðubandalagið) placed greater emphasis on making no cuts anywhere in public consumption or social projects. Natural resources were said to belong in social ownership, and in addition an unequivocal demand was made for the departure of the American military from Keflavík airport.

On the whole, the People's Alliance's proposals were by no means detailed enough to get a firm grip on, and the wish-list flavour was conspicuous. It was hard to avoid the feeling that everything the People's Alliance put forward was partly written for the front page of Þjóðviljinn in case the talks broke down. The text concerning wage matters in particular had the character of slogans. Wage matters were indeed one of the most sensitive parts of the talks. Svavar Gestsson and Ragnar Arnalds argued for the party's ideas at the meetings with us and the Social Democrats, and in addition Guðmundur J. Guðmundsson, "Jaki", sat in on many negotiating sessions. He was chairman of the Federation of General Workers (Verkamannasambandið) and of Dagsbrún. Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson occasionally attended meetings in Guðmundur's place.

The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) sent "the restless wing" to the talks. Kjartan Jóhannsson usually spoke for the party. Sighvatur Björgvinsson attended most meetings, and Vilmundur Gylfason early on. He kept a low profile. Magnús H. Magnússon took his seat as the talks wore on. The Social Democratic Party placed the greatest emphasis on restraint in taxation and public finances. The party's representatives were unsparing with comments but did not put forward their own proposals until near the end of the talks. Those were more radical than the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) proposals and aimed at bringing inflation down in an even shorter time. I thought I saw in them too great a tendency toward contraction and a risk of unemployment. The parties' policies were nonetheless easily reconcilable, in my view. That was also the opinion of the Social Democrats.

I was pleased with the Progressive Party's preparation for these talks, and the work of the party's economic committee weighed heaviest there. Its members included my kinsmen Bjarni Einarsson and his brother Guðmundur, Árni Benediktsson, Margeir Daníelsson, Gunnlaugur Sigmundsson, Bolli Héðinsson and Helgi Bergs. Much rested on their shoulders in formulating the party's plans and drafting proposals. Representatives from the labour movement and spokesmen of the main industries were also consulted. So a cross-section of society could be found there, so to speak. The economic committee met regularly to shape the party's proposals and respond to the ideas of the negotiating parties.
The National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun) was at once assigned to assess the proposals I presented at the start of the talks, and that assessment was in essentials positive. It was calculated

by it that at the end of 1980 inflation would be down to 37–38 per cent and a year later to 19 per cent. In other words, the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun) did not consider it possible to bring inflation down to 30 per cent in the first year, as the proposals aimed to do, but it considered the later stage achievable. Its assessment also said:
It is certain that bringing inflation down to what is set as the objective of the proposals in a shorter time than is reckoned with here is bound up with great difficulties.

Once this assessment was available, the setting of objectives in the proposals was changed to accord with the calculated results, and I considered that the party's proposals had gained considerable recognition. The results, however, also assumed that some reduction in living standards was unavoidable, and that worried the representatives of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). Svavar Gestsson said the party was not prepared to accept such a thing.
Clashes in the Althing

Since the Social Democratic Party's (Alþýðuflokkurinn) minority government was in power and the budget had not been passed, parliament was summoned only just over a week after the elections, on 12 December 1979. This delayed and soured the government-formation talks, because disputes over elections to parliamentary offices and committees stirred up bad blood in the parties' negotiations. In the very first days, difficulties arose in reaching agreement on the election of the Speaker of the united Althing.

I worked for cooperation among the left-wing parties in all the parliamentary elections in order to secure their influence and ease parliamentary business if agreement were reached on a left-wing government. That required the speakership of the united Althing, as well as of the upper and lower chambers. No less important was having a majority and the chairmanships in the main parliamentary committees. After the three parties had exchanged letters and proposals for several days, it became clear that agreement would be reached neither on the election of the Speaker nor on the committee elections.

These skirmishes had a substantial effect on the left-wing talks, though they probably did not decide the outcome. When the committee elections were to take place, I remarked at a negotiating meeting that those elections would test whether there was a genuine will for cooperation among the parties. The representatives of the People's Alliance concurred, and Svavar Gestsson said that "cooperation with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) would amount to little interest in cooperation here". Sighvatur Björgvinsson, however, stressed that these were unrelated matters. No agreement was reached.

Jón Helgason was indeed finally elected Speaker of the united Althing, but it took three rounds. The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) voted an Independence Party man into the Speaker's chair of the lower chamber and made a deal with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) on the committee elections. In the election to the budget committee, a Social Democrat cast his vote for the Independence Party list, with the result that a People's Alliance man lost his seat. The Social Democrats' votes also led to Geir Hallgrímsson being elected chairman of the foreign affairs committee. That probably stung the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) most. Both of the labour parties lacked the will to cooperate and did everything they could to spite each other. That did not improve an atmosphere that was bad already.

I did not exactly wear a halo when it came to the elections to the parliamentary committees, any more than the representatives of the labour parties. The Independence Party and the Social Democratic Party had a total of 31 members of parliament, in addition to Eggert Haukdal, who won election from a breakaway list of Independence Party men in the South. The old "Restoration" coalition parties (viðreisnarflokkarnir) could therefore form a working majority in parliament in both the upper and lower chambers. Many feared that possibility, not least because the Social Democrats' minority government was uncomfortably reminiscent of the corresponding Social Democratic government in the run-up to the Restoration coalition in the autumn of 1959.

To avert this, the Progressives entered into close cooperation with the People's Alliance in the elections to the upper chamber. The parties thereby secured for themselves half of the upper-chamber members, which sufficed to defeat measures on a tie against a possible Restoration government. I plotted the bloc-building together with Svavar Gestsson, Ragnar Arnalds and Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson. In fact, one can say that the two parties established good cooperation right away in that parliament.

These tactics of ours stirred up resentment among the Social Democrats, who considered them a sign of little trust toward them. That could no doubt be granted. Nor is it easy to say how matters would have turned out if the chamber elections had gone another way. The Restoration parties could have outmanoeuvred us but did nothing. It was hard to tell which party, the Independence Party or the Social Democratic Party, was more sensitive to any suggestion that a coalition between them was in the offing.

While this was going on, the Restoration parties seemed to be blundering. I found it beyond belief that they would deliberately rule out cooperation with each other, and so I felt certain that the indifference of the party chairmen, Geir and Benedikt, was to blame. But I did not know the whole story. In preparing this book I have learned on good authority that the chairman of the Social Democratic Party, Benedikt Gröndal, deliberately prevented cooperation between the Independence Party and the Social Democratic Party in the chamber elections. Benedikt was opposed to a Restoration government but feared

also that a large part of the parliamentary group was of the opposite opinion. At the forefront were those who had brought about the break-up of the government in Benedikt's absence in the autumn. By his inaction in the chamber election, Benedikt thus killed two birds with one stone. He prevented a Restoration coalition and got his revenge for the break-up of the government.

In the light of history, it mattered no less that Gunnar Thoroddsen offered to take a seat in the upper chamber for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). He had previously sat in the lower chamber, which was considered the broader arena, since the outcome of most matters was decided there. If Gunnar had not offered to do this, it would have been impossible for him to form his majority government. No one could have foreseen that. Gunnar in fact also stepped down as chairman of the Independence Party's parliamentary group at the start of this parliament. Some have pointed out that this suited him particularly well, giving him a freer hand in what followed. Afterwards, various people believed they could see in these decisions of Gunnar's at the opening of parliament that he had been laying the groundwork for his government formation from the very first day.
I do not put much faith in that. Not even Gunnar Thoroddsen possessed that much foresight.
"Anything is better than the Conservatives"

I had frankly declared during the election campaign that I wanted to aim for a left-wing government in the country. Nothing in that regard should have come as a surprise. Yet various supporters of the Independence Party seemed flustered when I held firm to this line after the elections. I said cooperation with the party was out of the question unless it changed its policy. In an interview with Vísir published on Saturday 8 December, I was asked whether the "lightning offensive" was the only reason for this view of mine on cooperation with the Independence Party. In my answer I put it this way:

I have always been doubtful about cooperation with the Independence Party. Perhaps that is an inheritance from my father, for he never entered a government under the leadership of the Independence Party men. It runs very deep in many Progressives that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) should be the adversary of the Independence Party. The late Tryggvi Þórhallsson said "Anything is better than the Conservatives" (Allt er betra en íhaldið), and I second that!

These remarks are included in this book because few things were more discussed in the Independence Party newspapers over the following days. It was as if all hell was about to break loose. Vísir wrote an editorial under the headline "The Insolence of the Progressives", which said among other things that my position was "a provocation to the whole nation

-loving Icelanders". Morgunblaðið was no less worked up and spoke of my "personal fanaticism". The editorial writer seemed chiefly to imply that anyone who let remarks of this kind fall condemned himself to political exile in Iceland.

At the end of my left-wing talks, Styrmir Gunnarsson, editor of Morgunblaðið, wrote a double-page article which he called "A Hopeless Left-Wing Game of Chess". This was some of the most unexpected and strangest writing Morgunblaðið has produced before or since. In it the editor argues that with my declarations I had brought political isolation upon the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn); left-wing governments, he said, had all been failures; and finally he argued at length the necessity for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) to enter a renewed Restoration coalition. In fact this first article was overshadowed by the one that appeared the following day, entitled "Historic Reconciliation". What surprised most there was the call for a coalition government of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið).

When Styrmir's first article is read, it is obvious that my remarks were the occasion for the writing. The Morgunblaðið men stood close to Geir Hallgrímsson, chairman of the Independence Party, at this time. They probably convened their war council after the interview appeared in Vísir and wanted by any means to break the isolation they believed hung over the party in the wake of my declaration. That effort began only three days after the Vísir interview with a short article by Björn Bjarnason, "The Art of the Possible". The editor's series of articles was intended to follow it up. Indeed, Styrmir says in his "reconciliation article" that my "campaign of exclusion" was the spark for the Independence Party's interest in the People's Alliance.

The purpose of the writing was not to make peace with the People's Alliance or to enter into government cooperation with the opponents of Western cooperation. On the contrary, the Morgunblaðið men dreamed of a new Restoration. The "commie-coddling", as they themselves would have called it, was only to make clear to the Social Democratic Party that it was not the Independence Party men's only option in the situation. The writing was meant to enable the Social Democrats to enter into cooperation with the Independence Party on the premise that otherwise the People's Alliance would do so.

The fear of political isolation weighed heaviest on the hearts of the Independence Party men. Only with that in mind does the paper's writing during those December days become comprehensible. I myself was in fact not much rattled by this, or by the cold air that blew my way from the Morgunblaðið building, for declarations of support rained down on me from Progressive people all over the country. In their minds, anything was better than the Conservatives.
Half-measures and half-spoken verses

As the left-wing talks wore on, it became clear that it would be difficult to bring the parties together on economic matters. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) could not be induced to make even the most trivial sacrifices in wage-earners' terms for the goal of bringing down inflation. The party seemed completely blind to the harm that wage-earners suffered because of inflation, and it was as if the party's leaders believed, deep down, that working people were better off with index-linked wages and high inflation than in economic stability where indexation would be unnecessary. This was phrased as the People's Alliance being opposed to "the inflation problem being solved at the expense of working people".

The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) was never enthusiastic about government cooperation with the People's Alliance. Influential men in the party are in fact said to have believed it was healthiest for it to stay out of government under all circumstances. When I had held the government-formation mandate for a little over two weeks, I considered the attempt exhausted for the time being. In interviews with the media I set out the reasons in detail, but said I did not rule out left-wing cooperation later on even though agreement had not been reached in these talks. I was above all relieved to be able to celebrate Christmas with my family without having to stand in this bickering.

After the Christmas holiday, on 28 December, the President entrusted Geir Hallgrímsson with attempting to form a majority government. He called me to a short meeting at his home the same day. There I confirmed to him what I had earlier declared in the media. I still considered cooperation with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) unlikely. Asked directly, I said a government of national unity was not out of the question if no other options were available.

Geir troubled neither me nor other political leaders much over the New Year and the first days of January. He let a week pass without any further discussion with me or the chairmen of the other parties. For a time the leaders of the Social Democratic Party thought Geir was talking with the People's Alliance men, and the People's Alliance men believed he was talking with the Social Democratic Party. Geir, however, talked with neither party. As so often before, this line had been given out in Morgunblaðið. Björn Bjarnason wrote a wistful article two days before Christmas in which he mourned the working methods of politicians from before the age of the "media microscope", when confidential private conversations took place without an exchange of words in written proposals or a single formal meeting being held. Geir truly practised these "ancient virtues".
It turned out that Geir had done little other than seek advice from Einar Olgeirsson and Gylfi Þ. Gíslason and
more old politicians instead of meeting with those who stood on the front lines and actually had some say. I found this way of working hard to understand.

Geir called the first formal government-formation meeting for 8 January 1980. The chairmen of the four parties were summoned there. But more strange things happened in the talks. When Geir presented proposals on economic matters, he declared that they were not the proposals of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn)! He also refused to disclose who their author was. In Tíminn they were never called anything but "the proposals of Mr. X". We used that name for them at the negotiating meetings as well. Each party appointed two representatives from its own ranks to a negotiating committee on economic affairs, where the situation was reviewed. Then it so happened that the Independence Party appointed Jónas Haralz on its behalf, even though he did not hold a seat in parliament. There was Mr. X.

The talks under Geir's leadership did not get far. Morgunblaðið had been badly mistaken when it considered it virtually out of the question that Geir would begin talks on a national unity government, but it came close on the consequences of doing so:
There is no likelihood that Geir Hallgrímsson will open the game by offering a national unity government. If it came to that, it would immediately deflate the tension.

Jónas Kristjánsson, editor of Dagblaðið, wrote around the time these attempts ended that the lack of news of the Independence Party chairman's government formation was not an example of a conspiracy by the forces of the right, who wanted to give him more peace to form a government than I had been given in the left-wing talks. Geir had simply done little that was newsworthy. After Geir had held his mandate for sixteen days, Jónas said he had gotten as far as I had gotten after the first three days in which I led government-formation talks. Jónas added:

At the same rate, it can be expected that it will take Geir all the way up to Easter to tread the same path that Steingrímur ran in two weeks before Christmas. 16 days have gone into examining the matter, preparing it, and possible attempts to bring about formal talks!

Many struck a similar chord as Jónas. I thought there was little leaderly bearing in the half-hearted dabbling of the Independence Party's chairman, and he was hesitant in all his actions and his presentation of the case. While the national-unity-government talks were under way, the discussions among the party chairmen were, in another thread, about whether there were not other possibilities on the table. Lúðvík Jósepsson in particular was diligent in pressing the rest of us about our position on that. He called a national unity government "an acknowledgment

a deadlock and the predicament of all the parties". At the chairmen's meeting on 13 January it emerged that everyone wanted to try other options before a national unity government. Geir's formal attempts were thereby at an end.

In the nearly three weeks that Geir held the government-formation mandate, we chairmen held only three actual negotiating meetings. It was hard to resist the thought that this time had been poorly spent. Geir's attempts bore not least the mark of the fact that the chairman of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) regarded it as his chief task to make use of the party's political isolation. He seemed, however, not to know which foot to step on in those matters. If the intention was to approach the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) through talks on a national unity government, the attempts were a complete failure. Geir did, to be sure, say that he had abandoned the "lightning offensive" policy. The proposals of Mr. X were nonetheless even worse in the minds of the People's Alliance than the ideas of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), let alone of us Progressives.
Scheming at Rauðarárstígur

Tómas Árnason was one of those who felt the chairman of the Independence Party was doing little while he held the government-formation mandate. He therefore set off on his own initiative and wanted to explore whether agreement could be reached among the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), the Social Democratic Party, and the Independence Party. At first, however, only minority cooperation between the Progressive Party and the Social Democratic Party was discussed. These talks were kept secret and were held on the premises of the State Development Agency (Framkvæmdastofnun) at Rauðarárstígur. From the Social Democratic Party came Sighvatur Björgvinsson, who was acting minister of finance, and along with him and Tómas, Bjarni Einarsson, who worked at the State Development Agency, and Björn Friðfinnsson, later a ministry permanent secretary, are said to have been present.

Morgunblaðið published a veritable bombshell report on these talks on the back page of the paper on Sunday 13 January. Tómas denied the report, both in a comment in the paper and at a meeting of the parliamentary group. In Tíminn he was even quoted as saying that he "could not put it more mildly than that this was pure 'Mogga-lies' of the worst kind". Sighvatur likewise denied the report in the news of the State Broadcasting Service (Ríkisútvarpið).

The talks between Tómas and Sighvatur did take place. Neither of them, however, was in a position to continue them or own up to them after word got out. Within the Progressive Party it was hard to tell who disliked these ideas more, Ólafur Jóhannesson or the agricultural leadership, which held the Social Democratic Party in as much contempt as Ólafur Jóhannesson did. The same story could certainly be told from the Social Democratic Party, where many regarded
the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) as their chief adversary. The talks at Rauðarárstígur were therefore kept extremely secret.

What even fewer knew was that Gunnar Thoroddsen, deputy chairman of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), met with Tómas several times while these talks were going on. In those conversations they discussed the possibility that Gunnar and a certain group of members of parliament from the Independence Party would give support to a minority government of the Progressive Party and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), or would even join it. Tómas says the talks revolved around government participation by Gunnar's men, and that the talks had been initiated in order to explore the possibility of a majority government of that shape. He also says he got the strong feeling that it was not far from Gunnar's mind to lead such a government, although that was never mentioned by name between them.
Gunnar Thoroddsen repeatedly denied both at the time, when the disputes within the Independence Party were at their height. In an interview with Tómas conducted for this book, he put it this way:

I spoke with Gunnar several times while this was happening. At that point the talk was that the Social Democratic Party would take part, together with Gunnar's men and the Progressive Party. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) came into the picture later, and without my knowledge.

No news got out about the part of the talks that concerned Gunnar. I do remember, though, that Sverrir Hermannsson came to me on one of those days and asked whether I knew about the conversations with Gunnar. I answered Sverrir, as I did others who carried such rumors to me, that I had no objection to individual members of parliament talking together. As chairman of the Progressive Party, however, I would not take part in such things while Geir held the mandate. Sverrir Hermannsson recounts our conversation in his memoirs, Skýrt og skorinort. His account, however, is heavily colored by the course of events that followed. No one could have foreseen it. When Sverrir spoke with me I did in fact have loose knowledge of the members' talks. The other thing I felt certain of: no one had mentioned that Gunnar would become prime minister, neither in such a government nor in any other.
A prime minister candidate chosen by drawing lots
When Geir had handed back his mandate, it was the turn of the People's Alliance. A change of leadership was under way in the party. Lúðvík was stepping down from

the chairmanship and therefore did not want to lead government-formation talks. In the first vote in the parliamentary group, the votes fell evenly between Svavar Gestsson and Ragnar Arnalds. A coin was tossed to decide which of them would go to see the president. Svavar won. If he had succeeded in forming a government, it would probably have been the first time in world history that the prime minister of a parliamentary state had been chosen by lot.

Svavar picked up the thread again in talks on forming a left-wing government. At the first meeting I declared myself ready for such talks in full earnest, and Benedikt Gröndal struck the same chord. On the other hand, I was not as taken with Svavar's starting point; he said a new report from the Central Bank (Seðlabankinn) indicated that the national economy was in good condition and made "further curtailment of wages unnecessary". The parties' negotiating committees were largely made up of the same men as before, three from each party. The state of the economy was reviewed and efforts were made to reach agreement on measures. The representatives of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) stood firm and showed little will toward forming a government.

After the parties' third meeting, Jón Helgason and I met Svavar and Ragnar at a special meeting. There it emerged that Svavar considered the matter fully tried if no agreement could be reached on the basis that lay before us. Ragnar also said he thought there was much in common in the policies of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). I agreed with that but considered a minority government a dubious path. If the Social Democratic Party could not be induced to cooperate, then only the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) remained. Svavar agreed with that and did not rule out a government with the Independence Party. He stressed, however, that cooperation with the Independence Party would be impossible unless there was complete solidarity and close collaboration between the Progressive Party and the People's Alliance.

It never came to the Independence Party being invited to three-party talks under Svavar's leadership. He tried no government configurations other than a left-wing government, any more than I had a month earlier, and handed back his mandate.

There was no mistaking, however, that there was a good spirit between the People's Alliance and the Progressive Party that winter. In part it could be traced to the breakup of the government in the autumn. At the same time, it was also the fruit of the fact that I had had more and better contact with the new leaders of the People's Alliance, inside parliament and out, than Ólafur Jóhannesson and Lúðvík Jósepsson had had between themselves while they were chairmen. Our sincere desire to form a left-wing government doubtless counted for much there. There were in fact many who believed that because of the People's Alliance's influence in the labor movement, it would have to be on board in the government if the economic problem was to be solved. Otherwise the whole of society would be ablaze with labor disputes.
The Social Democratic Party, on the other hand, seemed unable to bear the thought of ending up

in a government. To those Progressives who were most reckoned to the right, this seemed a great sin. They considered it clear that the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) was the political party with which the Progressives had the greatest common ground on substance, not least in economic matters. Tómas Árnason was one of them. He took a gloomy view of sitting again in a left-wing government and had not given up hope of cooperation with the Social Democrats. He therefore had good hopes when Benedikt Gröndal received the government-formation mandate after Svavar on 23 January. In fact I too, like my father, harbored the hope that the close pre-war cooperation between the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the Social Democratic Party could be revived. It foundered not least on agricultural matters.

Benedikt followed in Geir's footsteps and arranged all-party talks on a national unity government. At the first meeting, however, it became clear that the Social Democratic Party had no intention of forming a government, at least not with the Progressive Party. The Social Democratic Party's proposals called for a drastic overhaul of agricultural policy and for the squeezing of cooperative enterprise. It must have been clear to everyone involved in the talks that the Progressive Party could not enter into cooperation on this basis. Voices calling for cooperation between the parties fell almost completely silent, and Tómas's dreams came to nothing.

At a joint meeting of the Progressive Party's parliamentary group and executive committee on 24 January, many of the rural members of parliament had harsh words for the Social Democratic Party and its proposals. Páll Pétursson said the document was "not worth discussing", that the agriculture section was an impertinence and the wage-policy proposals "wage robbery and a seizure of power". Even Halldór Ásgrímsson, who was otherwise suspicious of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), said he was readier to support cooperation with it and the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) than a government of the Progressive Party, the Independence Party, and the Social Democratic Party. I put forward the following motion, which enjoyed broad support among those at the meeting:

A joint meeting of the parliamentary group and executive committee of the Progressive Party resolves that the proposals which the Social Democratic Party has now put forward cannot become the basis for the formation of a government with the participation of the Progressive Party.
In the wake of this it was decided to discuss the possibility of cooperation among the Progressive Party, the Independence Party, and the People's Alliance with the leaders of those parties.
"Man to man"

On Sunday 27 January I met Geir Hallgrímsson at his home and told him of the interest that had emerged in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) in a coalition government of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), and the Progressive Party. Geir said he was completely opposed to the idea and was more interested in forming a "Stefanía" government with the participation of the Social Democrats instead of the People's Alliance. Geir later confirmed this account but said he had been "unsuspecting" of the consequences of his words when he gave his refusal.

The next day I told the parliamentary group about the Independence Party men's answers and the progress of Benedikt Gröndal's talks. I said there appeared to be only two options for forming a majority government since the Independence Party ruled out the People's Alliance. These were a government of the Independence Party and the Progressive Party, or a three-party government of those same parties and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). "If this did not succeed, one might even expect a Restoration (Viðreisn) government." Few liked these ideas, and no decision on the next steps was taken in the parliamentary group. "Stefanía" was not ruled out, however, though opinion leaned mostly toward ideas of a national unity government.

In these last days of January the options for forming a government seemed nearly exhausted, except perhaps for those with the most unbridled imaginations. An unnamed member of parliament described the situation this way in a conversation with Morgunblaðið: "There are some men in all the parties considering all the possibilities, which other men in all the parties then rule out."

That was not far off the mark. At a parliamentary group meeting on 28 January the Independence Party resolved, among other things, that "every member of parliament should explore all possibilities through talks with members of other parties". It would be "man to man". At the same time, Guðmundur "jaki" was said to be sitting with five others in "New Deal talks" (nýsköpunarviðræður) among the People's Alliance, the Social Democratic Party, and the Independence Party.

Anders Hansen and Hreinn Loftsson give a detailed account of the government formation and the split in the Independence Party in their book Valdatafl í Valhöll. Although the account is in many places slanted against Gunnar Thoroddsen, the book is a considerable source, as it was published shortly after the events took place. It shows clearly, among other things, that in these January days every trick was employed, and influential men outside parliament worked for a solution to the government crisis no less than members of parliament did, if they thought they could tip the scales. Word got out that old classmates from primary school had met if it might help to resolve the government crisis. There gathered pupils of Skeggi Ásbjarnarson, a teacher at Laugarnesskóli, namely Styrmir Gunnarsson, editor of Morgunblaðið, Ragnar Arnalds, member of parliament for the People's Alliance,

Jón Baldvin Hannibalsson, editor of Alþýðublaðið, and Halldór Blöndal, member of parliament for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). Jóhann Einvarðsson, member of parliament for the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), was in fact also from this group, but he could not make it to the meeting.

Benedikt Bogason and Edgar Guðmundsson, two of Gunnar Thoroddsen's closest collaborators, were also active in these days. Benedikt was an engineer and an old workmate of Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson. They discussed the idea of Gunnar's supporters that there were possibilities for a maneuver among the parties in which Gunnar would play the leading role. Guðmundur G. put these ideas to me, but I did not give them much thought. Guðmundur recalls that I answered something to the effect that "such ideas could not be at the forefront for the time being".

These conversations probably took place about three days before Gunnar himself got in touch with me, and they later took on great weight in the disputes among Independence Party men about the run-up to the government formation. The truth, however, was that similar events were taking place in every corner of parliament. The whole of society was exchanging opinions about the government crisis. It may be that these conversations played some part in Gunnar's decision to take the initiative. But there is no way to assert anything about that one way or the other.
Gunnar takes the initiative

In the newspapers on Tuesday 29 January I was quoted as saying that there was interest within the Progressive Party in government cooperation with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and the Independence Party, but that I had been told the Independence Party men ruled it out. I was referring there to my meeting with Geir Hallgrímsson on the Sunday. These remarks found their way, among other places, onto the front page of Tíminn and were not contradicted by the leadership of the Independence Party. There was one important exception to that. That same Tuesday, Gunnar Thoroddsen and I ran into each other in the parking lot of Alþingi. A session of the united parliament was under way. On the agenda were questions I had little interest in, and after them debates on agricultural matters that I saw no reason to involve myself in. I therefore left parliament early.
As I was on my way out to my car, Gunnar Thoroddsen came along heading for his office in Þórshamar. We exchanged greetings and fell into conversation.

Gunnar said he believed the possibilities for forming a government had not been exhausted, and said he supposed it would be good for us to talk together. I agreed. He asked whether I had time to walk with him up to his office. I said I was glad to. Gunnar came straight to the point once the door had closed behind

us, and said he believed that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and part of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) could work well together. I said I had agreed with him, but recounted the answers Geir Hallgrímsson had given me two days earlier. Gunnar said little about that position but stated that he himself could secure the support of enough Independence Party members of parliament for such a government.

I was astonished at these words from the deputy chairman of the Independence Party and asked what he meant. Gunnar said that even though the parliamentary group of the Independence Party as a whole would not support such a government, he could guarantee the support of six to seven members of parliament. It was, however, an absolute condition that he become prime minister. I did not say much at first but was thoughtful, for it would probably have been considered more natural that I hold the premiership, whether one looked at the election results or the parliamentary strength of the Progressive Party. I quickly gathered from Gunnar, however, that he considered the prime minister's seat a precondition for his being able to secure the support that would be needed. On the other hand, he could not be induced to name his prospective supporters.
Gunnar said I would simply have to trust him with that part of the matter, for the time being.

My meeting with Gunnar lasted about half an hour. It ended with me saying that I did not rule out this possibility but wanted to talk with the leadership of the People's Alliance and with Ólafur Jóhannesson before going any further. Gunnar stressed that nothing of these plans must get out, but acknowledged that it was natural for me to speak with the People's Alliance and consult Ólafur. On parting we agreed to be in contact by telephone that evening.

I went straight over to parliament, where a session was in progress. As it happened, Svavar Gestsson and I sat side by side in the parliamentary chamber, at the far western end. I asked him to come see me, but Svavar was distracted. He was listening to a speech by one of the ministers of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) who was at the rostrum. Svavar was always ready for a scrap where the Social Democratic Party was concerned. I made it clear to him, however, that this was a serious matter. We walked over to a window in a side room between the lower and upper chambers. From there one looks out over Austurvöllur. Behind the curtains I told him what had happened and asked whether he could imagine entering into the formation of a government with the Progressive Party and Gunnar Thoroddsen.

Svavar perked right up and questioned me further about my conversation with Gunnar. I could not answer all his questions but told him that we had decided to be in contact that evening. I also asked Svavar not to tell this to a single soul, just as Gunnar had earlier asked me.
Svavar said, however, that he would have to consult Lúðvík Jósepsson, who was still chairman of the party. He was packing up his belongings in his office in Þórshamar. Svavar dashed off.

I could not find Ólafur Jóhannesson in Parliament. Ragnar Arnalds, however, crossed my path, and since there was good trust between us I told him the same story I had told Svavar, and with the same caveats. He sounded to me no less interested. Ólafur had not attended the parliamentary session that day, so I telephoned him at home. I said I needed to speak with him without delay, and Ólafur said I was welcome.

I have probably seldom been as deep in thought as on the way to that meeting. I fully realized that great responsibility came with taking part in splitting the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). It could have serious consequences and create conflict throughout society. At the same time I had to get used to the idea that Gunnar Thoroddsen would become prime minister. I met Ólafur in the library at Aragata and told him the news. He raised his eyebrows and leaned forward in his seat at the tidings. When I had finished speaking he asked one or two questions and then leaned back in his armchair. Ólafur pondered and puffed on his pipe without it showing the slightest sign that any ember still glowed in it. At first he said only "well, well," "remarkable," and sighed. After considerable reflection he said he agreed with me that this was a difficult and delicate matter.
All things considered, though, he thought it right to explore this option. I also heard that what he considered most important was that Gunnar had himself taken the initiative in the talks.

The Independence Party men believed Ólafur Jóhannesson capable of anything, both good and ill. It seemed to me they sometimes saw their late leader, Bjarni Benediktsson, in him. Some Independence Party members have firmly believed that Ólafur had arranged the formation of Gunnar Thoroddsen's government from the very beginning. In this way, they held, Ólafur wanted to repay Gunnar for supporting him in the Geirfinnur affair, when Geir sat silent while Gunnar mounted a defense. I do not believe this interpretation of history, although Ólafur and Gunnar certainly had a good working relationship, had worked side by side at the University's Faculty of Law, and knew each other well.

Ólafur played little part in the government formation — it would be closer to the truth to say that he neither pushed for it nor opposed it. He was largely absent from Parliament during the days when the talks began and attended only half of the parliamentary group meetings at which the government formation was discussed. Ólafur neither blessed these talks nor cursed them. It mattered greatly to me, however, to know that he agreed with me that there was reason to explore Gunnar's backing further. If Ólafur had opposed the arrangement, the parliamentary group would have hesitated. Ólafur was still strong in the party.

I telephoned Gunnar that evening, as we had agreed. I told him about my talks with Svavar and Ólafur Jóhannesson and that I was ready to explore the basis for further negotiations. Svavar is said to have brought Gunnar the same message from the camp of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). Svavar has recounted that after our meeting behind the curtains in the Parliament House he went to see Lúðvík in his office in Þórshamar. Shortly afterwards Ragnar Arnalds arrived there, out of breath and panting, from his meeting with me, bearing the same news. Those three decided, as I did, to keep this news from their own parliamentary group, and that Svavar would go to meet Gunnar before anything further was decided. Gunnar invited Svavar and me to meet him at his home the following morning.
Talks on Víðimelur

Wednesday 30 January began with a meeting of the party chairmen with the President of Iceland. There Kristján Eldjárn gave us all until Monday to form a majority government, without granting any one of us a mandate. We all knew that an extra-parliamentary government was in the air. After that meeting I went straight to Gunnar's home on Víðimelur. Vala, his wife, received us warmly and served us coffee and Danish pastry. When Svavar arrived at the meeting, however, he did not let the delicacies lead him astray, and said bluntly, just as he was greeting his host: "I hope you know that I have not come here to form a government with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). That is out of the question." Gunnar smiled to himself and replied with his well-known composure, "Nor had I expected so," as he offered Svavar a seat with a gentle wave of the hand.
From the beginning it was clear that the People's Alliance men were not least taken with the thought that cooperation with Gunnar would mean splitting the Independence Party.

At first there were only three of us — Gunnar, Svavar and I. We went over the state of affairs in general and the main policy areas. We benefited greatly from the fact that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance had already reached agreement on important points in the talks that had taken place earlier. Much of it was already down on paper. Gunnar declared at the outset that defense and foreign policy would remain essentially unchanged. No objections were raised to that, though the People's Alliance was accommodated on minor points in the final version of the government agreement. It was decided that the security affairs commission would continue its work and that plans to build a new air terminal would be subject to the approval of all the coalition parties.
On this first day of the talks I reported on them at a parliamentary group meeting

of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Many of the members were astonished, and not all were equally pleased. Many in particular thought it a reckless gamble to contribute to splitting the country's largest political party. I agreed, but said that I nevertheless believed there was a basis for further talks after the conversations that had taken place. So it proved.

Tómas Árnason was among the doubters. When he had last parted from Gunnar, they had still been discussing cooperation with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), not the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). Tómas was habitually wary of the latter's participation in government. He laid great stress on the chairman of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) being kept informed of the course of events. I had intended to do that myself, and in my consultations with Ólafur the day before we had reached the same conclusion. I was curious, however, to know whether there was more behind Tómas's insistence, and so I asked him why he was pressing the point. He answered with this sentence: "There will be a day after this one." No resolutions were passed by the parliamentary group at that point.

After the Progressive Party's parliamentary group meeting I had Geir Hallgrímsson called out of the Independence Party members' group meeting to inform him of the events that had taken place. Geir and I had a short meeting in the so-called ministers' room in the Parliament House. Geir was deeply shaken and considered it borderline whether we could justify taking part in a government without formally requesting such a thing from the Independence Party leadership. I told him frankly, however, that we would find it hard to refuse Gunnar after this long government crisis. Otherwise an extra-parliamentary government would be formed when the deadline the President had given us party chairmen ran out. No member of parliament could bear the thought of that.

I was glad to have had this meeting with Geir, even though it is hard to be the bearer of ill tidings. I had felt rather bad about going behind his back. I also think Tómas was right that this was in keeping with the long-term interests of the Progressive Party. Geir was grateful to me for this act of fair dealing and sometimes remarked, in his struggles with Gunnar, that he had met with "more candor and fair dealing" from his opponents than from the deputy chairman of the Independence Party. Geir and I always found it easy to talk to each other.

The talks threw the Independence Party leadership off balance, and Geir failed to get a grip on the situation. At first he chose to look past what was happening and called national unity government talks for the following day. There Geir and I met, together with Kjartan Jóhannsson and Ragnar Arnalds, on behalf of the four parties. No one said a word about Gunnar's talks, even though at that very time he was sitting with Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson and Svavar Gestsson
at Víðimelur. Ragnar Arnalds indeed believed that the only man in the room unaware of this was Geir Hallgrímsson.

At lunchtime that Thursday, Gunnar Thoroddsen met Eggert Haukdal and the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) members of parliament Pálmi Jónsson and Friðjón Þórðarson. Then came his talks with me. He was long reluctant to name his supporters, though he was pressed hard on the point. At this meeting of ours, however, he told me in complete confidence that in addition to those Independence Party men who had been his lunch guests, Albert Guðmundsson was one of his men. He also believed he had one or two more at his disposal. But he named no names. Gunnar stressed, however, that none of the members of parliament had yet made a firm commitment of support. I was uneasy about this. Everyone knew that the Independence Party leadership was working on those thought most likely to defect, applying persuasion and threats by turns — at least twice for every time Gunnar spoke with them.

Gunnar and I had no sooner finished our meeting than the balloon burst. Vísir published a news story about "Gunnar's private talks." For the next few days people talked of little else. That same day Dagblaðið in fact ran a story saying that Progressives and People's Alliance men had approached Gunnar about forming a government. Many thought they saw the fingerprints of Gunnar's men on those writings.

Despite the attention and the uproar the Vísir story caused, the meetings continued at Víðimelur. At four o'clock Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson and I sat down to a fresh platter of delicious refreshments together with Gunnar, Svavar and Hjörleifur Guttormsson. We were making good progress in most areas. As Gunnar felt he could see a basis for negotiations, he contacted his party chairman, Geir Hallgrímsson, and Ólafur G. Einarsson, chairman of the parliamentary group. He asked them to call a parliamentary group meeting to discuss forming a government with the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). I do not know how Geir and Ólafur took this news. What I do know is that the People's Alliance took it badly and feared that the whole Independence Party would join the talks. I believe Gunnar did not consider there to be much danger of that.
He knew his own people too well for that.

The Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) somehow ended up sidelined during these days, after running its own talks aground the week before. Benedikt Gröndal was chiefly occupied with pressing for an answer to his "Stefanía" ideas. That was readily granted. The Progressive Party rejected them, as had long been known. We were not only dissatisfied with the policy basis but no less with the Social Democrats' newly arrived idea that Jón Sigurðsson, director of the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun), should head the government. To us that seemed to come close

to installing an extra-parliamentary government. On the lips of the public, Jón had earned the nickname "þjóðhagi" (master craftsman of the nation), while the Social Democrats called him "a civil servant outside the parties." The Progressives entered Jón in their books as "a Social Democrat outside Parliament."
A Watershed in the Talks

Friday 1 February was the decisive day of the talks in many senses. That day Gunnar Thoroddsen went before his colleagues in the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and formally informed them of his talks and of the draft policy agreement of a new government. At the same time the Progressives sat in a meeting where I recounted the course of the talks. Among other things, this sentence is minuted after me: "In Steingrímur's judgment it still appears lacking that Gunnar has enough members of parliament with him for such a government formation." In other words, everything was still uncertain regarding the outcome of the government formation and support for Gunnar within the Independence Party.

At the parliamentary group meeting Gunnar was met with fire and brimstone. His attempts at forming a government were all but ignored, and the parliamentary group entrusted Geir Hallgrímsson with working toward the formation of a majority government on the party's behalf. Only Gunnar and Friðjón Þórðarson abstained when that motion was put. As a fallback it was resolved that Geir should explore forming a minority government with the support of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). Gunnar alone abstained on that decision. Gunnar's motion that the parliamentary group begin talks on a government formation of the three parties was thus never put to a vote! I do not know what the leadership of the parliamentary group was thinking.

Various Independence Party members of parliament left that meeting grinning. They were certain that Gunnar had been stopped once and for all. When I spoke with him after the Independence Party group meeting, he was so unsure of his position that he said that, judging by the parliamentary group's vote, he could only be certain of Eggert and Friðjón. I agreed to give Gunnar until morning to find out whether he had enough support to continue the talks.

Formal talks lay dormant that Friday evening. Instead, everyone involved sat glued to the radio and television broadcasts, where news could be expected from the Independence Party members' parliamentary group meeting. The reporter Stefán Jón Hafstein broadcast the first interview with Gunnar on the radio that evening. In that conversation Gunnar may be said to have confirmed that he had taken the initiative in the talks. He also recounted the state of the government formation talks and
the handling of the matter within the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in measured terms, and kept all avenues open.

The watershed was finally confirmed in the evening television news. It opened with an interview with Geir Hallgrímsson, in which he could barely speak for the frost and cold outside against the wall of the Parliament House. He had difficulty hiding his resentment. Geir could be forgiven. Most people, though, were quick to forget the red nose, the cold-stiffened face and the halting voice when the image of Gunnar Thoroddsen appeared in the floodlit television studio, where he was the special guest — dignified in dress, mild of eye and fatherly of speech. He answered the reporter's questions quickly and confidently.

Some of what Gunnar said in these interviews was perhaps a half-truth. He said, for example, that his thinking had been that the Independence Party would stand behind the government formation. That completely contradicted his declarations to the representatives of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) at the outset. He was also evasive when asked who had taken the initiative in the talks. Neither we Progressives nor the People's Alliance members of parliament quibbled over those vague answers. They were understandable in light of Gunnar's position within the Independence Party. Yet everyone with any knowledge of the matter knew that Gunnar was speaking against his own convictions when he said it was almost a matter of indifference to him whether Geir became involved in the government formation and took up the thread that Gunnar himself had spun. That was far from the truth.
There was no contact between them. Geir did not even have an inkling of where the government formation meeting called for the next day would be held. That was kept carefully secret.
The Ruble (Rúblan)

Gunnar did not take long to wrest the weapons from the hands of his opponents within the Independence Party and secure the support that was needed. After the evening's media interviews it was not long before Gunnar telephoned me. I could hear at once that the tune had entirely changed. Insecurity and uncertainty had given way to fatherly self-confidence and calm. He had received the response he had hoped for, and he confirmed the meeting for the following day.

The television news interviews proved decisive. After them, by far the greater part of the nation swung behind the government formation. A way had been found out of the government crisis. From every corner of the country, calls began pouring in to members of parliament urging them to work for this solution.

The supporters of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) were of one mind. A large share of Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) supporters followed Gunnar as well. It was no coincidence that many of the members of parliament whose support Gunnar had courted gave their assent over the weekend that was beginning. Their supporters back home urged them to do so.

After our government formation attempts became known on 31 January, there was little peace from the onslaught of journalists at Víðimelur. We therefore resorted to moving elsewhere. The choice fell on the office of Ásgeir Thoroddsen, supreme court attorney and Gunnar's son, on the upper floors of the Mál og menning building on Laugavegur. In the ranks of the most hardline Independence Party men, the building went by the name Rúblan — "the Ruble." The nickname rested on rumors that Icelandic communists had built the premises with Russian gold. That suited the Cold War generation at Morgunblaðið.

The talks progressed quickly compared with what had gone before. Svavar took it upon himself to put the government agreement into words, and we accepted gladly, for Svavar was an old newspaperman. The agreement was based to a considerable extent on the Progressive Party's policy as it had been presented at the start of the left-wing talks, with the compromises needed to accommodate the People's Alliance. Gunnar went over the drafts and made comments on what he thought could be improved. I put it this way in an interview with Vísir: that there was "relatively little of the Independence Party's viewpoints." That was the plain truth; Gunnar never mentioned the "lightning offensive" except in a disparaging tone. He was also undeniably much preoccupied with securing for himself the support he needed from the Independence Party's parliamentary group.

Before the meetings began on Laugavegur on Saturday 2 February, I went to talks with the other three party chairmen, where Geir Hallgrímsson was still straining toward national unity government negotiations. He seemed to me bewildered. Either he had not grasped the situation, or he refused to face the facts. At the end of the national unity government meeting he wanted a new meeting called later that day. Once the meeting was over, however, it so happened that Geir and Benedikt Gröndal came to speak with me and moreover proposed new talks between their parties and the Progressive Party.

The Progressive Party's parliamentary group received these offers coolly, especially as I also conveyed the message from Gunnar Thoroddsen that he had one man secured on his side and "the promise of three men of support for passing legislation and defending the government against a vote of no confidence." At this meeting the parliamentary group for the first time formally approved entering into talks with Gunnar on forming a government. It was done with all votes cast in favor. We broke off the national unity government talks thereafter. Geir had failed to seize the initiative

in the government formation. The national unity government talks were stillborn from the start. Lúðvík Jósepsson, chairman of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), put it well when he said it seemed to him that everyone had been wearing "other trousers over their national-unity-government trousers."

Following the parliamentary group's formal approval of entering into talks with Gunnar, a negotiating committee was elected according to the established rules. In reality, though, the weightiest part of the talks was finished and only points of detail remained. I proposed that Tómas Árnason and Jón Helgason be chosen for the committee, along with myself. Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson, who had figured prominently in events, I proposed as alternate in the talks. These resolutions of the parliamentary group were passed only six days after Gunnar Thoroddsen and I first spoke together, and five days after the first meeting was held at Víðimelur. By then, conventional government formation talks had gone on almost without interruption for nearly two months with little visible result. After five days' work, however, a government agreement was now essentially in place.
Events had unfolded at such speed that formal resolutions had been left to wait.
Hidden Men and Reprisals

Little was talked about more than who Gunnar's supporters were and how he would fare in bringing them on board the government. Eggert Haukdal was at once considered likely. He had fallen out with the party leadership, run on a separate list in the South, and been refused a seat in the parliamentary group of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) after the elections.

At the meeting of the central committee of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) held on Sunday 3 February, I sought support for forming a government under Gunnar's premiership. I said I could not present the policy agreement, since it was not yet finalized, and that in reality only Gunnar and Eggert Haukdal were secure in his band of supporters. Of the others little could be said at this stage. The meeting received the government formation remarkably well, and Eysteinn Jónsson remarked among other things that these events showed how "delightfully strange politics can be."

The government formation talks were going on almost simultaneously with the central committee meeting. Among other things, a declaration from Gunnar reached the meeting to the effect that he would procure the parliamentary support that was needed, and the policy committees that had been set up in five areas were presented: industry and energy, agriculture, transport, public finances, and wage matters.

It was put on record who held seats on these committees. There were the four of us who had been chosen for the negotiations on behalf of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), along with Svavar Gestsson, Ragnar Arnalds and Hjörleifur Guttormsson for the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). On Gunnar's behalf, Pálmi Jónsson sat on the committee on agricultural affairs, Friðjón Þórðarson on the transport committee, Björn Þórhallsson — a labor leader and the first chairman of the publishing company of Dagblaðið — on the wage-affairs committee, and Þóroddur Th. Sigurðsson on the committee on industry and energy. Gunnar attended to the state finances himself. With the appointment of the policy committees, the tone was set regarding the support of Friðjón and Pálmi. Soon they also began to make a habit of attending meetings at the Rúbla.
Still, several days passed before their support for the government became public.

In the book Valdatafl í Valhöll (Power Play in Valhöll), Pálmi is said to have informed Geir Hallgrímsson of his decision to support Gunnar's government the day after the aforementioned central committee meeting, Monday, February 4. It is also said there to be likely that Friðjón did not make his decision about his support until February 7. That must be considered rather unlikely, given that he took a seat in the working group of the government's supporters a full four days earlier.

More happened, however, on Sunday, February 3, and it settled the matter of the government coalition once and for all. Geir Hallgrímsson had gotten in touch with the leadership of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and requested that the Social Democratic Party support a minority government of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). He was promptly asked in return whether the entire Independence Party would stand behind such a government. Geir got no chance to answer. In the meantime he received a letter from Albert Guðmundsson in which he said he would defend Gunnar's government against a vote of no confidence. With that, all was lost for Geir. The battle was over.

The Morgunblaðið men, who had long been Geir's staunchest supporters within the Independence Party, did not sit idle, however. Over that weekend they cooked up great screeds in which scores were settled with Gunnar Thoroddsen — or so it was supposed to be. Those writings appeared on Tuesday, February 5, the same day that Gunnar Thoroddsen received the formal mandate to form a government from the President of Iceland. In an editorial under the banner headline "The Rúbla," it was recounted at length how Gunnar had repeatedly betrayed and repeatedly lied to all the nation's foremost sons. The "Historic reconciliation" that Morgunblaðið had proclaimed a few weeks earlier under no smaller headlines was now forgotten. Gunnar was said to be about to commit the sacrilege of leading the communists to the seat of honor in Icelandic politics through betrayal.
The Rúbla editorial was followed by the articles "The senior member strikes," "Historic betrayal" and "A winter of calamities in Icelandic politics," all

in a similar vein. What seemed to weigh most on the Morgunblaðið men, however, was that Gunnar had supposedly spoken disrespectfully about Bjarni Benediktsson at some point in 1968 — when Bjarni was in fact still alive and fully capable of answering for himself, prime minister and party chairman with his own organ, Morgunblaðið, standing undivided behind him. I have in fact never understood the Independence Party's (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) secret rites when it comes to the party's departed chairmen. It seems one may not speak of them as politicians but rather as sacred cows or holy icons. Gunnar could not have committed a more unforgivable sin. I believe, however, that these writings of Morgunblaðið, and the fury they displayed, drove people toward supporting the government, if anything.

While this storm of sorcery was at its height in the middle of the government-formation talks, those of us who stood behind them on behalf of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) discussed where this would end. We were afraid that Gunnar's supporters would be bent at the last moment when push came to shove. We could not bear to think of that. I often shook my head and remarked to Svavar Gestsson that this was quite the adventure we had gotten ourselves into. He, on the other hand, grinned all the wider the more uneasy I became.

All this time the prospective government seemed to be on the outermost edge. The leadership of the Independence Party held constant meetings with the members of parliament concerned, in between which Gunnar hammered courage and vigor back into them. Pálmi seemed tough, but some said that Friðjón Þórðarson had become hesitant. No one knew what the next day would bring.
The Endgame

Once the policy platform was ready, all that remained was to divide the ministries between the parties. That point was of no small importance to Gunnar. It was in fact quite a big pill for me to swallow that he should get the premiership of the government and two ministries besides. That division had come up in conversation early on and had not been dismissed. At that point, after all, it was being said that Gunnar had more members of parliament with him than turned out to be the case.

We understood, of course, why Gunnar placed so much emphasis on the seats. Only that way, he believed, could the knots be tied securely enough for the support to hold. In truth it may be said that we gave him free rein in these matters. Perhaps it was just as well, for when it came to the crunch, it was the ministers who proved the most steadfast in their support of the government among Gunnar's so-called supporters.
The final knot was tied on the negotiations on Thursday, February 7, the day before the government formally took power. That day the parliamentary group of
