of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) no fewer than three times. At the morning meeting the policy agreement was approved with all votes cast in favor. After that meeting I went into negotiations on the division of ministries.

The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) pressed hard to get the finance portfolio into its own hands, and many traced that to their clashes with Tómas Árnason in the left-wing government. I was correspondingly reluctant to give it up. In the afternoon of that same day I presented to the parliamentary group a proposal for a division of ministries on which it seemed possible to reach agreement with the coalition partners. It provided that each party to the government would get three ministers. The division of ministries, however, would be such that the Progressive Party would get five ministries, the People's Alliance four and Gunnar's men three. Gunnar was to get agriculture and the People's Alliance the finances. Objections were raised to most points of the agreement, and not least the ones last mentioned.

It fell to me to bring things ashore at an afternoon meeting with Gunnar and Lúðvík Jósepsson. Lúðvík took over the leadership for the People's Alliance men in these negotiations on the final day. Up to then they had been in the hands of Svavar Gestsson. I do not know the reason for that changeover. What I do know is that Svavar was very unhappy with the changes to the number of ministers that I achieved at the eleventh hour. Lúðvík agreed that the Progressive Party would get four ministers, one more than the People's Alliance and Gunnar's men. In return I conceded that the People's Alliance would get the Ministry of Finance. Perhaps Lúðvík's concession can be traced to his having wanted first and foremost to ensure that Tómas Árnason would not become finance minister again. They had fought hard battles over the passage of the budget during the left-wing government of 1978–1979.

In addition to the Ministry of Finance, the People's Alliance got industry, social affairs and health as its share. Gunnar's men got agriculture and justice, in addition to the Prime Minister's Office.
"The Old Man Said Yes"

I made no proposal regarding the Progressive Party's ministers, but instead arranged for a vote to be held among the members of the parliamentary group by secret ballot, as had always been the custom in the party. The day before the vote took place, I knew no better than that Ólafur Jóhannesson was not seeking a minister's seat. That position surprised no one. On top of that, ever since Kristján Eldjárn had declared in his New Year's address that he did not intend to stand for re-election, Ólafur's name had been mentioned in connection with a candidacy for the presidency. He had evaded answering questions about it. Certain

it is, though, that many pressed Ólafur for answers in the following weeks, and only two days before the government took power he was still considering putting himself forward. In a conversation with Morgunblaðið he said he had made no decision.

The only definite answers to be had from Ólafur in those days were that he was not seeking a ministerial post. He informed me of this in a private conversation of ours and made no secret of it to others. As chairman of the party I spoke with the members of parliament to sound out their views on possible ministerial candidates. Along with me, Tómas was an obvious ministerial candidate. He enjoyed broad support within the parliamentary group. Secondly, there was the question of which of the two, Ingvar Gíslason or Jón Helgason, would be chosen. They both enjoyed support and each represented the rural districts. It may be said that the choice between them hinged on whether the Ministry of Education or the Ministry of Agriculture would fall to our share. Ingvar was one of the party's leading spokesmen on educational matters, and Jón on agricultural matters.

I was firmly of the opinion that the party's fourth minister ought to be a member of parliament from an urban area. Ólafur was not putting himself forward, and Jóhann Einvarðsson, member for the Reykjanes district, was a new member of parliament and did not have support for a ministerial office. Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson, the party's second man in Reykjavík, was on the other hand an ideal ministerial candidate. He was young and up-and-coming and held the office of party treasurer. He had taken an active part in shaping the policy on economic affairs and fought the election campaign wholeheartedly, despite having had to yield the second place on the list to Ólafur. Few of our men had figured more prominently in the formation of the government. I therefore intended to use my influence so that Guðmundur would be chosen in the parliamentary group's vote.
I discussed this with Guðmundur and loosely with other members of parliament.

Ólafur Jóhannesson did not get much time to contemplate the presidency in those February days. The day before the selection of ministers took place, one man after another set about getting him to put himself forward — and not for the office of President of Iceland, but for a ministerial post. Tómas Árnason was in favor of getting Ólafur into the government. He considered it essential for it to enjoy his strength. There was of course a good deal to that. Defense matters were also close to Tómas's heart, and he had long been of the opinion that Ólafur was opposed to the military leaving the country. Ólafur, however, never let that slip within my hearing. Ólafur was the self-evident choice for the office of foreign minister if he made himself available for it. Tómas considered Ólafur an important counterweight to the ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið).
Kristinn Finnbogason, Alfreð Þorsteinsson and the group at

around them in Reykjavík did not hold back either. They considered themselves to have a double reason to pull at the oars. They wanted access to Ólafur in the government, and to prevent Guðmundur G. from taking a seat there.

On the day the appointment of ministers was decided, I approached Tómas between parliamentary group meetings and told him that I would propose him for the seat of foreign minister. Tómas thanked me for the confidence. He wanted to mention, however, that Ólafur Jóhannesson had seemed heavy-browed to him in recent days. The closer the selection of ministers had drawn, the heavier his brow had grown, if anything. Tómas said he did not know whether Ólafur was seeking a minister's seat, but suggested that I offer him the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. I followed Tómas's suggestion, even though Ólafur had in fact already declined, as related earlier.

At a parliamentary group meeting I asked Ólafur to step outside the meeting room with me. There I told him that he enjoyed unequivocal support to become foreign minister if he sought it. Ólafur was pensive about this and was perhaps waiting for me to urge him on. That I did not do. When the silence had reigned for a while, Ólafur nevertheless said: "Yes, Steingrímur, I accept this offer." I was surprised by this answer at first, and somewhat thoughtful. I believed renewal would be an improvement, and Ólafur seemed to me to be growing weary. Perhaps it would have been wisest for him to step aside. Tómas says one could hardly tell which of us was paler as we walked to our seats at the parliamentary group meeting, I or Ólafur. When I sat down beside Tómas I said little at first. When I found my voice again I grinned and said only: "The old man said yes."

Once I had come to grips with this about-face of Ólafur's, I was nevertheless in a certain way pleased with it. He was always a source of strength. I had likewise had some difficulty deciding whether I should become foreign minister myself or leave it to Tómas. To tell the truth, I had little interest in the office and believed that being abroad a great deal would take its toll on my work as party chairman. I was more interested in the affairs of the country's industries and rural communities and in what touched the voters in their daily toil. On the other hand, it gave me pause to hand such honors over to my deputy chairman. The foreign minister's seat was considered by most to be the most prestigious office in the government apart from the premiership itself. In the end, though, I had decided that Tómas would get this office. Now Ólafur took it upon himself.

The Ministry of Education fell to the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), in addition to foreign affairs, commerce, fisheries and transport. Ingvar Gíslason was thus chosen over Jón Helgason in the parliamentary group's vote. Ingvar had been one of the party's leading champions of educational affairs for many years. I took the fisheries

and transport portfolios, Ólafur Jóhannesson took foreign affairs, and Tómas Árnason handled commerce. I thought the government well composed, though I was sorry about Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson. He probably felt little gratitude toward me for how this turned out. It reinforced the individualist streak in him, which was strong to begin with.

It is a fair description of Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson that he was never easy on the rein. In parliament he very much went his own way. He was an industrious member of parliament and prepared his parliamentary business exceptionally well. I often remarked what a difference it made to have an engineer in the group to examine matters thoroughly. Guðmundur is exceptionally intelligent, has an excellent memory and is organized down to the last detail. He is artistic and fond of poetry and knows all of Shakespeare by heart. He delivers the splendors in nearly flawless English.

Guðmundur is at the same time a man of strong emotions and very steadfast. It seemed to me that he sometimes chose the course of consulting little with his colleagues rather than having to accommodate their views. More than once I remarked that he needed to remedy this. He was even known to draft entire bills on his own initiative, which he introduced without much consultation with the parliamentary group. I never worried that Guðmundur was dishonest in his work or plotting treachery. Over the years, however, he undeniably became isolated within the parliamentary group. Solo performances by rank-and-file members of parliament have been frowned upon in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) ever since the days of Jónas frá Hriflu.
Chapter Ten

I have never known two jobs as unlike each other as being minister of fisheries on the one hand and minister of transport on the other. In transport matters I was an engineer among engineers. The tasks were on a firm footing, planned and carried out by strong institutions that had large and capable staffs at their disposal and functioned well. My co-workers were mostly engineers who thought along straight lines, like myself. These were men of action. The tasks of the Ministry of Transport (samgönguráðuneytið) struck me as exciting and memorable. On these pages, however, they will fare as they did in my earlier ministerial work. They must wait their turn for discussion in the shadow of the fisheries, for the time being.

The fishing industry is the nation's most important industry. On that everyone was agreed, and surely still is. To the sale of marine products could be traced — and still can be — the largest share of the nation's foreign-currency earnings, as people were slow to tire of repeating. The national economy stood or fell with the fisheries. In this field the decisions were the most fateful, and the responsibility of those who dealt with them correspondingly great. At times, though, it seemed to me that nothing was as far from the minds of those involved as precisely this great responsibility.

The fisheries were like a circus. One incident followed another, disputes were daily bread and divided opinions were the rule, not the exception. Little seemed to be on a firm footing, and the minister had to content himself with dancing on the narrow line of compromise between the interest groups. They bared their claws at every step and made as if to tear the minister to pieces. If I made a misstep on this middle path, disaster was certain. There were lion pits on both sides. Time and again it was not only the disputing parties themselves that had to be
contended with. In the Althing (Alþingi) and in the newspapers, strong words were not spared. The minister of fisheries could long seem to be the most unpopular man in the country.
The Fish-Price Farce

In 1980, inflation was around and above 40 percent. For most of the preceding decade it had stayed in the range of 30–50 percent, and society had all but adapted to this reality as if to an immutable rule. Ordinary wage earners received pay raises quarterly in step with the rise in prices, as the wage agreements stipulated and the index showed. Price increases on goods and services followed in their wake, because employers believed they could not otherwise sustain the pay raises. The export industries also had to get more in krónur for their production. For that the currency had to be devalued, which in turn led to higher prices for goods and a higher index — and thereby higher wages. This was spiral inflation: inflation that arose not from overheating in the economy, where demand exceeds supply, but from the adaptation the economy went through in order to live with the inflation.

There were important exceptions to this. Fishermen received wages that were a share of the value of the catch brought ashore. They were thus virtually the only occupational class in the country whose wages were not indexed. It followed that their incomes depended on the fish price. The same story applied to the operation of trawlers and boats. The fish price determined their livelihood to a great extent. This marked out the battlefield. The fishermen and the fishing-vessel operators stood on one side of the battle line, while the fish exporters and the fish-processing plants were on the other, with opposing interests to protect. The processing plants were the buyers of the catch and saw their advantage in keeping the fish price low. The national economy could not afford for the fishermen to walk off the job, for the fleet to be steered ashore, or for fish processing to shut down.
That is why the fish price was one of the most sensitive matters of dispute in Icelandic society. Society could be turned on its head over the price of cod, capelin and herring.

The fish price was set several times a year. Often enough to guarantee that nearly constant disputes raged over it. According to law, the minister of fisheries was to play no part at all. The fish price was to be determined in negotiations between buyers and sellers. For these negotiations, the Fisheries Price Board (Verðlagsráð sjávarútvegsins) had been established, on which sat a total of twelve representatives of sellers and buyers, tugging over every króna. It was a fluke if this group agreed on the result — and perhaps no wonder.
When everything had become deadlocked, the matter passed into the hands of a so-called arbitration board

where two representatives of each party sat. At the end of the table sat the director of the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun). He was the fifth man and often cast the deciding vote. Even though the law had stipulated ever since 1962 that the determination of fish prices should not be in the hands of the Minister of Fisheries, in reality it fell on my shoulders and those of the government to cut the knot. The final settlement regularly took place at our table.

According to the law, fish prices were to be determined by the market value of marine products, by fishermen's incomes compared with other occupations, and thirdly by the operating results of the fishing and processing industries. To bring some sense to the decision-making, efforts were made to gather information on the position of companies at sea and on land. To this end the National Economic Institute assessed the performance of boats and trawlers and carried out reviews of the operations of fish processing plants and freezing plants. In reality this only served to crown the absurdity. Instead of leading to a compromise in which the negotiating parties met halfway, the disputes turned on the premises and results of the calculations.

The aim of the authorities was to find some sort of "zero point," as it was called, which could maintain a balance in the earnings of fishermen, the fishing fleet, and the fish processing industry, and at the very least keep the industry afloat. In my eyes a fish-price decision was not acceptable until preferably everyone was dissatisfied. Then moderation had been observed. Yet the price the fleet needed to get by usually seemed to be higher than the processing industry could bear. More often than not, measures were therefore taken after the fact, so-called side measures. To save the fish processing industry and the export companies, the króna was then devalued.

Devaluations added to the difficulties of the fishing fleet, which was heavily dependent on oil prices. It did not help matters that the price of oil rose rapidly in the winter of 1979–1980. That did nothing to lower the fleet's operating costs or simplify the picture. Whenever fish prices were being set, there loomed the threat that too low a price would bring the entire fleet to a halt, while a high price would wipe out onshore processing. Most of the companies were indebted to the hilt and vulnerable to the slightest setbacks. When a devaluation was carried out, the fleet's position therefore had to be redressed through special measures, transfers, or subsidies on oil.

When all is said and done, I believe the fishermen were the ones who came away with the shortest end of the stick in fish-price decisions, because the same parties commonly ran both fishing operations and fish processing. With low fish prices, fishermen's wages could be kept down, thereby lowering the total cost of fishing and processing. In other words, these companies could tolerate the fleet being run at a loss if the processing side profited correspondingly. That was often the case.
The Capelin Fails — and the Cod as Well

One of my first acts in the Ministry of Fisheries was to halt capelin fishing temporarily. It was my first administrative decision in the new government. It also caused the first disputes within the government and showed me in black and white that I would not have peaceful days in the minister's chair for fisheries. The leadership of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) reacted furiously and criticized me for not having sought the government's approval. Lúðvík Jósepsson referred, among other things, to a memorandum said to have been made at the formation of the government stating that "no major decisions on restrictions of fishing shall be taken without the approval of the government." I denied this.

It was true that such unofficial memoranda are often made when governments are formed. Representatives of the parties' negotiating committees signed two such documents when the government of Gunnar Thoroddsen took power on 8 February 1980. The first stipulated that no proposal would be made to the President of Iceland to dissolve parliament without the approval of all parties to the government. The second stated "that if disputes arise within the government, each government party shall have a veto, if it wishes to use it." Both of these memoranda are in my possession, signed by Gunnar Thoroddsen, Ragnar Arnalds, and myself. The third, which concerned fisheries matters, is however unsigned except that written on it in red is: "Rejected, SH." I had refused outright to be handcuffed by my fellow ministers when making decisions in fisheries matters.

Clashes between conservation and fishing grew ever more prominent. Capelin fishing was permitted again at the beginning of September 1980. At the same time an overall quota was issued for the fishery. Barely two months later, the fisheries scientists brought me the news that little capelin had been found in their research expeditions. There was nothing to do but to rein things in at once so that the stock would not collapse completely. Instead of immediately issuing a regulation, I summoned fourteen or fifteen of the country's leading capelin skippers to a meeting. These were the mightiest of strongmen. Nothing about them was small in scale, neither in word nor in manner.

I opened the meeting and delivered the news. The results of the capelin surveys were such that it was obvious the catch would have to be reduced. The skippers swelled to twice their size during this speech of mine. They positively bulged with rage. We were told that we knew nothing about capelin, landlubbers from Reykjavík. It was near enough said that the fisheries scientists could be trusted not to recognize a capelin even if they met one in the street.
I stuck to my guns and if anything pressed the point further. After a while I said that

they had heard the scientists' arguments and I had heard their opinion. I intended to leave the meeting for half an hour together with my men. When that time had passed, I wanted to hear their proposals. When we sat back down, the whole atmosphere of the meeting had changed. One of the most experienced skippers spoke for them. He said they agreed that it could not be risked that the stock might collapse. They would therefore accept the reduction in fishing effort in its essentials. I greatly respected the skippers for their good sense when it came to the crunch. At the same time I made concessions from my initial ideas to meet their suggestions. Instead of limiting the catch to 60% of the original fishing permits, as the Marine Research Institute (Hafrannsóknastofnun) proposed, I drew the line at 70 percent.
It was also agreed to examine whether capelin vessels could be granted permits to fish for cod.

The first attempts to limit fishing effort in Icelandic waters began alongside the extension of the fisheries limit to 200 miles, when the nation gained full control over the resource. A so-called "fisheries committee" drafted a bill on fishing within Iceland's fisheries jurisdiction. It was the first comprehensive legislation on fishing in Icelandic waters. I sat on the fisheries committee together with representatives of all the parties in parliament. This was remarkable committee work in many ways. We travelled all over the country and visited fishing operations, fish processing companies, fish-processing workers, and fishermen. In this way we gained not only insight into the fishing industry throughout the country but also a feeling for the attitudes of those who worked in it. This served me very well when I became Minister of Fisheries.

From 1977 onward, fish within Iceland's fisheries limits were caught under the so-called scrap-day system (skrapdagakerfið). It was based on amendments made to the aforementioned law of 1976 and was Icelanders' first attempt to manage their exploitation of the resources of the sea. The law's principal management tool was the minister's authority to prohibit vessels from fishing for cod for a certain number of days in each season. These closed days were also known as scrap days, from which the system took its name. The word "scrap" (skrap) comes from fishermen's parlance and means fish species less valuable than cod, that is, the species the vessels had to content themselves with catching on "scrap days." The proportion of cod in the catch could then not exceed 15 percent. The minister could, however, also ban all fishing during certain periods.

The scrap-day system proved an imperfect tool for protecting the cod stock. To respond to this, during my time as minister I revised the number of scrap days more than once in each season. In my first year in the ministry, the number of scrap days was increased three times. In 1980 and 1981 they numbered about 150, three times more than in the first two years of the scrap-day system.

With these measures I wanted to limit the catch so that it would come close to what the Marine Research Institute (Hafrannsóknastofnun) considered safe. It soon became clear to me, however, that this result could not be achieved with closed days alone. I therefore thought it right to set a target for the total cod catch. That had not been done before. I followed the advice of the Marine Research Institute, which considered it safe to catch 420 thousand tonnes of cod in 1981, and issued a regulation to that effect. It also provided for the division of the catch among trawlers, boats, and capelin vessels. Cod fishing was thus for the first time set in accordance with the recommendations of the Marine Research Institute. In fact, considerably better results were achieved in managing the fishery in those years than after the quota system was introduced in 1984.

The total catch was smaller than the Marine Research Institute's recommendations allowed for in both 1982 and 1983. It cannot be asserted, however, that my regulations weighed most heavily in that respect. An unexpected catch failure probably played a larger part in the fact that the quantity the Marine Research Institute proposed was not caught.

In 1981 about 450 thousand tonnes of cod were caught instead of the 420 thousand I had decided on. This was not viewed with alarm. The fisheries scientists believed the stock was on the rise, and the Marine Research Institute proposed that 450 thousand tonnes be caught in 1982. Optimism prevailed about the state of the fish stocks, the capelin alone excepted. The gloomy forecasts of earlier years seemed to have been built on weak foundations. Fisheries scientists and politicians regained their good cheer. This came through clearly in my remarks in the Althingi in October 1981, where I said among other things:

Despite all the dire predictions of past years, I believe everyone agrees with me that the cod stock is not at all in danger — indeed out of all danger and growing well. I, at least, am not afraid of a catch of about 450 thousand tonnes, as may happen this year. Admittedly I consider it imprudent to count on an increase next year, among other things because of uncertainty about the survival of the juveniles from this spring. The same can be said of most other fish stocks. It is, however, necessary that the capelin stock be given the chance to grow very substantially.

Shortly after these words were spoken in the Althingi, the capelin vanished like dew before the sun. Capelin fishing had to be halted almost entirely, with a great commotion, before the beginning of 1982. That year the cod failed as well. Only just over 350 thousand tonnes of a 450-thousand total quota could be caught. More fish simply could not be found. All the favorable forecasts failed, and the dire predictions that had earlier been written off seemed to be coming true in their worst form. The fisheries scientists offered little more to hold on to than the politicians in these setbacks. They had
no answers, though various people speculated that the cod stock had migrated to Greenland.
Dancing the Dance of Ruin

The state's involvement in the fishing industry was by no means limited to fish-price decisions and attempts to control the fishing itself. Into my office at the Ministry of Fisheries came a constant stream of representatives of companies facing insolvency. With that, unemployment and a string of costly bankruptcies loomed over entire communities. More often than not, some kind of rescue measures were undertaken. They were either general or tailored specifically to the needs of particular sectors. The causes of the difficulties were manifold. Indexation of capital was introduced in several steps during the government's time in power. As a result, it no longer paid to be in debt. For many, that change was a hard lesson. The rise in oil prices on the world market was also a heavy burden.
In the latter part of my time in the Ministry of Fisheries, catch failures and difficulties in foreign markets certainly weighed heaviest.

The fish processing industry recovered after a period of difficulty, and groundfish processing turned a profit as my years as minister went on. The fleet, on the other hand, was in constant trouble that seemed to worsen day by day. Imminent bankruptcies in the fishing fleet were dealt with in the ministry almost daily. The reasons for the difficulties were above all expensive loans, the consequences of indexation, and imprudent investments in new and larger ships. The trawler companies in particular had a hard row to hoe. Nevertheless, in the eyes of many these big ships were the lifeblood of the rural districts and of the whole country.

In every village it was a moment of celebration when a new trawler sailed into the fjord, and everyone who could lift a finger rushed down to the harbor to receive the marvel, even though the local companies, the municipal fund, or the cooperative society had gone into debt far beyond the limits of the possible to make the purchase. When the yoke of debt began to make itself felt, the minds and hearts of the local people reacted with fury, and the result was a very serious matter, both economically and politically. Difficulties of this kind afflicted not only the economic life of the communities but no less the souls of the people — and not least the souls of the constituency's members of parliament. It was not enough for politicians to refer the problem back to the fishing companies or back home to the district.

The difficulties of the fishing fleet were considered the difficulties of the entire nation, and as so often before, the public looked to its elected representatives in search of solutions. I did not want to be found wanting in that regard.
The government met the difficulties in the fishing industry variously with direct payments from the treasury, new loans, or refinancing. Often these expenditures were explained

or excused with the argument that they were a reimbursement of the trawler fleet's charges on various supplies that had flowed into the treasury. Transfers of various kinds were used to improve the position of individual branches of the fishing industry and to shield it from external shocks. Exporters' exchange-rate gains, for example, were confiscated and placed in an oil fund to ease the burden on the fleet. Money was even drawn from the banking system, by fair means or foul.

Indexation of capital and exchange-rate adjustments contributed to greatly increased profits for the Central Bank (Seðlabankinn) and the commercial banks. The Central Bank's reserves were in foreign currency, and their value in Icelandic krónur rose with every devaluation. The People's Alliance members in the government placed great emphasis on this accounting profit being used for the benefit of the industries. I did not want to go as far in this matter. I did bring it about that funds from the Central Bank's reserves were allocated to assist the fishing industry, despite the protests of the Central Bank governors.

It was all to no avail. Whenever some great danger had been averted, it would as often as not turn out that the time had come to review fish prices. The same old song began again. The fishermen demanded a correction of their wages. The fleet raised a cry of woe. The processing industry pleaded poverty more pitifully than ever. And once again the dance was danced.
"I Was Tricked"

Strange as it seems at first sight, every other fishing-vessel owner in the country was striving to acquire bigger and more expensive ships in these years, despite all the moaning about difficult operations. Yet ever since the build-up and renewal of the trawler fleet reached its peak in the mid-1970s, it had been government policy to reduce fishing capacity — especially after the left-wing government came to power in 1978. As mentioned earlier, there were serious failures in applying the brakes as needed, and the fleet grew steadily.

It could prove difficult to stand against the renewal of ships when it came to the point. One of my first acts in the Ministry of Fisheries was to authorize the replacement of the Guðbjörg from Ísafjörður, the greatest fishing vessel of the fleet. Her owners needed little or no borrowing for the purchase, and it therefore seemed to me absurd to refuse them approval. This decision was harshly criticized. The substance of the matter, however, was completely overshadowed by the fact that this was a trawler in my own constituency. My predecessor in the Ministry of Fisheries, Kjartan Jóhannsson, did not hold back in this debate. He regularly marched at the head of the group of Social Democrats who gave generous space in Alþýðublaðið to attacks
on me and the fisheries policy. I received no smaller helpings of abuse in the Althingi.

In my heart I agreed with those who worried about over-investment in the fishing fleet, as I had in 1976. On the other hand, I thought it dubious to prevent all renewal. This came through in my remarks in many places. In a speech on Seamen's Day, 4 June 1982, I put the problem facing a Minister of Fisheries this way:

We must go after the fish in good, fully equipped ships, and many of the older boats have become obsolete. They must be taken out of service. On many of these boats are capable men who have made seamanship their life's work. Are those who do not wish to give up the seafaring life to be refused permission to replace their boat? Are such men to be forced either to go ashore or to keep going to sea in old, obsolete, and even unsafe boats?

I added that in this field, as in so many others, the golden mean would have to be followed. It was also my view that these two goals — a suitable fleet size and normal renewal — could both be achieved if imports and new construction went hand in hand with the retirement of older ships.

When I became Minister of Fisheries, fishing vessels were on the so-called free list. There were thus few restrictions on their importation. My first winter in the ministry had not passed before I had this changed. Thereafter, importation was subject to the approval of the Minister of Commerce upon receiving the opinion of the Ministry of Fisheries. It was not enough, however, to set sensible rules. There were instances of them being circumvented, sometimes grossly.

One of the most talked-about cases was when two young businessmen from Tálknafjörður applied for a permit to import, and take foreign loans for, a trawler that later received the name Einar Benediktsson. Their application stated that they were the owners of a boat that had been condemned for scrapping and had owned a half share in another that had been lost off Látrabjarg. I accepted the men's assertions about their ownership of the boats as valid and recommended that the matter be approved. It fell to Tómas Árnason to review the documents. He handled import matters as Minister of Commerce.

It did not come to light that fraud was involved until the trawler had arrived in the country. It turned out that the pair had owned neither boat when they applied for the import permit. The one that had sunk was owned by an unrelated man, and the other had been sold at a forced auction before it came to be scrapped. The co-owner of one of the men had bought the boat at the auction in

to protect his financial interests. In a newspaper interview the skipper of the Einar Benediktsson said that despite the forced sale it was "they, and not the man who bought the ship, who were entitled to a new vessel!" The Minister of Commerce ordered an investigation following extensive public discussion of the case, and the businessmen were convicted of deception. When I was pressed in the Althingi about what my part in this affair had been, I put it in these words: "we were tricked." Some found this an undignified way for a minister to speak, and some even spoke of my resignation over the matter.
Favors and Regional Considerations

The opposition vied to cast suspicion on my policy of contracting the fishing fleet. Those of my official acts that seemed inconsistent with it were dragged into the light. They certainly existed. Much concerning my work and policy was, however, misrepresented. I tried to respond and defend myself with arguments. A special report on these matters was compiled in the Ministry of Fisheries, which showed that the renewal of the fleet, measured in gross register tonnes, had in fact slowed somewhat in my time compared with what had gone before — and the fisheries ministry years of Kjartan Jóhannsson were not excepted there. Indeed, the purchases of all the ships added to the fleet at the beginning of my ministry had been approved in the ministry during his tenure. The report appeared in the media in January 1982.

Neither the number of ships nor gross register tonnage, however, is an especially good measure of the fleet. Catching capacity matters more. Despite the government's policy, people regularly managed to enlarge their ships or alter them so that their capacity increased. Most of the new ships outperformed the older ones by a wide margin. There were also cases of vessel owners circumventing the rules by making modifications to their ships. Old trawlers were shortened by cutting off their bows. They were subsequently registered as boats and sent to fish in areas where trawling was prohibited. I responded with an amended regulation on trawling by fishing vessels and declared these boats to be stern trawlers, short though they were.

The government certainly had the power to prohibit the importation or construction of new ships by regulation. That, however, was a last resort. In the latter half of the electoral term, when the cod fishery had failed, it nevertheless seemed to me that every argument pointed that way. At my request the Minister of Commerce imposed an outright ban on all importation of fishing vessels by regulation. The Minister of Fisheries could, however, influence the renewal of ships without resorting to regulatory power. He could bring his influence to bear with the public funds. The Fisheries

Fund (Fiskveiðasjóður) played a large part in financing all renewal of the fishing fleet, and I was in good contact with its board. I did not control lending from the Fisheries Fund, but I could have considerable influence on whether applications were approved or rejected. That is how deals were done on the waterfront.

The board of the Regional Development Agency (Framkvæmdastofnun) pressed hard on the government to provide ships to communities where the employment situation was difficult. In all, five ships were added to the fleet on these grounds: trawlers came to Djúpivogur and Þórshöfn, a trawling vessel to Akranes and Suðurnes, and a shrimp vessel to Dalvík. These measures were heavily criticized, with Kjartan Jóhannsson and Kristján Ragnarsson foremost among the critics. The government, however, stood united on regional policy, as always.

The board of the Regional Development Agency had also approved assistance for the purchase of a trawler for Raufarhöfn. It was to be imported from Norway. Hjörleifur Guttormsson proposed that the permit for importing this new ship be revoked. He emphasized that new ships should be built at home. Ingvar Gíslason nonetheless succeeded in ensuring that the Agency's commitment was honored. Ingvar was tough on behalf of his constituency. These clashes never became public, but they are mentioned here as an example of one of the main points of dispute within the government in the field of fisheries. It was united only in limiting the growth of the fishing fleet as long as that did not hurt Icelandic shipyards.

Pressure to expand the fishing fleet came not only from vessel owners. The shipyards lacked work, and Hjörleifur Guttormsson, the Minister of Industry, took their interests very much to heart. He presented to the government a plan for serial construction of trawlers in Icelandic shipyards. It provided that they would thus be guaranteed work for several years, financed with foreign loans guaranteed by the state treasury. Considerable friction arose between me and Hjörleifur over this. He forced through permission for the serial construction of six new fishing vessels, but I managed to prevent there being more. I have counted myself lucky for that.

The foreign loans resting on the ships rose rapidly while the Icelandic króna's exchange rate slid. Regional considerations also figured heavily in this matter. Communities where the employment situation was poor welcomed the plans for new construction and pushed hard to get trawlers. But they bought a pig in a poke and spent years or decades paying the price for it all. Some of the ships were never fully paid for.

More successful was the regional initiative that Ingvar Gíslason championed as Minister of Education. Despite great opposition, he succeeded in having a technical university established at Akureyri. I doubt that any other effort has proved more beneficial to the rural districts of the country. Around this school
all kinds of knowledge industry now flourish. The champions of heavy industry might ponder that.
Good vessel owners and bad politicians

The reason it proved difficult to hold back the expansion and renewal of the fishing fleet lay, in my opinion, in the fisheries management system. The "scrap-day" system (skrapdagakerfið) meant that cod fishing was conducted according to the rule "first come, first served." There was no ceiling on the catch of individual ships, only on the fleet as a whole. With larger ships and more powerful fishing gear, vessel owners and crews could hope to bring more fish ashore on the days when fishing was permitted. They thereby secured a larger share of the total catch for themselves. This was the fundamental reason for the pressure to increase the fleet's fishing capacity, even though the fishing industry as a whole suffered for it.

Other factors mattered as well, though. Kristján Ragnarsson, managing director of the National Association of Icelandic Vessel Owners (Landssamband íslenskra útvegsmanna), was once asked why vessel owners pushed so hard for permits to buy new and larger trawlers when they were being operated at a roaring loss. Kristján answered, no doubt frankly, that they did so because they did not have to risk their own money on the investments. They could borrow nearly the full purchase price from public funds, and the collateral was only in the ships themselves. Vessel owners thus had nothing to lose. This struck me as rather dubious morality, though the explanation was doubtless well founded.

It is food for thought that a few years later these same men — who, according to Kristján Ragnarsson, risked their own capital only to a small degree when buying ships — were considered the self-evident holders, if not owners, of the quota when it came into being. Then the argument was that they had, through their own hard work, capital, and sacrifice, drawn the fish from the sea and brought it ashore for decades.

When assistance on regional-policy grounds was under discussion, various spokesmen for the fishing industry wanted to draw a distinction between the good vessel owners, who had risen by their own diligence and merit, and the duds who had had everything handed to them by virtue of a political rationing system or regional policy. Individual ship purchases were even harshly criticized, with the insinuation that assistance for them was inherently different from other assistance to the industry. In truth, I believe that was not so.

As Kristján Ragnarsson himself pointed out, few vessel owners risked their own capital except to a small degree. Then there was little difference between whether the assistance came from the Fisheries Fund (Fiskveiðasjóður) in the name of profitability and development, or from

the Regional Development Agency (Framkvæmdastofnun) in the name of regional policy. Both hard workers and duds were to be found among the borrowers of both funds. Many, in fact, received assistance from both directions, and from the banks besides.

The fact is that nearly all vessel owners sought their loan financing through public channels. The renewal of the trawler fleet at the beginning of the 1970s had, to take an example, gone mostly through these funds. Ship purchases were without exception financed in large part with loans from the Fisheries Fund (Fiskveiðasjóður). Like other loans, they carried negative real interest rates until indexation came along. In addition, vessel owners turned to the Regional Development Agency or the Regional Development Fund (Byggðasjóður) to finance what was still lacking. Those loans were even more favorable. The proportion lent from public funds for the renewal of ships could reach as much as 90–95 percent. This reflected the fact that the building up of the fishing industry all around the country was supported in the name of regional policy.

One would be hard put to find men or communities that did not seek assistance of this kind. Nor can there be any doubt that vessel owners were, as a group, deep in debt in those years. As evidence of this, it made a full-spread interview in Helgarpósturinn when a vessel owner in Hafnarfjörður turned out to be debt-free and could wave a blank certificate from the mortgage registry to prove it.

This is not said here to disparage vessel owners. On the contrary, I know that many of them are fully deserving of the success they have enjoyed. None of them, however, acted alone. The common funds stood firmly behind them. Admittedly, there are examples where the failure of a hopeless operation could have been foreseen and the involvement of politicians made things no better. I am willing to acknowledge that, and my own part in those matters. Yet public support has undoubtedly produced more good than some seem willing to admit. People have a strong tendency to explain success and well-executed industrial development by the diligence and drive of the vessel owner or businessman concerned. When things go badly, however, the mistakes are without exception recorded in black ink on the account of those who provided the assistance — the politicians and the authorities.
I believe the truth lies somewhere in between.
Powerful interest groups and fisheries management

On one occasion I met with the Canadian minister of fisheries. He had a great interest in Icelandic fisheries, since Iceland had the reputation of being one of the few countries in the world where the fishing industry was not dependent on the state. Conversation turned to the operations of the Ministry of Fisheries, and I told him that

it had fourteen outstanding staff members. "Fourteen?" said this fine man, his eyes going wide. He could not understand how so few individuals could handle the tasks of such an important ministry. Probably just as many people were employed distributing the internal mail in his own ministry. When the commotion was at its height during my years as minister, the strain on these excellent colleagues of mine was heavy. Yet they never failed.

Jón Arnalds was the permanent secretary and led his team with such energy that it was incredible how much his staff got done. Naturally, there are limits to what fourteen people can do. Because of the way the work was organized and the enormous tasks each person had on his plate, it is difficult to respond to unexpected events or undertake major policy-making. In such matters one must rely on advice sought from outside the walls of the ministries. Committees are not always appointed to smother issues, as is often said, but just as much for this purpose: to bring in knowledge and experience from outside the ministry. These are ideal conditions for powerful interest groups. The ministries are no match for them at the worst of times. In this way real power and policy-making can shift from the hands of the legislative and executive branches to those with the most at stake.
Perhaps this was most evident where powerful industry associations were involved — in policy-making in agriculture and fisheries.

In the Ministry of Fisheries I came to know this foundational industry well through acquaintance with the many first-rate people who worked in it. I greatly admired Icelandic fishermen, and closer acquaintance did nothing to diminish that, though I often had sharp disputes with various of their leaders. Óskar Vigfússon, chairman of the Seamen's Federation (Sjómannasambandið), was one of those I liked best. We were far from agreeing on everything. Nor did he hold back in criticizing my work. But I found him easy to talk to and understanding.

Much the same can be said of Kristján Ragnarsson, managing director of the National Association of Icelandic Vessel Owners (Landssamband íslenskra útvegsmanna). In my opinion, however, he went far too far in his domineering over everything that touched the fishing industry. Kristján regarded the industry as if it were his own kingdom. His pronouncements were unyielding and pointed. I did not always find them suited to the matter at hand. His strong words therefore missed the mark more often than not. Still, I respected Kristján for his energy and his persistence on behalf of his constituents. But I was not willing to let him run fisheries management.

I regarded the overhaul of fisheries management as one of my principal tasks when I took the reins at the Ministry of Fisheries. It was clear to me that fishing effort could not be controlled in the long run by

allowing fishing freely on some days and banning it on others. The scrap-day system had run its course. It would not do for the fleet to be tied up at the dock half the year and for the fish then to rot unprocessed when so much came ashore that the processing plants could not keep up.

To draft proposals on fisheries management I hired Baldur Jónsson, my old acquaintance from Ísafjörður. He had broader experience of fishing and fish processing than most other Icelanders. We immediately floated radical ideas that met with a mixed reception. Our proposals were for a quota system whose objective was to limit fishing effort in a sensible way. The total annual catch was to be as close as possible to what the authorities had decided; the quality of the catch and of processing was to be improved; and at the same time the system was to promote efficiency. One of the main points in our proposals was that the fisheries management system should not lead to the disruption of rural communities. To that end we defined landing zones. The quota was to be divided among the fish processing plants, ships, and boats in each zone.
It did not matter where the fish was landed within each landing zone, and within the zone it could also be transferred between fish processors or boats.

This was in fact a community quota. The landing zones were drawn so that the catch could be moved between places within each zone without great difficulty. Reykjanes, for example, was one landing zone. Another main point in our ideas was that within each zone the local people themselves were to manage the fishing, on the authority of and under the overall supervision of the Ministry of Fisheries. In allocating the quota, account was to be taken of the ships' catch history and the processing plants' production. The same rules were to apply to the division of the total quota among landing zones everywhere in the country. It was not to be permissible to transfer quota out of a landing zone except in absolutely exceptional cases.

I traveled around the country and held meetings on this policy, as I had done before as Minister of Agriculture. Community quotas were well received all over the country. People particularly liked the idea that the fish would not disappear along with the ships even if they were sold out of the community. I was optimistic about consensus on this approach, but I stressed that I would not force my ideas through without agreement on them. For the system to survive, consensus would have to be reached about it. As our ideas became clearer, the doubts we encountered grew stronger.

One of those I spoke with was Guðmundur Guðmundsson of Hrönn in Ísafjörður. He is a Social Democrat but a good friend of mine. Guðmundur said he was very skeptical of our ideas. I emphasized the advantages of moving power back home to the districts. Then Guðmundur said:
That is exactly why I have my doubts. It is out of the question for me to tell Ásgeir on the Guðbjörg that he may not catch more. You people can say that down south in the Ministry of Fisheries.

The local people wanted to spare themselves the unpleasantness and trouble that came with holding this power. They feared the responsibility and wanted to be able to point to "the crowd down south." I had not foreseen these difficulties, and I expressed my disappointment with these attitudes, which seemed to me to show little self-confidence. This was conspicuous in the Westfjords.

I first laid my ideas before the Fisheries Congress (fiskiþing) in November 1980, but there they found little resonance. As long as fish were plentiful and the catches good, there seemed to be no political basis for changes to the fisheries management system. When the policy work began, I appointed a cross-party committee on which representatives of all parties sat. Among its members the committee counted no fewer than three former ministers of fisheries. In its report, presented in 1980, however, the committee stated that it wanted to continue building on effort management with the scrap-day system and to make only minor changes. When it became clear that my ideas did not enjoy support, I declared that I would follow a largely unchanged policy, but set rules on total quotas by species and their division among ships, as recounted earlier.
The genesis of the quota system

Support for some kind of quota system grew in these years in the ranks of those close to the fishing industry. At the quarter assemblies of the fisheries associations, which are held before each Fisheries Congress, it emerged in 1981 that all quarters of the country except the Westfjords supported a quota system in some form. I, however, sympathized with the Westfjorders' cause and said in my speech to the Fisheries Congress that I would go slowly in placing quotas on ships. I stressed that a new fisheries management system had to have three objectives: conservation of fish stocks, quality, and efficiency. At the same time I argued the merits of community quotas with home rule. The Fisheries Congress reached no consensus on any changes in 1981 and voted to support the unchanged system. The same story repeated itself a year later.

Before the cod collapse began to make itself seriously felt in 1982, I continued working in the spirit of the "fisheries ministers" committee. At the end of March 1982 I said in an interview with Tíminn that for the time being it would be most sensible to mend the scrap-day system. Those improvements rested first and foremost on my trying to determine more precisely than before how much could be caught from each stock. The legal authority in force from 1977 empowered the minister to set

a ceiling on catch entitlements — quotas — if the Marine Research Institute (Hafrannsóknastofnun) considered the stock in question to be at risk. This condition was overlooked during my time as minister, and a total allowable catch was set even though stocks were not considered at risk. There was, however, no fully valid legal provision for that practice. For that reason a committee was established to strengthen the minister's legal powers for fisheries management. It began work in May 1982 and delivered a finished bill just under a year later, shortly before the end of the 1983 parliamentary session. By then it was too late to get the bill passed in the Althing. It was never introduced.

The quota system in the fisheries has wrongly been traced to this committee's work. The most remarkable example of this is found in the explanatory notes to the bill introduced in the 1983–84 session, which laid the foundation of the present quota system. There it says that the bill is "in essentials substantively identical to the proposals of the committee" that was appointed during my time as minister. The truth is that the committee only made proposals intended to give a legal footing to unchanged fisheries management, which rested on a weak legal basis, as said before. Indeed, the committee members specifically stated in their report to me that "although the committee has given some consideration to [the arrangement of trawling entitlements], it has not reached a final conclusion [on that matter], as this is a very sensitive subject that requires closer examination and discussion."

The quota system was brought in with haste at the turn of the year 1983–84. It was set up without any substantial discussion taking place in the political arena or in the Ministry of Fisheries. When I left the ministry, I did not suspect how soon Kristján Ragnarsson would get his way. I did not consider the ideas of community quotas to be dead. In my mind the discussion was just beginning.

Jón B. Jónasson, head of the fisheries management department of the Ministry of Fisheries, has confirmed in an interview for the writing of this book that within the ministry no work had been done to prepare a quota system resembling the one that was introduced — neither during my time as minister of fisheries nor, indeed, in the autumn of 1983. Work on the design of the quota system did not begin until Halldór Ásgrímsson, my successor in the Ministry of Fisheries, had had legislation to that effect passed in the Althing on December 28, 1983. It granted the minister broad power to manage fishing and determine quotas.

One need not look far afield for the true origin of the quota system. The Fisheries Congress passed a resolution on the arrangement of fisheries management in the autumn of 1983 in which the viewpoint of the National Association of Icelandic Vessel Owners (Landssamband íslenskra útvegsmanna) prevailed. The onshore processing industry and those who wanted fishing entitlements to remain attached to the communities were defeated. In this resolution of the Fisheries Congress are found the provisions

on which the quota system is actually based. It says, among other things, that quota shall be divided among ships according to their catch history in the three preceding fishing years, and for one year at a time. In addition, it provides that the transfer of allocated catch quota between ships shall be permitted. These provisions in the Fisheries Congress resolution have all come to pass and become law, though not all of them succeeded at the first attempt in 1984.

The lead-up to the introduction of the quota system in Iceland's fisheries is a story that has not yet been written, strange as that may seem. Once the vested interests in the fishing industry had agreed among themselves on a new fisheries management system, the politicians did not dare go against that outcome. Halldór Ásgrímsson supported the policy of the vessel owners' association (LÍÚ) and accepted the vessel owners' arguments for quotas on ships. My proposals for community or landing-zone quotas were finally laid to rest.
The whaling disputes

At the beginning of 1983, whaling came before the Althing in earnest for the first time. Conservationists had gained the upper hand in the International Whaling Commission. In that body, a ban on whaling had been approved for the first time. In accordance with the Commission's rules and international law, individual member states could lodge an objection to the resolution. They would then be considered unbound by it. Various nations had taken this route, among them the Norwegians, the Japanese, and the Russians. I wanted to take that route and proposed that it be the government's policy. I had a hard time getting it approved.

Powerful parties, with the fishing industry's marketing organizations at their head, were afraid of a head-on clash with the whale conservationists. They feared it could affect our market position, especially in the United States. While I was struggling to get my policy through in the government, Eiður Guðnason, a member of parliament for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), introduced in the Althing a parliamentary resolution on the same subject. It proposed that the whaling ban be objected to. I supported the motion and welcomed the Althing taking a position on the matter. Parliament would then bear responsibility for whatever the outcome would be.

Eiður's motion, however, had the opposite effect: doubters inside and outside parliament were given the opportunity to influence the matter. In the Althing there were loud disputes, no less than outside it. The seafood marketing organizations exerted themselves greatly, and their spokesman in parliament was Guðmundur H. Garðarsson, an alternate member for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), who was also press officer of the Icelandic Freezing Plants Corporation (Sölumiðstöð hraðfrystihúsanna). Many Icelandic nature conservation organizations supported not objecting to the ban.

The pressure from the United States was no less. From there came, among other things, a letter from the United States Secretary of State which many regarded as a letter of threats. I would not have put it quite so strongly. The Secretary mentioned fishing in American jurisdiction in exchange for the whaling ban not being objected to. There was no shortage of threats, however. The American authorities intimated that nations which did not comply with the resolutions of the whaling commission could expect trade sanctions. Organizations, senators and individuals in the United States said they would utterly destroy Icelandic companies in that country. Such threats were not to my liking, and I wanted members of parliament to disregard them.

I recalled that during my time as Minister of Justice I had had a Greenpeace ship brought to shore when it tried to disrupt whaling in Icelandic waters, without any repercussions resulting from that action.

The Foreign Affairs Committee of the Althingi split in its position on the whaling issue, and the ranks of both government supporters and the opposition were thrown into disarray. Halldór Ásgrímsson became the spokesman for the majority opinion of the Foreign Affairs Committee, which recommended against lodging an objection, thus going against my policy in the matter. This was not the last time we were on opposite sides in whaling matters. I had my doubts when Halldór pushed for Iceland's withdrawal from the International Whaling Commission (Alþjóðahvalveiðiráðið) some years later.

At a cabinet meeting on 1 February 1983 I finally got my proposal approved, that an objection should be lodged. The government's minute was published, among other places, in Morgunblaðið. When Eiður's motion came up for a vote in parliament the following evening, only a few hours remained before our deadline to object would expire. The vote was taken by roll call. The public galleries were packed and there was great tension in the air. The outcome was that the motion failed by a single vote. This was a disappointment to me. Halldór Ásgrímsson, Guðmundur Bjarnason and Páll Pétursson voted against the motion, alone among the Progressives. I was not particularly grateful to them for that. In fact all the parliamentary groups split except the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið).

All of its members voted against the motion even though the party's ministers had lent their support to a minute of the same kind the day before. That disappointed me most of all. There was, however, nothing I could do once the will of parliament was clear, and the objection was never sent.
Foreign Relations

In my ministries there were more quiet moments between battles than the account in this book suggests. There was nonetheless a fair amount of foreign contact, though it did not come close to the busy schedule of foreign travel that ministers have in

recent years. Many of the trips I took were instructive. I had barely settled into the chair of Minister of Fisheries when I was invited on an official visit to the Soviet Union. One of our main markets for marine products was there. That trip was not made, however, until June 1982. As has been mentioned, this was not the first time I visited the Soviet Union, and in fact not the last. Edda, my wife, came along, together with the permanent secretary of the ministry, Jón Arnalds, and Sigríður Eyþórsdóttir, his wife, as well as Haraldur Kröyer, ambassador in Moscow.

After good discussions in Moscow we flew to Astrakhan, at the mouth of the Volga. There we were shown sturgeon fishing and roe harvesting. The harbormaster of Astrakhan received us, Karakulsev by name. He was exceptionally cheerful and relaxed in all his manner. This was a change from Moscow, where gloom hung over everyone. In Astrakhan the whole atmosphere was freer, and it even happened that we saw people in love holding hands and kissing.

The breakfasts were lavish, as always in Russia. Sturgeon roe was on every table, and beer and vodka were pressed insistently on the guests. We declined the alcohol so early in the morning. At some point in the hotel elevator, Edda remarked to Sigríður that it would be preferable if we got champagne with breakfast instead of vodka. Lo and behold: an exquisite bottle of champagne stood on our table the next day. We suspected our escort of having arranged this. His name was Vladimir; he had been in Iceland for a time and spoke excellent Icelandic. Vladimir, however, was not in the elevator and thus was not a witness to our conversation — at least not as far as we knew.

We were invited on a trip aboard a fast river boat. At a dinner party on board, caviar and vodka were served no less generously. Our host Karakulsev pushed hard for toasts, preferably after every single mouthful. He maintained that the sturgeon roe so counteracted the effects of the alcohol that there was no need to worry about feeling poorly the next morning. The next morning we set out on another tour, and once again the same game began with caviar and vodka. When drinking was to begin anew, some in the group began to have second thoughts. I noticed that our hosts were being poured from a different bottle than the one offered to us. I commented on this and said I wanted to be served from the same bottle. The fellow was thus found out, and much fun was made of it. He had intended to drink water while serving us vodka.

In the autumn of 1980 I was invited on an official visit to Greenland. This attracted considerable attention, not least from the Danish ambassador to Iceland. The rules had been broken, according to which such invitations were to come through the Danish foreign service. Perhaps this was part of the Greenlanders' efforts toward independence. Jónatan Motzfeldt, chairman of the Greenland home-rule government and my host, and I were

in fact already good acquaintances. He had visited me informally when I was Minister of Agriculture, together with Lars Emil Johansen, who became Jónatan's successor at the head of the home-rule government. On that trip, Jónatan and Lars Emil spent a fine evening at Edda's and my home in Mávanes. They arrived dressed in white anorak jackets and were most ceremonious. The formality soon wore off, however, and the evening became very enjoyable. They were much preoccupied with questions about their country's independence, and in their speech they were very reminiscent of various Icelandic independence heroes.

I also held a banquet for the Greenlanders at the Ministerial Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn). As the evening wore on, their spirits rose considerably, and Jónatan had become slightly tipsy and was in high spirits. Icelandic lamb chops were served. Before long he tossed aside his fork and knife, seized the meat with his hands and began gnawing it off the bones. I decided to follow the example of the guest of honor and said that the priests were doubtless right that God's forks were far better than the factory-made ones. After the meal Jónatan sat down at the piano. The party did not end until around one o'clock after midnight.

My visit to Greenland in the autumn of 1980 was also extremely memorable. I attended the opening of the Greenland parliament and had good talks with Jónatan. Among other things, he invited me reindeer hunting at the innermost end of Góðravonarfjörður. We walked for ten hours through magnificent scenery but caught nothing. At a banquet held the following evening I remarked that I had walked across half of Greenland without seeing a reindeer. That remark was often quoted.

With us on the trip was one of Greenland's most skilled reindeer hunters. He seemed to have slept outdoors under the open sky for most of his life. His skin was hard as shagreen, and he was bony and light on his feet. After we had been walking for a while, the hunter asked, with the help of an interpreter, how old I was. Fifty-two, I said. He could hardly believe it; he himself was forty although he had the appearance of a man of seventy. I, on the other hand, was amazed at how much he smoked. Every half hour he paused the walk so that a cigarette could be lit. I found this rather tiresome and often walked on ahead.

My visit to Greenland was instructive, and I was deeply impressed to discover what children of nature the Greenlanders are. From my conversations with their leaders I also became convinced that the Danes had made a great mistake when they moved them, almost by forced relocation, out of scattered settlements and gathered the people together in population centers such as Nuuk. There, long and ugly apartment blocks were built to house the people. This did not suit their nature. The result was that dissipation and various socialproblems
are rarely as common as in Greenland. To tell the truth, I felt sorry for the Greenlanders and would have liked us Icelanders to lend them a helping hand.

I took an instructive trip to the Faroe Islands in 1981. The Faroese are a cheerful people and good hosts. Cooperation between the two nations in fisheries matters was the main topic of discussion, and those were excellent meetings. I found it instructive to get to know the Faroes and their economy. I admired much of what they had accomplished, but it nonetheless seemed clear to me that the islanders would find it difficult to stand on their own feet. The Danes paid a large share of the islands' public expenditures.

In 1982 I went on an official visit to Britain. With us on the trip was Már Elísson, Director of Fisheries. The fisheries minister in that country at the time was a certain Walker. Our talks have not stayed in my memory as well as the tours I took of Britain's main fishing regions. In Grimsby the harbor was like a ghost town. The only life to be found there was young people slouching against dilapidated walls who had evidently spent their unemployment benefits on cigarettes. From the fishing villages of Scotland, the story was in some ways the same, though conditions were not as striking. I was pleased to find that British fishermen bore no grudge against Icelanders on account of the cod wars and the extension of the fisheries limits. On the other hand, they criticized their own government very harshly, believing it had shown negligence and spinelessness in fisheries-limits matters.
The fishermen greatly feared that they would lose their own fishing limits to the control of the European Economic Community (Efnahagsbandalag Evrópu).
The Ministry of Transport

In the Ministry of Transport (samgönguráðuneytið) I felt right at home. The ministry itself had even fewer staff than the Ministry of Fisheries. Just as there, every post was filled by an able man. The permanent secretary, Brynjólfur Ingólfsson, bore clear witness to that. I had come to know him in my younger years in connection with track and field. He had been the fastest Icelander in the 400-meter run. Brynjólfur in fact retired during my time as minister. Ólafur Steinar Valdimarsson took over his position.

The workload was considerably lighter in the Ministry of Transport than in the Ministry of Fisheries. This was chiefly because its operations were largely in the hands of strong institutions, such as the Post and Telephone Service (Póstur og sími), the Road Administration (Vegagerðin), the Lighthouse and Harbor Authority (Vita- og hafnamálastofnun) and the Civil Aviation Administration (Flugmálastjórn). Each of these institutions had a good staff who knew the ins and outs of their field.

I met the heads of the institutions regularly. At these meetings we went over matters and decided what should be done. All plans held, and the work was carried out as requested. I was very pleased with this cooperation. Nor were the results long in coming. I got the opportunity to put into practice my old policy goals of automatic telephone service and television for every farm in the country. I had introduced bills on both in parliament. I considered such things just as fundamental in a modern society as electricity and water.

Jón Skúlason was Director of Posts and Telecommunications. He is a scrupulous man who was good to work with. Jón introduced me to innovations in the field of telecommunications, where technology was developing rapidly in those years. Among the innovations was the digital telephone, for whose rollout we undertook to make plans several years into the future. Many felt this was a big step, since we had scarcely finished connecting the entire population to automatic telephone service. It turned out that we were among the first nations to establish a digital telephone system. This bore clear witness to Jón's foresight.

In road construction I had a long-term plan drawn up. I had long found it strange that such projects were in fact decided from one year to the next, for one or two years at a time. The Road Administration (Vegagerðin) agreed with me wholeheartedly, and there Snæbjörn Jónasson, Director of Roads, was at the head of the column. He was as engineers ought to be, thoughtful and full of ideas but with both feet on the ground. After good work and a great deal of planning, I presented to the Althingi a twelve-year plan for road affairs.

It was clear to everyone that a long-term plan was a great improvement. The members of parliament acknowledged this too, one after another. When it came to a vote, however, parochial mouse-hole perspectives overpowered good sense. The people of the East Fjords felt some stretch of road came too late in the plan, and the people of the South wanted improvements somewhere else. Thus began a tug-of-war that could not be settled. I introduced the plan again at the next session of parliament. It went the same way.

The plan nevertheless had its effect, though it was never formally approved. By the time I had become Prime Minister, Matthías Bjarnason had taken over transport affairs. At some point when it was difficult to make ends meet in drafting the budget, there were proposals to cut funding for road construction. Matthías pounded the table. He said it was out of the question that he would take part in cutting back a plan that Steingrímur Hermannsson had put forward. Matthías did not intend to be a wrecker where I had meant to move mountains. I supported him in that, and so it stood.
The Flugleiðir Affair

The affairs of Flugleiðir (Icelandair) were very much on the government's agenda in its first year in office and, as time went on, became one of the bigger issues in politics. Sigurður Helgason, chief executive of Flugleiðir, came to see me shortly after I took over the Ministry of Transport and informed me that the company was struggling with difficulties in its North Atlantic operations. Flugleiðir had recently begun direct flights between the United States and Luxembourg in addition to the traditional service with a stopover in Keflavík. However, the fierce price competition of the preceding seasons, in which the airline Laker was in the forefront, was probably the main cause of the difficulties. The transatlantic operation had been run at a loss for two years.

At a meeting that I and the Prime Minister had with the leadership of Flugleiðir in the spring of 1980, it nevertheless emerged that the situation was not so bad that the company could not weather the difficulties if it received a small amount of assistance.

Flugleiðir had sent the government a request for the waiver of landing fees at Keflavík Airport in May of the previous year. It was raised by Benedikt Gröndal, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, outside a formal meeting but was never taken up for formal decision. His planned meeting with the authorities in Luxembourg also never took place. Around this time the Flugleiðir people had been in talks with the Luxembourgers about the future of their operations in that country. In January 1980 Luxembourg's transport minister had come to Iceland for discussions on aviation matters. These centered mainly on general issues and possible cooperation in passenger service between Luxembourg's national airline, Luxair, and Cargolux, which was largely owned by Flugleiðir. Those talks had been going on for some time but had not gotten far.

The first formal petition from Flugleiðir to come before the cabinet was taken up on 10 March 1980. It was a request for a state guarantee of a five-million-dollar loan. The Prime Minister raised the matter, and I was assigned to prepare its handling. The request received a great deal of discussion.

When these matters arose, I called on Agnar Kofoed-Hansen to advise me. He was Director of Civil Aviation, and we were good acquaintances. I had first come to know Agnar in my father's house. He often came there to see my father. My father appointed Agnar chief of police in Iceland in the 1930s, when he was very young. They had first met when Agnar was at officers' school in Copenhagen. My father was greatly taken with this young man. He considered it desirable that the chief of police have officer training, since war was looming in Europe. Ever since Agnar was appointed chief of police, it was said that he was my father's illegitimate son. That was pure nonsense. That much I know.

Agnar became head of civil aviation in Iceland in 1947 and was acquainted with the top aviation officials all over the world. He was my chief adviser in the field of aviation. When I put the Flugleiðir matter to Agnar, he did not think long before saying that we would have to get the aviation authorities in Luxembourg to assist us. Otherwise it would be difficult to find a lasting solution. I agreed with this and proposed to the chief executive of Flugleiðir that talks with the authorities in Luxembourg be resumed.

Agnar and I went for talks with the Luxembourgers on 24 and 25 March 1980. Representatives of Flugleiðir and a representative of the Ministry of Transport had previously held preparatory talks there. On this trip we spoke, among others, with Luxembourg's transport minister, Josy Barthel, and the heads of civil aviation in that country. Those talks moved us somewhat forward. Josy Barthel made a lasting impression on me. He was a former Olympic champion in the 1500-meter run and held in high esteem in his home country. It emerged clearly from what he said that keeping the America service going was no less a matter of interest to the Luxembourgers than to us. About 40 percent of the travelers passing through the airport were Flugleiðir passengers.
