It was agreed that we would propose to the governments of the two countries that Flugleiðir be given assistance to continue the North America service while a new basis for it was being explored.

While these talks were taking place, Flugleiðir's request for a state guarantee was under detailed examination in Iceland. A committee of members of parliament from all parties had been set up to study the matter, together with a three-man ministerial committee. On it sat Ragnar Arnalds and Friðjón Þórðarson, along with me. In the course of handling the matter, detailed discussions were also held with officials and the leadership of Flugleiðir. After my meetings in Luxembourg, I proposed in the cabinet that in addition to the state guarantee, landing fees on Flugleiðir's America flights at Keflavík Airport be waived while the basis for the service was being examined. The results of that examination were to be available no later than 1 September 1980. These ideas were based not least on the wishes of Flugleiðir.

The state guarantee was approved at a cabinet meeting on 28 April 1980, the same day as Flugleiðir's annual general meeting was held. It was subject to the conditions that increased maintenance work be carried out in Iceland and that Icelandic pilots have priority for the assignments of Flugleiðir and the company's subsidiaries.

In the wake of our talks with the Luxembourgers, exploratory discussions began on the establishment of a separate company for the transatlantic service. I had no direct involvement in these discussions but followed them from a distance. The main participants were the airlines Luxair and Flugleiðir. In the memoirs of Sigurður Helgason it is said that Cargolux and Luxavia also played a part. It was not
going to dispute that. Sigurður says, however, that these talks foundered because the authorities in Luxembourg had little interest in participating in airline operations. That is not correct.

The government of Luxembourg received the ideas about establishing a new airline very favorably and issued a special declaration to that effect. Flugleiðir's plans for the operation, however, were considered unrealistic. After they had been revised, the government promised extensive assistance with the establishment of the new company. It declared itself prepared to cover the projected loss on the route between Luxembourg and North America and also to provide investment assistance amounting to 3 billion Icelandic krónur at the value of the time. The Luxembourgers' conditions for this support, however, were that the company be registered in that country and that Luxair be a participant in the new company. There was a long wait for an answer from the management of Luxair, and their refusal caused the plans to collapse of their own accord.

The government of Iceland did not want to stand in the way of these plans, though I was not enthusiastic about a large part of Flugleiðir's operations moving out of the country. The same was surely true of others.
From Bad to Worse

I reported the "negative conclusions" of these talks at a cabinet meeting on 19 August 1980, after having had a meeting with Sigurður, the chief executive of Flugleiðir. Sigurður said he could see no alternative but for the company to discontinue the America service. This was unexpected news to me, and bad. I could not bear the thought of our air links with the United States being cut off. I was also surprised, because I had believed the company to be in much better shape after the state guarantee was granted in the spring. It was not long before further bad news arrived. Three days after my meeting with Sigurður, the board of Flugleiðir decided to lay off a large number of employees in light of the company's poor financial position. Following that came the company's request for assistance from the state.

To me this was an extremely serious matter that threw the future of Flugleiðir and Iceland's communications with the outside world into complete uncertainty. I began to explore what measures might be taken in this difficult situation.

It should have been clear to the management of Flugleiðir that there was political will to assist the company. Nevertheless, they announced that the transatlantic service would be discontinued as of 1 November. All the aircraft crews were also dismissed. The company's board had evidently lost its nerve. The company's entire marketing network came close to collapsing within a week, because the news spread quickly around the wide world. Complete helplessness seemed to reign in the management of the company, which was now at war with its own employees on top of its other difficulties. In

in the wake of the layoffs, unrest arose within the company, which among other things led the Ministry of Social Affairs to mediate the rehiring of staff, since the company's leadership did not feel able to handle the matter alone. At the same time, the government worked on resolving the issue. Ólafur Jóhannesson, among other things, explored the possibility of projects for the defense force, and a formal request was sent for new negotiations with the government of Luxembourg.

I presented proposals for assistance to Flugleiðir (Icelandair) on account of the transatlantic flights at a cabinet meeting on September 9, 1980. They provided for continuing the flights on a trial basis for three years. The state treasury was to provide a backup guarantee of up to three million dollars per year against projected losses. The amount corresponded to landing fees and rental charges at Keflavík Airport, revenue from the duty-free store, and other public charges connected with the flights. At settlement, the landing fees were to be deducted. A comparable waiver of landing fees in Luxembourg was anticipated. Finally, I proposed that the Icelandic state refinance the company's operations through share purchases corresponding to one-fifth of the share capital. The proposals were drafted with the knowledge and consent of Flugleiðir's top management.

In all, they were discussed at four cabinet meetings, and the ministerial committee also met outside of meetings to work them out further. The government's formal approval was obtained on September 16, 1980. These resolutions later became the foundation of a bill on the affairs of Flugleiðir which I laid before the Althing at the beginning of the parliamentary session.

Having obtained the government's approval, I traveled immediately to meet with the authorities in Luxembourg and held meetings there on September 17 and 18. On this trip I met Pierre Werner, prime minister of the grand duchy, as well as the transport minister Josy Barthel, who conducted the negotiations on behalf of the Luxembourgers as before. I particularly remember that the authorities there expressed their astonishment at how late I and the government had been informed of Flugleiðir's serious situation. Indeed, the ministers also expressed surprise that the company had managed to lose such large sums in as short a time as its accounts showed.

The authorities in Luxembourg nevertheless agreed to provide corresponding support, apart from the share purchases. This was assistance comparable to what had been offered during the summer. This time, however, it was not tied to the condition that a new company be established with its headquarters in Luxembourg. The government thereby made history in Luxembourg. There was no precedent for the authorities there providing such extensive assistance to a foreign company.
The Luxembourgers, however, wanted the trial period to be one year instead of three, as my proposals had envisioned. This stemmed among

other things from the fact that the authorities in that country found it incredible how late the leaders of Flugleiðir (Icelandair) seemed to have become aware of the company's difficulties. After talk arose of compensating the company for the losses on the America route with direct subsidies, Flugleiðir's forecasts for the operation of that route changed dramatically. It was as if the company intended to make a business out of the subsidies. This diminished the Luxembourgers' trust. I actually agreed with them that there was a slipshod quality to Flugleiðir's way of working. The company's projections held up poorly.

The fact is that the leaders of Flugleiðir did not seem to know what the company's real position was at any given time. After my meetings with the managing director, Sigurður Helgason, I often found it hard to resist the thought that the forecasts for the future were mixed with a good dose of wishful thinking. At the same time, I got the feeling that he was concealing important information from me and the government and did not show me full trust. At times it came close to wrecking everything.

One of the most serious examples of this kind arose the day before the government approved my aforementioned proposals for assistance to Flugleiðir. Two days before my trip to the negotiations in Luxembourg, more bad news arrived from the Flugleiðir people. They had previously spoken as if the North Atlantic route were the beginning and end of the company's difficulties. It turned out, however, that its entire operation hung by a thread. When the proposals concerning the America route were approved in the cabinet, it was in fact already clear that even if that part of the operation were given a helping hand, the company's operations as a whole would nevertheless remain in turmoil. In a letter from the managing director, a state guarantee of 12 million dollars was requested for the company, in addition to other support.

I was greatly shaken by this news, not least because I had been in constant contact with the company's managers for nearly a month without being told of this. My patience with the management of Flugleiðir diminished accordingly. This came out, among other things, when I gave an account of the matter in the Althing in October 1980. There I said that "the picture [was] ugly, very ugly, and even uglier than [had] emerged." In my speech I also said:

In actual fact, the difficulties of the North Atlantic route are mere trifles compared with the difficulties of the company as a whole, and those difficulties remain unchanged even if the North Atlantic route is discontinued.
Suspicion on Both Sides

The state's support for Flugleiðir (Icelandair) required substantial funds. Approval therefore had to be sought from the Althing through a special bill. The debate became highly political and had in fact been so for some time. Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, chairman of the parliamentary group of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), led a contingent of People's Alliance members who wanted to subject Flugleiðir to critical scrutiny. It was not the first time. He had put forward a proposal to establish a parliamentary committee of inquiry for this purpose in 1978. There he had, among other things, raised questions about Flugleiðir's investment policy and monopolistic tendencies. The proposal also stipulated that a comparable inquiry be conducted into the operations of Eimskip.

When Ólafur Ragnar spoke for his proposal in 1978, he predicted that a price war on the America route would, in due course, put severe strain on Flugleiðir's operations. For that argument he received little thanks from the company's leaders. It was perhaps to these clashes that their reluctance to provide the government and the Althing with information could be traced.

The opponents of the People's Alliance saw nationalization schemes in every corner and constantly accused Ólafur Ragnar of having a state takeover of Flugleiðir as his goal. Ólafur answered in kind and said that no one had contributed more to nationalization than the company's managers. Their mistakes in operations and management had forced the company to throw itself on the mercy of the state treasury. Within the government, a state takeover of the operation was never discussed, and I believe it was clearly understood that the state's increased share capital in the company was contributed only to strengthen it temporarily; indeed, the shares were sold as soon as the operation recovered.

I had in fact long considered it natural that the state should gain increased influence and the means to supervise Flugleiðir if it came to the company's aid in its operations. I had expressed that view, among other occasions, in 1975 when Flugleiðir received a state guarantee by act of the Althing during the coalition government of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Most of the conditions for state support that the Independence Party members criticized most harshly in 1980 in fact had direct precedents in their own handling of the matter in 1975.

Ólafur Ragnar certainly harbored no affection for Flugleiðir. He was vehement in his argumentation, as was his manner in political battle, and stumbled from time to time. Much of what he asserted about the operations and position of Flugleiðir, however, proved closer to the truth than the information served up by the company's spokesmen and the Independence Party members in parliament. That caused, for instance, great difficulties in the handling of the matter in the autumn of

1980 that the leaders of Flugleiðir (Icelandair) conducted their arguments as if they were at war with the company's sworn enemies, where the end justified the means. They repeatedly made false statements, published misleading figures about the company's position, and resisted providing information about collateral and assets that was necessary for the state to be able to undertake guarantees. They were also at the forefront of those who tried to cast suspicion on the government's case, and even went so far as to imply that the government was forcing assistance upon the company. Morgunblaðið danced along.

This extraordinary behavior stemmed from the deep-seated distrust of Sigurður Helgason, managing director of Flugleiðir, toward the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and thereby the government. I never knew where I stood with him. Because of what had gone before, Sigurður also had the greatest difficulty acknowledging the company's position. In personal conversations he seemed to me ever more embarrassed as the company's difficulties proved greater.

It may perhaps be considered strange that there was never any serious discussion of the state holding a larger share in the operation of Flugleiðir. Ever since the merger of Flugfélag Íslands and Loftleiðir in 1973, it may be said that Flugleiðir enjoyed the same status and facilitation as state airlines across Europe in those years. This applied both to the company's exclusive right to scheduled flights domestically and between countries, and to its ability to call for state assistance when its operations faced difficulties. The company's managers regularly turned to the public authorities for help during the 1970s, though the requests were never as extensive as in 1980 and 1981.

The biggest difference between Flugleiðir and the state airlines of Europe was that the representatives of the state always had difficulty obtaining information about the company's operations, guarding against its monopolistic tendencies, and protecting the taxpayers' other interests with respect to it.
Between a Rock and a Hard Place

The assistance granted to Flugleiðir by the resolutions of the government and the Althing in 1980 is without doubt one of the most extensive packages of support ever given to a private company in the country's history. The bill laid before the Althing provided for a large part of this support. As it turned out, the greater part of it was on account of operating difficulties other than those traceable to the America route. The government was authorized to grant Flugleiðir an absolute guarantee on a loan of up to 12 million US dollars for general operations. Flugleiðir was additionally granted an interest-free loan of up to 3 million US dollars on account of the America route. It would be paid out during the winter months. The repayments were to be based on the operating results of the company

and the public charges from the America route, which were to be counted as deductions from the repayment. At the same time, the company's unpaid landing fees for the years 1979 and 1980 were waived, and various other public charges were either waived or their payment deferred.

I discussed the affairs of Flugleiðir (Icelandair) not least with Ragnar Arnalds, the finance minister. I found it good to reach conclusions with him in these matters as in others. He was, however, a frugal finance minister and was therefore not particularly taken with waiving landing fees or with excessive burdens being placed on taxpayers. He saw particular objections to refunding Flugleiðir the landing fees for 1979, since those had already been paid into the state treasury. He agreed to it in the end, however. Ragnar was, on the other hand, adamant that it was necessary for the authorities in Luxembourg to grant Flugleiðir corresponding facilitation.

No sooner had the bill been introduced in parliament than the Flugleiðir people brought forward yet more new requests for assistance. They pressed hard for the 12-million state guarantee to be processed without delay, and preferably in the form of direct payments. No securities or collateral were in place, however, and this request was therefore refused until that was remedied. The Flugleiðir people would not take no for an answer and requested the disbursement of at least half the amount. Ragnar had had enough, no less than I. He made the "shifting attitude" of the company's spokesmen a topic in a parliamentary speech and traced how their requests had first been for backup guarantees, then a state guarantee, and finally direct payments.

Ragnar spoke in support of the government bill on assistance to Flugleiðir. In his remarks it emerged, among other things, that the requested state guarantee was equivalent to the entire net-wealth tax of Icelandic taxpayers. He did not consider it feasible to go further in assisting Flugleiðir. There were limits to how far companies in operating difficulties could go in sending taxpayers the bill. The moment was bound to come when the government would say: This far and no further. The government did not comply with further requests from Flugleiðir for assistance beyond what the bill provided for. At its urging, however, the National Bank (Landsbankinn) granted the company facilities to meet its short-term obligations, on the reasoning that the support of the state treasury would soon be forthcoming.

Various spokesmen of the opposition, with Morgunblaðið at the forefront, wanted to cast suspicion on the words and deeds of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) members in the Flugleiðir affair. In many respects this criticism was unfair. The ministers of the People's Alliance dealt with the affairs of Flugleiðir responsibly. Admittedly, they repaid the distrust and insinuations of the company's spokesmen in kind, and that sometimes made things difficult for me. The People's Alliance members did not, however, waver in their support
for the bill. The act on the affairs of Flugleiðir (Icelandair) was passed by the Althing with an overwhelming majority of votes.

Sigurður Helgason, managing director of Flugleiðir, gives me the assessment in his memoirs that I "trimmed my sails to the wind" in handling the Flugleiðir affair. Perhaps there is something to that. Because of the friction between the company and the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) members, I had to steer between a rock and a hard place. I spent considerable time convincing my fellow ministers in the government that the support for Flugleiðir must not be pared so close to the bone that it would fail to be of full use. I likewise held many meetings with the leaders of Flugleiðir where I made clear to them that the company would have to do its part for the matter to reach a successful resolution. I found them particularly reluctant to provide the requested information. That was nothing new either.
In 1975 this reluctance had been so pronounced that I put it into words, as was often quoted later, that the Althing was in effect granting a state guarantee to the company blindfolded.

In the Althing, various members went as far as the People's Alliance MPs in criticizing the management of Flugleiðir, and some went further. Eiður Guðnason, one of the opposition's spokesmen, said among other things in the debates:

To tell the truth, I think that to most outsiders looking at this, it must be incomprehensible why the current board and managing director of the company remain in place after all the sorry mess into which those parties have steered the company. It is at least incomprehensible to me.

At a meeting of the board of Flugleiðir in November 1980, a motion of no confidence in the company's managing director, Sigurður Helgason, was put forward. Behind it was the firebrand and my neighbor Alfreð Elíasson, who had been managing director of Loftleiðir. Sigurður rather belittles Alfreð's role in his memoirs. I consider that undeserved. Alfreð was one of the most remarkable pioneers in Icelandic aviation.

A shareholders' meeting of Flugleiðir agreed to accept the government's terms by an overwhelming majority, and the Althing approved the support. The America route was not discontinued. After these rescue measures, things began to brighten in Flugleiðir's operations. The state treasury got two men on the board in accordance with its shareholding. I appointed one of them, Kári Einarsson, an engineer and former cooperative-society manager at Bíldudalur, mentioned earlier. Ragnar Arnalds appointed Rúnar B. Jóhannsson, an accountant. From Kári I received news of how matters were progressing and thus kept track of the company's operations. I was in contact and communication with the leaders of Flugleiðir whenever the "trial agreement"

with Luxembourg had to be renewed a year later. In the following months, little was heard from the leaders of Flugleiðir (Icelandair) except when they needed further facilitation. Otherwise I had little to do with them.

Many years later I was passing through the airport in Luxembourg. There an employee of Flugleiðir came up to me whom I did not know, nor did I recall having met him before. He said he had long wanted to greet me and thank me for having saved Flugleiðir in the autumn of 1980. He said he suspected that little had been done to thank me for my large part in those rescue measures. Everyone in the know in Luxembourg, however, had known full well that those actions had been decisive in the company's survival.

I thanked this man for his warm words and, truth be told, they meant a great deal to me. He was at least right in the respect that thanks were scarce. It does not occur to me to complain about that, though. A warm handshake from an unknown man often matters more than empty speeches of praise delivered half-heartedly for courtesy's sake.
Monopoly, Arnarflug, and Íscargo

One of the conditions for the assistance to Flugleiðir was that the company meet its operating difficulties in part through the sale of assets. To me this seemed as natural as a family in payment difficulties drawing on its reserves before others came to its rescue. The leaders of Flugleiðir declared themselves of the same opinion and tried to turn various assets of the company into cash, though some of it was done grudgingly. The managing director of Flugleiðir sent me, among other things, a list in nine numbered items of assets that might conceivably be sold. When it came to it, however, the company's board considered it impossible to sell anything other than a portion of its shares in Arnarflug.

Representatives of the Arnarflug employees' association came to see me and expressed their interest in purchasing these shares. I considered that no sensible arguments stood against it. This was nevertheless one of the points that the government's opponents, Morgunblaðið and the Geir wing of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), tried to cast suspicion on, and indeed Sigurður Helgason follows faithfully in their footsteps in his memoirs. There he calls the sale of the shares in Arnarflug "coercive measures". After the sale, Flugleiðir nevertheless owned 40 percent of Arnarflug.

Flugleiðir's sale of the shares in Arnarflug had the political aim of increasing competition in aviation and was in line with the policy I wanted to adopt in the autumn of 1980 when I began to review the country's aviation policy. Flugleiðir's monopolistic tendencies were the occasion for this review, the company'

s underbidding on some routes and high prices on others. As it turned out, this policymaking unfortunately fell into the shadow of disputes over individual decisions on the granting of flight licenses. Every time a step was taken in the direction of breaking the company's monopoly on passenger flights to and from the country, there was an uproar, though none of those steps was large. All of them, however small, were harshly criticized by the company's leadership and the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) opposition.

The root of the problem lay in the merger of Flugfélag Íslands and Loftleiðir in 1973. I had had deep-seated doubts about the matter when it was under consideration in the Althing. In my heart I believed that two airlines in reasonable competition with each other would be the better option. The companies' operating figures, however, indicated that a merger was necessary. Flugleiðir (Icelandair) received a monopoly position as a christening gift: exclusive rights to scheduled flights on all domestic routes and in international flights. At the beginning of the 1980s, such licenses were in retreat in many places, though they were still customary in Europe. Aviation had, for example, been deregulated in the United States during President Carter's term.

In the autumn of 1980, Kristinn Finnbogason and Árni Guðjónsson, chairman of the board of the cargo airline Íscargo, came to see me and requested a license to fly passengers to Amsterdam. I told them that I considered it in various respects inadvisable. I promised, however, not to stand in the way of the matter being processed if, against the odds, the Aviation Council (flugráð) supported their application. Flugleiðir had not exercised its right to fly to Amsterdam for many years, and on those grounds Íscargo's request was approved in the Aviation Council by four votes out of five. Only Flugleiðir's operations manager abstained. I saw nothing standing in the way of granting the license other than my own political interests.

The granting of the license became entangled in the debates when the affairs of Flugleiðir were under consideration in the Althing, and it was clear to me that the matter would be interpreted in the worst possible light because of the party ties between me and Kristinn Finnbogason. Various opposition MPs indeed expressed doubts about this measure and wanted to attribute it to the company's owners being close to me.

Þorvaldur Garðar Kristjánsson, MP for the Independence Party, was the first to raise the matter in parliament after the board of Flugleiðir had distributed its protests against my decision to all members of parliament. The board of Flugleiðir considered it risky to set out on the path of competition in the field of scheduled flights between Iceland and other countries, and pointed to numerous examples of exclusive licenses in force across Europe. This was not Flugleiðir's only response, however. The competition was already having its effect. Around the time Íscargo's license was issued, Flugleiðir announced the novelty in its summer schedule of flying once a week to Amsterdam.

I thought it absurd that all international flights should be in one company's hands, although I declared myself in favor of that applying to the most common scheduled routes. In support of my case I cited examples showing that state airlines all over Europe held such rights without that preventing extensive charter flights on numerous routes. Charter flying was in fact growing in Iceland. On these grounds I granted, among other things, the Danish airline Sterling a license to fly charters for Samvinnuferðir-Landsýn. Arnarflug had in fact conducted such operations and flown between Iceland and Europe with good results during those difficult years for Flugleiðir (Icelandair). No real competition existed between them, however, as long as Flugleiðir held a majority on Arnarflug's board. That changed, though, following Flugleiðir's sale of a large portion of its shares in Arnarflug.

The new majority owners of Arnarflug soon expressed the view that the company needed to be allocated some scheduled routes to Europe in order to secure the foundation of its operations. Such a request did not seem unreasonable to me. I considered it right that Flugleiðir and Arnarflug should agree between themselves on a sensible division of these routes. I pushed for talks between the companies through the mediation of Agnar Kofoed-Hansen. An agreement on the division of scheduled routes could, I believed, prevent "unrestrained competition," as I often put it, even though I was of the opinion that increased competition was a good thing.

By 1982 it had become clear that no conclusion would be reached in the airlines' talks. I therefore considered it right to grant Arnarflug licenses on three routes. What complicated the matter, however, was that Arnarflug was in negotiations to purchase Íscargo, which was teetering on the brink of bankruptcy. The talks between the two companies had come about through the mediation of Kári Einarsson, my representative on the board of Flugleiðir. The idea had arisen in conversations between him and Magnús Gunnarsson, managing director of Arnarflug. After Kári had received a positive response from Kristinn Finnbogason on behalf of Íscargo, he informed me of these plans. He also asked me whether I had any objection to his becoming involved in these matters. I saw nothing standing in the way.

The outcome was that Arnarflug bought Íscargo's assets but neither its shares nor its name. Shortly thereafter I granted Arnarflug a license for scheduled flights to Amsterdam, Düsseldorf, and Zürich. Many believed that the Arnarflug men had in effect bought these flight licenses by rescuing my political allies from bankruptcy. That was wrong. Íscargo's licenses went with its name, not its assets; moreover, Arnarflug's representatives knew that they could expect the flight licenses before the Íscargo purchase was made.

Flugleiðir also had licenses to fly to Amsterdam and Düsseldorf. Ferociously hard competition began, and Flugleiðir's undercutting was highly conspicuous, since the company was at the same time requesting continued statesupport

on account of its operating difficulties. It seemed obvious to me that the goal of the Flugleiðir men was first and foremost to inflict damage on Arnarflug and bring its European flights to their knees. I came to the conclusion that there was nothing to be done but revoke Flugleiðir's licenses on these routes. I received harsh criticism in the aftermath, and it was claimed that I had begun working against the very competition goals I had previously advocated. I will not accept that. Even though the companies did not fly the same routes, there would still be some competition in the European flights. On the other hand, it would prevent "unrestrained" competition, which could lead to both companies losing money until the smaller one gave way and consumers were once again stuck with a monopoly.

I am still of the opinion that the decisions I made to stimulate competition in aviation were essentially correct. Some things could no doubt be criticized, for example allowing my representative on the board of Flugleiðir to act as intermediary in the dealings between Íscargo and Arnarflug. That was questionable because of his work on the Flugleiðir board and gave my opponents an opening to strike at me. It would never occur to me, however, to blame Kári Einarsson in this matter. His conduct bore witness above all to his initiative and drive. Still, such things gave suspicion wind under both wings, and the dust storm whipped up around Íscargo undeniably overshadowed my objective: competition in aviation.
Controversial Appointments

In all matters concerning aviation I worked closely with Agnar Kofoed-Hansen. Edda and I also came to know both Agnar and his wife Björg well personally. On one occasion, as so often, Agnar and I were discussing aviation matters in my office. He seemed somehow unlike himself, and I noticed that he winced when he rose from his seat. When I asked him whether something was wrong, he replied that the man with the scythe was after him. "He will not succeed in his errand, though," Agnar added, straightening up. He had developed cancer. This illness eventually led to Agnar's death, far before his time.

I made Pétur Einarsson Agnar's successor in the post of director of civil aviation after careful consideration. This was surely one of the most controversial appointments of my political career. Pétur had long been a great aviation enthusiast and was considered vigorous in all his work. I regarded that as no small matter, for strong bones are needed to hold that office.

Pétur's strongest rival for the position was Leifur Magnússon. He was considered to have a better education than Pétur. In that respect he was probably better prepared for the job. To me, though, there did not seem to be much difference between these two fine men.

Perhaps it may be said that I took as my guiding light something Bjarni Benediktsson once said: if two men are equally good but one of them is a fellow party member, that tips the scales. Pétur had long worked within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Later I in fact received praise from many quarters for having hired him for the job. He proved himself at once in his work and took a firm grip on the office.

Spears were also aimed at me when I gave Jón Skaftason the office of city magistrate (borgarfógeti) in Reykjavík during my time as Minister of Justice. He had lost his seat in parliament in the 1978 elections. Jón had everything that could adorn a good magistrate, both in education and in ability. No doubt many others could have handled the office. I was always opposed to the attitude that men who had worked in politics and in parliament were unfit for other work. On the contrary, I believed that the experience gained from years of sitting in the Althing was valuable, and that few had as good an insight into and understanding of the inner workings of society as experienced parliamentarians. I have never heard anything other than that Jón performed well in the job.

During my time as Minister of Justice I also appointed one judge to the Supreme Court, Sigurgeir Jónsson, who had been district magistrate (sýslumaður) in Kópavogur. He was a staunch Independence Party man. Predictably, there were various people within the Progressive Party who expressed displeasure that I had not appointed a Progressive to the judgeship.
Skirt-Hem Capitalism

My acquaintance with Icelandic business in these years gave me considerable food for thought. When things went well, businessmen beat their chests, talked about free enterprise, and cursed all interference by the state. It went without saying that success was due to their own hard work. When things went badly, however, government assistance was demanded, and the government was blamed for how matters stood. Icelandic business life was not private enterprise in the sense that companies and individuals stood or fell by their own actions. This was private enterprise under the shelter of the government, which critics called skirt-hem capitalism (pilsfaldakapitalismi).

As different as my ministries were in other respects, they had one thing in common. Under them fell strong companies and powerful industries that had grown accustomed to doing business with the state and with politicians. When difficulties arose, their first reaction was often to call for state support. Such rescue operations were criticized above all from the left wing of politics. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) argued

against excessive coddling of "the 200 fishing-industry families" and "the companies of capital." The Independence Party men, on the other hand, sided with the spokesmen of business when the state treasury was being tapped.

Politicians of all parties took part in the game wholeheartedly, and the power of allocation was used to gather votes. In the government of Gunnar Thoroddsen it went beyond all bounds in the election spring of 1983, when a special appropriation was approved from the state treasury for "rationalization in fish processing and the fishing industry." In these measures, some 120 million krónur were distributed across the whole country on pretexts large and small. A special committee was appointed to allocate this money, and fifty-nine companies received "rationalization loans," from 500,000 krónur up to 7 million.

Rationalization was only a pretext for these measures. Difficulties certainly existed, but the upcoming elections were what decided the matter. The fishing industry had, among its regular threats, that of sailing the fleet into harbor if the government did not meet its demands for assistance. The government could not bear the thought of a stoppage, with every boat and tub tied up at the dock while the public cast their votes on election day.

Although short-term interests in politics and business coincided in measures such as these, long-term interests were sacrificed. That must be admitted. Some of the businessmen's criticism of government policy and the government's measures was also justified. The businessmen deserved some sympathy. The foundation was weak and the fluctuations were great. Ever since the "Innovation Government" (nýsköpunarstjórnin) of 1944–1947 squandered the wartime profits with its purchases of an obsolete trawler fleet, which was distributed around the country by government decision, it had been endemic in Iceland that the good years were not used to ease the burden when times grew hard. All attempts at counter-cyclical stabilization had failed. For these reasons I have long been of the opinion that the Innovation Government was the most unnecessary of all governments in the history of Iceland.

Most government measures since the end of the war bore the mark of being makeshift. The main objective was usually no more ambitious than keeping the economy afloat. This was an unhealthy operating environment in which incentives to perform well were lacking. Instead of being able to concentrate on their operations, the energy of businessmen went into procuring for their companies all manner of grants and public support. The political rationing system was, moreover, far from perfect, to put it mildly. Those whose operations fared worst received the most assistance. The experience in Gunnar Thoroddsen's government brought out, to my mind, many of the worst flaws of this system.
Chapter Eleven

Gunnar Thoroddsen's formation of a government in 1980 demonstrated his talents and his strength as a politician better than almost anything else. He had most of the qualities politicians need — a fine mind, elegance, resourcefulness, and eloquence — such that his equal in that field was hard to find. Few could have pulled this off. His story has scarcely any parallel in Icelandic politics. This was certainly not the first adventure in a colorful career. It was a long road from Gunnar's first involvement in politics to the moment he split the country's largest political party, the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn).

Gunnar Thoroddsen is still the youngest man ever elected to a seat in the Althing of the Icelanders. Nor has anyone been older in the prime minister's chair. Forty-six years passed from the time he was first elected to parliament until he formed his own government. Something tells me it will be a long wait before anything like that is repeated. Gunnar took his seat in the Althing at 23 years of age in 1934, and thus became a member of parliament the same year as my father. Gunnar, however, used his first term partly for postgraduate studies in law while my father sat in the prime minister's chair. He became a professor of law at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands) in 1940, at thirty years of age. At that point he in fact held no seat in parliament, for in the 1937 elections he fell to Ásgeir Ásgeirsson in Vestur-Ísafjarðarsýsla.
That was easily avenged, though, as the wits said: Vala, Ásgeir's daughter, fell for Gunnar during that same election campaign, and they married shortly afterward.

Gunnar became mayor of Reykjavík in 1947 and held that office all the way to 1959, when he took up a ministerial post. For most of that time he was also a member of parliament and a professor, and thought nothing of "betraying"

the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in 1952 — so much so that he came close to being expelled from the party. Gunnar's high treason consisted in supporting his father-in-law for the presidency instead of following the Independence Party line and backing Bjarni Jónsson, the cathedral pastor. Many in the innermost circle of the Independence Party never forgave him for it. That did not, however, prevent Gunnar from taking over the office of finance minister in the "Reconstruction Government" (viðreisnarstjórnin) in 1959.

The time came, however, when Gunnar's opponents in the Independence Party got the chance to get their own back on him. Gunnar himself stood in the presidential election of 1968, as I have recounted earlier. Many then seized the opportunity to repay him in kind. That worked to the advantage of Kristján Eldjárn. A few years earlier, in 1965, Gunnar had withdrawn from politics, or so it seemed, and become ambassador in Copenhagen. After the presidential contest he was then appointed a justice of the Supreme Court (Hæstiréttur). All these offices were granted by virtue of the political power of the Independence Party, though Gunnar certainly possessed the education, ability, and experience the offices demanded. The Independence Party men went so far in these matters, however, that they even took to "creating" special positions for Gunnar, whether at the Supreme Court or at the University.

Gunnar Thoroddsen's political career reads like a tall tale. He had not sat long on the Supreme Court before he grew restless. Before the 1971 parliamentary elections he therefore resigned his office and took third place in the Independence Party's primary in Reykjavík, behind Mayor Geir Hallgrímsson and Jóhann Hafstein, the party chairman. Following that, Gunnar ran against Geir for the deputy chairmanship at the party's national convention. He fell barely fifty votes short of victory. With these elections the struggle between Gunnar and Geir began in earnest. Gunnar held his own for a long while even though Geir became party chairman and prime minister in 1974. Gunnar then became a minister, deputy chairman of the party, and also chairman of the parliamentary group.
After the battle for the deputy chairmanship, however, the Independence Party members split into Gunnar's men and Geir's men. Some say they still do.
A Nimble Leader

Gunnar's hallmark was how easily he made himself understood. He reached the general public and was the first of the old chieftains to grasp how utterly different a manner and style the new medium, television, demanded. He could deliver a thundering speech from the rostrum with the firmness a meeting hall demands, and speak calmly but with conviction about the same issue on television a few minutes later. He changed skins as the occasion required. In Gunnar,
demeanor became an art. His artistic nature was strong and a large part of his personality and bearing.

In the struggle with Geir he considered himself the representative of the broad Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), a party of all classes that also took to heart the circumstances of the worst off. The "lightning offensive" (leiftursókn) was, in his mind, conservatism of a different strain. He regarded his government and the ministers from the coalition partners as his allies in the fight for social equality in Iceland. For that goal, and to keep a functioning government in place, he was ready to give his all.

Gunnar's leadership abilities probably should not have surprised me. Yet I did not fully realize until the coalition was under way how industrious he was, how unsparing of himself, and how ready to listen to his colleagues. I never felt I detected the slightest sign of old age in him. The disputes within the Independence Party had in many ways given a different picture of him than the man I came to know. His fiercest opponents all but held that he was descended from the Devil himself. And that in the direct male line.

I found it good to work with Gunnar. He was a gentleman to his fingertips and tremendously well informed about everything that concerned Icelandic society, whether people or issues. Gunnar also had good command of this knowledge of his and put it well into words. He and Ólafur Jóhannesson had it in common that they were on home ground where the law was concerned. Yet much was different between the two. Gunnar was far more open in all dealings. I could always turn to him when the need arose.

Under Gunnar's leadership this became a government of compromises. Many of the ministers were hard-working but rigid in their opinions. Gunnar had a knack for winning people over to his side, was light-hearted, and I usually found it difficult to rebel or go against him. Gunnar chose, however, not to play the mediator's role alone. In order to build consensus between the parties he held frequent meetings of us party chairmen. Svavar Gestsson and I thus sat through many a midday over sandwiches and pilsner in Gunnar's office. That took a heavy toll on my lunchtime swim, which had long since become a fixed habit.

Gunnar went incredibly far in getting people to reach agreement. Sometimes too far, in my opinion. It often seemed to me high time for the prime minister to cut through the knots that formed in the coalition. In particular, he seemed to me to have unbelievable forbearance when waiting on the countless councils and committees of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), which had a hundred opinions on every issue, and preferably all of them impossible. Gunnar, however, undeniably showed great skill in holding the government together.
"Water on the Devil's Mill"

It took strong bones to join forces with Gunnar from the Independence Party's parliamentary group while the government formation was at its height. That much is certain. Ellert B. Schram later described the reactions of the Independence Party members by saying that first they became angry, then astonished, and finally sorrowful. No doubt that was true of some. It seemed to me, though, that somehow the anger was always the most conspicuous. The inner life of the Independence Party leadership showed itself then, as so often before, in the writings of Morgunblaðið. Morgunblaðið was at first astonished, then gentle, and finally angry. The Moggi never became sorrowful. It turned gray with rage, ash-gray, and that did not change as long as the government lived.

Among the labels chosen for the government formation in the paper's writings were "water on the Devil's mill" and "a malignant tumor in our national life," as recounted in Gunnar Thoroddsen's memoirs. Gunnar's supporters were not given more dignified names. They were the "sewage" of the "political sewers," which the editor of Morgunblaðið said Geir Hallgrímsson need not worry about.

Those who stood behind the government paid little heed to the agitation of the Morgunblaðið men. I can hardly suppress a smile when I recall these writings so long afterward. The ministers went cheerfully about their work and encountered great support everywhere. Dagblaðið published an opinion poll on the public's attitude toward the government on 18 February 1980. In it, 70.5% of voters said they were in favor of the government, 21% declared themselves undecided, and only 8% said they were opposed to it.

Morgunblaðið took this popularity lightly. The "historic betrayal" was shelved but not forgotten. In a Reykjavík Letter (Reykjavíkurbréf) a year and a half after the government's formation, the paper reached this conclusion:

The crux of the matter regarding the government of Gunnar Thoroddsen is not whether, or what, success it achieves in economic affairs or in other areas of public life. Nor is the crux of the matter whether the prime minister is personally popular with the public at this moment or not. What remains is simply this: that the formation of the government has opened so deep a wound in the nation's strongest political movement, the Independence Party, that it will take many years to heal those wounds. The government's formation is a malignant tumor in our national life, and so it will remain as long as this government sits.

Pálmi Jónsson became minister of agriculture, and this much is certain: Pálmi had great sympathy for the interests of farmers. He was wholehearted in that, as in everything else he has undertaken. That, however, unfortunately meant that he showed no effort to move agricultural production further out of the export-subsidy system. He let matters rest with the small progress I had achieved, and the review that had nevertheless begun essentially came to nothing. Meanwhile, things drifted aimlessly.

I attended the Agricultural Assembly (búnaðarþing) as former minister of agriculture only a week after the government took power. There I heard Pálmi deliver his first speech as my successor, and I remember well how I felt inside. I grew ever more restless in my seat as it went on. The last straw came when the newly minted minister cheerfully read that it "[should be] carefully examined whether it might not be advantageous for society as a whole to continue producing sheep products for export, even though it costs something in export subsidies." To my mind, such an experiment had been running for two decades and had cost the state, the public, and the farmers inefficiency and untold sums of money.

The consequences should have been foreseeable to everyone. When Jón Helgason took over the reins in the Ministry of Agriculture in 1983, the meat mountain had become a fact. Unfortunately, it seemed to me that Jón fared just like Pálmi. Despite the sharp intelligence and good will of this fine friend of mine, I could not come to any conclusion other than that it was a bad idea to have a minister of agriculture from the ranks of the farmers, and it mattered little how worthy the men were in other respects. A farmer in the Ministry of Agriculture is simply under the heel of the agricultural leadership. The leading men of the farmers' organizations are more often than not on close personal terms with him, and their associations are his school and training ground in social affairs and politics.

I am almost inclined to say that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) should preferably not hold the agriculture portfolio, and I tried to avoid it after this experience. On that point, however, many of my fellow party members disagreed and still disagree with me.
Regarding Pálmi Jónsson it should be added that our acquaintance became closer later in life, and I count him among the worthier of men.

Friðjón Þórðarson held the justice portfolio. He regularly chaired cabinet meetings in the prime minister's absence. As minister of justice he did not leave deep footprints. I have, however, always liked Friðjón. He is a peaceable man and calm in all his conduct. It also seemed to me that he was a supporter of a mixed economy and clearly understood the role of government in shaping economic and industrial policy. Perhaps that is where his path and Gunnar Thoroddsen's first converged, in those ideals.
Eggert and Albert

Gunnar's supporters from the ranks of the Independence Party members did not turn out to be as numerous as he had implied at the outset. No one joined the group of those who had figured in the story while the government formation was at its height. Various people thought Sverrir Hermannsson was likely to support the government. That came to nothing, and he has in fact repeatedly sworn off any such notions. I cannot settle that question.

Of Gunnar's supporters, Pálmi and Friðjón became ministers, but Eggert Haukdal and Albert Guðmundsson did not. Eggert became chairman of the board of the State Development Agency (Framkvæmdastofnun ríkisins). Considerable power could come with that, if matters were handled accordingly. Some thought Eggert rather too free-handed when he traded support for individual projects and grants across the board table.

Eggert Haukdal is hard-working and mulls things over a great deal. He approaches every matter with the prudence of a good husbandman: he checks the weather and then sets to work. In that way he ran his politics from day to day according to how the wind seemed to blow each time. This made Eggert in many ways a peculiar politician, and it was often hard to predict his reactions. He was apt to stray far off the beaten path and never fit in well in a party. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) was in constant trouble with him, and we did not escape this trait of his in the coalition government.

Gunnar spent many hours in meetings with his allies from his own party. That was necessary to hold that band together. There were plenty of flare-ups all the same. Gunnar turned nothing away when these men were concerned. At one point, when Eggert Haukdal was locked in a bitter dispute with the priest at Bergþórshvoll over a mare that had given up the ghost in the wrong paddock, the government offices were given over to those private matters. At one conciliation meeting, nothing less would do than to convene the priest and the member of parliament, the Bishop of Iceland, the minister for church affairs, the chairmen of both coalition partners in the government, and of course the prime minister himself, who hosted this rather ludicrous gathering. Svavar and I looked at each other and tried to keep from laughing.

No less remarkable was watching how Morgunblaðið built Eggert up as time went on and his support for the government grew shaky. If Morgunblaðið found a weak spot in the government's policy, it made sure to get Eggert to declare himself in opposition on the issue. Thus Eggert was celebrated and exalted, while at the same time being egged on not to betray "his" ideals — and Morgunblaðið's. As time went on, someof
the ministers felt that Eggert had gone too far in making his support on one issue an article of trade in exchange for favors on another.

Albert Guðmundsson was called by many the godfather of the government because of his declaration of support for its formation. He had long been one of the most colorful politicians in the country. At the start of his political career, Albert was first and foremost known as one of the nation's foremost football players. He earned a good name as a professional with major clubs abroad and soon became involved in politics after returning home. In his new arena he earned the nickname "friend of the little man" for his helpfulness and willingness to serve those who turned to him. There seemed to be few limits to either. He therefore had a powerful and fervent group of supporters who followed him through thick and thin. His backing within the sports movement was no less strong. Gunnar handled the negotiations with Albert Guðmundsson entirely on his own.
No one else came anywhere near them, and so it remained while the government sat.

As was customary, the coalition parties divided among themselves the board chairmanships of the three state banks. The chairmanship of one bank fell to each of them. Albert was made chairman of the board of the Fisheries Bank (Útvegsbankinn). Some were uneasy about that arrangement, not least because of Albert's natural inclination to smooth the way for every man who turned to him. Tómas Árnason held the formal power of appointment in the banks, and he delayed somewhat in granting Albert the office. It happened in the end, though. Gunnar decided it. Albert, however, took it into his head to demand a letter of commission from Tómas. There was no precedent for this, and he was refused. There followed threats from Albert to resign if he did not get the letter.

Tómas was entirely unruffled and took leave of Albert some three times with the words that he should just let him know if he wanted out of the bank. It never became clear what Albert intended to do with the letter of commission. Stories circulated that he meant to open an office in the bank where people could come to him for favors. I do not know what truth there was in that.

Gunnar would surely have offered Albert a ministerial seat if he had sought one. Albert, however, was far along in his preparations for a presidential candidacy while the government formation was under way and had other fish to fry. Otherwise, the 1980 presidential election figured little in party politics. It is nowhere mentioned by name in the minute-books of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), which is a sign of changed times. I myself supported Guðlaugur Þorvaldsson, who had been rector of the university, and many considered him to enjoy the support of most Progressives. Nothing can be said with certainty
about that. Although a great many Progressives doubtless supported Guðlaugur, few of them declared their position publicly, and that was the case with me.

Guðlaugur and I met several times for talk and planning while the election campaign was under way. Our consultations, however, came nowhere near my work in connection with Kristján Eldjárn's candidacy twelve years earlier. My position was also different. Instead of being a substitute member of parliament for the Westfjords, I was a minister in the government of Iceland and chairman of the largest governing party.

Two candidates were counted as Independence Party men, Albert Guðmundsson and Pétur Thorsteinsson. From the start it was clear that Pétur had little chance. Many were surprised that Pétur did not withdraw before the election came. That would certainly have changed the outcome.

Albert enjoyed the support of Gunnar Thoroddsen but had little following in the ranks of the Progressives. Various people asserted that Albert had let word go out that he intended to withdraw if Ólafur Jóhannesson made himself available for the office of president. Perhaps in that way he was trying to secure the support of those close to Ólafur. The party members who did declare their views were mostly those who supported Vigdís Finnbogadóttir. The ambassador Hannes Jónsson was prominent among them, along with left-leaning Progressives around the country and a great number of Progressive women. Halldór E. Sigurðsson, a former minister of the party, likewise came out in support of Vigdís after he was asked to chair a large meeting of her supporters. She declared her candidacy late, after I had firmly pledged my support to Guðlaugur.

I regarded Vigdís's candidacy favorably, though I believed that left-leaning voters would split between her and Guðlaugur. I am convinced that most of Vigdís's supporters would have voted for Guðlaugur if her candidacy had not come about.

When Vigdís emerged victorious, some felt that Albert took rather too keen an interest in the affairs of government and made demands on the cabinet as if he owned every bone in its body. He was unabashed about seeking assistance within the government's ministries and did not always trouble himself to knock before he swept into the ministers' offices. They often went on these errands as a pair, Albert and Guðmundur "jaki", who also had a seat in parliament. The two of them could often be seen playing chess in the parliament building during sessions. Many found it difficult to stand in their way when they joined forces. I believe the ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) in particular felt the presence of that pair. Most often, though, these were minor matters or favors for individuals that did not weigh heavily on the treasury's purse.
I, on the other hand, had little to do with Albert in this government. He had no business with me, neither in
neither in fisheries nor in transport matters. It was not until later that I came to know him well, and we became good friends.
Svavar and Public Services

It has sometimes been said that politics and political debate in Iceland have been almost exclusively confined to economic matters. In keeping with this, governments have been judged by only one yardstick: how high inflation was during their time in power. On those grounds, Gunnar Thoroddsen's government has not received a flattering epitaph. Nevertheless, few governments have enjoyed as much popularity during their term of office, if opinion polls are anything to go by. It enjoyed broad public support, not for inaction or because it was inept at managing the economy, but for its work in other fields. Progress and development are not easily measured by the yardstick of inflation.

Among the government's principal achievements was ambitious legislation in the fields of social and health affairs. The coalition agreement stated that one of the government's main tasks was to "increase social services and equalize living standards." There it was not least the ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and the labor movement that consulted with each other. The coalition agreement stipulated that maternity/paternity leave would become the right of all parents, that entitlement to unemployment benefits should be broadened, and that improvements should be pursued in the affairs of the elderly, the disabled, and those living with impairments.

All these promises were carried out, not forgetting the comprehensive housing legislation that marked a turning point. A great number of people were thereby enabled to acquire their own homes. A social housing-loan system was also established, and new legislation on student loans was passed in which, for the first time, it was stipulated that students could borrow enough to cover their full living costs during their studies. Progressive equal-rights legislation was likewise passed, the first comprehensive laws on the affairs of the elderly were enacted, along with legislation on rents and tenants' rights. Many of the items pursued in social affairs became part of the collective wage agreements in the autumn of 1980 through a special declaration by the government.
It contained various of the items listed above, in addition to provisions that substantial funds would be devoted to building day-care centers.

Many of the causes the government championed in the field of social affairs were long overdue and matters of plain justice. Previously, only some women had had the right to maternity leave, and one needed special goodwill in the banking system to obtain a loan to put a roof over one's head. The major steps the government took toward having all Icelanders save into a pension fund were

also unquestionably steps forward. Still, I felt the government was getting rather too strong a reputation for social spending. After the wage agreements had been concluded, I stressed that in the next round of negotiations the primary aim should be to reduce inflation and increase purchasing power. There had been enough "social-affairs packages." The ministers of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and their allies in the labor movement, however, were in the highest of spirits.

Social development and public services were the apple of Svavar Gestsson's eye. He is a socialist through and through and can talk a whole house into a fever when the ideals of the welfare system are at stake. I share many of his views on those matters. Svavar, however, is almost a pure-bred idealist in politics, with the virtues and flaws that entails. I often found Svavar lacking in groundedness and realism, especially when it came to economic affairs and the struggle with inflation. Then he proved reluctant to resort to the measures that were needed. Svavar also refused to face the fact that the greater part of the economy is free and beyond the reach of government. He had far too strong a tendency toward interventionism. Ragnar Arnalds, it seemed to me, had a sharper understanding in those matters.

Svavar took great pains to cultivate his relationship with the grassroots of the People's Alliance. That was certainly no easy task, since gathered together in one party were labor bosses and opponents of the military base, pacifists, redstockings and feminists, intellectuals and old Möðruvellingar, rural-minded farmers and migrant laborers, revolutionary Marxists, and God knows who else. The main factions, though, were the socialists and those who liked to call themselves the democratic generation. The innermost core of the socialist wing traced its roots back to the former Socialist Party (Sósíalistaflokkurinn) and Communist Party (Kommúnistaflokkurinn) and commonly went by the name of "the party owners' association" (flokkseigendafélagið). Svavar was considered to stand closer to the socialists.

He nevertheless managed to hold these diverse threads of the party together so well that he received a "Russian election" as chairman of the People's Alliance in November 1980. On that occasion he said the party had the distinction of being "united." That did not last long.

In a certain way I respected Svavar's grassroots work, though it created problems for the government where the labor wing of the People's Alliance was concerned. No economic reforms emerged unscathed from that assembly, even when they enjoyed the support of the People's Alliance ministers. Svavar seemed neither to be a leader in that group nor to feel up to a fight with it. Svavar came back winded from his labor-movement meetings no less during Gunnar Thoroddsen's government than in the days of the left-wing government. It seemed to make no difference that he had in the meantime been elected chairman of the party.
Right-leaning Progressives sometimes asked, half in jest and half in earnest, howit

felt to sit in a government with "such hard-line commies." By that they meant Svavar and Hjörleifur. It would never have occurred to anyone to use the word communist about Ragnar Arnalds. When our cooperation in government began, I knew good things of Ragnar, as has already been mentioned. Nevertheless, it surprised me what a good finance minister he was. Ragnar was far more prudent with money than I had expected. The treasury had almost without exception been run at a deficit every single year for more than a decade. Under Ragnar's leadership there was a turnaround in this respect, and the budget showed a surplus. The treasury was run without a deficit throughout the government's years in office, despite the costly build-up in social affairs.

Ragnar certainly benefited from the work of Tómas Árnason from the days of the left-wing government, and in his first year in office he presented Tómas's budget bill almost unchanged. He showed, however, determined will and ambition in the office of finance minister. His good sense and the respect he enjoyed meant that there was no need to battle the most extreme viewpoints within the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) over the management of state finances. He managed to steer the government clear of them with finesse. Composure was Ragnar's hallmark.
Hjörleifur and the "Increase at Sea"

If any one word describes Hjörleifur Guttormsson, it is industriousness. He is one of the greatest workhorses I have ever known. I liked to think I started the day early, often arriving before eight o'clock. Yet without fail the lights were already on in Hjörleifur's office. Often a light was still burning in his office when I went home. Despite his long workday, Hjörleifur was always impeccably turned out. His clothes were in the latest fashion, pressed and neat, and any barber would have been proud of the chin-beard that framed the set of his mouth.

Hjörleifur was no less diligent in assigning tasks to his subordinates. Report-writing was his bread and butter. And then everything was photocopied for the cabinet. The photocopier in the ministry seemed to grind away in three shifts around the clock. Hjörleifur can hardly have stood over it himself morning and night. There was no possible way to get through reading more than a fraction of what he served up to us. On one occasion, when Hjörleifur had delivered yet another mountain of paper at the start of a cabinet meeting, I remarked that the prime minister would have to revoke the industry minister's photocopying license.

Hjörleifur had his hands full during his time as minister. He believed he had discovered that the Icelandic Aluminium Company (Íslenska álfélagið) was cheating Icelanders out of large sums through accounting tricks. In his investigations he had the assistance of Ingi R. Helgason and

a British auditing firm. The Swiss owners "sold to themselves" alumina which they shipped from their own mines in Australia via Rotterdam to Iceland. By the time the alumina reached the aluminum smelter at Straumsvík, its price had risen by a total of 16.2 million US dollars over a five-year period beyond what could be considered normal. The result was that the company paid much lower taxes in Iceland than it otherwise would have.

Spokesmen for the smelter protested vigorously that anything irregular had taken place. An investigation, however, revealed that Hjörleifur was right about the markup. The price of the alumina had "risen at sea," as the phrase went. On the other hand, he had difficulty getting the upper hand over the Swiss in the drawn-out negotiations and war of nerves that followed. They had done nothing illegal, even if the ethics of it could be debated.

On 16 July 1981 the government approved, on Hjörleifur's proposal, the presentation of maximum demands in talks with the Swiss. This was done with reference to the fact that Alusuisse had "not honored its contractual obligations." The objectives of the talks were threefold: first, to obtain payment of unpaid taxes; second, to revise the production levies of preceding years; and third, to demand an increase in the price of electricity. At the same time, a demand was approved for at least half Icelandic ownership of the smelter, and that the production of anodes and other technical equipment be moved to Iceland. These objectives were fully in line with the resolutions of the parliamentary group of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), although some members of parliament had doubts about individual points, especially the provision on Icelandic ownership of half the smelter.

A special negotiating committee was established which now took charge of the negotiations with the Swiss. Because of the People's Alliance's (Alþýðubandalagið) historic distrust of Jóhannes Nordal, Hjörleifur pushed him aside. The party's spokesmen held him responsible for overinvestment and greatly increased borrowing by the National Power Company (Landsvirkjun), and said he was therefore intent on selling the electricity "no matter what it cost."

Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson, director of the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins), was appointed chairman of the new negotiating committee. Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson was the representative of the Progressive Party. It soon became clear that the only way to improve the Icelandic state's position lay in negotiating a higher electricity price. There everything was deadlocked. Hjörleifur remarked on that occasion that the electricity price the smelter paid was so low that "by far the cheapest power-development option for the nation" would be to shut off the electricity to the smelter.

I think Hjörleifur was right about the "rise at sea," although the figures in that regard actually decreased as the investigations multiplied. He handled the situation badly, however. Hjörleifur proved to want to dictate

with the negotiating committee and made liberal use of his ministerial powers. Toward the Swiss he stood inflexible on all of Iceland's demands. Things moved neither forward nor back. At the end of 1982 Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson resigned, saying that the minister wanted to run the negotiations like a "Russian chicken farm." Guðmundur was convinced that Hjörleifur had no intention at all of reaching an agreement, but rather believed that unilateral measures served his propaganda and his interests better.

In the aftermath, Hjörleifur dissolved the negotiating committee amid great commotion. The disputes that followed became so fierce that he remarked it would be logical for a motion of no confidence to be brought against him. I did not endorse that, though I had grown weary of waiting for "serious negotiations" on raising the electricity price. Negotiations on revised energy prices were left on the back burner throughout Hjörleifur's entire time as minister because of disputes over other, unrelated matters. As a result, Landsvirkjun and the state treasury lost considerable revenue. It would have been better to keep the dispute concerning taxes and fees separate from the negotiations and resolve it before the courts.

It fell to Sverrir Hermannsson to conclude the agreements with Alusuisse in 1984. He made it his first task to call Jóhannes Nordal back to work. A considerable increase in the electricity price was obtained. I believe the outcome was acceptable for Icelanders.

Hjörleifur's other major undertaking was policy-making in heavy industry and power development. The shaping of an energy policy was one of the policy points stipulated in the government's coalition agreement, and the opposition pressed hard for action. More often than not the refrain was that "millions of krónur were flowing out to sea every day, benefiting no one." Resolutions and projects were in fact not long in coming. Power generation began at the Hrauneyjafoss power station in 1981, and at the same time its expansion and that of the Sultartangi station were decided upon, in addition to which it was decided to build a power station at Villinganes.

At a cabinet meeting in April 1981, Hjörleifur presented a bill on power stations. The parliamentary group of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) had approved bringing it before the government. Its objective was that within ten years work would begin on harnessing the Blanda river and the first phase of the Fljótsdalur power station. These projects were the mainstay of the implementation plan for electric power that the Minister of Industry later presented and championed.

Environmental issues were not uppermost in Hjörleifur's mind in those years, any more than in mine or that of others involved in these decisions. Heavy industry was still considered the cure for every district's ills. He did, however, emphasize that ownership should remain in Icelandic hands. He and Ragnar Arnalds argued over whether the Blanda river or Fljótsdalur should be harnessed first. Hjörleifur lost that battle, but at the close of the spring session

in 1981 he nonetheless got a bill passed authorizing the minister to grant Landsvirkjun a license to build a power station in Fljótsdalur. It is on this authorization that the hydroelectric plans now most fiercely disputed — plans that will submerge the Eyjabakkar wetlands — are based. The bill contained no provisions for environmental impact assessment, which was indeed not in the spirit of the time.

Hjörleifur's dreams of a power station in Fljótsdalur were closely tied to a plan to build a silicon metal plant or some other energy-intensive industrial enterprise at Reyðarfjörður. He got a proposal to that effect approved by the government in November 1981. These silicon-plant dreams became a most troublesome affair before all was over. When the plans were finally scrapped in 1987, the board and managing director of the factory — which was never built — had been drawing salaries for years.
Economic Affairs and Internal Strife

The coalition agreement was quite clear where economic matters were concerned. One of the government's chief objectives was bringing down inflation in stages. The foundation for this was above all the detailed policy of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). On the Progressives' side, an economic plan had been fairly well worked out already in the run-up to the formation of the government, unlike the situation when the left-wing government took power in 1978. Throughout that government's entire term, one might say, continuous discussions were held about a long-term economic plan that never made it onto paper.

In Gunnar Thoroddsen's government, however, it fell to the Progressives to push for the measures that had been promised. The coalition partners had, unfortunately, opposed committing to paper the precise figures and dates of the countdown strategy. For that reason every step had to be negotiated, and it tried one's patience. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) dragged its feet and Gunnar mediated.

Necessary measures were greatly delayed during the first year in office. All of 1980 passed without the People's Alliance ministers being brought to any decisions. During the spring session, all the government's work went into putting together the budget and taking necessary short-term measures. The governing of the country had been left almost entirely on the back burner during the Social Democratic Party's caretaker government. Cooperation within the government was nonetheless good, and parliament was more productive than usual. Once the spring session was over, the People's Alliance still considered it out of the question to announce economic measures while wage negotiations were under way. Those proceeded slowly, and economic measures awaited their outcome for a time. As mentioned earlier, they concluded with the government's "social package" at the end of October.
In November 1980 the congress of the Icelandic Federation of Labour (Alþýðusambandið) was approaching. A new leadership was to be elected there. Decisions on economic matters also had to await those

results. Some said the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) did not want to upset its allies in the labour movement in any way before those elections. The government coalition affected the power struggle within the labour movement. Behind the scenes, People's Alliance men exploited the split in the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). It was felt in the labour movement as elsewhere. The People's Alliance candidate, Ásmundur Stefánsson, defeated Karvel Pálmason, who had been put forward by the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the Geir wing of the Independence Party. Elected vice-president was Björn Þórhallsson, a Gunnar man from the Independence Party, who among other things had taken part in drafting the wage-policy section of the coalition agreement, as mentioned earlier.

The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) supported Ásmundur in the presidential election and greatly strengthened its position within the Federation of Labour (ASÍ) at that congress.
