This was celebrated at a meeting of the party's executive committee. The party's leaders hoped that the government would enjoy greater understanding from the labour movement as a result. Those hopes were utterly dashed. The government enjoyed little goodwill and limited understanding. All its work was held hostage by the labour movement.

In December 1980, comprehensive economic measures by the government were finally prepared in talks among the parties. The goal was for inflation to be brought down to 40 percent by the end of 1981. It had been around 60 percent for some time. As Christmas approached, I believed that consensus had been reached, and so did others. I therefore considered it safe to go on holiday over Christmas and New Year. In my work as Minister of Fisheries I had become acquainted with a Spaniard, a high-ranking official in the foreign trade ministry. He urged me to come to Formigal in the Pyrenees for a skiing trip with the family. That is what we did.

As it turned out, there was fierce wrangling within the government throughout the holidays. Considerable fuss was made about my absence, not least in the media. I was asked repeatedly by reporters whether it was not difficult to be away. I always answered that the telephone connection was good. Tómas Árnason took charge of my ministries in my absence and also handled relations with the coalition partners. The course of events in those days was typical of the state of affairs in the government. Agreement with the People's Alliance was never fully concluded. No sooner had I left for Spain than Svavar came with new demands.

On 30 December 1980 the parliamentary group of the Progressive Party met for the last time before the parliamentary recess. There Tómas presented a compromise that had been reached in the government earlier that day. He moved that the parliamentary group approve that outcome. Tómas expected that the People's Alliance men would return from a meeting of their labour council, as was their habit, with a changed position. He proposed that the party's members of parliament hold a month-long
their Christmas recess, each going to his own home, so that it would be impossible to negotiate any further concessions on the part of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn).

Tómas's prediction came true. Svavar Gestsson came to see him only half an hour after the parliamentary group meeting ended, with the news that his party would have to demand changes. Tómas replied that this was out of the question; the parliamentary group had gone home and would not convene again until after the recess. They parted at that. The next day the government met yet again on the economic issues. The task at hand was to finalize the economic plan and issue provisional legislation. Tómas had prepared himself to set out the parliamentary group's non-negotiable position.

Before he got the floor, however, Svavar Gestsson presented a joint proposal from himself and Ólafur Jóhannesson in which concessions were made to accommodate the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið).

Svavar had gone to see Gunnar Thoroddsen the evening before, so late that he found the couple in their dressing gowns. Gunnar thought it could hardly be a great matter to accommodate the People's Alliance, but advised him to consult Ólafur Jóhannesson. Svavar visited Ólafur early the next morning, shortly before the cabinet meeting. He received as good a reception there as he had from Gunnar. Svavar assumed, however, that Ólafur would consult his fellow ministers in the Progressive Party before the cabinet meeting. He considered himself to be working merely on minor changes that mattered little to the government but a great deal to himself, both personally and politically vis-à-vis the labour movement.

Tómas understood this quite differently. In his eyes it was an assault following fierce clashes between the coalition parties, and it came from the most unexpected quarter. Tómas felt he had been the victim of treachery and demanded a recess. He and Ólafur then went out in front of the meeting room and had a sharp exchange of words there. Tómas has said that they had rarely quarrelled as bitterly as in that conversation. Ólafur, however, showed little change of expression under the tirade and said nothing but: "It makes no difference. Shall we just break it off? Shall we just break it off? And with the chairman absent?"

I did not hear of this quarrel until I came home shortly after the New Year. It was symbolic of two things. First, Tómas Árnason's battles with the People's Alliance. He was a staunch advocate of radical measures against inflation and wanted to mount an assault on the indexation system to achieve those goals. Second, this sequence of events illustrates Ólafur Jóhannesson. He was prone to making decisions without consultation.
Otherwise Ólafur attended to little besides his work in the foreign ministry in this government. He led our dispute with the Norwegians over Jan Mayen

to a successful conclusion and earned the enmity of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) and the opponents of the military base by preparing the construction of an air terminal at Keflavík airport. In these years Ólafur did little work within the party but spoke, as was his habit, at formal meetings of the parliamentary group and the executive committee. Ólafur will hardly be counted among the country's more travel-happy foreign ministers, and he readily avoided trips abroad unless it was urgently necessary that he go himself. He sometimes got other ministers to attend to foreign assignments in their own policy areas, as when he had me sign the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on behalf of the government.
Short-Lived Comfort

The measures agreed upon at the beginning of 1981 were based on the one hand on a price freeze and on the other on limiting wage indexation payments. They were introduced alongside the currency reform in which two zeros were "clipped" off the króna. This was meant to renew public confidence in the currency and strengthen people's sense of prices. The Progressives felt the measures came late. At a meeting of the party's executive committee I recounted the development of the matter and remarked among other things that the People's Alliance's first ideas had been "utterly absurd and proved preposterous upon examination by the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun)."

The measures were based in essence on the countdown strategy according to the Progressives' ideas. We realized from the outset, however, that not enough was being done; this was only the first step of the countdown. The measures nevertheless produced the intended results. Inflation was down to 40 percent eight months later, sooner than projections had anticipated. In fact, the favourable outlook at the end of 1981 misled the government. In October 1981 an economic forecast was presented to the Althingi that anticipated continued growth in national income and a still further decline in inflation.

This forecast created not only optimism but also reluctance to undertake further measures that would entail a reduction in living standards. The People's Alliance could not be brought to any agreement, and various Progressives felt the Prime Minister showed feeble leadership in getting them to the negotiating table. Tómas Árnason would not have minded presenting the People's Alliance men with an ultimatum in the autumn of 1981. He believed they could not afford to blow up the government. It was more popular than ever. I was of another opinion. I considered the outlook acceptable, the coalition important, and that it was right to keep seeking agreement between the government parties.

At the beginning of 1982 the government issued a new economic plan. There was less substance in it than in the measures of the year before. In reality it was merely a collection of promises and policy declarations. No agreement was reached on the next step toward bringing down inflation. The declaration did, admittedly, provide for the drafting of proposals to change the wage indexation system, which we Progressives cared about greatly. Otherwise inflation was not confronted. On the contrary, it was thought safe to increase freedom in economic affairs in light of the promising situation. The price freeze, which had been in effect with only brief interruptions for more than a decade, was loosened, and pricing was liberalized. Furthermore, it was considered safe to allow full indexation of bank deposits and loans for the first time in the history of the republic.

It soon became clear that the economic forecast for 1982 had been built on excessive optimism. Its projection of economic developments had to be revised again and again as the year went on. With each revision the picture painted grew darker. Instead of one percent growth in national income, a contraction of three and then five percent appeared likely. Toward autumn the outlook worsened still further. By then a contraction of national income of as much as 7–8 percent was projected for 1982 and 1983 according to the forecast of the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun). The inflation forecast turned from decline to growth of 80–90 percent, and everything else followed suit. New wage agreements, deteriorating terms of trade abroad, and a failure of the catch all combined against us.
In June 1982 the Independence Party men used their influence among the employers to hand wage earners a pay rise on a silver platter. It amounted to 15 percent.

The difficulties of economic management likewise intensified greatly during 1982. It was clear that radical measures had to be taken so that the country's economy would not grind to a halt. The situation was discussed in the cabinet meeting after meeting. Gunnar described the state of affairs in 1982 thus:

The world depression meant that the outlook worsened in some sectors, while recovery failed to appear in others. Stockfish did not sell. Capelin was not caught. The fishing season fell short of hopes.

The situation can hardly be described more briefly or more clearly. There was no mistaking that tendencies toward depression were being felt in the world in 1982. Unemployment grew by rapid strides throughout Europe. In Britain it more than doubled in three years and had reached 13–14 percent by 1983. In the countries of the European Economic Community, 40 percent of people under the age of 25 went unemployed. Although the worst pessimistic forecasts of the National Economic Institute for

for 1982 did not in fact come true in the end, national production nonetheless contracted by 2–3 percent, for the first time since the Reconstruction years. The Chamber of Commerce (Verslunarráð) compared the position of the fisheries to the situation after the collapse of the herring stock in 1967. At the same time spending was heavy and the rush for foreign currency enormous. That was not unnatural, since the exchange rate was steadily sinking. The only way to secure the value of one's money was to exchange it for foreign currency.

At the beginning of summer 1982 the serious state of the nation's monetary affairs was under discussion in the parliamentary groups of the coalition parties. A greatly increased deficit in foreign trade was looming, and job security was threatened by shrinking national production. In addition to a ministerial committee on economic affairs, a special committee on necessary measures was established, on which sat one member of parliament from each of the coalition parties. Halldór Ásgrímsson was called to this work from the ranks of the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) backbenchers. He had also taken a seat on a special negotiating committee on the indexation issues.

I was among those who believed the only way out of this impasse was to break the spiral of wage-price inflation. I therefore stressed that both things needed to be reviewed: the indexation of wages and of capital. I also believed that no better way had emerged to achieve these goals than the countdown policy that had brought the Progressive Party victory in the 1979 elections. The People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), however, considered that it had entered the coalition with the promise that no economic measures would be undertaken in opposition to the labour movement.

At the end of July I presented the Progressive Party's proposals in the cabinet. They comprised 15 points and provided among other things for a 15 percent devaluation that would not affect the wage-compensation index, and for the indexation periods to be lengthened from three months to six. These measures, along with other accompanying actions, were meant to slow the inflationary spiral considerably. Special measures were to be taken to reduce the looming trade deficit, the living standards of the lowest paid were to be protected from the effects of these measures, and special steps were to be taken to address the difficulties of the fishing fleet.
The Greatest Mistake

We Progressives felt it most urgent that the next steps of the countdown be taken at once. It seemed to me that Ragnar Arnalds also understood this clearly, though his priorities were different. In an article in Þjóðviljinn he rejected the idea that the government should sit idle for a whole year waiting for elections. Ragnar also raised the point, however, that it was uncertain whether the government had a parliamajority
to push through the necessary measures. Eggert Haukdal had threatened to withdraw his support from the government.

Earlier in the year a trade agreement had been concluded with the Soviet Union. Þórhallur Ásgeirsson, permanent secretary of the Ministry of Trade (viðskiptaráðuneytið), bore the brunt of the negotiations. He had done so ever since 1953, when the first agreement was made. As is famously told, Bjarni Benediktsson, who was then foreign minister, is supposed to have said: "This is great news, and good news," when he heard that the agreements had been secured. In 1953 the Icelandic national economy was under serious strain. In the summer of 1982, however, Morgunblaðið whipped up a storm over the negotiations and cast suspicion on the agreement in every possible way. That campaign sprang first and foremost from political roots. Morgunblaðið's aim was to give government supporters in the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) an opportunity to jump ship. Eggert took advantage of it.

This meant not only that the progress of legislation in the lower chamber of parliament was uncertain, but also that every single government backbencher held a veto in his own hands. That hindered all radical measures.

I was no less worried about this than Ragnar Arnalds during those summer months, but Svavar Gestsson seemed to me to be singing a different tune. We spent many a lunchtime with Gunnar Thoroddsen outside cabinet meetings trying to agree on new solutions while "the nation [was] bleeding to death economically," as Eysteinn Jónsson put it around the same time. The tension within the coalition had become great, and in effect hard negotiations were taking place in which the prime minister sat between me and Svavar and tried to mediate. At a meeting of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) parliamentary group on 13 August I said, among other things, that the declarations of the People's Alliance members were "wholly unsatisfactory," and I stated that the prime minister had taken the same view.

I told the parliamentary group that I felt progress toward a decision on the necessary measures was far too slow. I went so far as to say that I considered the coalition effectively at an end if matters did not improve, and that I intended to inform the prime minister of this. After the parliamentary group meeting I went to see Gunnar and told him that our patience was exhausted. We needed to get real responses to our proposals. Otherwise the breakup of the government loomed.

Gunnar asked us to show patience a while longer. A conclusion would not be long in coming. Three days later the prime minister presented a draft of provisional legislation together with a proposal for a changed index-reference system for wages. These contained quite a few concessions compared with the Progressive Party's original proposals. After long discussions, however, both received the approval of a large majority

of the parliamentary group, along with other items connected to the proposals. Two days later the parliamentary group gave the party's ministers a mandate to "take these matters forward and get the best outcome available". The approval was unanimous. Tómas Árnason, however, entered a formal reservation which said:

I say yes, but underline the proposal of the party chairman that the parliamentary group introduce a bill in Alþingi on changes to the indexation system on the basis of [the conclusions of the coalition parties' indexation committee] if agreement on it is not reached among the government partners.

While negotiations proceeded between the parties, answers from the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) were long in coming. This time its labour council was not to blame; rather, Guðmundur J. Guðmundsson had gone to Luxembourg together with his wife Elín Torfadóttir. There they had rented a car and driven off into the blue. Nobody knew where. There would have been no reason to make a fuss about this except that Svavar Gestsson flatly refused to give any answers about the party's position until he had spoken with Guðmundur! So the issuing of provisional legislation on economic affairs in Iceland had to wait until the labour leader reported his whereabouts!

On 21 August 1982 the answers and proposals of the People's Alliance finally arrived. Gunnar Thoroddsen immediately put forward counter-proposals. They were not as bad as the People's Alliance's ideas, but were nonetheless even further from our original ideas than Gunnar's first proposals. The most significant change was that talks were to be entered into with the social partners about changes to the wage-indexation reference system instead of changing it by law immediately.

By this point many party members had lost patience. Tómas Árnason was one of them. We were of course in constant contact while my wrangling with Svavar went on, and it was not always quiet. My lot was to try to reach a solution without the government breaking apart, but at the same time that solution had to be as close as possible to the policy of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). The latter proved difficult.

When the prime minister's compromise proposal came before the parliamentary group, Tómas argued for "backing the People's Alliance up against the wall", and others shared that view. I, on the other hand, hoped that the government's resolutions meant that changes to the indexation system were finally just around the corner. I therefore did not consider it right to bring about the fall of the government, and argued for accepting the prime minister's compromise proposal. The entire parliamentary group, with the exception of Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson, ultimately approved that course of action.
Tómas nonetheless referred to his earlier reservation. Svavar Gestsson thus succeeded in getting limited measures approved, which we decided to accept.

In hindsight I believe it was a mistake to agree to concessions. That became clearer and clearer to me over the course of that winter. Especially as changes to the indexation system were continually delayed. As before, our measures were only temporary, even though the short-term solutions already applied were quite enough. As matters developed, it would have been wiser to force through the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) policy, or otherwise to break up the coalition.
A Winter of Troubles

In the early autumn of 1982 my work was characterized above all by hard clashes with the fishing-vessel owners. Elections were in the air and the political situation was combustible. The National Association of Icelandic Vessel Owners (Landssamband íslenskra útvegsmanna) demanded corrections on behalf of its members with greater vehemence than almost ever before. The government's measures at the end of August had included, among other things, considerable support for the trawler industry. Spokesmen for the LÍÚ said these fell far short of being sufficient. The vessel owners followed up their demands by sailing the fleet ashore. The national economy could by no means withstand such a blow on top of everything else.

In response, substantial additional support for the fishing industry was approved in the government on 17 September 1982, and provisional legislation to that effect was issued shortly afterwards. It included a considerable reduction in oil prices, an interest-rate cut, debt restructuring and a lowering of capital costs. The measures were considered to cut the losses of fishing companies by half on average. History seemed set to repeat itself. The vessel owners said they needed still further assistance, and ships did not leave harbour. In the media I exchanged shots with Kristján Ragnarsson. We had in fact been at odds since early summer.

In the autumn warfare every trick was employed. Among other things, the tiresome practice arose that accounts damaging to me were "leaked" from my meetings with the vessel owners and appeared in the evening news on radio or television. All of this caused quite a commotion, which was the last thing that was needed. I still have handwritten comments on television news broadcasts which I evidently wrote in front of the set, to use in rebuttals in the evening news the following day.

In the middle of this propaganda war, Ólafur Jóhannesson authorized two sailings to foreign ports with unprocessed catch. He was then serving as Minister of Commerce in Tómas's absence. I had declared that sailings would

not be permitted because of the fish-processing plants' shortage of raw material, and Tómas had agreed to enforce this. Ólafur pointed out, however, that no resolution to this effect had been adopted in the government. That was correct. Yet he well knew that he was going against my declared policy. The decision came at the worst possible time for me. I was locked in fierce conflict with the leadership of the vessel owners, who of course declared their full support for Ólafur's actions. A large part of the fleet lay in harbour on the orders of the LÍÚ, and in many parts of the country the fish-processing industry was running out of raw material. The sailings added still further to that problem.

The LÍÚ's negotiating committee did not become fit to talk to until LÍÚ solidarity began to crack within its own ranks and the occasional ship had put out of harbour. The trade unions had by then passed resolutions on "the LÍÚ's war against the government". The Federation's fishing operations (Sambandsútgerðirnar) contemplated resigning from the vessel owners' association, and more and more fishing companies and communities intended to defy the fishing halt and sail their ships out of harbour. Agreement was finally reached. The fish price was raised by four per cent — which was in fact what the vessel owners had been offered before.

These disputes were only a foretaste of what went on that winter. Few matters made their way through Alþingi without a struggle. Eggert Haukdal finally withdrew his support from the government in the wake of the provisional legislation of 21 August. With that, the government no longer had a secure majority in the lower chamber of parliament. As we had feared, this made things very difficult for us. It was probably a mistake not to summon parliament together at once and put to the test whether the opposition would stand by its big words. If the provisional legislation had been voted down, the obvious course would have been to dissolve parliament and call elections immediately. This was not done.

When parliament convened in October it was clear that the entire opposition was against the provisional legislation. I considered it a genuine option to force a showdown and put the provisional legislation to a vote in the lower chamber of Alþingi without delay. If the matter were defeated, parliament would be dissolved and elections held in mid-November. This was also the proposal of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) parliamentary group, put forward in the government. But there were also weighty arguments against immediate elections. It was pointed out above all that the economic measures would thereby be sacrificed for political gain. Those views had some merit. However, the economic measures proved to be of little worth when it came to the crunch. So it may be said that little would have been sacrificed even if elections had been held before the end of the year.

Many Progressives would have supported autumn elections. But there were also those who thought the government had already suffered such a setback that it would be wisest to let the effects of the economic measures emerge and fight the elections in the spring. Among them was Tómas Árnason. It was Gunnar Thoroddsen, however, who was chiefly responsible for the government's remaining in office.

Given how things stood, I considered the only responsible course to be to invite the opposition to talks on the handling of the most urgent matters. The Progressive parliamentary group supported this unanimously. Once parliamentary business had begun and the opposition held all the weapons in its hands, there were no political grounds for dissolving the coalition. A break-up of the government would have been seen as total capitulation. The government had to sit until spring, whatever became of action on the economy. At first the opposition showed little disposition to negotiate. They said they would only negotiate about a dissolution of parliament and elections. This was followed by a demand for the government's resignation. This fencing disappointed me. I was of the opinion that the state of the economy and the national finances called for a more responsible attitude.

The reality was that the passage of most government bills that winter had to be negotiated. Often I felt I was dealing with intransigence and vindictiveness. As an example, the first negotiations concerned the conditions set by the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) for entering into negotiations on any other matters at all. The conditions were three: that the provisional legislation be laid before Alþingi without delay, that the constitutional committee speed up its work, and that elections be held in the month of April. The constitutional committee was working on changes to the electoral law and the constituency system, along with other general matters.

I found it irksome to accept these conditions. They were, however, of such a nature that it was impossible to reject them. The provisional legislation was to be introduced at once in any case; there was no alternative to the constitutional committee speeding up its work, and a conclusion was expected from it; and elections had already been planned for April. It seemed to me that the terms were put forward first and foremost to raise the Social Democrats' banner up off the ground.

Shortly afterwards the Social Democratic Party did in fact resolve to bring a motion of no confidence against the government. I did not think there was much sincerity in that. Everything ran along these lines during that winter of troubles. Disputes arose, among other things, over the point in the economic measures that part of the exchange-rate gain on stockfish should flow into an oil fund for the benefit of the fishing industry. The opposition, with Matthías Bjarnason at its head, altered my proposals and I could mount little defence. Thus the fishing industry was made to suffer so that a political blow could be struck at me and the government.
The Constituency Issue

My energies that winter did not go only into negotiations and disputes in Alþingi. A large part of my time went into talks on changes to the electoral legislation and the constitution, the so-called constituency issue. That issue was so extensive that
ministers in the government have described it by saying that the government was virtually like a caretaker government because of these preoccupations and the government's weak position in parliament.

Ever since the winter elections of 1979 it had been in the air that the constitution would be amended. People's eyes were very much fixed on the position of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) in that connection. The party had never joined with other parties in making such changes. Some remarked that the next elections would partly revolve around the constitution and new electoral laws, which would be enacted with or against the will of the Progressives.

Changes to the electoral arrangements had always been politically difficult for the Progressive Party and had left wounds in its dealings with the other parties. They led to the fall of a government and long-lasting disputes between my father and Ólafur Thors after the so-called "oath-breaking affair" of 1942. The electoral system had next been changed in 1959, in the run-up to the formation of the Viðreisn government. The Progressive Party stood alone among the parties against those changes. This cost an almost complete rupture of cooperation between the Progressive Party and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), which did not work together in government until nearly two decades later. Friendships between the parties' leading figures were also broken. My father and Gylfi Þ. Gíslason, who had been very close companions, were an example of that.

The constituency system settled on in 1959 had proved better than most Progressives had thought likely. In the time that had since passed, however, the imbalance of votes between urban and rural areas had greatly increased because of population displacement. As an ever larger share of the nation moved from the countryside to the capital area, the number of votes behind the rural members of parliament fell, while conversely the number of votes needed to win a seat in Reykjavík and Reykjanes rose. This was among the things that called for change.

These migrations from countryside to city had, however, also produced an imbalance between the parties. The Progressive Party was considered to benefit from an unchanged electoral arrangement. It was proportionally strong in the rural areas but weak in the urban southwest corner.

The other three parties were thought to have more to gain from a changed electoral system. So the threat loomed that, just as earlier in the century, they would agree on changes without consulting the Progressives. For that reason I was all the more determined that the Progressive Party should, for the first time, take part in changes to the electoral law and the constitution. In that way it could influence the outcome.
Gunnar Thoroddsen was chairman of the constitutional committee, which had been at work for a decade. He announced that a bill for a new constitution would be laid

before the autumn session of parliament in 1982. The committee's work did not proceed without difficulty, however, and in 1982 it seemed clear that its work would drag on still further. The remedy adopted was that the chairmen of the four parties holding seats in the Althing began talks among themselves about changes concerning the electoral legislation. In the spring months Þorkell Helgason began working for the chairmen's committee, and it immediately became easier to explore the various ideas. Þorkell is a great master of calculation, and those talents were sorely needed.
The Most Difficult Issue of My Political Career

Within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) a great many party members were suspicious of changing the electoral laws in favor of the urban areas. This attitude was very much in evidence in the party's discussion of the constitutional amendments. At the party's open meetings and gatherings, however, many agreed that it was important to respond to the critical voices concerning the unequal weight of votes. There was also growing understanding that the party needed to establish itself more firmly in the capital region. I emphasized that it was essential for the party not to isolate itself in opposition to changes in the electoral system in step with the development of settlement patterns.

I supported equality between the political parties but did not consider it unnatural that the rural areas should have proportionally more members of parliament than the urban areas relative to the number of voters. That is how matters stand in most of the Nordic countries, and no less in the United States, to name some examples. In fact it may be said that these priorities were accepted. Before it was over, the chairmen — Geir Hallgrímsson, Svavar Gestsson, Kjartan Jóhannsson, and I — had met at dozens of meetings and examined a vast number of ideas, chiefly concerning the design of a new electoral system. We reached agreement on the main points.

They were: an unchanged constituency structure; that the number of members of parliament would not be increased significantly; that each constituency would have a minimum of five members; that complete equality would be achieved between parties; that inequality between constituencies would be no greater than in 1959; and that the geographic distribution of members would be no worse than under the existing law. This conclusion was important. Everything that followed was based on these fundamental premises.

The work on the electoral legislation was to a large extent technical, since it proved complicated to correct the imbalance between parties without increasing the number of members of parliament substantially. Both the Progressive Party and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) opposed increasing the number of members. At the end of November a solution came into view that provided for a minimal increase in the number of members, from 60 to 63. Neither the Progressive Party nor the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), however, could accept the method of allocating seats that was envisioned to be used.

After the new year of 1983 we chairmen picked up the thread again and shut ourselves away in the tower room of the Rúgbrauðsgerðin building on Borgartún. The working method was like that of cardinals choosing a pope. They are not let out of the Vatican until they have chosen someone for the office. At our meetings we examined dozens of variants. Each and every one was combed through and calculated against all election results since 1959. The options that seemed most promising were then put through a test in which 100 simulated election results were computed into parliamentary seats. It was not enjoyable work, but I believe it was done with great care.

Although various criticisms could be made of our final conclusion, it is certain that it would have been difficult to design a better system if the many different viewpoints we started out with were to be accommodated. Many of them were, of course, debatable, no less than the implementation. At a special central committee meeting that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) held on the "constituency issue," opinions differed widely. That meeting was the decisive moment. It determined the Progressive Party's participation in the constituency issue.

The central committee meeting lasted ten hours. I introduced the matter at the beginning of the meeting and then spoke last, after having listened to some 35 speeches, many of them detailed, and criticism was not spared. Judging by the minutes, I did not have many supporters in the party. In my closing remarks I said that this issue was the most difficult I had dealt with in my political career. Perhaps that was an overstatement, suited more to the occasion than to my feelings. It is a fact, however, that it would have been easier for me, as chairman of the Progressive Party, not to take part in negotiations on changes and to oppose them instead. In my view, however, that would have shown cowardice and short-sightedness and gone against my convictions. My proposal before the meeting was essentially that the conclusion of the chairmen's committee should be followed.
It was approved almost unanimously, with minor changes.

After the four parties had reached a common conclusion and the chairmen each had it approved in their own arenas, the matter passed peacefully through parliament. Occasional voices of dissatisfaction were heard about the implementation of the electoral laws, and I could myself agree with some of that criticism. I believe, though, that in the main the changes were an improvement. Since a constitutional amendment was involved, the new electoral system did not take effect immediately. It was not put to the test until the elections of 1987.
Tómas Considers Resigning

The changes made to the government's economic measures on 21 August 1982 to accommodate the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) proved fateful. The government's indexation committee — Halldór Ásgrímsson; Þröstur Ólafsson, assistant to Ragnar Arnalds; and Þórður Friðjónsson, the prime minister's economic adviser — had agreed on the main elements of changes to the indexation system after consulting numerous parties. Instead of these being put into effect, new negotiations with the social partners on those matters began in the autumn. They produced no result.

Within the cabinet, Tómas Árnason was tireless in raising the indexation issue and inquiring about its progress. Outside meetings he pressed no less hard for action. I tried to the utmost to reach agreement between the coalition parties. I probably clung too long to the hope of a joint conclusion. Inflation, however, did not wait for the People's Alliance's approval. It rose steadily and was heading toward three digits by the spring of 1983. The heat in my conversations with Tómas rose in step with the inflation. We often spoke on the telephone, frequently late in the evening. Þóra Eiríksdóttir, Tómas's wife, recalls that she was often quite alarmed when her husband raised his voice in our conversations, more than she had ever heard him do before. I raised my voice somewhat as well.

When these matters were at their height, Tómas seriously considered resigning his ministerial office. He did not want to bear responsibility for the inaction. This went so far that he consulted Ólafur Jóhannesson about the matter. Ólafur believed the resignation would not be seen as directed against the economic situation but against my leadership in the struggle with the problem. Tómas says Ólafur put it this way: "that it would be a grave matter to rebel against one's chairman." They also came to the conclusion that some might side with Tómas and withdraw their support from the government. It is not unlikely that this would have led to a split in the party.

Tómas therefore decided to stay. He has always been loyal to the party and never told me of these deliberations of his. I first heard of them when this book was in preparation. These thoughts of Tómas's about resignation do not really surprise me, though. He often snapped in our conversations that he "would then simply have to part ways with the government" and other things in that vein. I never worried much about those declarations and considered them first and foremost bluster. Tómas evidently was more serious than I suspected, however.
A final attempt to achieve changes to the indexation system was made in

the government in February 1983. The Prime Minister himself introduced a bill on the matter. Svavar Gestsson presented a resolution of the central committee of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) in which all changes to the indexation system were vigorously opposed. Gunnar responded by placing on record that the bill was based on the government's economic programme from the beginning of 1982 and the agreement of the coalition partners from 21 August. He also declared that despite the opposition of the People's Alliance, the bill would be introduced in the Althing by the Prime Minister on behalf of the ministers of the Independence Party and the Progressive Party. The discussions of the matter in the cabinet became long and hard and were taken up again at the next meeting.

Despite a compromise proposal by the Prime Minister, Svavar could not be persuaded to accept that this would be a government bill. Gunnar said that it would nevertheless be introduced in parliament and enjoyed the support of seven ministers.

The bill came before parliament late, and the People's Alliance turned against it there as it had in the cabinet before. Svavar Gestsson objected to it chiefly with three kinds of arguments. He criticized it for being of little use, for having been drafted without consultation with the labour movement, and argued that it would be more proper to let measures of this kind wait until after the elections. The first point had some justification, first and foremost because too much ground had been given to the People's Alliance in the hope of solidarity within the government. The fact was that the measures were almost useless. They came nowhere near striking at the roots of inflation. In the mind of the Prime Minister, however, the bill was important despite this. It had symbolic significance.

Ideas of radical changes to the indexation system never won through with the support of the People's Alliance, any more than in the days of the earlier left-wing government. It made no difference that one of the chief goals of Gunnar Thoroddsen's government had been the gradual winding down of inflation. The People's Alliance used its veto power against all attempts to unwind the inflationary spiral. The opposition of the labour movement was surely decisive there.
The Government's Epitaph

The Prime Minister's bill on a new reference system for wages did not pass in parliament. Inflation spun even further out of control, and by the time of the 1983 elections it stood at about 80 per cent. In the last three months the government sat, it was close to 130 per cent on an annualized basis. Those facts say more than many words and became, for most people, the most memorable epitaph of the government.

Shortly after Gunnar Thoroddsen's government left office, the outgoing Prime Minister sat down to write. He put on paper "Eight Points on Economic Affairs at the Change of Government". There he drew a rather different picture than the media had presented to the nation in the summer of 1983. By then the government's legacy had led a new government under my premiership to resort to radical and unpopular measures. The outgoing Prime Minister compared forecasts and outcomes for the development of the economy for the years 1982 and 1983 and drew conclusions about the achievements of his government from the comparison. With them he wanted to send back where they came from the claims of "the worst parting legacy in the history of the republic" and "the most dreadful state of affairs in half a century".

In essentials, Gunnar seems to have been content with his government's parting legacy. He pointed out that the deficit in trade with foreign countries had been reduced by the government's measures in the autumn of 1982 and that employment had been plentiful in its time. Unemployment had admittedly increased from 0.3 to 0.9 per cent according to measurements, but both figures testified to a good employment situation. It was first and foremost a sign of the harsh propaganda against the government that a "state of emergency" was proclaimed and much made of the fact that registered unemployment had tripled. Gunnar also pointed out that the nation's foreign currency reserves were good, the state treasury stood well, and the public's savings were fully index-linked in the banks, as the coalition agreement had stipulated.
Index-linked savings accounts were probably one of the government's most popular measures.

Gunnar says in his report that at the change of government the problems to be dealt with were manageable and chiefly of two kinds. On the one hand, the wage compensation system had been unworkable and had led to constant leapfrogging increases of prices and wages, to the detriment of all economic management. On the other hand, external conditions and a failure of the fishing catch had led to lower national production and lower national income than had been anticipated. Together with inflation, this led to "appreciable difficulties for the industries". Unfortunately, however, he glosses over the fact that the government failed in tackling the problem it faced. It was for that purpose first and foremost that it was formed, but it proved not to have the strength for it.
Held Hostage by the Labour Movement

The chief problem of the Icelandic economy was inflation. Its causes were to be sought in the economic system. The reasons why it proved so difficult to overcome inflation, however, were political in nature rather than there being any lack of means to defeat it.
The consequences of the "solstice agreements" of 1977 for the economic development of the years that

that followed can hardly be overestimated. The enormous wage increases contained in the agreements were more than the economy could bear, and the indexation provisions made it nearly impossible for the authorities to tackle the problems that resulted. Unfavorable conditions certainly poured oil on the fire of inflation. The instability of the national economy in 1977–1983 could not, however, be traced solely to setbacks and external circumstances. The governments of that era were all agreed that unemployment was completely unacceptable. Full employment was the chief goal of economic management. Devaluations were the authorities' only remedy when the export industries were headed for ruin, since unemployment, which would otherwise have been the outcome, was considered even worse than inflation.

Out of sympathy for wage earners and the struggle of the labor movement, devaluations were, moreover, usually too small to give exporters a sound operating basis. The indexation of wages also meant that a reduction in the value of the króna led before long to wage increases. Devaluations thus fueled the spiral of inflation and were by nature short-term measures against imminent unemployment, which solved the problem for the moment but not for the long run.

The effects of the "solstice agreements" of 1977 became permanent for political reasons. Inflation was their unavoidable consequence unless the interplay of prices and wages was cut off. Most people soon realized this. The first attempt to respond to the spiral inflation was the February legislation of 1978. The chain of events it set in motion led to the great victory of the two labor parties (the A-parties) in the summer of 1978.

It fell to the left-wing government of Ólafur Jóhannesson, which took office in the autumn, to remedy the problem. The coalition of 1978–1979 disappointed me. I was not convinced, however, that it was impossible to carry out a sensible economic policy in cooperation with the A-parties. The fact that I reached agreement with both coalition partners in the economic committee in the spring of 1979 was, in my view, evidence that it could be done. Ólafur Jóhannesson seemed to me to display more rigidity than I encountered among my colleagues in the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) or the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) when he blew that agreement sky-high and introduced the "Ólafur laws" (Ólafslög). I therefore did not blame the labor wing of the People's Alliance for the lack of progress in economic matters during that government's term.
After its collapse it was in fact the Social Democratic Party that was the greater problem in my eyes. The "restless faction" that held sway there was unpredictable and hard to trust.

I was, and still am, convinced that the "countdown" policy (niðurtalning) that we Progressives put forward in the 1979 elections was a sensible way to work toward bringing down inflation. In the government-formation talks of that winter of conflict

it also mattered greatly that I was likewise of the opinion that in the longer term an economic policy would have little strength if it was not decided in good consultation with the labor movement. That was the lesson I drew from the 1978 elections. In my mind, cooperation with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) was necessary because of its influence within the labor movement. In that respect I considered the composition of the government good. In my mind, Gunnar Thoroddsen's government was formed to get a grip on the nation's economic problem, inflation.

The People's Alliance, however, had drawn the conclusion from its election victory of 1978 that its main role was to defend the index-linking of wages. In the 1979 elections the party went even further and declared that the People's Alliance would make no decisions in economic matters against the will of the labor movement. I had some sympathy for this viewpoint. I had inherited from my father the view that it would be difficult to get a grip on Icelandic economic affairs without consultation with the labor movement. It never occurred to me, however, that the labor movement should have the last word on the management of economic affairs in Iceland, nor did it cross my mind that the People's Alliance members held that view either. There I was mistaken. The leaders of the People's Alliance truly kept their election promise, and in the literal sense.

As a result, Gunnar Thoroddsen's government was held hostage by the labor movement at every step. The People's Alliance defended the indexation system tooth and nail, unaware, it seemed, that in doing so it was standing guard over inflation far more than over the living standards of working people. Inflation hit hardest those who had the least to spare.

The reality was also that the labor movement lacked the maturity and perspective needed to tackle the inflation problem. This was a great disappointment to me. Despite this principal conclusion, I was still of the opinion that in the long run the labor movement should be consulted. However, I believed that the connection between it and the political parties had to be severed so that cooperation could be rebuilt on a new foundation. Political leaders rarely think further ahead than the next elections, and labor bosses no further than the next wage settlements. When such short-term perspectives combine, no good can be expected.

By the time of the 1983 elections, all the political parties except the People's Alliance had become united in the view that the wage-compensation system, which was one of the main causes of inflation, needed to be revised. After the experience of the coalition, however, I considered it clear that the nation's economic problems would not be solved in cooperation with the People's Alliance. I began to ponder ever more often whether the only feasible way out of the impasse was legislation in defiance of the labor movement. That seemed to me a sad conclusion.
Chapter Twelve

When the political leaders crossed swords in the television studio before the 1983 elections, the scene was different from what it had been barely four years earlier. Then I had been the only newcomer in the group of four party chairmen, the newly elected chairman of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Of those who took part in the debates in 1983, Geir Hallgrímsson, chairman of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), was the only one remaining apart from myself. He, however, had had his wings clipped after a poor showing in the Independence Party's primary in Reykjavík.

In place of Lúðvík Jósepsson, Svavar Gestsson now held the chairmanship of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), and Kjartan Jóhannsson had relieved Benedikt Gröndal in the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). Even he had become unsteady on his feet after a short career as chairman. A new star had appeared on the scene in the party's primary in Reykjavík. There Jón Baldvin Hannibalsson had taken the top seat after a hard primary battle with Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir.

Two new slates had also joined the ranks of the four established parties. The Women's List movement (Samtök um kvennalista) fielded candidates in three constituencies: Reykjavík, Reykjanes, and Norðurland eystra. Its vanguard consisted of Sigríður Dúna Kristmundsdóttir, anthropologist; Guðrún Agnarsdóttir, physician; Kristín Ástgeirsdóttir, historian; Þórhildur Þorleifsdóttir, theater director; Málmfríður Sigurðardóttir, housewife; and Kristín Halldórsdóttir, housewife.

The Women's List had its roots in the Women's Slate (Kvennaframboðið), which had fielded candidates in many parts of the country in the local government elections the year before. In those elections the other main news was that a young Independence Party man by the name of Davíð Oddsson played a large part in toppling the left-wing majority on the Reykjavík city council. Davíð became mayor after the elections and made his presence
felt in the political debate that election winter, as indeed he has done ever since.

There was no shortage of strife within the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). Vilmundur Gylfason split off from his old comrades after coming out the loser in the vice-chairmanship election and ran his own party in all constituencies. It was given the name Alliance of Social Democrats (Bandalag jafnaðarmanna). Sighvatur Björgvinsson, who had long been Vilmundur's political sworn brother, remained loyal to the Social Democratic Party. He, however, was defeated by Karvel Pálmason in the party's primary in the Vestfirðir.
Election Jitters in the Progressive Party

Fratricidal feuds and conflicts have seldom been greater on the stage of Icelandic politics than before the 1983 elections. This applied almost equally to all the parties, and the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) was certainly no exception. Svanur Kristjánsson, professor of political science, puts it thus in his book, Frá flokksræði til persónustjórnmála (From Party Rule to Personality Politics), that the run-up to these elections confirmed that a watershed had occurred in the Progressive Party in 1978, when five members of parliament lost their seats. Up to that time, or ever since the party's split in 1934, the Progressives' candidacy matters had been resolved with little upheaval and the party's support had been stable. Previously, members of parliament had kept their seats unless "age, illness, or death" prevented it. There is considerable truth in this analysis of Svanur's.

I traveled around the country holding meetings in the run-up to the 1983 elections, discussed the political situation, and urged that as many party members as possible take part in arranging the candidate lists. The response to this appeal varied. Primaries were held in several constituencies, and where constituency councils decided the list, they were generally doubled in size. That meant that alternates attended the meetings with the same rights as full members, and thus the number of those involved in the selection increased considerably.

In Reykjavík the same play was repeated as four years earlier. Kristinn Finnbogason and Alfreð Þorsteinsson asked me to make myself available as a candidate in the constituency. I refused flatly. They then again put pressure on Ólafur Jóhannesson to run. Among other things, they collected the signatures of a large number of Progressives on a petition to that effect. The outcome was that Ólafur once again made himself available as a candidate. With that, Guðmundur G.'s patience was exhausted. He announced that he would not take part in the party's primary despite appeals. I was among those who thought it bad

to lose Guðmundur, though I understood his position. In his place an excellent man, Haraldur Ólafsson, university lecturer and anthropologist, was chosen for second place. He had held third place, after Guðmundur, in the 1979 elections.

The departure of Guðmundur G. attracted no less attention outside the party than within it. Lúðvík Jósepsson put it, among other things, this way: that the Progressives had let Guðmundur G. Þórarinsson go „overboard“ during the parliamentary term, „and he was, after all, the party's rising star in Reykjavík“. Guðmundur himself said that „the time had come for him to make way for men older than himself“.

The Progressives' candidacy affairs in the East Fjords (Austfirðir) trailed the heaviest wake behind them, all things considered. In the elections of 1974 and 1978, Tómas Árnason had held second place on the list and Halldór Ásgrímsson third. Vilhjálmur Hjálmarsson had led the Progressives in the east on both occasions. When he retired from parliament in 1979, Tómas and Halldór both moved up one place. In the run-up to the 1983 primary, Tómas knew nothing other than that there was an unwritten agreement between himself and Halldór Ásgrímsson to keep the slate unchanged. He believed he enjoyed nearly undivided support for first place.

Ásgrímur Halldórsson, Halldór's father, was of another opinion. It was asserted that he had mustered forces and urged people to vote for his son in place of Tómas. By the time Tómas heard of these proceedings it was too late to act. He had exerted himself little in the primary campaign, and the efforts of his supporters in the final days were not enough. Turnout in the primary was low. Halldór Ásgrímsson took first place, though in fact there was little between him and Tómas, who came second. Jón Kristjánsson of Egilsstaðir came third. Tómas was greatly shaken by these results and felt that a plot had been hatched against him. But there was nothing to be done about it. Tómas accepted second place.

The fiercest clashes within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) before these elections took place in the Northwest constituency (Norðurlandskjördæmi vestra). There Páll Pétursson had been the party's first member of parliament and Stefán Guðmundsson had held second place on the list. Ingólfur A. Guðnason occupied third place, and he had won election to parliament in 1979 by a rather narrow margin. It did not look as though the party would hold three parliamentary seats in the 1983 elections.

During the parliamentary term, Páll and Ingólfur had been locked in bitter disputes over the planned hydroelectric development of the Blanda river. Páll was suspicious of these plans and wanted to reduce the area of land that would go under water. Ingólfur was a staunch supporter of the Blanda power project. These disputes meant that opinions were sharply divided when it came to arranging the list. Páll's supporters wanted the list unchanged, while Ingólfur's men wanted Ingólfur in the top seat. In the end Ingólfur declared that he would not be on the list if Páll remained on it.

To settle the matter, a constituency assembly was convened. Both principal delegates and alternates were summoned to the meeting. A vote was held on the composition of the list. There Páll took first place and Stefán second. Third place went to Sverrir Sveinsson of Siglufjörður, while Ingólfur received only fourth place. At these results, Ingólfur's supporters rose from their seats and marched out of the meeting in a body. In the aftermath they decided to field a separate list and applied to the executive board of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) for permission to use the list letters BB. That meant the candidacy would in effect be under the party's auspices and these votes would benefit it in the allocation of equalization seats.

I pushed for the approval of this proposal, even though the majority of the constituency association's board opposed it and Páll Pétursson reacted furiously. I feared that otherwise we would drive away many good party members in the constituency. Suffice it to say that Ingólfur did not make it into parliament and did not stand again. Many of his supporters later became close collaborators of Páll's. Although Páll harbored a grudge against me for some time over these matters, he now considers that this was the right and sensible way to handle the case. If Ingólfur's men had been forced to run on a list outside the party, it is quite likely they would not have returned to the ranks of the Progressive Party, as in fact they have done.
Clashes and renewal

It is safe to say that momentous events occurred in many places when the political parties began their election preparations for the 1983 parliamentary elections. None of the four main parties was spared. Much suggested that primaries were transforming the political parties. Renewal and clashes made themselves felt everywhere. At the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), the chief news was that Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson fell to fourth place on the party's list in Reykjavík. Guðrún Helgadóttir won the battle for third place by a margin of one vote. This was the first time a sitting member of parliament had been moved down on a People's Alliance candidate list.

Baldur Óskarsson, Ólafur's old comrade-in-arms from the Möðruvellir movement (Möðruvallahreyfingin), received a drubbing in the People's Alliance primary in the Southern constituency (Suðurland) that same spring, and this proved his last attempt to get into parliament. In the Northeast constituency (Norðurlandskjördæmi eystra), Stefán Jónsson retired from parliament. A young geologist, Steingrímur J. Sigfússon, won his seat after a primary battle, at 28 years of age. In second place was Svanfríður Jónasdóttir, a teacher in Dalvík.
At the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), what Gunnar Thoroddsen intended to do was awaited with the greatest anticipation. Much has been whispered about that, but

little is known for certain, however. Some have believed that Gunnar avoided autumn elections in 1982 because he intended to stand as a candidate. He would therefore have wanted more time to prepare. I do not put much faith in this. From my conversations with Gunnar I am convinced that he first and foremost wanted to steer the government coalition to a successful conclusion, and by no means intended to leave it at that. Admittedly, he never ruled out a candidacy when asked, and it was plain to hear from him that he would not run again for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). Yet neither could I detect that he intended to enter the electoral fray anew. Svavar Gestsson, however, tells a different story.

Gunnar took good care not to quash the talk of his candidacy until he had seen how his supporters fared. The government's supporters in parliament who came from the ranks of the Independence Party all ran in primaries under the party's banner. All of them won splendid victories. Friðjón Þórðarson took the top seat in the Western constituency (Vesturland) and Pálmi Jónsson won an overwhelming election in the Northwest constituency (Norðurland vestra). Eggert Haukdal did not appear to pay any price for his revolt against the government and came third on the Independence Party's list in the Southern constituency (Suðurland). There a newcomer took first place, a certain Þorsteinn Pálsson, who had been managing director of the Confederation of Icelandic Employers (Vinnuveitendasamband Íslands) and editor of Vísir. The biggest news, however, came in Reykjavík.

Albert Guðmundsson ran in Reykjavík and there contended with many of the party's leading figures, among them the chairman of the Independence Party, Geir Hallgrímsson. Before the primary, few expected anything other than that Geir would poll well, despite what had gone before. He had won a secure victory and taken first place on the list before the 1979 elections. There was more uncertainty about Albert, who had taken second place in the 1979 primary. It was thought difficult to predict the consequences of Albert's having supported Gunnar Thoroddsen's rise to power in defiance of the party leadership.

Albert truly pulled out all the stops in the primary campaign, together with his supporters. He won a splendid election to the top seat on the list. In second place came Friðrik Sophusson, who had previously held fifth place, and Ellert B. Schram rose from eighth place to fourth. These were young men on the way up. It was another matter with the party chairman. Geir Hallgrímsson, to everyone's surprise, fell to seventh place in the primary. He took his defeat manfully and accepted a place on the list even though it was clear he risked losing his seat in parliament. I had no inkling of what consequences these results would have for my political career.

“Why should I tell the truth when it would suit me better to lie?” So run the opening words of the biography of Ludwig Wittgenstein, one of the most influential philosophers of this century. Ray Monk wrote it. This question was the first philosophical problem that pressed upon Wittgenstein, as a child. As plain and straightforward as the question may seem, it must nonetheless always weigh on the mind of anyone who sets his life down in a book. Not least if that life has held headwinds and triumphs, matters of historical controversy and bitter disputes, backroom dealings and decisions that proved decisive at delicate moments in Iceland's political history. All of this is woven into the biography of Steingrímur Hermannsson.

“Why should I tell the truth when it would suit me better to lie?” When all is said and done, the answer must turn on the honesty, self-image and self-respect of the one telling the story. He must have the determined will to do his part so that light may be shed on the truth. In the pages that here meet the reader's eye there are no few contentious questions and disputed points. A story of conflict always has many sides. In the work here presented in print, an effort has been made to bring out those facts and events that could give the clearest possible picture of the political history of recent decades as it appears to one of the most prominent politicians of the period, Steingrímur Hermannsson. The aim of the book is thus first and foremost to convey the story of Steingrímur Hermannsson.

It is safe to assert that various people who figure in the story will find their part either too small or even uncomfortably large from Steingrímur's vantage point where individual incidents, decisions or the course of the narrative are concerned. That cannot be helped.

An individual's biography is, by the nature of things, told only from his point of view and always bears the marks of that. In that sense it can never be neutral. On a great many points, judgments and opinions, Steingrímur is the sole source. I hope, however, that we have succeeded in writing an impartial account where Steingrímur's opinions leave off. Those behind this work will also be the first to welcome it if the publication of this book brings forth new information or perspectives that can shed still better light on the disputed events discussed here.

In order to deepen the narrative and trace the lines of conflict and the course of the story, extensive use has also been made of numerous contemporary sources and Steingrímur's own personal papers, and in addition interviews have been conducted with a great many of his fellow travelers, allies and opponents. The interviews were recorded on tape and are listed in the bibliography. Without the assistance of these informants — their recollections, suggestions and confirmation of particular points touching this story — the result would have been the poorer. To all of them the warmest thanks are given, while at the same time it is reiterated that none of them can in any respect be held responsible for the information found in this book, the context in which it is placed, or its presentation in any other regard.

Having said this, it is proper to pass on corrections that were received after the publication of the first volume of the biography of Steingrímur Hermannsson. The writer Páll Eggert Ólason was wrongly called Ólafsson; the businessman Þorvarður Árnason was called Þorvaldur; the director Stefán Bjarnason was called Ólafsson; Skafti Stefánsson of Siglufjörður was called Jónsson; and Geir Gunnlaugsson, farmer at Eskihlíð, was called Kristjánsson. In addition, the name of Sverrir Scheving Thorsteinsson was omitted from the list of interviewees consulted in the preparation of the book. Apologies are offered for these errors.

Like the first volume of this biography, the contents of this book are based on numerous interviews with Steingrímur himself, his family and friends. I have had unrestricted access to all the documents in Steingrímur's possession: private letters, diaries, personal card files and memoranda, handwritten notes from government-formation negotiations, Steingrímur's extensive collection of speeches, together with newspaper articles and manuscripts, in addition to public and printed sources as detailed in the bibliography. In gathering many other kinds of material I have enjoyed the invaluable assistance of the staff of the National Library (Landsbókasafn), the National Archives (Þjóðskjalasafn), the ministries of agriculture, fisheries and transport, the Institute of Regional Development (Byggðastofnun) and the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun).
To all of them I offer my best thanks. Among those who have provided useful suggestions in the search for sources or particular details

of this story, one may name the historians Valur Ingimundarson and Professor Helgi Skúli Kjartansson, Sigurður Líndal, professor of law, Svanur Kristjánsson, professor of political science, and Sigurður Snævarr, economist at the National Economic Institute (Þjóðhagsstofnun). They are thanked for their part. It should be stated that these distinguished men bear no responsibility whatsoever for the handling of sources, neither in particulars nor as a whole.

Pictures are important sources no less than what is set down in print. Eygló Stefánsdóttir, an employee of DV, deserves special credit for the book being as rich in pictorial material as it evidently is. She has proved invaluable in tracking down old photographs from the archives of Tíminn, Dagblaðið, Vísir and DV. With a fraction of the best from these gold mines, a fairly complete overview of the period under discussion has been obtained. Most of the oldest pictures are from the collection of Guðni Einarsson (GE), press photographer of Tíminn, who kindly granted permission for their publication. The same positive response came from Tryggvi Þórhallsson (Tryggvi) and Guðni Róbert Ágústsson (Róbert), who both worked at Tíminn for a time. They all receive heartfelt thanks for their assistance. Gunnar V.

Andrésson (Gunnar) was no less obliging and also acted as intermediary for the publication of pictures from the archives of Dagblaðið, Vísir and DV, and he is thanked for his contribution in that regard. Sigmund Jóhannsson in the Westman Islands (Vestmannaeyjar) has not only been the country's best cartoonist for years on end but has also been one of the shrewdest political commentators in the Icelandic media. It proved easy to obtain his permission to publish his “documentary drawings” of historic incidents from the political stage. The book's picture pages, and the story told there, would be blander without them. In addition, numerous pictures from the personal collection of Steingrímur Hermannsson appear.

I have had no cause to complain of poverty where proofreaders are concerned, no more than before. Gunnar Steingrímsson, my grandfather, has read the entire manuscript and given me precious encouragement. My parents, Eggert Gunnarsson and Bergþóra Jónsdóttir, have tried to convince me that the book is interesting and readable. My brother Gauti shared with me his gift for bringing out what is worthwhile and shortening whatever slows the story's progress. Kristín Jónsdóttir, my maternal aunt, a specialist in Icelandic and office director in the Ministry of Education (menntamálaráðuneytið), has read more autobiographies than anyone else I know. Kristín read the first half of the manuscript in its first draft and the final version in its entirety. From her I received numerous invaluable comments.
My strictest reader, where facts, accuracy and needless verbosity were concerned, was Steingrímur Hermannsson himself. There, in fact, Edda Guðmundsdóttir, his wife, also played a part. They have

husband and wife read the manuscript in its entirety a good four times, and some parts of it even more often. The historian Sverrir Jakobsson read the manuscript in full with care and acuity. His comments bore clear witness to his breadth of vision and learning. The lawyer Kristrún Heimisdóttir has always been my most critical reader as to form, content and substance. With her innate ambition she urged that we look beneath the surface of the story wherever there proved reason to. Sigríður Rögnvaldsdóttir has supervised the publication of the book on behalf of Vaka-Helgafell. Truth be told, I could not imagine a better collaborator in those matters. Good taste in language and style there goes hand in hand with clear reasoning, meticulousness and the ambition to deliver good work.

My conversations with this formidable group and other friends of mine have strengthened my ambition to do well. I owe many of them a great deal. Whether that undertaking of mine has succeeded, others must judge. The inspiration for the writing, and the energy to finish it, I have nonetheless drawn first and foremost from Arna Einarsdóttir, my fiancée. Her forbearance where this book is concerned seems to know few limits.
Stockholm, September 1999.
Dagur B. Eggertsson
